10028-spalding-s-official-baseball-guide:
Spalding's Official Baseball Guide for 1913, edited by John B. Foster and sold for ten cents, served the game's fans and officials. Published by the American Sports Publishing Company in New York, it opens with an introduction on the progress of America's national game.

Inside are the personnel of the National League, the oldest base ball organization, with editorial comment by Foster and records of leagues from Illinois-Missouri to Indiana-Illinois-Iowa and the International League. The guide is a snapshot of organized baseball in 1913, when the modern game was coming of age.
10838-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction opens its thirteenth volume with the number of January 3, 1829, priced at two pence. Its leading engraving shows Bruce Castle, Tottenham, as it appeared in 1686, copied from a print after Wolridge. The text traces the ancient castle to Earl Waltheof, who married Judith, niece of William the Conqueror.

An old brick tower over a deep well, once used as a dairy, marks the site's age. The Mirror's mix of picture and short history aimed at family readers. Modern readers get a neat sample of how the 1820s learned local history, one engraving at a time.
10950-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A weekly miscellany for general readers, The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, issued this number on Saturday, February 7, 1829, priced twopence. The lead piece describes villas in Regent's Park, including the Marquess of Hertford's villa designed by Decimus Burton, with its six-column portico, Venetian roof, and glass lanterns.

Other items mix history, biography, and anecdote, from Roman villas larger than Versailles to a king returning from chapel at Windsor, watched by crowds from Cheapside. Engravings illustrate the articles. The issue shows early nineteenth-century popular learning: short, varied pieces meant to amuse and instruct a family audience in one sitting.
11112-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction for Saturday, January 10, 1829, opens with Macclesfield Bridge in Regent's Park. Designed by Mr. Morgan, the bridge crosses the canal near Primrose Hill, with cast-iron columns of the Grecian Doric order, arches over canal, towing path, and banks, and ornaments praised by architect Mr. Elmes for lightness, elegance, and originality.

Other items in the number mix travel, history, and anecdote, including a battlefield story of Scotch soldiers cooking beefsteaks in a French cuirass, used as frying pan and dish. The Mirror's short, illustrated pieces aimed to amuse and instruct a family audience for twopence. This number shows early Victorian popular journalism at its most varied.
11322-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated March 7, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Rugby School, founded in Elizabeth's ninth year by Lawrence Sheriff, a London grocer, as a free grammar school for Rugby and Brownsover children. The article traces the school's endowment. from eight acres at Lamb's Conduit Fields worth little at first to a London property that rose sharply in value as the metropolis grew, funding master and almsmen.

The school's rise among classical seminaries is the article's theme, told through deeds, leases, and salaries. Shorter items complete the sheet. For historians of English education, the number preserves a concise, contemporary account of how a provincial grammar school became famous on the back of London land.
11331-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The March 28, 1829 Mirror leads with Guy's Cliff, a mile and a half northeast of Warwick, where the Avon winds through fertile meadows beside rock and wood. Leland's phrase, a home of pleasure, a place meet for the Muses, heads the article, which traces a Saxon oratory. a hermit's cell under Edward III and Henry IV, and Guy of Warwick's retirement after his duel with the Danish Colbrond. Henry V's charmed visit is also recalled.

Felice, Guy's neglected countess, is said to have buried him there. The article blends legend with topography in the Mirror's usual manner. Readers of Warwickshire history will find a compact, romantic account of a site where poetry, chivalry, and landscape meet.
11338-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This supplementary Mirror number, numbered 373, reviews Scott's Anne of Geierstein, or The Maiden of the Mist, praising the Waverley novels' knowledge of the human heart and mastery of passions. The reviewer argues Scott's free, conversational style strikes feelings and common sense at once, identifying readers with heroes' impulses. That chapter endings work like good stage exits, leaving readers curious for the next scene. Scott's incognito, now removed, has not dimmed his fame.

The review treats Scott as a national author whose popularity may outlive matter-of-fact works. Shorter items accompany it. For Scott scholars, the number preserves a contemporary verdict on a late Waverley novel, admiring but no longer rapturous, as the reviewer admits.
11340-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 30, 1829 Mirror leads with Epsom's new race stand, built by the Epsom Grand Stand Association with twenty thousand pounds capital in thousand twenty-pound shares, patronized by Jockey Club stewards. Modeled on Doncaster's stand but larger, it accommodates four to five thousand persons, measures 156 feet wide and 60 deep. A Doric portico, a terrace ten feet above ground, and a magnificent central flight of steps. Temporary accommodation was promised for the spring races beginning June 2.

The article avoids competing with racing lists, offering architecture instead of tips. Shorter items follow. For sporting historians, the number records Epsom's commercial growth, as racing became a business with shareholders, stands, and crowds.
11342-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated January 17, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Prince Rupert's palace in Barbican, a Beech Lane house where the prince lived under Charles II. The article notes Charles's visit, when Cripplegate ringers earned a guinea for a merry peal, and praises Rupert as a man of science: inventor of Prince's Metal. firearm locks, and gunpowder improvements, fellow of the Royal Society, Board of Trade member, and first governor of the Hudson's Bay Company, whose influence founded it.

Rupert's military fame, the writer argues, will fade before his artistic and useful legacy. Shorter items follow. For London historians, the number preserves a lost City house and a reminder that a Civil War cavalier could also be an experimental philosopher.
11343-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated May 9, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Cornwall Terrace in Regent's Park, designed by Decimus Burton and named for the king's ducal title when regent. The article praises its regularity and beauty, with a rusticated ground story, Corinthian stories with fluted shafts and well-proportioned capitals, and a facade of great architectural elegance. Adjoining York Terrace, engraved in number 358, it was among the park's earliest and most admired buildings.

A Cosmopolite column and a concluded piece on the Times newspaper follow, dissecting how readers consume court circulars and money-market news. The terrace piece and the newspaper piece together show the Mirror's range: buildings and media in one sheet. Regent's Park enthusiasts will value the contemporary praise for Burton.
11347-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 16, 1829 Mirror leads with Laleham Park, a villa on the Thames between Shepperton and Staines, lately the temporary residence of the young Queen of Portugal. The article describes an elegant villa on forty acres with fine elm timber, laid out under the Earl of Lucan, and a lively, light-haired child queen. nearly the same age as Princess Victoria, who arrived in London the previous October and stayed at Grillon's Hotel before ill health required country air.

Laleham's fame for angling and its transparent shallows complete the picture. The piece is celebrity reporting in 1829 form: a royal child, a pretty house, and a river. Shorter items fill the sheet, but the young queen gives the number its news value.
11348-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 2, 1829 Mirror leads with Clarendon House in Piccadilly, the splendid mansion of the Earl of Clarendon facing St. James's Street, on the site of present Grafton Street. Built with stone intended for St. Paul's, it cost fifty thousand pounds and employed three hundred men, and enemies called it Dunkirk House, claiming it was built with money from selling Dunkirk to France. Clarendon himself later apologized for its vanity and expense, which embarrassed his affairs.

George Monck, Duke of Albemarle, later bought the house. The article balances admiration for the pile with the political scandal it caused. Shorter items follow. For Stuart historians, the number preserves a famous house and the envy that helped ruin its builder.
11350-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The June 20, 1829 Mirror leads with Exeter 'Change in the Strand, celebrated for its menagerie and merchandise: wild beasts and cutlery, kangaroos and hosiery, elephants and pins. The article recalls Burleigh's house, where Elizabeth visited her treasurer, becoming a receptacle for beasts upstairs and shopkeepers below, including Clarke the cutler, who amassed a princely fortune. Improvement has now condemned the building, and the beasts move to the King's Mews at Charing Cross.

Two doors east of this world of wonders, the Mirror itself first appeared. A building for public societies is planned for the site. The article is both obituary and memoir, mourning a London curiosity. For city historians, it preserves Exeter 'Change at the moment of its removal.
11361-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The June 27, 1829 Mirror leads with Loch Goil Head in Argyleshire, a small village at the end of Loch Goil. rendered interesting as the residence of Thomas Campbell, author of The Pleasures of Hope. Campbell's château or retreat appears on the left of the engraving, its romantic position probably inspiring many soul-stirring compositions. Nearby stand Carrick Castle, said to be built by Danes, Ben Cruachan at 3,300 feet, Inveraray Castle, Loch Lomond, and Glencoe.

The article sells Argyleshire as Alpine sublimity within Britain, with poetry as its guide. Shorter items follow. For Campbell readers, the number locates the poet in his landscape, showing how literary fame turned a loch-head village into a destination.
11382-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The January 31, 1829 Mirror leads with the Colosseum in Regent's Park, a polygon of sixteen sides, 130 feet in diameter, whose exterior the engraving shows. Each angle bears a double square Doric pilaster supporting an entablature, above which sit a blocking course. attic, and majestic cupola on three receding steps, glazed above and copper below, finished with an immense open circle. The portico, copied from Rome's Pantheon, is praised as among the best Graeco-Doric in the metropolis.

An earlier number guided readers through the interior; this one treats the architecture. The Colosseum housed a vast panorama, and the Mirror's attention shows its novelty. For Regent's Park historians, the number preserves a building now vanished, described while it still astonished visitors.
11390-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The January 24, 1829 Mirror presents villas in Regent's Park, with engravings of Hanover Lodge and Grove House seen from Macclesfield Bridge. Hanover Lodge, residence of Colonel Sir Robert Arbuthnot, offers a handsome portico, a dining room, and drawing rooms sixty feet by eighteen, with nine chambers above and domestic offices complete. Its grounds avoid geometrical formalities, unlike old gardeners who carried square and compasses. Grove House, home of George Bellas Greenough, was designed by Decimus Burton.

The villas exemplify a light, elegant style, unlike southern London's brick monstrosities. Shorter items follow. For Regent's Park enthusiasts, the number pairs two villas in one sheet, showing how the park's domestic architecture complemented its terraces.
11486-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 22 August 1829, priced at twopence, opens at St. Peter's Church, Pimlico. The church stands east of Wilton Place in St. George, Hanover Square. Henry Hakewill designed the Ionic building. It runs east and west as a parallelogram.

A small chancel and vestries extend the east end. A six-column portico fronts the west. Steps lead to three entrances. Columns carry an entablature and pediment. Notes after the main piece turn to insects and cruelty to small creatures. Royal visits get a note as well. The weekly blend stays the same.
11487-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The May 23, 1829 Mirror leads with the Fortune Playhouse in Golden Lane, Barbican, built by actor Edward Alleyn, founder of Dulwich College, in 1599, burnt in 1624, and rebuilt in 1629. A treasure reportedly found digging foundations probably fell to Alleyn, and the name Fortune may derive from it. The spacious brick building showed royal arms in plaster, retained in the engraving even as its lower part became shops, base purposes for a temple of drama.

Ben Jonson and others called Alleyn the first actor of his time, playing leading roles in Shakespeare and Jonson, drawing crowds wherever he performed. Shorter items, including Royal Academy pictures, follow. For theatre historians, the number preserves a Shakespearean playhouse in its decayed, shop-filled state.
11611-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 6 June 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Holland House, Kensington. Sir Walter Cope built it in 1607. Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, gave the house its name. Its form is a half H, and Inigo Jones designed the entrance piers.

Francis Cleyne decorated the gilt room, which keeps its first state. Kensington has housed celebrated men since William the Third. He was the first royal tenant of the palace there. A later piece turns to Old Charing Cross. It was one of Edward the First's memorials to Queen Elinor, later destroyed by Reformers.
11710-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 13 June 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Cumberland Terrace, Regent's Park. The terrace completes the magazine's series of architectural illustrations there. Nash designed the terrace, raised above the road, with a carriage sweep and balustrades.

A garden promenade lies below, level with the road, for residents of the terrace. Centre and wings join by two handsome arches, with Doric columns and a balustrade above. Allegorical figures of seasons, quarters of the globe, and arts and sciences crown the masses. A later piece solves the fate of La Pérouse through the massacre of the Hunter's crew at the Feejee Islands in 1813.
11740-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 4 April 1829, priced at twopence, opens at the tomb of Gower the poet in St. Mary Overy, or St. Saviour, Southwark. Dr. Johnson, the writer notes, dignified Gower as the father of English poetry, so no apology is needed for the memorial.

Three Gothic arches, rich in cinquefoil tracery, roses, and carved work, form the tomb, with trefoil niches behind and a Doric column rising between. Cherubim descend from the interior arches, and foliage crowns the whole. A later piece shows the Hirlas Horn, a piece of plate given at the Denbigh Eisteddfod of 1828 to Dr. Jones, its honorary secretary.
11742-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Saturday, 25 April 1829, priced at twopence, opens at Sussex Place, Regent's Park, said to be built from Nash's designs, though counted among his least successful works. It was among the earliest terraces in the park, and its contrast with chaster neighbours drew critical pasquinade.

A centre with pediment, two octagonal towers, and wings with four towers each, all topped with cupolas and minarets, make the range. The effect, the writer says, is far from pleasing, though a landscape painter might enjoy its picturesque outlines. Later notes cover Loch Katrine, ten miles long, never freezing, and portrait painting.
12017-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
This volume of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction contains original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, sketches of society, topographical descriptions, novels and tales, anecdotes, and poetry. It opens with a portrait of the late Sir Humphry Davy. Its subtitle promises the spirit of the public journals and discoveries in the arts, for twopenny readers.

The Davy memoir notes that a few days before his marriage he received knighthood from the Prince Regent, the first dignity of that kind the prince conferred. It follows his discoveries relating electricity and chemistry, with Davies Gilbert's speech awarding him a royal medal. Science, biography, and miscellany share the volume in the magazine's familiar mix.
12089-letters-of-travel-1892-1913:
Rudyard Kipling's Letters of Travel, 1892 to 1913, in the Dominions Edition published by Macmillan in London in 1920, gathers travel letters from three sources. From Tideway to Tideway appeared originally in The Times, Letters to the Family in The Morning Post, and Egypt of the Magicians in Nash's Magazine.

Kipling writes as an imperial traveller and reporter, moving between Canada, South Africa, Egypt. Other parts of the empire with a journalist's eye for harbors, railways, soldiers, and settlers. The letters, spanning two decades, show his style hardening from youthful impressionism to the confident, sometimes combative voice of his later public writing.
12213-odd-charges-odd-craft-part-13:
A stranger eating and drinking in the warm tap-room of the Cauliflower meets a withered ancient nursing an empty mug in Odd Charges, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. The old man blows through a cold churchwarden pipe, waiting for charity.

The stranger, generous with his mug, draws out tales of Bob Pretty and village feuds, including a coat dropped on a head from a window and thanks sent down for kindness. Jacobs lets the tap-room talk wander from poaching to revenge, with each anecdote sharpening the last. The title puns on odd charges: the bills, accusations, and favors that pass between drinkers. The story is a small masterpiece of pub narration.
12477-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 14 February 1829 and priced at twopence, this number of the Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction opens with an engraving of the interior of the Colosseum. A key explains the print in detail, from its central tower and galleries to its refreshment room, music rooms and the old ball from St. Paul's Cathedral.

That blend of picture, explanation and short reading typifies the weekly miscellany, which mixed literature, science, history and curiosity for a broad audience. Later pages would carry anecdotes, sketches and notices in the same accessible style. The issue is a small window on cheap illustrated print in the 1820s, when a panorama print could teach as well as entertain.
12498-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated 21 March 1829, this Mirror number leads with Chester Terrace, Regent's Park, in a spirited engraving. The range of palatial residences, named from the royal earldom of Chester, stands between the Colosseum and St. Katharine's Church, with the Colosseum's cupola in the distance. Nash, architect of York Terrace, designed it.

Like most of the park's terraces, Chester Terrace presents a noble appearance, the article says, as fine as any similar structure in the park. Short pieces around it keep the weekly mix. The number shows Regency London in print, a new park, new terraces and a public eager to see them pictured.
12897-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, February 21, 1829, this Mirror number leads with Warwick Castle, inhabited from its foundation for nearly a thousand years. The town on the Avon, debated as Roman or Saxon in origin, gets its own history before the castle's towers and sieges. Antiquaries Rous and Dugdale supply the learned notes.

Later pages turn to encyclopaedias, tracing the word from the Greek circle of liberal learning to the vast modern works of human knowledge. Short notes and anecdotes fill the rest. The issue shows the weekly's habit of pairing a grand old building with light learning for general readers.
12898-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, February 28, 1829, this Mirror number leads with York Terrace in Regent's Park, a splendid range of homes that looks like one unique palace. Entrances at the rear, uniform doors and windows, and undivided gardens give the terrace a princely, little-Versailles air. Its Græco-Italian design, with rusticated piers and round-headed windows, earns praise.

Later pages travel to Mecca, where unpaved streets turn to dust in summer and mud in rain, and no house is thought older than four centuries. The mosque itself, repaired by many sultans, counts as modern. The issue pairs London architecture with foreign travel notes.
12899-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
Dated Saturday, April 18, 1829, this Mirror number opens at Harrow School, founded by John Lyon under Elizabeth with letters patent and a code of rules. The archbishops of Canterbury once kept a residence on the hill. The free grammar school grew from Lyon's small gift of thirty marks a year into one of England's eight great schools.

Later pages turn to South America, where Bolivar leaves his army to Paez and repairs to Angostura as Morillo advances toward the Orinoco. Foreign friends who flew to freedom's aid earn the writer's praise. The issue pairs English school history with stirring news from abroad.
13578-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
A supplementary number of the Mirror of Literature, volume thirteen, number 361, opens with the Naturalist, illustrated by the talipot tree, the glowworm, and the deathwatch magnified. A new Journal of a Naturalist, with the motto plants, trees, and stones we note, earns praise as a delightful volume almost synonymous with this division of the Mirror.

London building follows, with Belgrave Square rising in about four years, houses of the largest size round spacious squares and wide streets, built by gentlemen and tradesmen as a pre-eminent example. A confederate in knavery, needy and outcast, links his destiny with Fitzroy, who lives by plundering the unwary and is hailed as Magnus Apollo. Nature, building, and rogue memoir share the supplement.
13644-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement:
The Mirror of Literature for March 14, 1829, opens with the grand entrance to Hyde Park, designed by Decimus Burton. A screen of handsome fluted Ionic columns, three carriage archways, two foot entrances, and a lodge stretch about one hundred and seven feet, with a bold central projection. Lord Burleigh's maxim, that a realm gains more by one year's peace than ten years' war, frames the praise.

A chronological table follows rulers from Cromwell's interregnum, 1648 to 1660, through popes, emperors, and kings of France, Spain, Portugal, Denmark, and beyond. A review of Penelope, or Love's Labour Lost, praises a mixture of satire and fashion without starch or silly affectation. The number mixes architecture, chronology, and novel criticism.
16760-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-:
This slice of Holinshed's Chronicles covers Stephen, earl of Boulogne, from his swift crossing after his uncle Henry died in 1135. Stephen was son of Stephen of Blois and Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror. He seized the realm with help from his brother Theobald. His brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, aided him too. Yet he had sworn to uphold the Empress and her heirs.

The same day he landed, a great winter tempest of thunder and lightning struck, which chroniclers read as a sign of trouble to come. The slice opens the Anarchy in Tudor prose, with side notes naming its sources. Readers who push through the old spelling get a reign that starts in oath-breaking, storm, and civil war.
17320-political-and-literary-essays-1908:
The Earl of Cromer's 1913 set gathers political and literary essays from the Edinburgh Review, Quarterly Review, Nineteenth Century, and Spectator. Topics run from the government of subject races and army reform to free trade, China, Egypt, Disraeli, Russian romance, the Greek anthology, and the future of the classics. Pieces on Wellington, Burma, and Portuguese slavery widen the range.

Cromer writes as an imperial statesman and man of letters, firm in view and clear in prose. His essays show Edwardian Britain debating empire, trade, and culture at full stretch. Historians and essay lovers will find a rich, opinionated volume from a leading voice of its age.
2113-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle closes the First Silesian War in Book Thirteen, from May 1741 to July 1742, leaving the general European war ablaze all round. The British king, paladin of the Pragmatic Sanction, carries the axis of the world on his shoulder. The Pragmatic Sanction, which secured Maria Theresa's throne, drew Britain into German war.

Carlyle writes of a small gentleman with proud eyes and poor sight, trying to unriddle a waste of diplomacy under pain of death. The volume ends Frederick's first war with a peace that settled Silesia but not Europe. Carlyle's small gentleman is George II, whose German lands pulled him into a continental tangle.
22242-the-youth-s-companion-volume-lii-n:
The Youth's Companion was America's best-loved family weekly for a hundred years. This number, volume 52 number 11, is dated Thursday, March 13, 1879. J. T. Trowbridge, a regular contributor, supplies the lead story. In it a one-eyed hostler leans on a bar and lectures on bears. Let them alone, he says, and they will mostly let you alone. A vicious one turns up now and then.

Stories, poems, household pages, and a children's corner fill the issue. The Companion reached more American homes than any magazine of its century. Mark Twain and a dozen presidents wrote for it. One surviving number shows the wholesome, story-rich mixture that made it a fixture by the fireside.
30186-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Rossiter Johnson edits volume 13 of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a chronological history told in the words of eminent historians, with brief links by specialists. Charles F. Horne supplies an outline narrative, then Louis Adolphe Thiers tells how John Law promoted the Mississippi Scheme in 1716 and how the South Sea Bubble burst in 1720. Prince Eugene's own account covers the siege and battle of Belgrad in 1717, and Bach lays the foundation of modern music in 1723.

The National Alumni published the volume in 1905, promising a non-sectarian, non-partisan account with thorough indices, bibliographies, chronologies, and courses of reading. Each event reads as a complete narrative, not a summary, so the book suits readers who want history in strong period voices. Later volumes carry the chain forward, but this one stands well on its own.
3089-original-short-stories-volume-13:
Old Judas closes the series in volume thirteen, beside a wild black lake. The opening story surveys a wild lake of stagnant black water, reeds waving in a vast circle, with a grandeur almost religious and an air of sinister desolation. The volume adds The Little Cask, Boitelle, A Widow, The Englishmen of Etretat, Magnetism, A Father's Confession, and A Mother of Monsters. Later tales include An Uncomfortable Bed, A Portrait, The Drunkard, The Wardrobe, The Mountain Pool, A Cremation, Misti, Madame Hermet, and The Magic Couch.

A father's confession tells of a month of horrible anguish and hatred toward a child blocking his path to happiness. The final volume shows Maupassant's full range, from horror to irony.
30954-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume thirteen of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds The Wrecker, with a prologue set in the Marquesas and a front showing the back verandah at Vailima.

The yarn opens with a sound commercial education and Roussillon wine, then introduces Mr. Pinkerton, a figure who shapes the hero's fortunes. Chapters follow extremes of fortune, bad luck in Paris, going west, irons in the fire, and faces on the city front. Then comes the wreck of the Flying Scud and the vanishing of its crew. It is a sprawling adventure of business, ships, and mystery, in Stevenson's late, Pacific style.
31288-the-conscript-a-story-of-the-frenc:
Erckmann-Chatrian's The Conscript, in the Scribner translation of 1911, is the French authors' sustained sermon against war. It follows their Madame Thérèse with the tragic story of 1812 and 1813 rather than Napoleon's victories. Its first part follows the grande armée through Alsace toward Moscow and the Beresina, with anxious waiting, rumors of disaster, and a demoralized, straggling retreat.

The second and larger portion follows the fatal campaign that opened doubtfully at Lutzen and Bautzen and ended at Leipsic and the capitulation of Paris. Joseph Bertha, torn from his betrothed and peaceful trade by conscription, tells the story with shrewd, simple reflections that make his fate stand for a generation's.
31289-waterloo-a-sequel-to-the-conscript:
Erckmann-Chatrian's Waterloo, translated from the French and published by Scribner's in New York in 1911 as a sequel to The Conscript of 1813, tells the campaign from a private soldier's standpoint. It describes only what he saw. The introductory note argues that this limit still admits events of the greatest importance and incidents of intense dramatic interest, from the combat at Hougoumont Farm to the Emperor's departure for Paris.

The narrative also pictures France after the first Bourbon restoration, when the unbounded joy at Louis XVIII's return in the spring of 1814 gave way, through the new regime's stupidity. That stupidity prepared the gradual return of Napoleon. As familiar history and historical commentary, the novel shows how a restoration lost a war-weary people.
3246-the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-:
This volume of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction dates from the spring of 1829. Number 365, priced at twopence and dated Saturday 11 April 1829, opens with an engraving of Old Somerset House. The editors call it one of the greatest antiquarian treasures they had lately offered readers. The house took its name from Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset.

The Mirror was a weekly miscellany, mixing pictures, history, and light reading for a popular audience. Each number packed short pieces and engravings into a cheap sheet. This volume preserves that format intact: a window onto what ordinary London readers browsed in 1829, from old buildings to anecdotes, before the age of the illustrated newspaper.
34150-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Alexander Leighton revised this thirteenth volume of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, published in London and Newcastle in 1885 by Walter Scott, with a glossary. Tales run from The Unknown by John Mackay Wilson and The Trials of Menie Dempster by Leighton to the Professor's Tales, the natural history of idiots, and the Floshend Inn.

Lottery Hall, the dominie and the souter, the dominie's courtship, the souter's wedding, Roseallan's daughter, the two sailors, and the Dream complete the set. The opening tale finds a young Spanish woman in faded silk, faint and weary, bearing an infant on the road to Rothbury in 1785. The volume offers Border tales of mystery and life.
3563-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This thirteenth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers Napoleon in 1815, the year of his return from Elba and his final fall. Bourrienne writes as a former secretary watching the Hundred Days unfold: the emperor's landing, his march to Paris, and the gathering of armies against him. The Hundred Days read here as a rush of hope followed by a second, harder reckoning.

The narrative carries the excitement of a comeback and the speed of its collapse. Old loyalties revive for a season, then break again at Waterloo and after. Bourrienne gives the view of a man who knew Napoleon's court in its prime and now saw it dissolve. The volume suits readers reaching the end of the long story.
3593-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This thirteenth volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters thirty two through thirty seven of Book Two. They include a defense of Seneca and Plutarch and the story of Spurina. Other essays treat war according to Julius Caesar, three good women, the most excellent men, and the resemblance of children to their fathers. Montaigne opens by noting how much help Seneca and Plutarch lent to his age and to his book.

The essays show Montaigne reading the ancients as friends and guides, not as distant authorities. He defends them against critics, borrows their tactics, and compares their lives with his own family. The volume suits readers who enjoy classical learning worn lightly, with personal comment at every turn.
3803-file-no-113:
Emile Gaboriau opens this early detective novel with a Paris bank robbery that fills the evening papers. On a February morning in 1866, thieves force an impregnable safe at the bank of Andre Fauvel in the Rue de Provence and take three hundred and fifty thousand francs in notes. Police arrest a clerk, known in the papers only by initials, and the town talks of nothing else for four days.

Then the case deepens, as the papers prove wrong or at least careless, and private passions surface behind the crime. A billiard room quarrel, where Gaston confronts Jules Lazet over a remark about a nobleman's daughter, shows how honor and money tangle. Readers who like the roots of detective fiction will find a tale where the mystery matters less than the human wreckage around it.
5287-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's thirteenth volume opens with St Julian's Prayer, a tale that begins by laughing at charms, philters, secret spells, and prayers. So many place all their cares in such things. The author admits he never believed in them, yet notes that with the fair such words are viewed as sacred virtues, working wonders in love.

Saint Julian's prayer, repeated by Reynold D'Ast, produces a benefit classed as good fortune. The tale that follows turns prayer into comic proof. Readers get a volume in which La Fontaine mocks superstition while granting it a storyteller's power, in verse that is sly rather than scolding.
5915-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
An interpolated novel anchors this Don Quixote portion, chapters thirty-three through forty. Chapter thirty-three relates the novel of the ill-advised curiosity, set in Florence among two gentlemen of wealth, Anselmo and Lothario, friends so great that all called them by a special distinction. Chapter thirty-four continues that novel, chapter thirty-five stages a heroic battle at the inn, and chapter thirty-six adds more curious incidents there.

Chapter thirty-seven continues the story of the famous Princess Micomicona, chapter thirty-eight gives Quixote's curious discourse on arms and letters, and chapters thirty-nine and forty let the captive relate his life. Readers get Cervantes's nesting tales at full stretch, as inn guests tell stories within the story. The part suits readers who enjoy the novel's digressions as much as its knight.
7598-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part thirteen of The Caxtons turns toward departure, as Pisistratus prepares to leave home. The call cannot be refused: an old sea-roving strain in his blood will have its way, and he must be a soldier or a rover. His family will mourn and miss him, but no chain holds young eagles to the eyrie. Lytton makes the old theme of leaving home fresh again, through a son who must argue his freedom politely.

The argument itself is managed with love and cunning. The young man seeks to insinuate his project into favor with his unsuspecting family through innocent arts. Saint Chrysostom on the priesthood supplies his cover, defending deceit for a good purpose by scriptural examples and calling it good management instead. The part thus joins a son's ambition to a scholar's excuse, and both to affection.
813:
813 is a 1910 Arsène Lupin novel by Maurice Leblanc, in which the gentleman thief must clear his own name. When one of Lupin's victims is found dead in a way that points to him, he insists on leading the police search for the real murderer himself. The hunt that follows is one of the strangest in the series.

The mystery turns on a package of letters once written to Bismarck and on a clock where the number 813 carries a hidden meaning. A reigning emperor is drawn into several journeys in disguise as the case widens. Murders multiply, and Lupin works both sides of the law to reach the truth first.
arxiv-2509-00013:
Rakshit Poudel, Daya Nidhi Chhatkuli, and Madhav Kafle propose a fix for the center of a Schwarzschild black hole in Anti-de-Sitter space in 2025. In the standard account, the fully stretched form of that spacetime holds a singularity, a point where the math breaks down. The authors propose swapping that point for a tiny de-Sitter patch, a small region of outward-pushing space that does not last.

The swap counts as a deep change to the entangled sector, or to its dual paired state. The authors speculate that the core could shift late-time signals, tame runaway values, and show in how holographic complexity, a gauge of state depth, grows. They also discuss a link to the Page curve puzzle of evaporating holes. The idea is a proposal, not a proven result.
arxiv-2509-00213:
Farhan Fuad Abir, Abigail Elliott Daly, Kyle Anderman, Tolga Ozmen, and Laura J. Brattain build a multimodal model in 2025 to classify phyllodes tumors of the breast. These rare fibroepithelial lesions look much like benign fibroadenomas on scans, so they are hard to classify before surgery. That overlap leads to needless surgical removals.

Their dual-branch network fuses breast ultrasound images with structured clinical data from eighty-one confirmed subjects. Class-aware sampling and subject-stratified cross-validation guard against imbalance and leakage. The fused model beats single-mode baselines at telling benign tumors from borderline or malignant ones. Among six image encoders, ConvNeXt and ResNet18 lead in the fused setting. Sharper pre-surgery calls could spare patients needless operations.
arxiv-2509-00713:
Junghoon Justin Park leads five authors in total, with Huan-Hsin Tseng, Shinjae Yoo, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, and Jiook Cha, in applying quantum reinforcement learning to Super Mario Bros. Quantum learners promise compact models with vast state spaces, but current noisy quantum hardware limits qubits and adds noise.

Their multi-chip ensemble splits high-dimensional game observations across several small Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks, each on its own circuit, then classically aggregates outputs inside a Double Deep Q-Network. The modular design reduces information loss from dimensionality reduction and remains implementable on near-term hardware. It achieves better performance and learning stability than classical baselines and single-chip quantum models, opening complex environments to quantum agents.
arxiv-2509-00813:
Gyehun Go leads six authors in total, with Satbyul Han, Ahyeon Choi, Eunjin Choi, Juhan Nam, and Jeong Mi Park, in introducing AImoclips, a benchmark for emotion conveyance in text-to-music generation. Systems now create expressive music from natural language prompts, but how faithfully they convey intended emotions has been little studied.

The team selected twelve emotion intents across four quadrants of the valence-arousal space, which maps feelings by pleasantness and intensity, and used six leading systems to generate over one thousand clips. One hundred eleven participants rated perceived valence and arousal on a nine-point scale. Commercial systems skew more pleasant than intended, open-source systems the opposite, high-arousal emotions convey best, and all systems bias toward neutrality.
arxiv-2509-00913:
Disha Shetty leads a team of eight authors on quantum linear solvers for network problems. Network-based linear systems arise naturally from graphs. They connect to many real-world applications. A quantum solver's advantage depends on two scalings. They are the condition number and the sparsity of the graph matrices.

The team analyzes fifty graph families for advantage prospects. Only twenty-one show prospects for exponential advantage with the HHL algorithm. That comparison is against an efficient classical solver. Some families gain prospects with improved algorithms like Childs-Kothari-Somma. The team also introduces a unified graph superfamily. It contains infinitely many good graph families within it. They conjecture rules for judging a family's prospects by eye.
arxiv-2509-01113:
Soft robot hands bend as they grip, which helps them handle people and fragile objects but makes control tricky. Haiyun Zhang, with four co-authors, offers a simpler way to model a soft hand driven by air pressure. Their method treats each bending part as if it were a stiff body on a hinge, a stand-in called a pseudo rigid body model.

To set the model's values, the team uses the logarithmic decrement method, which infers traits from how motion fades over time. On a test hand, their controller tracked position and force far better than a standard PID controller, with much smaller peak errors. The result supports faster, more accurate control of soft hands in real time.
arxiv-2509-01213:
When a model learns new tasks one after another, it often forgets what it knew before, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Ege Sualp and Mina Rezaei test whether growing a model, training a larger one from a smaller one's progress, can soften that loss. Growth by stacking transformer layers was known to speed training, but its effect on forgetting was unclear.

The pair compared a stacked large model with one trained without growth, across fine-tuning tasks in domain knowledge, reasoning, reading, and bias. Both models gained domain knowledge, yet their retention of reasoning and reading skills diverged in telling ways. Sualp and Rezaei present the study as evidence on when model growth helps continual learning, a key need for language models that must keep learning.
arxiv-2509-01913:
M A Garcia-Marquez, H M Moya-Cessa, I Ramos-Prieto, and F Soto-Eguibar solve a continuity equation in the Madelung-Bohm view of quantum motion. That view rewrites quantum flow in terms of a density and a phase, like a fluid. They assume the phase splits into a space part times a time part plus a time shift. Operator methods then reshape the wave amplitude into a handy form for any starting state.

The reshaped amplitude acts like a squeezed version of the position operator applied to the start. Two cases show the power of the form. In one, no outside potential acts, so motion stems only from the Bohm potential. In the other, the form mimics light spread in waveguide arrays, where even complex values still obey the core equation.
arxiv-2509-02513:
Tuval Danenberg wrote a 2025 solo political science theory paper on how polarisation and issue alignment can grow together under rational learning. Polarisation means views split toward opposite extremes; alignment means one person's views across issues become more consistent with each other.

The model uses Bayesian agents, ideal learners who update beliefs from public signals by the rules of probability. Danenberg characterises which public signals can keep agents polarised on every issue dimension at once. Evidence of alignment itself can push Bayesian agents apart. However, stronger forms of polarisation, beyond marginal beliefs, clash with Bayesian rationality. Whether belief splits become position splits also depends on whether issues can be separated from each other in agents' thinking.
arxiv-2509-02613:
Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay present a 2025 mathematical paper building a formal model of an evolving internal state, inspired by the flow of thought. Their state space is a topological space, possibly an infinite-dimensional Banach space, and each trajectory is a continuous path through it.

Ideas from Brouwer's intuitionism treat the sequence of states as a choice sequence, freely unfolding rather than pre-set. The authors prove that evolutions exist and are unique under continuity conditions, using a fixed-point argument. They also show some sets of states cannot carry a classical measure at all. A Tarski-style truth definition for statements about states completes the logical side. The work deliberately avoids category theory while blending classical analysis with intuitionistic views.
arxiv-2509-02813:
Tessa T. Frincke and nine co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper reporting early brightness measurements of 3I/ATLAS, only the third known object visiting the solar system from interstellar space. Observations came from the SOAR telescope in Chile on three July 2025 nights, days after discovery.

Twenty-eight photometric points in a red filter feed the object's growing light curve. No obvious long-term brightness trend appeared. Two apparent brightening events on later nights were tested with contamination, stacking, and aperture experiments. Both turned out to be artefacts of poor seeing and nearby field stars. Reported mean magnitudes for each night give clean reference values. Cometary activity in matching images hides any rotation signal, and activity stayed near discovery levels with no outburst.
arxiv-2509-03313:
Miguel Molina-Hernandez and 3 co-authors extended a radiation chemistry simulator in 2025 to handle FLASH dose rates. FLASH radiotherapy delivers dose at ultra-high rates and seems to spare healthy tissue, an effect researchers are racing to explain. One clue is that radical-radical reactions, where reactive fragments react with each other, speed up under FLASH conditions.

The upgraded GPU-based Monte Carlo tool, gMicroMC, now simulates many pulses in sequence. Water exposed to proton pulses showed a clear threshold in average dose rate. Below it, radicals drained fully between pulses and product yields stayed flat. Above it, reactive species piled up across pulses, raising reaction rates and hydrogen peroxide yields. The buildup between pulses, the authors argue, matters more than interactions between separate particle tracks.
arxiv-2509-03813:
Parth Ashokbhai Shiroya and six co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to classifying indoor surfaces with LiDAR so wireless networks can predict how signals scatter. Millimetre-wave and sub-terahertz links depend on reflections because their signals block so easily. Whether a surface reflects cleanly or scatters diffusely depends on material and roughness.

Their framework sorts surfaces by how specular their reflections are, taking optical reflectivity as a stand-in for electromagnetic behaviour. Over seventy-eight thousand LiDAR points from fifteen materials were divided into patches, letting the system classify from partial views. Patch features capture geometry and intensity, among them elevation angle and intensity ratios. Random forest, gradient boosting, and neural network classifiers are trained and compared. Ensemble tree models give the best balance of accuracy and robustness, confirming LiDAR features capture roughness-driven scattering. Outputs feed scatter-aware maps and digital twins for beam management.
arxiv-2509-03913:
Jiajun Yuan and five co-authors survey STSR, a framework for speech super-resolution, rebuilding wideband speech from low-resolution input in a 2025 research paper. Faithful rebuilding must keep harmonic coherence, the pattern of overtones, and local transients, the sharp attacks that make speech crisp. Diffusion models achieve fidelity but cost too much for many deployments.

Efficient time-domain designs are cheaper, yet they lack frequency views for spectral structure and harmonic alignment. STSR instead works end to end in the MDCT domain, a compressed frequency form of the signal. Its attention mechanism uses layered windowing to gather non-local context, keeping harmonic structure consistent up to forty-eight kilohertz. A sparse-aware regularisation counters the suppression of transient parts that compressed forms cause. Across tests, STSR beats leading baselines in perceived fidelity and in zero-shot reach to unseen conditions, while staying fast enough for real-time restoration.
arxiv-2509-04013:
Testing whether standard benchmark scores for large language models survive simple rewording is what Riccardo Lunardi and three co-authors do in a 2025 research paper. Benchmarks like MMLU present questions in one fixed, standardised wording. Real users phrase the same questions many ways, so a model that only handles the canonical wording is less capable than its score suggests.

The authors generate paraphrases of every question across six common benchmarks, then measure how effectiveness changes for thirty-four leading language models . Model rankings stay relatively stable under paraphrase: the best models mostly remain the best. Absolute scores, however, change and decline significantly, showing the models struggle with linguistic variability. That drop undermines trust in benchmark-based evaluation, since high scores may not reflect robustness to real-world input variation. The authors emphasise robustness-aware benchmarks, designed to measure performance across rewordings, as a better guide to practical deployment.
arxiv-2509-04113:
Sudheer Mishra and one co-author, E Natarajan, develop a numerical method for slow fluid flow problems in a 2025 thesis-style paper. The target is the generalized Oseen equation, which models fluids pushed along by a steady current. Their method is called a virtual element method, since it works on many-sided mesh cells without fixing each cell's inner shape. Equal-order approximations for speed and pressure can turn unstable, so the authors add stabilizing terms built from local projections.

Proofs show the scheme stays stable in a standard energy measure. The same setup also covers the Brinkman and Stokes equations with no extra conditions. Error bounds stay even as diffusion, meaning spreading, gets very small. Computer tests in slow and fast flow regimes back the theory.
arxiv-2509-05013:
Liquidity on a decentralised exchange forms a surface that moves over time and price ticks. Jimmy Risk, lead author with two co-authors, study those dynamics for Uniswap v3 in a 2025 paper. They model liquidity as a time-tick surface and analyse three pools over several sample periods.

Functional principal component analysis and dynamic factor methods reduce the surface to a few interpretable components. For the tightest fee pools, the leading components explain most variation and stay stable, aligning with simple polynomial shapes. Their factor coefficients follow persistent time series patterns with heavy tails and changing volatility, giving a compact statistical picture of automated market maker liquidity.
arxiv-2509-05213:
Federated training of large neural networks struggles when each client's data differ and communication is expensive. Jiaojiao Zhang, lead author with three co-authors, propose FedSub, a subspace algorithm for that setting, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Client drift from heterogeneous data is the other main obstacle they target.

Each client updates only inside a low-dimensional subspace, cutting communication, computation, and memory costs. Low-dimensional dual variables counteract client drift. Their convergence analysis shows how step size and projection choices affect the rate. Experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the design for large-scale federated learning.
arxiv-2509-05513:
First-person video of human hands at work becomes training data for dexterous robots in OpenEgo, a dataset introduced by Ahad Jawaid and Yu Xiang in a 2025 paper. Egocentric video scales well for imitation learning, but older collections lack either precise action labels or detailed hand tracking.

OpenEgo unifies six public datasets into more than a thousand hours of footage. It covers hundreds of manipulation tasks across hundreds of environments. Hand poses are converted to one standard layout, and actions are described with time stamps aligned to the actor's intent. To validate the resource, the authors train language-guided policies that predict hand trajectories. All materials are slated for public release.
arxiv-2509-05613:
Collisions of light atomic nuclei may or may not create droplets of quark-gluon plasma, Lucas Constantin and three co-authors predict in a 2025 nuclear physics paper ahead of a 2025 collider run. Signs of collective behaviour have appeared even in proton collisions, blurring where this exotic matter begins to form.

The team simulates oxygen-oxygen and neon-neon collisions at the Large Hadron Collider with three models. One couples fluid dynamics for the plasma stage to a hadronic transport stage, one runs the transport alone, and one serves as a no-collectivity baseline. Comparing the evolutions on equal footing shows what each ingredient contributes. The predictions target the light-ion run held in July 2025.
arxiv-2509-05913:
Spotting muscle and joint injury risk in athletes from video and body tracking is the aim of a 2025 paper led by Md. Abdur Rahman with five co-authors. Most current tools need controlled settings and a single data type, so they falter at real games and training. The authors combine images with skeletal coordinates in one model, called ViSK-GAT.

Their dataset, MusDis-Sports, pairs pictures with joint coordinates and labels each sample into eight risk grades from the Rapid Entire Body Assessment system. Two new modules refine features within each data type, then align image and skeleton information before judging. Scores passed ninety-three percent across key measures, beating strong standard backbones. The authors pitch the system as a route to earlier, AI-guided interventions in sport.
arxiv-2509-06013: Kalyan Banerjee proves a negative result about cubic threefolds in a 2025 paper: a very general cubic threefold admits no universal codimension-two cycle. Cubic threefolds are three-dimensional shapes cut out by a degree-three equation, a classic testing ground in algebraic geometry. A universal cycle would parametrize all codimension-two cycles at once. Banerjee shows no such object exists for the very general member of the family. He concludes that the threefold is stably irrational, meaning it cannot be made rational even after standard stabilizing tricks.
arxiv-2509-06213:
How would anyone certify that an AI system follows rules it must discover itself? Christo Mathew and six co-authors explore that metrology problem in a 2025 paper. Their testbed is the Game Of Hidden Rules, a puzzle where an agent must infer secret rules to clear a board by sorting pieces into buckets. Only partial observations are available, so rule inference and policy learning must proceed together.

The team trains a transformer-based advantage actor-critic agent under two state representations, one feature-centric and one object-centric. Experiments vary the rules and trial lists to measure transfer and the effect of representation on learning speed. The work frames hidden-rule games as measuring instruments for artificial intelligence itself.
arxiv-2509-06413:
Judging the quality of super-resolved images made by modern generative methods is the challenge summarized in a 2025 paper led by Yixiao Li with thirty co-authors. The VQualA challenge at ICCV 2025 built a dataset of images upscaled by GAN and diffusion methods, whose artifacts differ from classic super-resolution. One hundred eight participants registered; four teams submitted valid final solutions.

The paper describes the dataset, the competing methods, and the results, with the best submissions reaching state-of-the-art quality prediction on the benchmark. The project is public, and the authors aim to standardize how perceptually convincing, but possibly invented, detail in generated super-resolution gets scored.
arxiv-2509-06613:
Electron pairs from heavy-ion collisions are reported by Florian Eisenhut in a solo 2025 conference paper on the ALICE experiment. Dielectrons matter because they escape the hot, dense matter made in such collisions without being reshaped by later hadronic interactions. They offer a direct look at the earliest moments.

Results cover proton-proton collisions taken with the upgraded ALICE detector, plus the status of the lead-lead analysis at a higher collision energy. Eisenhut explains how prompt and non-prompt dielectron spectra are extracted across a wide mass range. The discussion also covers what these measurements could reveal about the Drell-Yan process in a regime where simple theory struggles, and about the first signs of thermal radiation from the hot matter. The paper is a progress report rather than a final measurement.
arxiv-2509-06813:
Wind turbine maintenance logs, written as messy free text, are labeled by language models in a benchmark by Max Malyi and three co-authors in a 2025 energy informatics paper. Cheaper wind power depends on good operations and maintenance data, but unstructured logs resist automated analysis. The authors build a reproducible, open-source benchmarking framework for the classification task.

A diverse suite of proprietary and open-source models is evaluated for reliability, efficiency, and calibration, meaning whether stated confidence matches accuracy. A clear hierarchy emerges, with top models aligning well with a benchmark standard and showing trustworthy confidence. All models agree more when the task is naming a component, an objective call, than when it is interpreting what maintenance action was taken. Since no model is perfectly accurate, the authors recommend a human-in-the-loop setup, with models accelerating and standardizing labeling for human experts.
arxiv-2509-06913:
Massive galaxies that stopped forming stars surprisingly early are counted by Struan D. Stevenson and twenty-four co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The sample holds two hundred twenty-five quiescent galaxies seen when the universe was young, drawn from the PRIMER and JADES surveys. Only areas with optical coverage in three Hubble filters were used, a restriction the authors show matters for clean, complete samples.

Contamination was checked with JWST spectroscopy, Chandra X-ray imaging, and ALMA observations, coming out modest. Dropping the Hubble data would add star-forming interlopers and lose a fifth of the candidates. Number densities at early times are three times pre-JWST estimates, and most simulations now match the counts at moderate redshift but fall increasingly short earlier. About half the most distant subset shows faint active nuclei, matching recent results.
arxiv-2509-07013:
Sima Najafzadehkhoei and 3 co-authors give a fast way to fit epidemic models to data in a 2025 paper. Agent-based models, which track each person in a fake outbreak, are a key tool for studying how disease spreads. But fitting them to real data takes huge computer time, which hurts when health teams must act fast.

Their method, DeepIMC, learns the link in reverse: from a curve of cases over time, it reads off the traits of the outbreak that made it. A neural net is trained on thousands of fake outbreaks made by agent models, so at use time it can fit fresh data at once, with no new sims. In tests with five thousand varied outbreaks, the method beat a standard Bayesian route on how well it got the true traits back, and its doubt ranges were sharp and well set.
arxiv-2509-07113:
Junfeng Xu and 2 co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on functions of several complex variables. Complex variables are numbers with real and imaginary parts, and here functions can depend on many of them at once. One tool in the field is the logarithmic derivative, which measures how fast a function grows compared with its own size.

The authors first bound the logarithmic partial derivative for a broad class of such functions, extending older one-variable results to higher dimensions. Next they carry Wiman-Valiron theory, a method for studying growth near a peak point, into several variables. Last, they study how fast solutions of a class of partial differential equations can grow. Each result widens tools that were once limited to a single complex variable.
arxiv-2509-07213:
Finding the exact outline of a breast tumor in ultrasound images is hard when lesions are small or faint. Raja Mallina and 1 co-author present XBusNet in a 2025 research paper. XBusNet is a model that segments, or outlines, lesions by combining images with clinical text. One branch reads the whole image with help from prompts about lesion size and location. A second branch sharpens the edges.

The text prompts describe shape, margin, and standard reporting terms, and the system builds them automatically from stored metadata. No manual clicks are needed. Tested with five-fold cross-validation on a breast lesion dataset, XBusNet beat six strong baselines on standard overlap scores. Small lesions improved the most. Separate tests confirm that global context, edge modeling, and text guidance each add value.
arxiv-2509-07413:
Yuhan Pang and 7 co-authors present a control scheme in 2025 for robots that collect luggage trolleys in airports and warehouses. In their system, mobile manipulators form leader-follower groups, and each base must dock precisely to line trolleys into neat queues. Docking is hard because precision demands are high, surroundings disturb the robot, and the base cannot move sideways.

The scheme, DA-VPC, uses active infrared markers that stay visible across lighting conditions for robust visual guidance. It models the robot's motion limits and camera visibility inside a predictive controller solved by optimization. An extended state observer, a module that estimates hidden disturbances, counteracts pushes while the robot shoves trolleys. Experiments in varied settings show the system docks accurately and stably, supporting fully autonomous trolley fleets.
arxiv-2509-07513:
Charmonium particles, made of a charm quark and its antiquark, act as thermometers inside the hottest matter made on Earth. Ingrid McKibben Lofnes reports recent measurements in 2025 conference proceedings from Quark Matter 2025. Heavy quarks form early in a collision. Charmonia therefore trace the whole life of the quark-gluon plasma. That plasma is the hot, dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.

The proceedings present published results from the ALICE experiment on lead-lead collisions. They cover prompt charmonia and those born later from beauty hadron decays, which reveal how beauty quarks lose energy. A first preliminary result compares two charmonium states at forward rapidity in newer data. Color screening melts some charmonia in the plasma, while recombination builds others back. Comparing the measurements with theory helps physicists tell those competing stories apart.
arxiv-2509-07613:
Fangqi Cheng's 2025 paper, with 2 co-authors, adapts medical vision-language models to diagnose Alzheimer's disease with little data. Medical models often underuse patient metadata, lack clinical knowledge, and are trained on flat 2D image-text pairs at great cost, leaving 3D imaging poorly served. The pipeline instead fine-tunes a 3D CT-based model for 3D MRI, the scan type central to Alzheimer's workups.

Two innovations carry the method. Structured metadata are converted into synthetic reports, enriching the text side so images and words align better. An auxiliary token is trained to predict the MMSE score, a standard clinical measure of cognition tied to disease severity, adding supervision. Lightweight prompt tuning adjusts only small parts of both encoders. The approach aims at accurate diagnosis without the vast datasets medical AI usually demands.
arxiv-2509-08213:
Error bars compress every kind of doubt into one tidy whisker on a chart, and two visualization researchers find that suspicious. Michael Correll and Lane Harrison write a provocation on uncertainty visualization in a 2025 research paper. They argue the error bar rests on a large hidden metaphysics of probability. Other traditions, including religious ones, carve up uncertainty very differently.

Drawing on religious examples, the authors present alternative views of what uncertainty is. Some doubts concern fate, providence, or unknowable will rather than sampling noise. The point is to widen what designers think is worth visualizing. It is also to ask who the audience for an uncertainty display really is. The piece is deliberately provocative. It invites the field to match visual forms to the actual kinds of not-knowing people face.
arxiv-2509-08313:
Thermal glow from the telescope itself is traced and corrected in a 2025 instrumentation paper by Jayke S. Nguyen and 4 co-authors. Mid-infrared imaging from the ground can find older, colder exoplanets that other methods miss. The catch is background: the atmosphere and telescope radiate heat, laying a slowly varying, uneven glow under every image taken with the Keck II telescope.

Understanding where that background originates, in instrument design and in atmospheric conditions, allows its systematic patterns to be modelled and removed. Better photometry in the mid-infrared tightens constraints on exoplanet atmospheres. Ground telescopes cannot escape their own warmth, so characterising the glow precisely is what makes cold-planet imaging from Earth credible at all.
arxiv-2509-08613:
Ke Ma and 4 co-authors improve a model of silicon absorption in the Lyman-alpha forest in a 2025 paper. The forest is a set of absorption lines in distant quasar light, used to study gas between galaxies. Silicon absorption adds a correlated signal that can distort measurements.

Using the Sherwood-Relics simulations, the team finds extra small-scale power that earlier work missed. Their new fitting function allows different line shapes and a changing ratio of silicon to hydrogen absorption. It matches simulated data across a wide range of redshifts. The model matters for future precise tests of dark matter and cosmic gas.
arxiv-2509-08713:
Ziming Luo and 2 co-authors warn about hidden pitfalls in AI scientist systems in a 2025 paper. Such systems run the full research loop, from ideas and experiments to writing papers. Their inner workflow has rarely been examined closely.

Four failure modes are named: poor benchmark choice, data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias. Controlled experiments isolate each mode in two open source systems. Several failures appear, at varied severity, and are easy to miss in a final paper. Access to trace logs and code makes detection far easier. The authors urge venues to require those artifacts with submissions.
arxiv-2509-08913:
Sin-Yu Huang and 1 co-author propose user-oriented image semantic coding in a 2025 paper. Semantic coding sends the meaning of an image rather than every pixel. Users often care about a specific region tied to their intent, which older systems ignore.

A text query from the user guides which features are extracted and sent. The receiver rebuilds an image from those features alone. Large vision-language models, CLIP and LLaVA, support generalization and a loss that scores match to user intent. In zero-shot tests on unseen objects, the method beats prior query aware coding on answer match rate.
arxiv-2509-09413:
Microbes that thrive together in one pond may ignore each other in the next, so a single universal interaction network misleads. Daniel Agyapong and 4 co-authors build an algorithm that respects place and time in a 2025 research paper. Standard co-occurrence methods pool samples from many environments into one snapshot. The team instead studies how microbial associations change across locations and time points.

Their evaluation framework trains and tests models both within one environment and across combined environments. Their proposed algorithm, fuser, keeps each sample group's own signals while sharing information across environments during training. It produces a distinct predictive network per environment rather than one averaged network. Within single environments it matched strong baselines. Across environments it cut test error notably. Ecologists get a tool for asking how communities rewire as conditions change, not just who coexists on average.
arxiv-2509-09813:
Amira Abbas and 5 co-authors design methods to learn sparse quantum Hamiltonians in 2025, judging success by measures a physicist would actually care about. Earlier work often lacked matching lower bounds and graded errors with yardsticks chosen for mathematical ease. Their Hamiltonians involve few Pauli terms, and access comes through watching the system evolve over time.

Two distances anchor the study: one based on telling systems apart through bounded-time motion, another through thermal states at bounded temperatures. Sparse systems with bounded strength can be learned in both settings with modest experiment counts. Fresh lower bounds for the time-based distance nearly match the method's cost, certifying it as close to optimal. Along the way every Pauli coefficient of such a Hamiltonian can be recovered.
arxiv-2509-10013:
Ting-Jung Kuo and 2 co-authors study dome-like metrics on a flat torus that blow up at three marked cone points in a 2025 geometry paper. The cone at the origin opens with angle six pi, while a mirrored pair of points carry angle four pi each, and the whole metric is required to be even. The question is when such a family of spherical metrics can exist at all, and the answer turns out to be written in the torus's own shape.

Existence holds exactly when the torus's Green function possesses a matching pair of nontrivial critical points, and then the cone location and monodromy data are forced. A transformation links this family to a simpler one-cone case. For rhombic tori the authors add a rigidity statement, closing off extra freedom.
arxiv-2509-10113:
Junfeng Xu and 3 co-authors hunt for meromorphic solutions of a special algebraic differential equation in a 2025 complex analysis paper. The equation mixes a polynomial in a function and its derivatives with terms built from a linear combination of those derivatives and a product involving two distinct target values. Questions of which functions can satisfy such a relation sit inside value distribution theory, where normal family ideas often decide what shapes are even possible.

Borrowing exactly that idea, the authors pin down the candidate solutions of their equation. The outcome sharpens and widens earlier findings by Li and Yang and by Xu and collaborators, covering a far larger family in one sweep. For specialists, the paper is a consolidation: scattered special cases collapse into a single broader statement about admissible solutions.
arxiv-2509-10213:
Ming Zhou and six co-authors published this computer security paper in 2025. Their subject is how to fix software flaws on small embedded devices, such as medical equipment, without shutting them down. Such devices have little spare memory or processing power, and they come in many different hardware designs, which makes live patching hard.

The team builds a framework called StackPatch, which prepares patches by rebuilding the saved layout of a running program's stack. It uses exception handling built into common processors to redirect program flow, so the same approach adapts across chip families. In tests on ARM, RISC-V, and Xtensa devices, the group fixed over a hundred known flaws in real-time operating systems, each fix finishing in under 260 processor cycles.
arxiv-2509-10413:
Guojun Tang and seven co-authors map the world of Bitcoin cross-chain bridges in this 2025 survey. Bitcoin has limited scripting. It also lacks built-in ways to work with other chains. That walls it off from wider blockchain finance and multi-chain applications. Bridges are the workaround. The authors sort them into three families. Some simply swap tokens. Others issue pegged assets. A third group passes arbitrary messages between chains.

Each family is graded on several points. Trust assumptions come first. Speed, capital efficiency, and fit with decentralized finance follow. Newer ideas get attention as well. BitVM and recursive sidechains could make interoperation safer and programmable. The survey then turns to the Artificial Intelligence of Things. It sketches bridge uses in energy trading between devices. Health data integration and supply chain automation appear too. The taxonomy is offered as a design foundation.
arxiv-2509-10513:
Mixture-of-experts models switch on only a few specialized sub-networks per input, and Sugyeong Eo with three co-authors improve how those experts specialize in this 2025 study of instruction tuning. Diverse instructions strain the usual routing, where each token is sent to experts with little sense of the whole request.

Their Mixture-of-Clustered-Experts routes in two stages. First, features of the whole sequence steer the input toward an expert group matched to its knowledge needs. Then, inside that group, individual tokens pick their top experts as usual. The design encourages groups to become genuine specialists while keeping fine-grained token routing. Across a broad set of benchmarks, the clustered design consistently beat strong baselines and generalized better, and the authors' analysis points to the routing structure itself as the source of the gains.
arxiv-2509-10713:
Christian Escarrega and 4 co-authors built a low-cost energy manager as an undergraduate design project, reported in this 2025 paper. Electricity bills for homes and small firms include demand charges, which punish short peaks in use. Commercial systems that shave those peaks are expensive. Their prototype joins grid power with an iron-phosphate battery bank under real-time control, at a small fraction of commercial prices.

A Raspberry Pi runs the control logic, switching between grid and battery based on live price, load, and charge readings. Data flow through an IoT platform to a phone-friendly display. Real-world tests confirmed the system cuts demand charges and keeps power flowing. The authors also pitch it as a teaching tool for energy control courses.
arxiv-2509-11313:
Camila Cristiano, Ludmila Viotti, and Paula I. Villar examine quantum batteries through the lens of geometric phase in this 2025 quantum physics paper. A quantum battery stores energy in a quantum system, and charging it quickly means the system's state traces a path whose geometry leaves a measurable imprint.

The authors simulate non-adiabatic charging under the kinds of noise reported in superconducting circuits, and they add exact results for the noiseless limit. They find a direct link: the geometric phase a battery picks up during charging tracks the total energy it stores over the same transition. The same relation held for a two-part battery charged through a noisy, dephased charger. Because both quantities are measurable with current techniques, the phase could serve as a handy dial for reading a quantum battery's charge.
arxiv-2509-11413:
Grigori Fursin and Daniel Altunay propose treating AI benchmarking itself as a learning problem in this 2025 paper. Standard benchmarks such as MLPerf freeze a fast-moving field into fixed tests, and deployment decisions made from stale results go wrong. If benchmarking were a learning task, models could be re-evaluated and re-tuned continuously across data, software, and hardware.

Their FlexBench extends the MLPerf language model inference benchmark in a modular way and plugs into the Hugging Face ecosystem. Results and metadata flow into an open data set that the community can extend and mine for predictions. The concept was validated through real MLPerf submissions, including large recent models on commodity servers, with the aim of cheaper, better-informed deployment choices.
arxiv-2509-11513:
Zhongyang Hu and four co-authors improve how substitute words are ranked in this 2025 natural language processing paper. Lexical substitution replaces a word in a sentence with a fitting alternative, and the ranking step must judge which candidate keeps the sentence's meaning best.

The usual method swaps each candidate in and compares the sentence before and after, but it struggles to capture how the swap affects both the target word and its surrounding context. The authors investigate two fixes: one based on attention weights, and one using integrated gradients, which is more interpretable. Both measure how context tokens influence the target token and combine that with the similarity between the original and substituted sentences. On the standard LS07 and SWORDS datasets, both approaches improved ranking performance.
arxiv-2509-12013:
Quantum-corrected black holes, placed in a universe with a cosmological constant, ring and bend tides in ways Yunlong Liu and one co-author compute in 2025. Two metric frameworks that build the constant into the quantum modification frame the study.

The authors derive the axial and polar disturbance equations. Pseudospectral methods then give the ringing tones, called quasinormal modes. Direct integration gives the tidal Love numbers, which measure how a companion's gravity deforms the hole. A quantum parameter steers both. Higher overtones react to it most. One framework keeps purely imaginary tones throughout, while the other flips modes between real and complex. Tidal responses rise and fall non-monotonically for axial disturbances yet climb steadily for polar ones.
arxiv-2509-12113:
Roman V. Ovcharov and 3 co-authors propose a new shape for spin-Hall nano-oscillators in a 2025 paper. These tiny devices produce microwave signals from electric current and magnetic effects. Their asymmetric nanoconstriction design lets two oscillators placed very close together influence each other through stray magnetic fields.

Using computer simulations of magnetism, the team first studied a single device and found a wide range for tuning its frequency. Two devices could then lock together using only that magnetic coupling, with no wires or spin waves between them. Depending on the settings, they settled in phase or exactly out of phase. When one oscillator grew much weaker, the pair tended toward out-of-phase locking and the weaker signal faded. The design pairs strong coupling with separate control of each device.
arxiv-2509-12313:
The Milky Way's retinue of tiny satellite galaxies tests theories of galaxy birth and of dark matter itself, but telescopes miss many of them. C. Y. Tan and eighty-six co-authors deliver a careful census in 2025, measuring exactly how complete three big sky surveys are at finding these faint companions.

The team runs detection software over the combined survey ground, recovers forty-nine known satellites above a strict threshold, and injects fake galaxies to learn what gets missed. A fitted model then predicts a few hundred satellites in total across a wide range of brightness, size, and distance, with a mild clustering tied to the Large Magellanic Cloud.
arxiv-2509-12513:
