Stars ring with sound waves, and the pitch of that ringing reveals their mass, size, and age. Sophia Grusnis and two co-authors listen in 2025 to eighty-two subgiant and lower red giant stars watched by the TESS telescope in its continuous viewing zones, using a new open-source analysis package.

The measured oscillation peaks give masses, radii, and surface gravities with modest errors for the whole sample, filling the gap between earlier dwarf and giant studies. Four modeling grids then supply ages, which broadly match neighboring star samples, though a consistent offset from model predictions appears and grows at higher gravity. The ages feed future galactic archaeology.
arxiv-2509-12613:
Abhishek Chakraborty and Angelia Nedic study hard balance problems in 2025 where the allowed region is the overlap of many curved sets. Direct steps that project onto the whole region can cost too much or fail, so a cheaper path is needed.

They use random checks that fix one rule at a time inside two known methods, one due to Korpelevich and one due to Popov. With a new gap measure they prove how fast the methods close in on a solution. Tests on a two-player matrix game show the approach works and keeps the cost low.
arxiv-2509-12913:
Hojat Ardi, Amir Jahanshahi, and Ali Diba present T-SiamTPN in a 2025 paper on tracking objects from drones. Aerial tracking is hard because of scale variation, dynamic backgrounds, clutter, and frequent occlusions. Most trackers emphasize spatial cues and overlook how appearance changes over time, limiting robustness during long tracking or occlusion.

Their system extends a Siamese transformer pyramid architecture with explicit temporal modeling. Temporal feature fusion and attention-based interactions strengthen consistency over time and produce richer feature representations. Link-based Siamese trackers are limited by the linear nature of link, which struggles with complex non-linear appearance changes; the new design addresses that weakness. Despite added temporal modules, the tracker preserves computational efficiency while achieving results competitive with leading trackers, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-13313:
Xixi Wu and 15 co-authors present ReSum in a 2025 paper on long-horizon search by language model agents. Agents that browse the web are good at tasks that demand a lot of knowledge. But they face a basic squeeze. Good searching means roaming widely, while the window of text an agent can hold at once stays small.

ReSum takes a lighter path. It is a plug-and-play scheme that lets an agent roam without a fixed bound. From time to time it calls an outside tool. The tool squeezes the history of the search so far into a short summary, and the agent carries on from there. So the authors add ReSum-GRPO. It reshapes a policy optimization method so that the final reward is broadcast back across the separate stretches of the long task. Wide testing showed clear gains over the relevant benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-13413:
Param Rekhi, Sahar Shahaf and five co-authors link in 2025 Gaia main-sequence plus white dwarf pairs to classical barium stars. Astrometric pairs near one AU with mild eccentricity strain synthesis models. Barium enrichment proves a white dwarf partner and past mass transfer with slow-process yields.

FEROS spectra for thirty Gaia pairs find ten barium enriched. With archive data, thirty-eight barium dwarfs now hold dynamical white dwarf masses, versus six before. Low metal content aids enrichment, even in eccentric pairs. Post-giant transfer can pump or spare eccentricity. Gaia pairs trace the parent pool of barium stars.
arxiv-2509-13513:
Kevin Wagner, Ewan Douglas and six co-authors simulate in 2025 astrometric exomoon hunts around imaged planets, centered on a hypothetical giant in Alpha Centauri A habitable zone. Planet-star wobble from moons is the signal. Candidate detections motivate the target.

Observatory options span upcoming sites to a purpose-built space telescope with set size, wavelength, and contrast. Such a facility could find Earth-mass moons in five years around a Saturn-mass planet. Precision and cadence maps give broad limits: small moons on short orbits need fine precision with hourly cadence. A large ground telescope could find Earth-sized moons with daily cadence.
arxiv-2509-13613:
Yi-Ming Jiang, Xiao Lu, and Shan-Gui Zhou study the shapes of radon nuclei in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Some nuclei deform into a pear-like form called octupole deformation, and experiments have hinted that several radon isotopes vibrate in this way. The team asks which of four isotopes actually settle into the deformed shape.

Using multi-dimensionally constrained covariant density functional theory, a method that computes nuclear structure from nucleon interactions, they map the ground states and energy surfaces of the isotopes. Octupole deformation appears in two of the four, but not in the other two. Pairing between nucleons shifts as deformation grows, falling for neutrons and rising for protons, and single-particle levels near the Fermi surface explain why.
arxiv-2509-13713:
Tae-Wook Um and 3 co-authors present UM-Depth in a 2025 paper on monocular depth estimation. Inferring scene shape from a single camera is more and more adopted in robotics and autonomous driving. In self-guided systems, a network jointly creates depth and pose estimates during training, eliminating the need for depth labels.

These methods remain challenged by uncertainty in input data, such as low-texture or dynamic regions, which reduces depth accuracy. UM-Depth joins motion- and uncertainty-aware refinement to enhance quality at dynamic object boundaries and in textureless regions. A teacher-student training method embeds uncertainty estimation into both the pipeline and the network architecture, strengthening supervision where photometric signals are weak. Prior motion-aware approaches incurred inference-time overhead and relied on extra labels or auxiliary networks, limitations the design addresses.
arxiv-2509-13913:
Carl Johan Casselgren and Kalle Eriksson compare three cousins in graph coloring in a 2025 combinatorics paper. List coloring gives each vertex its own palette; the variants here are single conflict coloring, adapted list coloring, and choosability with separation, where neighboring lists may share at most one color. Each notion has its own chromatic invariant, and how they order against each other was not fully mapped.

The pair construct explicit families of graphs where the first two invariants agree but strictly exceed the third, and other families where all three coincide. For planar graphs they ask which triples of values can occur together and settle parts of that classification. Many questions are left open, with connections drawn to adapted coloring and related invariants.
arxiv-2509-14013:
Peñil and five co-authors search for clockwork in gamma-ray skies in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Jetted active galactic nuclei are galaxies firing plasma jets toward Earth. They sometimes seem to pulse periodically. That hints at orbiting black hole pairs or precessing jets. Confirming any period needs long, patient observations in gamma rays.

Using twelve years of Fermi-LAT data, the team ran a robust pipeline of nine different detection techniques. The sample held nearly fifteen hundred jetted sources from the 4FGL catalog. It is the largest sample ever analyzed this way. Two dozen earlier candidates were set aside for a companion study. They found no evidence of periodic signals in any light curve. The clean null result tightens what periodicity hunters can claim.
arxiv-2509-14313:
L. Theerthagiri, Rajesh Narayanan and R. Ganesh propose a way in 2025 to count dark states in a light and matter system. In the Tavis-Cummings setup, two level atoms sit in a leaky cavity. Destructive interference can trap excitation in states that emit no light.

Their protocol starts with some qubits excited and watches for photons leaving the cavity. Detecting no photons signals that the system has fallen into a dark state, much like a Stern-Gerlach measurement sorts particles. Counting trials in a set way yields the number of independent dark states. The authors show that count stays robust even when coupling strengths vary in a disordered way. A robust count helps characterise storage like behaviour in cavity systems.
arxiv-2509-14513:
Bart Rosenzweig and Jonathan Stanfill prove a broad integral inequality in 2025 by basic means, for cases with higher order rates of change. Splits of second and fourth order operators drove the work. One shared frame should give back many known results and yield new ones too.

Their frame widens two known tools: Hardy improving potentials and Bessel pairs, both used to sharpen classic bounds. Many cases follow, some new and some known, all proved in the same way. Basic proofs travel well in analysis, since readers can adapt them without heavy kit. A single unifying bound also shows scattered results as cases of one split idea, not lone tricks.
arxiv-2509-14613:
M. Kıyami Erdim, Emine Gülmez and Murat Hüdaverdi study the isolated relic galaxy Mrk 1216 in 2025 through X-ray observations of its hot gas. Relic galaxies are red nuggets that barely interacted since the early universe. They preserve a record of how massive galaxies first assembled.

XMM-Newton data give radial temperature and element abundance profiles for the interstellar medium. The centre shows an elevated magnesium to iron ratio against typical early type galaxies. That pattern fits a brief, intense burst of star formation during early assembly, a hallmark of relics. A nearly flat supernova Ia ratio adds detail on enrichment history. Chemical fingerprints let astronomers read a quiet galaxy past without watching it form.
arxiv-2509-14813:
Ferdinand Omlor, Florinda Viñas Boström, and Martin Leijnse propose a ring-shaped device for linking electron spins with microwave photons in a 2025 quantum devices paper. Such spin-photon interfaces are building blocks for quantum networks and processors. Their design uses a circular double quantum dot, motivated by recent experiments on nanowires showing unusual g-factors and ring states.

A theoretical model captures how spin-orbit coupling and magnetic flux through the ring shape the states. Ring states form where states of opposite geometric parity cross, and detuning the dots can turn them into single-dot states, giving strong control. A tilted magnetic field mixes spin and charge, which enables the spin to couple to photons. The paper also examines how disorder changes the coupling mechanism.
arxiv-2509-14913:
Mitsuo Higaki, Jiajiang Liao, and Franck Sueur ask whether a patch of fluid can be steered to a target by remote action inside a perforated domain, in a 2025 fluid mechanics paper. The domain is riddled with many small holes, like a porous solid. Lagrangian controllability of viscous flow near solid walls is notoriously hard because of boundary layers.

The paper treats perforated domains where holes occupy a small fraction of the volume. Results distinguish cases quantitatively by hole size, hole spacing, and the size of the initial flow data. The approach builds on recent homogenization results for time-dependent problems, which replace the perforated medium by an effective one, plus stability estimates for flows in measure. Classical Runge-type approximation arguments complete the proof strategy for the Navier-Stokes setting.
arxiv-2509-15213:
Yicheng Zhang and five co-authors expose security holes where language models meet extended reality in a 2025 systems security paper. XR headsets increasingly call large language models to understand scenes and even generate executable content, and such AI glasses are reaching consumers. The integrated pipeline creates attack surfaces neither field faced alone.

The authors survey LLM-integrated XR systems in research and practice, sorting them along system dimensions to find a shared threat model. Proof-of-concept attacks then run on several platforms, including major headsets and smart glasses driving different underlying models. Though each integration differs, all share a weakness: an attacker who alters the public context around a legitimate query can corrupt what the user sees or hears. The demonstrations press vendors to treat context as untrusted input.
arxiv-2509-15313:
Anne Dattilo and a large team of co-authors announce two young Neptune-sized planets in the Alpha Persei cluster in a 2025 astronomy paper. Young planets with measured properties are rare and precious for studying how atmospheres lose mass, because stellar activity makes them hard to confirm. The host star is only about seventy-five million years old and Sun-like.

Three sectors of TESS data, dozens of CHEOPS orbits, and ground-based follow-up confirm both transiting planets. The inner and outer worlds have nearly equal radii, each close to five times Earth's, on orbits just outside a three-to-two resonance, where their periods nearly form that simple ratio. A near-resonant pair around a young cluster star offers a snapshot of planetary systems still settling into maturity.
arxiv-2509-15413:
Andrew Zeolla and a team of twelve present design work for a neutrino hunter called HERON. Neutrinos are faint particles that pass through almost all matter. HERON aims at tau neutrinos that skim the Earth at very high energy. It pairs tight groups of radio antennas with a wide, sparse array on a mountain side. That mix gives sharp aim and broad reach.

The team ran a full chain of mock tests, from how the particles move to how antennas reply. They used the tests to pick the array layout with the best reach at their target energy. They also chose the antenna design and checked how well events can be rebuilt. The paper lays out the plan and its results for a future build.
arxiv-2509-16113:
Many computing tasks can be cast as a search for the best point on a curved space of matrices known as a Stiefel manifold. Dinh Van Tiep and three co-authors improve the geometry used for such searches when the space has an indefinite form. Their new way to measure distance on the space avoids a costly matrix equation that older methods had to solve at each gradient step.

They build the full tool kit for the new geometry, plus a path-based way to step across the space. Tests show the resulting descent method performs well next to the older approach. Cheaper steps could widen the use of these searches.
arxiv-2509-16313:
Many cosmic blasts shine by synchrotron light, but the quick formulas used to model that light break down at high speeds. Ross Ferguson and Ben Margalit build a full numerical model that solves the light transfer problem in such shocks with all speed effects counted. The model handles shocks of any velocity and aims to serve many kinds of transient events.

Tests show the simple formulas go wrong by large factors once shocks move at a fair slice of light speed. That bias may skew traits read from fast blue transients and jetted tidal events. The code is shared in public for the growing set of such sources.
arxiv-2509-16413:
Building small language models is still more craft than science, since tight budgets make each design choice count and few tools test those choices cleanly. Richard Diehl Martinez and five co-authors release Pico, a light modular frame for hypothesis-driven work on small and medium models. Two libraries let researchers change one part of a model or its training and watch the effect directly.

A suite of baseline models, trained under standard settings, is open-sourced with the frame. Case studies show how the sandbox supports step-by-step design and analysis. The goal is a more systematic path to better small models.
arxiv-2509-16513:
AI supercomputers now swing power grids with demand spikes of staggering size, and planners need a safe place to test greener schedules. Wesley Brewer, Matthias Maiterth, and Damien Fay extend an open digital twin that replays real job traces from a university supercloud. The twin tracks power, cooling, and timing in fine detail while jobs are reshuffled in simulation.

Early learning-based scheduling trials show energy-aware choices are within reach. The platform supports tests of incentives and hardware ideas without risking the real machine. Better schedules could lift throughput while easing the load such centers place on utilities.
arxiv-2509-16613:
Hyungsung Yun studies edge behavior of hard equations in a 2025 solo math paper. The equations track change over time and can turn degenerate or singular based on the slope of the solution. At a boundary, control is hardest to prove. Yun seeks bounds on how the slope behaves right at that edge.

Such bounds are called Hölder estimates, after a classic form of smooth control. The time part of the equation adds snags past the steady case. Gradient-linked degeneracy makes the work harder still. Firm edge bounds help prove that rough models still behave well. They matter for flows, finance models, and other time-based systems.
arxiv-2509-16813:
Devin R. Wright, Jisun An, and Yong-Yeol Ahn score identity fusion from text in a 2025 paper. Fusion is the sense that the self has merged with a group or cause. It shapes much group behavior, from fandom to politics. Their score blends language theory with large language models. Metaphor use in text is a key signal.

The score is named CLIFS. Models and code are shared in public. The team flag a new task for language research in this work. They also call for larger, more varied datasets across targets and cultures. A sound text score could help researchers track fusion without costly surveys.
arxiv-2509-16913:
Pedro Ramoneda, Masahiro Suzuki, Akira Maezawa, and Xavier Serra generate piano practice pieces at set difficulty in a 2025 paper. Sight-reading means playing a new score at first sight. Students improve fastest with pieces matched to their level. The team build a generator that targets a chosen difficulty.

Automatic scores and expert judges both rated the output. Control over difficulty beat prior approaches. Experts also saw real teaching value in the pieces. Tailored practice could keep students in the zone where learning is fastest. The work is a step toward personal music training that adapts as a student grows.
arxiv-2509-17013:
Raphaël Giordano extends two classic coloring theorems to richer sets in a 2025 solo math paper. Van der Waerden's theorem guarantees long arithmetic patterns in any finite coloring of the integers. Rado's theorem does the same for solutions of certain equations. Giordano proves versions of both for IP-sets, which hold all finite sums of an infinite set.

A bounded variant allows each summand to repeat a limited number of times. Patterns must still appear inside these sparser sets. Such results show that arithmetic structure is hard to avoid, even in thin sets. They sit in Ramsey theory, where order is proved to lurk inside apparent randomness.
arxiv-2509-17113:
Kai-Wen Huang, Xiang-Jian Hou, and Ying-Hai Wu study phase changes in layered quantum Hall systems in a 2025 physics paper. Each layer alone hosts a known fractional state, of Laughlin or Moore-Read type. The systems stack two or three such layers of bosons. The team map what happens as tunneling and interaction between layers are switched on.

With both effects present, composite fermion liquids and Jain states can appear. The resulting phase diagrams are intricate, with many transitions. Exotic critical points may hide among them. The transitions they find are of third order, a rarer class. Layered Hall systems are a playground for phases that could one day host robust quantum bits.
arxiv-2509-17213:
Yassine Kebbati, Naima Ait-Oufroukh, Vincent Vigneron, and Dalil Ichala wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on steering self-driving cars along a set path. Road scenes change fast, and wind, slope, and sensor error can throw off fixed controllers. Sideways control is the weak point, since a small drift grows into a lane error if the controller cannot adapt.

Their controller uses model predictive control, which plans steering over a short horizon at each step. A swarm search tunes it, and its settings adapt online through two learning tools: neural networks and a fuzzy neural system. In tests with a triple lane change and path tracking runs, the adaptive design beat the standard version. The authors post their code in a public repository for others to check.
arxiv-2509-17313:
Zixiang Yin, Jiarui Li, and Zhengming Ding built a model that reads visual signals from the brain across many people. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles neural decoding, which tries to rebuild what a person saw from brain recordings. Past methods rebuild the image but say little about how the brain does its visual work.

Their model, called iMIND, first builds a shared neural space across subjects with a masked autoencoder based on a vision transformer. It then splits neural features into parts tied to the person and parts tied to the object seen. Two decoding heads use those parts, one for identity cues and one for meaning. Tests give the best decoding scores so far with little trouble scaling. The model also yields voxel-object fingerprints that point to where each object lights up the brain.
arxiv-2509-17413:
Masako Kishida, writing alone, works on proving neural networks safe when inputs are uncertain. Her 2025 arXiv paper grows out of a known verification frame that uses quadratic constraints and semidefinite programs. That frame checks a network against sets of inputs, but it treats all bad outcomes alike, with no eye for rare tail events.

Kishida adds worst-case conditional value-at-risk, a tail-risk measure, over a set of distributions fixed by mean and covariance. The new conditions can still be checked by semidefinite programs, and the tail risk is priced in plainly. The input sets grow broader too, covering ellipsoids, polytopes, and hyperplanes. Tests on closed-loop control reachability and classification show how the risk level trades caution for tolerance of tail events. The computing shape of the older methods survives intact.
arxiv-2509-17913:
Ruixi Huang and David Waxman model how a shifting world can wipe out one of two life strategies. Their 2025 paper uses a large group of organisms that breed without mates, such as microbes. Fitness peaks at two trait values, with a dip between them, so two clones can live side by side.

Each clone holds its peak in part through shared mutations. When the world shifts at a steady pace, the group tracks it by using larger mutations. Past a pace threshold, one peak fades and the trait spread turns single. That shift marks a loss of bio variety driven by pace of change.
arxiv-2509-18413:
Voice anonymization hides who is speaking, but standard scores may hide how much privacy really leaks. Efthymios Tsaprazlis and four co-authors argue that the usual equal error rate is too blunt. Their 2025 paper introduces VoxGuard, a test frame built on membership inference attacks. Such attacks ask whether a given voice was in a target set at all.

VoxGuard splits privacy into two parts: hiding the speaker, and hiding traits like gender and accent. The key test zone is where false alarms are rare, since even a few true hits breach privacy there. Informed attackers, using tuned models, scored far stronger attacks in that zone than the standard score suggests. Simple attacks even recovered gender and accent almost perfectly after anonymization. The authors urge the field to judge voice privacy at low false alarm rates.
arxiv-2509-18713:
Customer service agents built on language models forget past chats and repeat their own mistakes. Yizhe Huang and five co-authors present MemOrb, a memory layer that plugs into such agents, in this 2025 paper. It needs no fine-tuning of the base model. The goal is steady, reliable behavior across many sessions.

MemOrb distills multi-turn chats into compact strategy reflections, short notes on what worked. Those notes sit in a shared memory bank and are retrieved to guide later decisions. The team judges agents on task success and on consistency across repeat trials. With MemOrb, multi-turn success rose by up to 63 points in their tests. Performance also grew steadier across trials. The authors argue that structured reflection is a strong tool for frozen models. It offers long-term improvement without retraining.
arxiv-2509-18913:
Why does an image model give the answer it gives? Nguyen Van Tu and two co-authors survey ways to make computer vision models easier to understand. Deep learning now leads image analysis, but its models often act as black boxes. In fields where errors carry real risk, that lack of clarity is a serious concern.

The survey covers four families of explanation tools. Saliency maps highlight the parts of an image that drove a choice. Concept bottleneck models route choices through named ideas a person can check. Prototype methods compare inputs with stored examples, and hybrid methods mix these ideas. For each family, the authors explain how it works, where it is strong, where it falls short, and how its quality is measured.
arxiv-2509-19013:
M. Ferro and twelve co-authors examine a laser experiment on muonic hydrogen, an atom made of a proton and a heavy cousin of the electron. Lasers aim to flip the atom between its two hyperfine levels, states split by the spins of its parts. To boost the light, the beam bounces through a multi-pass cell. Simple ray tracing treats that light as if its waves never interfered.

Wave interference can pile light up in some spots and drain it in others, which changes how saturated the atoms get. The team builds a simple model that bounds the largest effect interference could have, without needing the exact field inside the cell. For their setup the bound shows the effect can be safely ignored. The method, though, can be reused by other groups with similar cells.
arxiv-2509-19113:
David Marco and two co-authors show how to make pulses of light that last only a few hundred attoseconds and carry a skyrmion pattern in their polarization. A skyrmion here is a swirl in which the light's polarization states cover every possible state exactly in a mapped way. Such patterns had been made with steady beams, but not in the ultrafast regime. Their route is high-harmonic generation, where a strong laser drives atoms to emit far higher frequencies.

Simulations that join single-atom physics with light propagation show the recipe works. A special infrared beam with fractional orbital angular momentum yields extreme-ultraviolet harmonics with nearly identical skyrmion patterns across a broad color range. Filtering that output in a realistic setup gives a train of skyrmion pulses about 500 attoseconds long. The authors see uses in ultrafast control, imaging, and spectroscopy.
arxiv-2509-19613:
Verified compilers must move programs between languages without changing what they do or leaking safety. William J. Bowman describes work in progress that models a whole compiler inside one multi-language system. Older models split the job in two: one translation for compiling, another for the run-time boundary between languages. That split doubles the work and can hide mismatches.

In Bowman's approach, compilation itself becomes steps of evaluation in the shared system. Running those steps early gives ahead-of-time compilation; running them late gives just-in-time compilation. If the shared steps can reach the same end from any order, compiler correctness follows. The talk reports early semantic insights from the attempt. A single model for both jobs could shrink proofs that secure compilers are right.
arxiv-2509-19713:
A single camera cannot tell scale: a near small object and a far large one look alike. Saimouli Katragadda and Guoquan Huang pair the camera with motion sensors to recover dense, true-scale depth. Their framework, VIMD, leans on a proven visual-inertial tracker for motion. Multi-view cues then refine the scale pixel by pixel, rather than fitting one global correction.

The design is modular, so many depth networks can plug in as backbones. Even ten to twenty known depth points per image suffice for strong results. Tests on two standard sets, plus a zero-shot trial on table scenes, show accuracy and robustness. Robots and augmented reality glasses both need cheap depth that works indoors. A camera plus tiny motion sensors is far cheaper than laser scanners.
arxiv-2509-20113:
Erkan Karabulut and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on data mining. Association rule mining looks for simple if-then patterns between features in a dataset. Such rules support knowledge discovery and models that people can inspect. In wide datasets, though, the number of rules explodes and searches grow costly.

The authors study Aerial+, a neural-symbolic method built to tame that explosion. They show it scales far better than leading algorithmic and neural baselines on five real datasets. They also define a new hard setting: wide data with very few rows, like gene data with thousands of features and dozens of samples. Two fine-tuning tricks that use tabular foundation models then improve rule quality. The gains held across the five datasets they tested.
arxiv-2509-20213:
A. Yu. Orlov wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics. It presents a family of solvable multi-matrix models tied to a graph with a single vertex. Each edge of the graph carries corner matrices, and the model's partition function depends on their behavior around the dual graph. The paper sorts out when that function has extra integrable structure.

Orlov selects the cases where the partition function becomes a tau function of known integrable hierarchies. Those hierarchies include the KP, two-component KP, and BKP families. He compares integrals over the unitary group with integrals over its special unitary subgroup. The unitary case allows graphs with any number of vertices. Mixed ensembles drawn from several matrix groups are also treated.
arxiv-2509-20613:
How wide a fitting window should astronomers use when measuring a star's brightness? Sebastian Espinosa and four co-authors replace the usual rule of thumb with information theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. Standard practice picks the radius that maximizes signal-to-noise ratio. That criterion ignores the joint estimation of flux and background, and the statistical floor on precision set by the data itself.

The alternative uses the Fisher information matrix and its Cramer-Rao bound, the theoretical limit on estimator accuracy. Numerical experiments traced information and estimator behavior as the fitting radius varied. Classical estimators were checked against that bound. Radius choices guided by Fisher information proved more robust for reaching optimal precision. The result gives photometry pipelines a principled way to set a parameter usually chosen by habit.
arxiv-2509-20713:
Hong Su argues that language models reason too passively, answering questions without noticing what has changed. The solo author sets out a fix in a 2025 paper called difference-guided reasoning. The framework aims to mimic how people start thinking when they spot a difference.

The model first extracts features and marks changes across time and space. It then ranks those changes, putting the newest and most important first, and links each one to a suitable action. Extra parts handle abnormal behavior detection. Other parts pull in fresh information from users or sensors. Su presents the design as a way to keep model reasoning grounded, timely, and more active than simple question answering.
arxiv-2509-20913:
Crime clusters in particular blocks at particular hours, and people's movements shape those patterns. Ariadna Albors Zumel, Michele Tizzoni, and Gian Maria Campedelli test how much mobility data helps crime forecasting in a 2025 study. They cover four United States cities over the years 2019 to 2023.

The team combines police incident records with census demographics and fine-grained human mobility data. Everything is aggregated into small grid cells, and a deep learning framework forecasts crime at fine spatial and temporal scales. The cities are Baltimore, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia. At sixty-four pages, the study weighs whether micro-level movement features genuinely improve predictions over history and demographics alone, a question with direct policing implications.
arxiv-2509-21013:
Training a huge language model just to test a dataset idea is prohibitively expensive, so researchers use small proxy models. Woosung Koh and four co-authors show proxies can even predict reasoning skill in a 2025 paper for ICLR 2026. Reasoning was thought to emerge only at large scales, making proxies unreliable.

Their method, rBridge, aligns the small proxy with the target in two ways. It weights the training loss by task alignment, with gold-standard reasoning traces taken from frontier models. Small models of at most a billion parameters then rank datasets in a way that tracks large-model reasoning. The authors report cost cuts of more than a hundredfold for dataset ranking. That makes data curation for reasoning models far cheaper to explore.
arxiv-2509-21113:
A video model can land on the right answer while its reasoning wanders away from what actually happens on screen. Sicheng Tao and ten co-authors fix that drift in MOSS-ChatV, a 2025 reinforcement learning framework for video temporal reasoning. Process consistency, not just final answers, is the target.

The reward is rule-based and built on dynamic time warping, which aligns the model's reasoning trace with temporally grounded references. That alignment supervises the process directly, without training a separate reward model. The authors also identify dynamic state prediction as a key subskill for video understanding. By rewarding faithful intermediate steps, MOSS-ChatV aims at multimodal models whose explanations of events over time can be trusted, not just their conclusions.
arxiv-2509-21313:
Torsional rigidity for the k-Hessian operator obeys bounds that depend on the shape of the region. The work is by Alba Lia Masiello and Francesco Salerno. A shape functional assigns a value to a region based on a partial differential equation. The authors study torsional rigidity linked to the k-Hessian operator. The setting is a bounded, open, convex set with smooth boundary. They work in any dimension.

They first prove a Polya type lower bound for the k-torsional rigidity. Such a bound limits how small the rigidity can be for a given set. They then study optimal sets for that inequality. Two quantitative estimates measure how close a set is to the optimal case. The results extend classic rigidity bounds to a wider class of operators.
arxiv-2509-21413:
Merging fine tuned models without their training data is the problem behind a 2025 paper by Zihuan Qiu and 9 co-authors. A merged model should stay stable on old tasks and stay plastic on new ones. Stability and plasticity pull in opposite directions. Past methods lack a bridge from data level goals to parameter space optimization. No task data is available to guide that bridge.

Their framework, NUFILT, uses null space filtering. Task vectors roughly align with representation subspaces, which serve as structural stand ins for the missing data. A null space projector filters overlaps to preserve prior responses. That protects earlier tasks while new ones are absorbed. The method is data free and continual, built for backbones that evolve task by task.
arxiv-2509-21613:
Optimizing a language model for several goals at once is a challenge of balance. Lingxiao Kong and 3 co-authors survey multi objective reinforcement learning for that task in a 2025 vision paper. Their taxonomy organizes methods for optimizing large language models. Advantages and limitations of each approach are examined. Personalization and the inherent complexity of language models strain current methods.

The authors propose a vision for a benchmarking framework. It would measure how methods behave under diverse objective relationships. Meta policy approaches, which learn how to adapt policies at a higher level, are a focus for future work. Their bi level learning promises better efficiency and flexibility. Key research questions and potential solutions are highlighted for the field.
arxiv-2509-21813:
Brief flashes of light can change how a doped Mott insulator absorbs energy. A Mott insulator is a solid that blocks current even though it has free charges. Sumal Chandra and four co-authors model such a material as narrow ladders of atoms in this 2025 paper. They ask where the energy of a very short light pulse actually goes.

Using a heavy numerical method, the team tracks how the material absorbs light after each pulse. A pulse tuned to the free-charge band weakens that response and lifts a middle band, though the lift fades as the pulse grows stronger. A pulse tuned to the middle band leaves a different mark. The reason is that the middle band comes from magnetic effects, which do not couple to light directly. The authors note that labs can test these predictions on cuprate materials.
arxiv-2509-21913:
Radiation therapy guided by daily scans relies on cone-beam CT, which is cheap and quick but noisy. Alzahra Altalib, Chunhui Li, and Alessandro Perelli present EqDiff-CT in this 2025 paper, accepted in Medical Physics. Cone-beam scans suffer from scattering and blockage, so their tissue values drift. Those values feed dose calculations, so drift hurts treatment planning. Standard CT is accurate but is taken offline and cannot show changes during treatment.

EqDiff-CT uses a diffusion model to synthesize a clean CT image from a cone-beam scan. Its backbone is built to respect rotation symmetry, which helps keep fine structures intact while noise and artifacts are removed. Trained and checked on a public head and neck data set, it beat advanced rivals on structure, tissue-value accuracy, and standard scores. The authors report sharper soft-tissue borders and more realistic bone in the results.
arxiv-2509-22113:
David Benfield, Phan Tu Vuong, and Alain Zemkoho study how to keep prediction models honest when the people being predicted fight back. In spam filtering, malware detection, and fake-image spotting, adversaries reshape their data to slip past an established model. Game theory captures that contest. A recent tool, pessimistic bilevel optimization, has proven strong for classification. It assumes the adversary plays as badly as possible for the defender, without assuming their best move is unique or well-behaved.

That tool, however, had not been carried over to regression, where the model predicts a number rather than a class. This 2025 paper proposes a pessimistic bilevel program for the regression setting. It keeps the same freedom from assumptions: no convexity of the adversary's problem, and no uniqueness of their optimal response. The aim is predictors that stay resilient when the data-generating side adapts.
arxiv-2509-22213:
Ossi Räisä, Antti Koskela, and Antti Honkela work on a flexible style of privacy protection for data analysis. In accuracy-first differential privacy, the analyst sets an accuracy target and lets the privacy bound adjust until the target is met, instead of fixing the bound in advance. Their 2025 paper examines a property that style had neglected: post-processing immunity, the guarantee that no later manipulation of the output can weaken the privacy promise.

The authors determine which existing accuracy-first definitions keep that immunity and which lose it. They therefore propose a new definition built on Rényi differential privacy, which does keep immunity, and they develop the basic theory around it. That includes a counterpart of the standard Gaussian noise mechanism and a check for whether accuracy on a private validation set is high enough.
arxiv-2509-22713:
Kaishuai Xu and 3 co-authors let a medical model's own reasoning decide what to look up. Fetching outside facts can curb knowledge gaps and made-up answers in language models. But hard medical questions need deep reasoning, and the surface wording often hides the true knowledge need. Their framework, RAR2, builds a line of thought first. That thought lays bare the hidden needs and guides both the search and the final answer.

Training uses pairs of ranked replies with a method called direct preference optimization. Two test-time tricks push the frame further. Across several medical question data sets, RAR2 beat search-based rivals with and without fine-tuning. The joint design sharpens both the search and the reasoning it feeds.
arxiv-2509-22913:
Jake S Rhodes and 5 co-authors improve manifold alignment, a way to learn shared codes across data domains. Many older alignment methods cannot extend to fresh data, which limits real use. Their framework uses twin autoencoders with a geometry penalty to keep the learned codes faithful. A pre-trained alignment model and a multi-task setup add support.

Across several alignment methods, their approach raised code consistency and cross-domain transfer. It also kept more of the source information. The team then applied the framework to Alzheimer's disease diagnosis. Patient data from mixed sources helped cases where only one data type was on hand. Predictive accuracy rose in those single-domain cases.
arxiv-2509-23113:
Fault diagnosis from sensor streams could gain a lot from language models that explain themselves. Xian Yeow Lee and 3 co-authors test LLM systems on industrial fault tasks. They vary the setup in three ways. Architecture is single model or multi-model. Inputs are raw values or summary statistics. Context window size also changes.

Summary statistics worked far better than raw streams. Multi-model systems with specialized prompts caught faults with higher sensitivity. The models wrote detailed, readable justifications for their calls. But they adapted poorly over repeated fault cycles in continual settings. Calibration drifted as cycles repeated. The study maps both promise and current limits.
arxiv-2509-23313:
Irregular time series, sampled at uneven gaps across many channels, resist standard forecast tools. Xvyuan Liu and 6 co-authors built ASTGI to forecast from such data without distortion. Each raw observation becomes a point in a learnable space-time embedding. A neighborhood module then builds a causal graph around each point. Nearest neighbor search drives that graph build.

A propagation module passes messages on the graph with weights from relative positions. A query module gathers neighborhood data to make the final forecast. On several benchmarks, ASTGI beat top prior methods. Health and finance data are the motivating cases.
arxiv-2509-23813:
Forecasters often throw away the humble index: the timestamp and the variable's identity carry meaning too. Beiliang Wu and 5 co-authors build IndexNet, an MLP-based forecaster that feeds those indices back in. A timestamp embedding turns times into vectors, helping the model catch long, complex periodic patterns. A channel embedding gives each variable a learned identity, so similar-looking series do not collapse into identical forecasts.

Across twelve real-world data sets, the model matched mainstream baselines. Plug-and-play tests and visualizations add evidence for generality and interpretability. The authors argue that index awareness is an underexplored, cheap source of accuracy in multivariate forecasting.
arxiv-2510-00013:
Liu and colleagues introduce ProTDyn, a foundation protein language model built to replace costly molecular dynamics simulations. Such simulations track how a protein moves atom by atom, but their tiny time steps make long processes too expensive to follow. Earlier learning models handled only one half of the problem: sampling the shapes a protein takes at equilibrium, or mimicking how those shapes change over time.

ProTDyn does both jobs in one framework. It samples fresh equilibrium ensembles and also rolls out trajectories across timescales from nanoseconds to microseconds. It learned from hundreds of thousands of protein sequences and more than a million conformations. On test proteins it matches reference simulations closely, and it keeps that accuracy on proteins outside its training data. Its longer-step dynamics module also proved steadier than a short-step one, which drifts as small errors pile up step after step.
arxiv-2510-00113:
Antonio Herrero-Brocal and Avelino Vicente, both at institutes in Valencia, Spain, wrote this 2025 theory paper on neutrino mass models. Neutrinos may be Majorana particles, meaning each one is its own antiparticle. Many models can produce their tiny masses, and the authors want a map of the simplest ones. They extend a standard parametrization so it covers every such model.

With that map, the authors can pick out the models with the fewest free parameters. In some cases the key combination of couplings shrinks to a single real number. Such tight models make definite predictions that experiments can test or rule out. The paper works through examples tied to heavy neutrino decays and rare charged-lepton decays. The result is a guide for builders of neutrino models who want the leanest options.
arxiv-2510-00213:
D. Gorbunov and E. Kriukova wrote this 2025 theory paper on making dark photons in pion-proton collisions. Dark photons are hypothetical particles that could link ordinary matter to a dark sector. The authors study negative pions striking protons, a setup several experiments can realize. They focus on dark photon masses between a few tenths and a few GeV.

Two production routes are estimated within a splitting-function framework. One is inelastic pion bremsstrahlung, where the pion sheds energy as it scatters. The other mimics the Drell-Yan process from quantum chromodynamics. For each route they compute the total production rate and the energy spread of the dark photons. They give concrete predictions for the NA64h experiment's reach. Mean energies are also reported for the secondary pion beams at T2K, DUNE, and SHiP, guiding future dark photon hunts.
arxiv-2510-00613:
Wen Shen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper classifying exotic shapes that share the algebraic shadow of a classic space. The reference space multiplies complex projective three-space by a seven-sphere, making thirteen dimensions. Many smooth manifolds can share its cohomology ring while differing in fine structure. Shen sorts them completely under three notions of sameness: smooth, topological, and homotopic.

The classification pins down exactly which shapes occur in each equivalence class. Under extra conditions, each shape, or that shape joined with an exotic sphere, carries a nicely curved metric. Non-negative sectional curvature is a strong geometric prize in high dimensions. As a bonus, the machinery classifies certain circle group actions on a product of two seven-spheres. Diagonal actions of the circle on that product fall out of the same analysis. The paper closes a chapter in the topology of thirteen-dimensional manifolds.
arxiv-2510-01313:
Singhi rescues a standard holographic claim from an apparent counterexample involving imaginary black holes. Rotating, cold anti-de Sitter space should be governed by a gas of thermal radiation, implying a confined dual theory. Yet complex-valued black hole solutions seemed to beat that gas in the path integral.

Careful steepest-descent analysis shows those extra saddles never actually contribute. The small, unstable rotating black hole is likewise excluded at every temperature. The original picture survives intact in five dimensions and, by extension, higher ones. Thermodynamics of the dual gauge theory keeps its clean interpretation. Euclidean path integrals are the arena where the saddles compete. Mini-superspace reasoning simplifies the steepest-descent bookkeeping. Complex parameters mark where real black holes cease to dominate. Four dimensions and up share the same qualitative story. A corollary clears the small black hole from every ledger.
arxiv-2510-01513:
Rizk, Walsh, Core, and Nye build a framework for assembling video-analysis pipelines out of pre-trained models without heroic engineering. Multimodal content mixes visual, auditory, and textual channels, and fusing existing models over such data is costly and fiddly. Their framework lets builders prototype pipelines by marrying methods into a candidate recipe.

The recipe converts videos first into a temporal semi-structured format. A further translation produces a frame-level indexed knowledge graph that users can query directly. The graph supports continual learning, so new domain knowledge enters through an interactive medium. A proof-of-concept system demonstrates querying a video database while adding fresh annotations. Static-image models abound; temporal fusion is the scarce craft. Open-source components keep the recipe reproducible for other teams. Search and understanding of video are the target uses named. Annotations become durable knowledge instead of exhaust.
arxiv-2510-01613:
Lau and Marin-Marquez ask when a polynomial whose coefficients vary continuously over a space admits continuously varying approximate roots. Exact roots can fail to exist even for friendly equations, so approximation is the practical fallback. The setting mixes algebra with topology, since the coefficient functions live on a compact space.

For one-dimensional spaces, the answer runs through maps from a pro-version of the fundamental group into braid groups. Braids record how roots wind around each other as the input point travels. A worked example builds an acyclic space where a degree-four equation lacks even an exact root. Shape theory supplies the language that makes the criterion precise. Approximate roots relax equality to closeness, which topology can sometimes grant. One dimension is where the braid criterion becomes decisive. Continuous coefficients model sensors and signals that vary smoothly over a space.
arxiv-2510-01913:
Rollano and co-authors characterize a superconducting detector material in darkness in this 2025 instrumentation paper. Their devices are titanium-aluminum lumped-element kinetic inductance detectors, tuned for the W-band of radio frequencies. That band, from seventy-five to one hundred ten gigahertz, suits searches for axions and other faint cosmic signals. Dark tests reveal how the material itself behaves without any light falling on it.

A Mattis-Bardeen analysis described the bilayer's thermal equilibrium well and matched its measured transition temperature. That fit confirms the devices suit the full W-band range. Phase-noise measurements then probed how quasiparticles recombine after disturbances. The kinetics departed from the standard BCS prediction in clear ways. Simpler models with gap unevenness and phonon bottlenecks captured the data instead. Knowing these limits helps designers predict detector noise before any sky deployment.
arxiv-2510-02213:
O'Reilly and five co-authors count objects of many categories at once in crowded scenes in this 2025 computer vision paper. Density map estimation counts where detection fails, in dense and occluded crowds. Single-category counters dominate the field, forcing one pass per class. Their framework, MMDEW, estimates all categories jointly.

A Twins pyramid vision transformer supplies the backbone features. A specialized multiclass head builds on a state-of-the-art multiscale decoder. A segmentation-based category focus module suppresses cross-talk between categories during training. On the VisDrone and iSAID benchmarks, counting errors fell by a third to nearly two thirds versus prior multicategory methods. Comparisons with a leading detector underscored why density methods remain necessary in dense scenes. A biodiversity monitoring dataset showed the same machinery counting wildlife for conservation. One model now watches mixed crowds, traffic, and animals alike.
arxiv-2510-02313:
Yang and co-authors teach models to name the object that made a sound. Their 2025 computer vision paper defines a task called sounding object detection. A spoon on hardwood sounds nothing like a spoon on carpet. People link such sounds to objects without thinking. Models must learn that link from real life video. The team trains on first-person videos of daily actions. An automatic pipeline marks the objects taking part. Those masks steer the model toward the interaction spot. A slot attention encoder adds a further object focus.

The model both finds the sounding object and judges if an action sounds at all. It reached state-of-the-art scores on the new task. It also improved results on older action understanding tests. Visual clusters grouped scenes with similar sounds. Sound aware models could help robots and home assistants. Hearing which object acted is a basic life skill.
arxiv-2510-02413:
Apinyan and Sahakyan argue that gated monolayer graphene can host unusual spin-triplet superconductivity. Their 2025 physics paper models a single carbon sheet under a gate voltage. Local Coulomb repulsion at each lattice site enters the model. Phonons, the lattice vibrations, pair the electrons in their scheme. They discretize excitations near the Fermi wave vector. A special split turns single excitations into paired ones. Self-consistent equations then govern the chemical potential and order parameter. A numeric solver handles those equations exactly within the model.

The superconducting order survives across a broad temperature domain. A large energy gap appears even without an applied field. Only a narrow band of coupling strength supports the state at high temperature. Charge imbalance between the two lattice sublattices also emerges. Chemical potential plays a central role in forming the state. Graphene superconductivity would be a prized laboratory platform.
arxiv-2510-02613:
Singh and co-authors scale mixture-of-experts language models up and down without downtime. Their 2025 systems paper presents a framework called ElasticMoE. These models activate only a few experts per token. That sparsity promises cheap, efficient scaling for serving. Traffic in the cloud arrives in bursts, though. Copying whole replicas wastes accelerators and provisions slowly. Restarting instances for vertical changes causes outages. ElasticMoE decouples running inference from memory operations. Scaling steps then proceed while serving continues. A memory module remaps weights and caches with zero copying.

High bandwidth links move data directly between devices. Another module pre-builds target setups before they are needed. Tests showed faster scale-up than baseline approaches. Throughput stayed stable through the transitions. Peak memory overhead stayed low as well. Bursty demand is where serving money gets wasted. Elastic expert pools match capacity to the moment.
arxiv-2510-02913:
Naghavian and Tavassolipour harden vision-language models against attack. Models like CLIP can classify images they never trained on. Tiny, invisible tweaks can still fool them badly. Standard defenses fine-tune the model on attacked examples. Their method is called Confidence-Aware Weighting, or CAW. It has two parts that work together during fine-tuning.

One part is a loss that stresses shaky cases. It scales a mismatch measure for attacked inputs the model finds unclear. The other part keeps the tuned encoder near the frozen one. That anchor guards the model's semantic knowledge. Tests ran on TinyImageNet plus fourteen more data sets. Strong attacks, including AutoAttack, formed the test bed. CAW beat recent rivals like PMG-AFT and TGA-ZSR. It won on both clean and attacked accuracy. It also used less memory than those rivals. The result keeps zero-shot skill while adding real toughness.
arxiv-2510-03013:
Wu, Zhao, and Wu rethink how machines infer what an expert wants. Inverse reinforcement learning reads reward from observed behavior. Most methods return one fixed reward number per action. Real rewards, though, are often random in nature. An expert may also care about risk, not just averages. Their framework learns a full distribution of rewards instead. It also learns the spread of total returns.

The method cuts violations of first-order stochastic dominance. In plain terms, clearly better options must rank better. Distortion risk measures then shape a risk-aware policy. That policy can favor safe gains over flashy ones. Tests spanned fake benchmarks and real brain-behavior data. Robot control tasks from MuJoCo joined the list. The method matched expert behavior better than prior art. It also recovered richer reward structure from the same demos. Such tools suit behavior science and careful imitation.
arxiv-2510-03213:
Lamb and co-authors push polarization-maintaining fiber amplifiers into a new pulsed power regime. Pulsed power, though, fights nonlinear effects inside the fiber. Large mode area designs spread the light to tame them. Higher-order modes then threaten the clean output beam. Recent fibers dump those stray modes with heavy loss. This work builds the amplifier around such a ytterbium fiber.

The fiber keeps polarization while guiding a wide fundamental mode. Nanosecond pulses reached one millijoule at a kilowatt average power. Lower repetition settings pushed pulse energy half again higher. Polarization purity stayed strong across the operating range. Beam quality sat near the diffraction limit throughout. Almost all measured energy stayed inside the pulses themselves. Stray light between pulses measured below a tenth of a percent. The results match what non-maintaining fibers achieved before. Coherent lidar at long range is a named target application.
arxiv-2510-03313:
Subramanyam, Chen, and Grossman present a 2025 arXiv paper that adds data quality to the scaling laws for language model training. Classic laws link model loss to model size and data volume only. Yet trainers know that clean, well covered data teaches better than noisy repeats. The authors define a single quality score and rebuild the classic Chinchilla style law around it. Their view treats poor data as shrinking the useful size of a data set.

Tests on translation and word prediction used data with controlled amounts of noise. Loss followed the new law closely as quality rose and fell. Cleaner data let smaller models reach the same loss, which saves computing cost. The team also gives two practical ways to estimate the quality score for a real corpus. Trainers can now weigh the cost of cleaning data against the cost of building bigger models with hard numbers.
arxiv-2510-03413:
McInnes and dozens of colleagues report on a 2025 workshop about the future ecosystems of scientific computing. The meeting ran in Chicago in spring 2025 and drew experts from national labs, universities, and industry. Their report asks how community, software, and AI should grow together for team science across fields. Computing now faces AI integration, tangled teamwork across disciplines, and demand for software that lasts. The report records what the group agreed must change.

Three domains drew focus: software infrastructure, cross disciplinary teamwork, and training. Two themes cut across all of them: the transforming role of AI and the need to build the workforce and community. The group calls for modular software with AI woven in by design. It also urges new habits and tools for mixed human and AI teams. This report opens a multi year workshop series, so its roadmap will guide later meetings and funding choices.
arxiv-2510-03613:
Manikandan presents a 2025 arXiv paper introducing Hill-ADAM, an optimizer designed to escape minima and hunt for the global minimum of a loss landscape. Gradient methods settle into the valley they find, and random restarts add uncertainty. The paper derives an approximation of the ADAM optimizer's step size at a state. From a formula comes a condition explaining when ADAM cannot climb out of a valley. Hill-ADAM alternates phases: it minimizes error, then maximizes it to climb out, then minimizes in fresh territory.

This cycle explores it instead of relying on kicks. The author tested the method on five loss functions and twelve image color correction cases, shifting amber heavy images toward cooler tones. Exploration makes runs repeatable, which debugging and science value. If the approach scales, image and signal models could dodge valleys reliably. The analysis of ADAM's step size stands as a diagnostic for training runs.
arxiv-2510-03813:
Kim, Um, and Ye present this 2025 arXiv paper on making text-to-image models produce more varied pictures. Diffusion models follow text prompts closely, but strong guidance often makes every output look nearly the same. Earlier fixes adjusted images midway through generation and gave modest gains. This team instead changes the starting noise for each image.

Their method, Contrastive Noise Optimization, adjusts a batch of starting noise vectors before generation begins. A contrastive loss pushes batch members apart for variety, while an anchor keeps them near a reference for quality. The authors also give theory that explains why this shaping of early noise works. Across several image models, the method improved the balance between variety and prompt fidelity. It also stayed robust when its settings were changed. Varied outputs give users wider creative choice per prompt.
arxiv-2510-04013:
Liu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on reading a language model's mind through its internal activations. Models often state wrong answers with total confidence, which makes their errors hard to catch. Retrieved context can help, but only when the context itself is correct and relevant. The authors ask whether the model's own hidden signals reveal when an answer is right and when context is helping.

Across six models, a simple classifier trained on middle-layer activations of the first output token predicted correctness about three times out of four. The team also built an internals-based metric that separates correct context from incorrect or irrelevant context. It beat prompting-based checks by a clear margin. Polluted context is a real danger in retrieval systems, so a reliable internal alarm has practical value. The findings show interpretability tools can serve as working safety instruments, not just research curiosities.
arxiv-2510-04413:
Muhammad Umar Farooq Qaisar and eight coauthors wrote this 2025 tutorial on sixth generation wireless networks. Future 6G systems aim to merge two jobs that radios used to do apart: sending data and sensing the world. One shared signal and one shared device would do both jobs at once. That merger is called integrated sensing and communication. The paper explains why the merger matters and how it works.

The tutorial traces the idea from early radar and radio coexistence to modern transceivers. It covers the core designs, the system variants, and the tools that make them work, such as large antenna arrays and smart surfaces. The authors also map the open problems, from signal design to privacy risks. They close with design advice for engineers who will build these networks. The paper serves as a map of a field that standards bodies treat as a core 6G feature.
arxiv-2510-04613:
Balázs Bárány and Manuj Verma wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the dimension of wedding cake surfaces. Such a surface rises over a triangle in stacked fractal layers, like the tiers of a cake. It is built by a fractal interpolation scheme driven by self affine maps. Breakthroughs settled the dimension theory for strongly irreducible systems, but these surfaces fall outside that class. Their maps mix directions in a way the new theory does not cover.

The pair proves that the Hausdorff dimension of the surface equals its affinity dimension for all scaling choices. The exception set has zero length in the parameter line, so the formula holds. For a range of parameters, they go further and pin the dimension down for every scaling choice. That step uses an overlap count for a system named after Furstenberg. Dimension tells how much detail a fractal carries at fine scales.
arxiv-2510-05013:
Theodore Jerome Tinker, Kenji Doya, and Jun Tani ask how babies learn words and actions together so fast in this 2025 arXiv paper. Infants generalize from very few examples. Large language models, by contrast, need billions of training tokens. The team looks for the missing mechanism inside robot simulations.

Their simulated robots learn commands such as push the red cube by exploring on their own. The design blends active inference with reinforcement learning to create curiosity. Curiosity plus motor noise beat learning without curiosity by a wide margin. Simple actions emerged first, and complex ones built on them later. Rote word-action pairs came before true compositional generalization.
arxiv-2510-05613:
Meng and colleagues generate 3D point clouds one scale at a time. Autoregressive generators have lagged diffusion models in point cloud quality. Forcing an order onto unordered points biases generation toward local patches. Their 2025 PointNSP framework instead predicts whole levels of detail in sequence.

Coarse scales lock in global structure like symmetry and topology first. Finer scales then add geometric detail step by step. This factorization respects the permutation-invariant nature of point sets. Rich interactions inside each scale replace brittle fixed point orderings. On ShapeNet, PointNSP sets a new quality record for autoregressive generation. It also beats strong diffusion baselines on parameter, training, and inference efficiency. Its edge grows further at dense settings with over eight thousand points. The team aims next at foundation-scale models on larger datasets.
arxiv-2510-05913:
Allen, von Blanckenburg, and Olum rebuild pulsar timing array analysis on Legendre polynomials. Pulsar timing arrays hunt a stochastic gravitational-wave background through pulse arrival times. Standard analyses expand signals in Fourier modes. Their 2025 paper uses the Legendre basis to simplify pulsar timing-model effects.

Timing models always remove constant, linear, and quadratic terms from residuals. In the Legendre basis, that removal simply zeroes the first three coefficients. The authors build an optimal quadratic estimator of the Hellings-Downs correlation there. Its variance follows the established Allen-Romano construction. For power-law spectra, many quantities obtain analytic closed forms. Covariances are computable in closed form even across unequal observing spans. Conversion between Fourier and Legendre bases runs both directions cleanly. Scalar results are basis-independent when the basis is complete, as expected. Cleaner bookkeeping for the background search is the practical payoff.
arxiv-2510-06013:
Agarwal, Chen, Garg, and Kettinger tackle a basic question in group theory in a 2025 algebra paper. Given a finite abelian group, when can a symmetry of the group carry one chosen element onto another? Such elements are called automorphically equivalent, and they form orbits inside the group.

The team proves that two elements are equivalent exactly when the quotient groups left after removing each element's subgroup match in structure. That single test yields the two fastest known algorithms for deciding whether two elements are equivalent. A related method lists all the orbits of a group, and one algorithm runs in near-linear time for groups of moderate exponent. These tools make orbit questions practical to compute for large finite abelian groups. Earlier work mostly counted automorphisms or orbits rather than testing pairs of elements.
arxiv-2510-06713:
Frédéric Marin leads a team observing the bright galaxy at the center of the Perseus cluster. Their 2025 paper reports optical spectropolarimetry of NGC 1275, an active galactic nucleus. They used an instrument on the Nordic Optical Telescope in the Canary Islands. The observations ran alongside an X-ray polarimetry mission studying the same cluster.

Polarimetry measures how light waves align, which reveals hidden geometry around the black hole. The total-light spectrum confirms an edge-on system whose core is obscured. That matches a type-2 classification. The polarized light told a subtler story. Its angle lines up with the galaxy's radio jet axis, which is exceptional for type-2 objects. Continuum polarization sits at two to three percent and varies with wavelength. Emission lines stay narrow, under a set width expected for narrow-line radio galaxies. The team concludes that NGC 1275 is a jet-dominated narrow-line radio galaxy.
arxiv-2510-06813:
Giorgio Di Russo and Anna Tokareva use black hole vibrations to test a conjecture about gravity and charge. Their 2025 paper studies charged Reissner-Nordström black holes that sit near their maximum charge. Such holes ring with quasinormal modes after a disturbance, and some modes fade very slowly. Corrections from effective field theory shift those ringing frequencies.

The Weak Gravity Conjecture says nature must let every charged black hole evaporate. That demand fixes the sign of a certain mix of theory corrections. The authors compute the corrections to the slow modes analytically. Their route borrows a duality with a supersymmetric gauge theory curve. The main result is a clean match. Demanding that the ringing theory stay causal gives exactly the same condition on the corrections as the conjecture does. Two very different lines of reasoning, causality and evaporation, converge on one constraint. Such agreements build confidence in the conjecture.
arxiv-2510-06913:
Ke Guo, Haochen Liu, Xiaojun Wu, and Chen Lv make simulated traffic behave more like real traffic. Their 2025 paper improves imitation learning, where driving agents copy human behavior from recordings. One popular method pits agents against a judge network that scores realism. In multi-agent scenes, that judge often punishes a good driver for its neighbors' bad behavior.

The team names this failure irrelevant interaction misguidance. Their fix, DecompGAIL, splits realism scoring into two parts. One part judges the driver against the map, and the other judges it against nearby cars. Signals about neighbor-to-neighbor and neighbor-to-map interactions get filtered out. A social training objective also rewards each agent for keeping agents realistic. On the WOMD Sim Agents 2025 benchmark, the system reached state-of-the-art realism scores. Training also grew more stable than decentralized approaches. Better simulators mean safer testing grounds for self-driving software.
arxiv-2510-07213:
Zhong and co-authors locate where a language model tracks which language it is speaking. Their 2025 paper builds on a known pattern. English-centered models seem to think in English-like form in their middle layers. They then switch into the target language near the end. The team guessed that a small, sparse set of internal dimensions drives that switch. Those dimensions sit at the same positions across late layers.

A simple method finds those dimensions using as few as fifty sentences. No retraining is needed. Twisting just those dimensions flips the output language while keeping the meaning intact. The trick beat older neuron-based methods at far lower cost. It also makes the model's language choice easier to inspect and explain. Cheap, precise control could help multilingual products serve users in their own tongue, and it sharpens understanding of how models organize languages.
arxiv-2510-07513:
Liu and co-authors teach multimodal language models to read time series by looking at them, the way human analysts do. Their 2025 paper introduces MLLM4TS, a framework for general time-series analysis. Numbers alone hide patterns that the eye catches instantly in a plot. Each channel of a multivariate series is drawn as a color-coded line, and all channels stack into one composite image. A temporal-aware alignment strategy ties image patches back to the time segments they depict. A dedicated vision branch then fuses the picture's global context with the raw sequence's fine temporal detail inside the language model.

Experiments span classification, anomaly detection, and forecasting across diverse datasets. Ablations credit both modalities: the visual branch captures cross-channel structure, while the numerical branch preserves precision. The framework is deliberately task-general rather than tuned to one benchmark.
arxiv-2510-07713:
Yu and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on personalizing language models with user text history. People now leave long trails of written interactions online. Those texts reveal interests far better than clicks alone. Most systems treat that history as a flat list to search. That shallow approach misses how interests evolve and connect. The authors propose weaving the whole history into a layered memory.

Their framework, MemWeaver, builds two memory parts at different levels. Behavioral memory stores specific user actions with their timing and meaning. Cognitive memory distills long-term preferences from those actions. Together they let a model reason over both concrete acts and stable traits. Tests on the LaMP personalization benchmark favored MemWeaver across six datasets. The memory also updates incrementally, so it can keep pace with active users. Deeper personal memory could make generated text feel far more tailored.
arxiv-2510-07813:
La Gatta, Mutzari, Kraus, and Subrahmanian wrote this 2025 paper on a pursuer that must hide while it hunts. In contested settings, asking for information can reveal your position. The authors capture that tension in a pursuit-evasion game with exposure and concealment. A pursuer may request the evader's location, but each request exposes the pursuer to being targeted. Both agents learn movement by reinforcement learning, and the pursuer also learns when to communicate.

Their framework, SHADOW, mixes continuous navigation, communication choices, and a model of the opponent's behavior. Sequence modeling across time proved essential in ablations. SHADOW pursuers beat six rival baselines on capture success. As the risk of being shot grew, SHADOW communicated more selectively, while rivals barely adapted. Its policies also held up across risk levels and physical asymmetries. The work offers a template for agents that must weigh information against survival.
arxiv-2510-08213:
Majid Bastankhah and colleagues offer a 2025 arXiv paper that extends a classic theory of how turbine rotors affect flowing air or water. The old actuator disk theory treats a rotor as a thin, porous disk. It works well near the rotor but assumes smooth flow behind it. That assumption fails farther downstream, where swirling wakes mix with nearby fluid. It also gives unrealistic results for rotors under heavy load.

The new theory joins the classic disk view with a model of the turbulent wake, meaning the rough, mixed flow behind the rotor. It tracks speed, pressure, and stream width at any distance, both upstream and downstream of the disk. By counting how the wake pulls in outside fluid as it grows, the model gives more realistic thrust and power values. This holds even for heavily loaded disks, where the old theory broke down.
arxiv-2510-08313:
Kosuke Matsui and co-authors count how many qubits a general quantum operation truly needs, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum instruments are the broadest class of quantum operations, covering measurements with several outcomes. Scaling processors is hard, so knowing the minimum hardware for a task matters. The count was unclear when mid-circuit measurements and delayed inputs are allowed.

The team characterizes upper and lower bounds on the needed qubits through the instrument's causal structure. Causal structure describes which parts of the operation can influence which later parts. Signaling conditions, which track possible information flow, drive their bounds. They apply the results to protocols that distill entanglement using stabilizer codes. There the bounds meet, fixing the exact optimal count. It is three qubits for the nine-qubit code protocol and four for the five-qubit code protocol.
arxiv-2510-08413:
David Madras, Joshua Safyan, and Qiuyi Zhang explain why prompt tuning works with little data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Engineers search huge spaces of possible prompts using only small task data sets. Intuition says such searches should overfit badly, yet they often generalize well in practice. Earlier PAC-Bayes bounds explained this only when data was plentiful.

The authors argue the missing piece is perplexity, a measure of how natural text feels to a model. Perplexity acts as a prior that steers search toward prompts natural for the task. They derive new generalization bounds that stay non-vacuous, meaning informative, in data-scarce settings. The bounds show formally how perplexity regularization tightens guarantees by limiting exploration. Experiments checked both the bounds themselves and the practical gains of this regularization. Both supported the claim that naturalness helps prompts generalize.
arxiv-2510-08513:
Md Kowsher and co-authors explain why fine-tuning tiny slices of a pretrained network works so well, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts large models by changing only a small part of them. SliceFine updates randomly selected slices of the original weight matrices, adding zero new parameters. The puzzle is why such small, arbitrary pieces suffice for adaptation.

The authors prove pretrained networks have a universal winning slice property, from two phenomena. First, spectral balance: different slices of a weight matrix share remarkably similar eigenspectra. Second, high task energy: backbone representations retain rich, task-relevant features before any tuning. Together these form their Universal Winning Slice Hypothesis for parameter-efficient tuning. Empirically, SliceFine matched leading methods across language and vision tasks. It also improved training speed, memory efficiency, and model compactness significantly.
arxiv-2510-08613:
Xinnan Dai and co-authors map the internal wiring of language model reasoning as a graph in a 2025 arXiv paper. How models turn sequential text into structured reasoning remains poorly understood. Their framework, GraphGhost, represents neuron activations and signal propagation between them as graph networks. Graph algorithms like PageRank then characterize which neurons matter most.

Across diverse data sets, the graphs reveal both shared and model-specific reasoning behaviors. The team identified the neurons activated within GraphGhost and tested them by intervention. Editing key neuron nodes triggered reasoning collapse, breaking both logical flow and semantic understanding. Small structural edits thus have outsized effects on model reasoning. The authors position GraphGhost as a tool for analyzing and intervening in models. It targets the structural foundations of reasoning rather than surface outputs alone.
arxiv-2510-08813:
Mishra, Boutet, and Magnana show that the language a model trains on changes how much private data it leaks, in this 2025 arXiv study. Most privacy tests for large language models use English only. The team instead trained models on medical text in English, Spanish, French, and Italian. They measured six traits of each language and then attacked every model in three ways.

The attacks tried to extract training text, to test whether swapped facts were memorized, and to guess whether a record was in the training set.
