Leakage grew with how repetitive a language is and with how coarsely it gets chopped into tokens. Italian leaked the most, while English records were easiest to pick out as training members. French and Spanish resisted better, which the authors link to their richer word forms. They call for privacy tools tuned per language.
arxiv-2510-08913:
Chen and Li argue that the gravity of a star cluster's own birth cloud can tear the young cluster apart, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Stars are born in clusters inside cold molecular clouds, yet old stars are spread evenly across the galactic disk. Something must dissolve the clusters. Once newborn stars blow their leftover gas away, the cloud's uneven pull, stronger on the near side than the far side, keeps stretching the cluster.

Working analytically, the pair show this tide drives runaway expansion on a timescale set by the cloud's density at the cluster. The effect lasts a few million years, until feedback wrecks the cloud or the cluster drifts clear. In that span a cluster can swell tenfold. The stretching also pulls clusters into bar-like strands. The authors propose those strands are the string-like groupings the Gaia telescope has spotted across the sky.
arxiv-2510-09313:
Roman Prosanov, the sole author, studies bent surfaces inside anti-de Sitter spacetimes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Anti-de Sitter space is a model universe with constant negative curvature, here in two space dimensions plus time. A Cauchy surface is a slice that captures the whole spacetime at one moment, and Prosanov asks which curved surface metrics can appear as such slices.

He proves that any hyperbolic cone-metric on a closed surface of genus at least two, with cone angles above a full turn, embeds as a bent Cauchy surface, convex toward the future. The embedding lands in a spacetime whose left representation is a fixed Fuchsian one, a standard starting representation. He also shows that any two such metrics can be embedded together in one spacetime, one facing the future and one the past. For small enough metrics, the spacetime and the embeddings are unique.
arxiv-2510-09513:
Albert Belenguer-Llorens, Carlos Sevilla-Salcedo, Janaina Mourao-Miranda, and Vanessa Gómez-Verdejo propose a Bayesian method for messy clinical data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Real patient cohorts combine several data types, such as biology, psychology, and social background, and some views are often missing. Sample sizes are small, which strains ordinary machine learning and hides how conclusions were reached.

Their approach joins two formulations in one model. A generative part learns how the different views relate to each other, helped by a semi-supervised strategy, and it can fill in missing views automatically. A discriminative part is aimed at a specific downstream task, picking out the information that task needs. Together they give both a general understanding of the cohort and task-specific, interpretable answers. Applied to multimodal clinical data, the method captured and disentangled how biological, psychological, and sociodemographic factors interact in complex ways.
arxiv-2510-09913:
Shangbin Feng and co-authors argue for model collaboration in this 2025 arXiv paper, titled Don't Throw Away Your Pretrained Model. Alignment training makes language models better at reasoning and following instructions. But it can also cost skills where the raw base model is stronger, such as creativity and calibration, knowing how sure to be.

Instead of picking one model, the team lets models from different stages of the training pipeline work together and cover each other's gaps. The aligned model handles tasks where instruction following matters most. The base model contributes where its older strengths still win. The paper frames the pretrained model as an asset worth keeping in play, not a draft to discard after alignment.
arxiv-2510-10013:
Yuyi Huang and co-authors identify a safety failure in large reasoning models in this 2025 arXiv paper, which they call path drift. Reasoning models think in long chains of thought before answering. Early alignment steps, such as training from human feedback, set guardrails at the start of that chain.

The authors show that first-person commitments made early in the reasoning can pull the whole trajectory off the aligned path. Once the model commits to a stance in its own voice, later steps follow it into content that breaks safety constraints. The vulnerability was largely unexplored before this work. It suggests that checking only the start or end of a reasoning chain misses where safety is lost.
arxiv-2510-10113:
Mi and co-authors release ImmerIris in this 2025 arXiv paper on biometric recognition. Iris recognition identifies people from the eye's iris pattern. In headsets for augmented and virtual reality, the cameras sit at a tilt and capture off-axis irises in open, uncontrolled scenes, unlike classic systems with frontal sensors.

ImmerIris is a large-scale dataset and benchmark for this immersive setting. It lets researchers train and compare methods on the tilted, loosely controlled images that headsets actually produce. The authors argue that recognition tuned on clean frontal images will not transfer directly. A dedicated benchmark is the first step toward seamless, accurate identification inside everyday AR and VR devices.
arxiv-2510-10213:
Kalimullin and Eduard Lerner link graph colorings to spanning trees in this 2025 arXiv paper in combinatorics. Tait coloring colors the edges of a graph with three colors so that edges meeting at a vertex all differ. The authors associate a weight from a three-element field to each edge of a connected pseudograph.

They introduce an alpha-representation connected with these colorings and with sums taken over all spanning trees of the graph. A spanning tree reaches every vertex with no cycles, and there can be enormous numbers of them. Tying colorings to tree sums gives algebraic tools for a classical problem. Tait colorings are historically linked to the four color theorem, so new representations still draw interest.
arxiv-2510-10713:
Yuan-Sen Ting reviews how deep learning is changing astronomy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Neural networks now complement classical statistics across the field. This science is a special test bed because physical symmetries, conservation laws, and differential equations can be built straight into model designs. Such models can generalize beyond their training data. The challenge is data: unlabeled observations number in the billions, while confirmed examples stay scarce and costly.

Ting evaluates where deep learning gives genuine advances and where claims deserve scrutiny. Highlights include inference from simulations and anomaly detection, which extract information where classical likelihoods fail, and multi scale models that learn small scale physics from costly high fidelity runs. He also surveys newer directions: reinforcement learning for telescope operations, foundation models that learn from few examples, and language model agents that automate research tasks. These, he notes, show promise but are still developing.
arxiv-2510-11013:
Tatsuru Kikuchi borrows fluid dynamics to find where a policy's effects fade out, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Difference in differences studies compare treated and untreated places over time, but researchers rarely know how far effects reach. Starting from the Navier-Stokes equations of fluid flow, Kikuchi derives conditions for treatment effects to decay exponentially in space and time. That decay yields explicit boundaries beyond which effects become undetectable, for both simple diffusion and richer flow regimes with reactions.

Scope conditions are testable through two dimensionless numbers from physics. He demonstrates with air pollution from coal fired power plants in the western United States. The data cover 791 ground monitors for fine particles and about 190,000 satellite cells for nitrogen dioxide over 2019 to 2021. Within 100 kilometers of plants the decay pattern validated the framework. Beyond that range, urban sources took over and the method correctly flagged its own assumptions failing.
arxiv-2510-11313:
Breaking a broad job skill into small teachable parts is slow, so skill lists often stay too coarse. Luyen and Abel test whether large language models can do that splitting work in this 2025 arXiv paper. They judge output against an expert skill map, called an ontology, not a quick read. Their setup fixes each stage, from the prompt sent to the model to the cleaning of its reply.

One score checks if each part means the right thing, using word vector matches. A hierarchy-aware F1 score, their second score, gives credit when a part lands in the right branch of the skill tree. Tests used their ROME-ESCO-DecompSkill benchmark, built from parent skills in two large job maps. Zero-shot prompts gave a strong starting point across many models. Adding a few safe examples steadied wording, kept detail more even, and often made replies faster.
arxiv-2510-11413:
Carrying a cable-suspended load with several drones usually relies on the carriers hovering or stopping, which fixed-wing aircraft cannot do. Sofia Girardello, Giulia Michieletto, Angelo Cenedese, Antonio Franchi, and Chiara Gabellieri present the first closed-loop control framework for carriers that never stop in this 2025 arXiv robotics paper. The challenge is regulating the payload's pose while every carrier keeps moving throughout the transport.

Their design builds on grasp-matrix formulations and internal force redundancy among the carriers. A feedback wrench controller regulates the payload's position and orientation, while a second layer shapes oscillations in the internal forces to guarantee persistent carrier motion. Early tests with multirotor drones validate the model assumptions behind the controller. Simulations then show the method preventing carrier stagnation, tracking the load well, and producing feasible trajectories with smooth velocity profiles for the whole formation.
arxiv-2510-11913:
Gabriela Barenboim, Yeji Park, and Liliana Velasco-Sevilla hunt for gravitational waves from a quiet corner of particle theory. Extensions of the Standard Model often contain flaton fields, whose energy landscapes are nearly flat. Flatons can drive a brief second burst of inflation, called thermal inflation, which dilutes dangerous leftover relics from the early universe. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies flat potentials tied to the breaking of lepton number.

When the universe cools, a flaton eventually rolls off its plateau and settles into its true minimum. If the potential develops a barrier along the way, that settling becomes a first-order phase transition, violent enough to radiate gravitational waves. The team determines the conditions the potential must meet for such a barrier to form. They map when the resulting waves could actually be observed by detectors.
arxiv-2510-12113:
Sangho Suh, Rahul Hingorani, Bryan Wang, and Tovi Grossman reinvent the timeline as a chat. Timelines are basic for showing how events and ideas unfold, yet they sit static, answering only questions their makers foresaw. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents the generative timeline, which expands or contracts in response to a user's growing curiosity, and builds it as KnowledgeTrail.

Users co-construct timelines of past events and knowledge formation, drilling deeper or ranging wider on demand. Two user studies found the system fostered curiosity-driven wandering and lucky finds. Users could trace complex relationships between ideas and events that fixed timelines fragment. Citation features backed checking of the generated content. Yet trust proved fragile, shaped by views of source credibility: a link to a doubted source reassured nobody. The authors offer design insights for balancing luck against credibility, a tension every generative interface will face.
arxiv-2510-12213:
Greco and a large team explore adding text and meaning based search to sky coverage maps, in a 2025 arXiv paper published in Astronomy and Computing. The Multi Order Coverage map, a standard of the International Virtual Observatory Alliance, encodes irregular regions of the sky in a hierarchical structure. Such maps help astronomers cross match catalogs and visualize surveys, but they normally hold no descriptive text.

The authors define Textual MOCs, which store written descriptions inside sky regions, and Semantic MOCs, which convert that text into embeddings, numerical vectors that capture meaning. The embeddings sit in vector databases built for fast retrieval. In their experiments, textual maps supported game based learning tools, while semantic maps enabled similarity searches and context aware queries. They also show how these maps can feed generative artificial intelligence systems for richer, agent based analysis of astronomical data.
arxiv-2510-12413:
Pognan and co-authors model how lanthanide elements shape the late time infrared spectra of kilonovae, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. In the nebular phase, months after a merger, the glow is mostly infrared light from forbidden emission lines of neutron capture elements. Lanthanides have complex atomic structures with many infrared transitions, so their fingerprints could dominate.

Using radiative transfer models that go beyond local equilibrium, the team varied ejecta mass and lanthanide fraction. Lanthanide impact grew at higher densities, meaning earlier epochs and heavier ejecta, and was strongest below about four micrometers. Two ionized species, cerium and neodymium, contributed most to forming the spectrum. Lines proposed from data, including tellurium and selenium features, appear. The tellurium line is always blended. The models could not match the smooth continua seen in one event. Line opacity alone, they argue, cannot make the ejecta optically thick.
arxiv-2510-12513:
Pandey and a large team measure the sizes of black holes in two active galaxies by watching how their light echoes, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Reverberation mapping times the delay between changes in an active galaxy's central light and the response of its broad line region. Combined with spectroastrometry, it can yield geometric distances tied to the Hubble constant dispute.

The campaign monitored two narrow line Seyfert galaxies, Mrk 1048 and Mrk 618, with telescopes in India over about five months. Continuum and emission line light curves were well sampled, with variability between a few percent and the low teens. Three methods measured the hydrogen line lags, around ten days for one line and fifteen to nineteen days for another. Line widths from the variable part of the spectra gave black hole mass estimates for both galaxies. The results will anchor absolute distance calibration once space based measurements are combined.
arxiv-2510-12913:
Patuzzo reconstructs a medieval sundial formula with modern tools in this 2025 arXiv paper. The formula came from Arab astronomers between the ninth and thirteenth centuries, including al-Battānī and Ibn al-Shāṭir. It gives the path traced by the tip of a vertical gnomon's shadow during the day. Traditionally the derivation used spherical trigonometry with complex geometric reasoning.

Patuzzo shows the same result follows directly from elementary vector algebra and rotation matrices, mathematical tools that rotate vectors in space step by step. The shadow path depends on latitude, the Sun's declination, and gnomon height. The vector approach recovers it through successive rotations of the Sun's direction, the gnomon, and the dial plane. The same framework extends naturally to other classical relations used in sundial construction, which Patuzzo offers as a simpler, more intuitive route to the classical results.
arxiv-2510-13013:
Luo and co-authors review a decade of QCD sum rule studies of excited heavy baryons in this 2025 arXiv paper. Singly heavy baryons contain one heavy quark, either charm or bottom, and experiments have observed many of their excited states in recent years. The review covers P-wave states, where the internal orbital motion carries one unit of angular momentum.

Working within heavy quark effective theory, the authors' program applied QCD sum rules and light-cone sum rules systematically across the charm and bottom families. Those calculations explain many observed states across the lambda, xi, sigma, and omega families, matching names and masses reported by experimental collaborations. The review also lists predictions for additional P-wave states not yet observed, including several in each family, giving experimentalists concrete targets. The authors present the collected results as a map of where sum rule methods succeed for heavy baryon spectroscopy.
arxiv-2510-13113:
Chen and colleagues use atom-level simulations to explain how metastable titanium alloys deform in this 2025 arXiv paper. These alloys, built on a body-centered cubic beta phase, can gain great strength and ductility when several deformation modes compete: a diffusionless phase transformation, twinning, and dislocation slip. Which mechanism wins under given temperature, composition, and loading was poorly understood.

Simulations of how each mode nucleates revealed that twinning pathways emerge through reversible transformations between the beta phase and an orthorhombic phase. This matches crystallographic theory. Two energetic numbers governed the outcome: the free energy barrier for switching between the phases, and the misfit strain energy along certain phase boundaries. Both vary with conditions. That explains the transitions seen in simulations and experiments. The authors propose them as design metrics for future alloys.
arxiv-2510-13213:
Saeed, Javed, and Nauman track particle creation across a cosmic bounce in this 2025 arXiv paper. In bouncing universe models, imposing a fundamentally discrete physical volume replaces the big bang singularity with a bounce, where contraction reverses into expansion. The authors ask what quantum fields experience as they propagate through that bounce.

Using quantum field theory on a curved background, they numerically followed the number of particles created in a field's vacuum across the bounce. Production in all modes rose initially, peaked sharply at the bounce itself, then varied slowly afterward. Compared with a purely expanding universe, the bounce left distinct imprints, notably a late-time particle spectrum across modes resembling a thermal distribution. Semiclassical gravity calculations gave similar qualitative results, and the authors also determined how the created particles feed back on the geometry's evolution.
arxiv-2510-13713:
Roux, Zimmer, D'Aspremont, and Pokutta prune large language models with a relaxation solved by the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Their 2025 arXiv paper attacks layer-wise pruning, where each layer is thinned on a small calibration set. Picking the best set of weights to drop is a hard combinatorial problem. Greedy heuristics ignore how weights interact inside the pruning objective.

Instead of greedy choices, the authors relax the yes-or-no constraints into a smooth convex problem. Frank-Wolfe, a classic projection-free method, then solves that relaxed problem layer by layer. The method slashes per-layer pruning error compared with strong baselines on modern GPT models. It stays light on memory while doing so, a key constraint at this scale. Theory backs the recipe: known Frank-Wolfe convergence guarantees carry over to the setting. Rounding the relaxed answer back to whole weights gives a provably near-optimal mask.
arxiv-2510-14013:
Valentina Peralta Clarke and co-authors examine how the definition of compatibility affects fairness in kidney exchange programs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These programs match patients who need a kidney with living donors brought by other patients, swapping so each recipient gets a compatible organ. Compatibility is judged by HLA markers, immune-system proteins, and the science has moved from antigen matching to finer allele and eplet levels.

The authors show that effectiveness and equity both shift across the three paradigms. Their equity analysis, focused on ethnic disparities, confirms a risk. Moving to the finer allele and eplet definitions can enlarge inequities between groups. To counter this, they present new optimization models that weight equity directly in the matching objective. These models remedy the inequities under all three paradigms without sacrificing patients' access to transplants. That combination matters for programs deciding which science to adopt.
arxiv-2510-14113:
Matan Levi and co-authors present CyberPal 2.0, a family of language models trained to be cybersecurity experts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cybersecurity has lagged in adopting language models because high-quality, domain-specific training data and models are scarce, and frontier models are expensive to deploy on security work.

To train models ranging from four to twenty billion parameters, the team built an instruction data set of chain-of-thought reasoning for security tasks using their SecKnowledge 2.0 pipeline, which combines expert steering of reasoning formats with multi-step grounding. Across cybersecurity benchmarks, CyberPal 2.0 beat its baselines and matched or surpassed much larger open and closed frontier models. On threat-intelligence knowledge tasks, the models outranked almost every frontier system tested. On threat-investigation tasks, such as linking vulnerabilities and bug tickets to weaknesses, their largest model ranked first. It beat GPT-4o and other leading systems.
arxiv-2510-14513:
Juheon Choi and co-authors build an AI assistant that asks users to state their intention before working on a computer, in this 2025 arXiv paper. It gently nudges them when their activity drifts from it. Digital distractions erode productivity and well-being, but blockers and timers are blunt instruments that cannot tell focused research from doomscrolling.

The assistant uses a large language model to analyze screenshots, application titles, and visited URLs, judging whether activity aligns with the stated goal and notifying the user when it diverges. Initial clarification dialogues and continuous user feedback refine its detection accuracy. In a three-week field deployment with twenty-two participants, using a within-subjects design, the assistant was compared against a rule-based intent reminder and a logging baseline. The authors report it supported users in maintaining focus and aligning digital behavior with their intentions, and they release the source code.
arxiv-2510-14613:
Leclere and colleagues, in a 2025 arXiv paper, use a large cosmological simulation to ask which pairs of supermassive black holes pulsar timing arrays might soon hear. These arrays watch for gravitational waves by timing radio pulses from spinning stars. The combined signal of many distant binaries forms a background hum. A few loud individual binaries might stand above it as continuous waves.

Working with the Horizon-AGN simulation, the team built realistic populations of black hole binaries and estimated their signals. With current European array sensitivity and a ten-year baseline, the chance of detecting one is about four percent. For the future Square Kilometre Array, it rises to about twenty percent. The background is dominated by hundreds to thousands of binaries in massive, quiet galaxies. The individual candidates are heavier, closer, and mostly active galactic nuclei rather than bright quasars.
arxiv-2510-14913:
Montgomery and co-authors study, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how to spend a fixed computing budget wisely when a language model checks its own candidate answers. Test-time scaling generates many solutions and picks the best, but generative verifiers, models that write out an assessment, are expensive. The authors champion discriminative verifiers, which simply score each candidate.

Alone, discriminative verifiers underperform. Combined with self-consistency, the majority-vote method, they form a hybrid that is both cheap and strong. Under a fixed compute budget, this hybrid beat state-of-the-art generative verification clearly, reaching up to 15.3 percent higher accuracy on the AIME2025 mathematics benchmark in the reported comparison. The authors argue the hybrid is not merely a free upgrade over self-consistency. For real deployments it is the more effective and efficient route to reasoning, and they release their code openly.
arxiv-2510-15013:
Neuman, Smiljanić, and Rosvall import, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a principled fix for a scandal in data analysis: clusters that are not there. From neuroscience to ecology, researchers cluster data to find modules. But methods like hierarchical clustering, k-means, and WGCNA offer no principled way to choose the model. Noise then crystallizes into phantom groups. The workaround, deleting weak correlations first, inserts arbitrary thresholds that can distort the structure.

The authors unite sparsification and clustering under Bayesian community detection with model selection by minimum description length. They test two methods from network science, the Degree-Corrected Stochastic Block Model and the Regularized Map Equation. On synthetic data they beat standard approaches, recovering clusters under high noise and with fewer samples. On gene data, the Map Equation found modules more robust and more functionally coherent than WGCNA's. The pitch: a noise-resistant framework that can say which clusters deserve belief.
arxiv-2510-15113:
Anutam Srinivasan and Aaron Nielsen work on navigation that uses Earth's magnetic field instead of GPS, in this 2025 paper. Magnetic anomaly navigation matches readings of local magnetic patterns against stored maps, but shifting background fields from space weather blur the signal. Ground stations normally correct those disturbances, yet their readings are trusted only within about a hundred kilometers, which limits long survey flights.

The pair built the Extended Reference Station Model, which stretches one distant station's usefulness through a longitude-based correction plus a regression model, a statistical tool that learns the correction from past data. They tried three regression styles, including a small neural network, and the best setups kept typical errors under ten nanotesla even across thousands of kilometers. Median errors fell below five nanotesla in favorable cases. The study also checks how space weather, oceans, and polar locations change performance.
arxiv-2510-15413:
Po-Yu Tseng, Po-Chu Hsu, and Shih-Wei Liao build a database that answers SQL queries without ever decrypting the data. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents FHE-SQL, built on fully homomorphic encryption, a method that computes directly on encrypted values. An untrusted server can then run queries while learning neither the questions nor the records.

Older encrypted databases leak patterns through deterministic or order-preserving encryption, and trusted-hardware designs inherit the risks of their chips. FHE-SQL avoids both traps by keeping every computation under encryption. To tame the size of encrypted data, it separates small metadata in a fast store from large ciphertexts in blob storage. Selection happens through homomorphic boolean masks, which hide which rows matched. Caching and garbage collection keep the system practical, with security proven in a standard framework. They pitch SQL support, not just niche searches, as the system's main advance.
arxiv-2510-15813:
S Raman and colleagues address a stability problem in a 2025 paper. The authors work at Fermi and Berkeley national laboratories. The problem sits in control loops of particle accelerators. These machines run in continuous-wave superconducting mode. They use a self-excited loop, a positive feedback design. Safe operating limits come from amplifier calibration. But real amplifiers respond non-linearly. The usual straight-line calibration then introduces errors.

The authors describe how this non-linearity distorts the calibration. It bends the link between drive signal and output power. They present compensation inside the loop controller. The derived limits stay trustworthy as a result. A misjudged limit can push a cavity into unstable operation. That can happen during routine running.
arxiv-2510-16413:
Wenbin Li, Ken K. T. Hung, and Shingyu Leung present a 2025 method for mapping what lies below ground. Their tool uses first-arrival times of waves that pass through rock or soil. From those times, it infers slow and fast zones and the sharp lines between them. Old shape tools could track just one such line at a time.

Their method stacks many shape levels in one function, so many zones fit at once. Extra steps keep the shapes smooth and the maths stable. Tests show it rebuilds complex maps with many zones and sharp edges. Such maps aid quake studies, oil hunts, and scans of the ground. The error checks help judge how much to trust each map.
arxiv-2510-16613:
Olga S. Rozanova and Evgeniy V. Chizhonkov find a smoothness guard for plasma waves in a 2025 paper. They study cold plasma, a gas of charged parts, in one dimension with Einstein rules. The core task asks when waves stay smooth for any set span of time. Blow-ups, where slopes spike without bound, are the risk to rule out.

Their guard is a plain test on the start data of the wave. In the Einstein case, both start slopes and start values must be small. That is stricter than the non-Einstein case needs. Number tests check how sharp the guard is in practice. They also map the shape of spikes when the guard fails. Such guards help labs know safe ranges for plasma runs.
arxiv-2510-17013:
Lanni Bu, Lauren Levine, and Amir Zeldes build a harder reading test for language models in a 2025 paper. Most benchmarks ask about facts stated plainly in single sentences. Real understanding means tracking meaning across whole documents. Pronouns, salience, and unstated links all live between sentences.

Their benchmark, DiscoTrack, covers twelve languages. Tasks sit at four levels of discourse understanding. They include recognizing what stays salient and tracking mentioned entities. They also include discourse relations and bridging inference, guessing unstated links. Even the strongest current models found these tasks hard. The results expose a gap between sentence-level scores and true reading. DiscoTrack gives researchers a multilingual yardstick for that deeper skill.
arxiv-2510-17113:
Mengzhen Liu and four co-authors survey antennas that can change their form in this 2025 article. Such antennas can shift their beam, tone, and wave slant on demand. Sixth-generation wireless nets will need that kind of flex. The article links antenna hardware with signal handling as one joint topic.

The authors review main hardware types and new array layouts. They show uses in joint sensing and messaging, secure links, and near-field links. A case study shows gains in beam aim, link strength, and power use. Open problems include better models, firm hardware, and channel checks. The piece gives a map for work on future wireless systems.
arxiv-2510-17313:
Learning systems often need to separate the many factors that shape a sound, a video, or a time series. Tal Barami and five co-authors point out that past work mostly split data into just two kinds of factors, static and dynamic, which made gathering data easier. Real recordings mix many more factors that change and interact over time.

Barami and his co-authors supply the first standard benchmark for this harder multi-factor task, covering six data sets across video, audio, and time series. The package adds tools for adding data, building models, and scoring results, plus a step that lines up hidden units with real factors. A new model they propose reached the best scores in their tests.
arxiv-2510-18013:
Yiran Wang and three co-authors collect real crashes from machine learning notebooks into the first benchmark of its kind. Notebooks are the main sketchpad for ML work, yet few debugging tools target them, partly for lack of test data. JunoBench gathers over a hundred curated crashes from public Kaggle notebooks, each with a verified fix.

The set spans major libraries and includes notebook-only faults like running cells out of order. Every crash reproduces in one shared environment, with labels and plain-language notes on each fault. Debugging researchers gain realistic material for building tools that find, explain, and repair notebook errors.
arxiv-2510-18313:
Bohan Li, with Zhuang Ma and eleven co-authors, presents OmniNWM in a 2025 paper on driving world models. A world model predicts how a scene evolves, letting driving software rehearse choices safely. Earlier models handled only fragments of state, action, or reward, and drifted over long horizons.

OmniNWM generates panoramic video across color, semantics, depth, and occupancy in one consistent model. Semantics here means labels for what each part of the scene is. Its action encoding separates motion from camera details, enabling control on new camera setups without retraining. Rewards come from the generated three-dimensional volumes, closing the loop for testing driving plans.
arxiv-2510-18513:
Suman Kunwar, writing alone, describes DWaste, a vision platform that sorts waste in real time on ordinary phones and small edge devices, even while offline. Sorting well matters more as convenience packaging floods the waste stream. Kunwar tested several image classification and object detection models on a labeled recycling data set, looking for the best balance of accuracy, speed, energy use, and size.

The most accurate classifier was right about ninety-six percent of the time but answered slowly and produced higher carbon emissions. Lightweight detection models reached up to eighty percent on the detection measure while answering in a small fraction of the time and fitting in under seven megabytes. A compression step called quantization shrank model size and memory use by up to seventy-five percent. The results support a greener design: small, fast models that ordinary devices can run continuously.
arxiv-2510-18813:
Soumyabrata Kundu and Risi Kondor re-derive steerable convolutional networks from geometry rather than group theory. Steerable networks are built so their internal features rotate in a controlled way when the input rotates, which suits physical and molecular data. Most introductions lean on abstract algebra, making the machinery hard to intuition-check.

Starting from pattern matching and basic geometric principles, the authors give an intuitive derivation valid in any number of dimensions. Along the way they explain naturally why two fixtures of the theory appear: the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition, which governs how rotations combine, and spherical harmonics, the natural basis for functions on a sphere. They also propose building the convolution layers with interpolation kernels, a construction they argue improves on existing implementations and tolerates noisy data better. The paper doubles as a teaching resource for a difficult corner of geometric deep learning.
arxiv-2510-19413:
Yasser Hamidullah, Josef van Genabith, and Cristina España-Bonet describe a submission to a sign language translation task, converting Swiss German Sign Language video into German text. Standard systems use generic sequence models fed with frame features, often wasting the time structure of signing, so this entry learns space and time features together with translation in one end-to-end model.

The system was expected to generalize better to new data. It scored moderately on the development set, but performance on the test set dropped sharply, a gap the authors report plainly. That honest failure data point is useful evidence about how brittle end-to-end sign translation remained at the time.
arxiv-2510-19513:
T. S. Kosmas, R. Sahu, and V. K. B. Kota work out how neutrinos and antineutrinos scatter off molybdenum nuclei, to test the metal as a detector material. The recent first sightings of coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering opened new ways to probe weak-force physics. The team focuses on the stable even-even isotopes of molybdenum.

Their cross sections, for both coherent and diffuse scattering, come from a deformed shell model of the nucleus. That model earlier fit data from the COHERENT experiment better than simpler form factors did. The sums cover beams from stopped-pion sources and reactors, plus solar and supernova neutrinos, and they guide future detector choices.
arxiv-2510-19713:
Zehra Akbulut and four co-authors study a duality between two-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories with N=(0,2) supersymmetry. Dualities claim that two seemingly different theories describe the same physics, and a sharp way to test them is comparing their elliptic genera, refined counting functions attached to each theory. The authors build new Bailey pairs for these genera.

Bailey pairs are identities between special functions that can be applied again and again. Using them, the team establishes the equivalence of the elliptic genera for quiver gauge theories generated by repeatedly applying a basic seed duality. The framework turns one proven duality into a whole family of checked dualities.
arxiv-2510-20013:
Paata Ivanisvili and Xinyuan Xie record a short counterexample in a problem called Non-Interactive Correlation Distillation with erasures. The question asked whether the majority function is always the best choice among unbiased Boolean functions. A suggestion from GPT-5 Pro, found through numerical experiments on an open problem list, pointed to a five-bit function that does better.

The note states the problem precisely, gives the explicit function, and checks the computation by hand so readers can verify it without a computer. The counterexample works when the erasure rate is 0.40 in the tested case. The authors also show majority stays optimal near zero erasure for each fixed odd input size.
arxiv-2510-20213:
Vanshika Datta, C. Nahak, and J. C. Yao build a robust plan for ground cover by drone-based sensors whose spots may shift. Each drone sensor casts a sector shape on the ground. Its size is set by height, view field, and aim. Cover drops fast when a sensor drifts from its planned spot. Their plan bakes drift room right into the task.

A score called the radius of robust feasibility gauges how much drift a plan can take. The hard worst-case task has no smooth form and is NP-hard. So a shared greedy step turns each sensor by local facts and aims at high-value zones. In sim tests, the plan keeps strong cover on rough land and in mixed states.
arxiv-2510-20413:
Aditya Gopalan, Sayak Ray Chowdhury, and Debangshu Banerjee show that Direct Preference Optimization, a popular way to align models from preference data with supervised learning alone, is a misspecified estimator. The method implicitly solves a statistical problem over reward functions expressible through the policy class. When the true reward behind the preferences cannot be expressed that way, failure modes appear, including reversed preference order and worsening policy reward.

The authors also study two-stage reinforcement learning from human feedback locally and link it to a natural gradient step in policy space. That geometric picture motivates AuxDPO, which adds auxiliary variables to the DPO loss to steer training toward the reinforcement learning solution. Experiments on toy bandit settings and language model alignment tasks favor the fix.
arxiv-2510-20913:
Poonam Chandra, writing alone, reviews how supernova debris crashing into gas shed by the star before explosion lights up across the full spectrum. That surrounding gas carries the fingerprints of the dying star, so the glow from the crash reads like a record of its final years.

Studies across supernova types show the interaction starts on varied timescales and reaches varied depths, with mass loss rates differing sharply between subclasses. Radio, X-ray, and optical views each probe a different layer of the encounter. Chandra gathers this multi wavelength picture into one account of how explosions reveal the hidden histories of their progenitor stars.
arxiv-2510-21113:
Maitreyi Swaroop leads two co-authors on distributionally robust feature selection, choosing a small set of features to observe so models trained on them perform well across many subpopulations at once. Features can be costly, each survey question or sensor adds burden, so the chosen few must serve everyone.

Their method relaxes the discrete choice into a continuous problem through a noising mechanism, avoiding any need to backpropagate through model training. Optimization targets worst case quality across groups rather than average quality alone. Robust selection suits health surveys and sensing deployments where one instrument must serve diverse communities.
arxiv-2510-21413:
Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi and three co-authors study how open-source developers brief AI coding agents before work begins. Modern agentic tools read standing context files, often Markdown, that record project structure, code style, and build steps, and a shared format named AGENTS.md has recently emerged to replace tool-specific versions.

The team examines 466 open-source projects that adopted such files, sorting what developers write, how they phrase it, and how the files change across commits. No settled structure exists yet: content swings widely, and instructions arrive as plain description, firm prescription, bans, explanations, or conditions. Commit histories give early clues about how this context craft evolves, and the authors see the files as a rare window into practical context engineering for AI agents.
arxiv-2510-21513:
Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz, Max Hort, and Leon Moonen test whether teams of coding language models beat a single champion model. Chasing one best model costs heavily and ignores complementarity, the chance that different models shine on different problems, so the authors measure that effect directly across ten models from five families.

Three benchmarks cover writing code and repairing broken programs. In principle, an ensemble that always picked a correct answer when one existed could beat the best single model by over eighty percent. Picking by consensus backfires, though: popular answers are often popular and wrong. Picking for diversity fares far better, reaching up to ninety-five percent of the ideal, and even two-model teams gain. The results sketch a cheap route to stronger software engineering assistants.
arxiv-2510-21613:
Eleon Bach and three co-authors propose judging an algorithm the way practitioners actually meet it: implemented, tuned, and fed realistic data. Algorithm theory often idealizes both the input and the algorithm itself. This helps explain why famous methods behave far better at work than worst-case bounds suggest, a gap the field has long wanted to close.

Their test case is the simplex method for linear optimization, a workhorse with stellar practice and dreadful worst-case theory. Earlier smoothed analysis narrowed the gap by jittering inputs. But left weaknesses the new by-the-book framework repairs by modeling the implementation's own habits, like feasibility tolerances and input scaling, alongside the data. Under those grounded assumptions, they prove the method indeed runs in polynomial time, matching what practitioners have always observed.
arxiv-2510-21813:
Samuel J. Barrett and Docko Sow introduce SITS-DECO, a generative model for satellite image sequences that borrows its design from large language models. Most Earth observation models are rigid, tied to one data source. Need extra adaptation for each job, whereas language models learn many tasks at once simply by predicting the next token in a unified stream.

SITS-DECO casts satellite data the same way, using a plain decoder-only network and symbolic prompts to switch between jobs such as classifying crop types pixel by pixel across time and sensing modes. Despite having no spatial context and a simple build, it beat much larger Earth observation foundation models on a standard crop classification benchmark. The authors argue that rich temporal sequences, not bigger architectures, are the missing ingredient.
arxiv-2510-22113:
Zitiantao Lin, Yongpeng Sang, and Yang Ye let a robot arm take orders from a glance. Robot helpers fetch objects for people with mobility impairments. Joysticks are the usual control, but they demand precise hand control. They also force users to think in the machine's frame, not their own.

Their system, RaycastGrasp, pairs a wearable mixed reality headset with the arm. The user simply looks at the wanted object. The headset reads the gaze fixation from a first-person view. Augmented cues confirm the intent. A pretrained vision model and the arm then carry out the grasp. Experiments showed clear gains over conventional control. The authors position eye guidance as a more accessible front end for assistive robots.
arxiv-2510-22213:
Yaokun Li, Lihe Ding, Xiao Chen, Guang Tan, and Tianfan Xue make real trees sway, bend, and answer a push, in three dimensions and in real time. Virtual worlds need such trees, but earlier methods produced motion that broke the tree's structure, crawled through slow optimization, or ignored complex real specimens entirely.

DynamicTree starts from a Gaussian Splatting reconstruction of an actual tree and drives it with a compact sparse voxel spectrum, a compressed description of how the tree can move. Mesh motion comes first from that spectrum, then the visual splats are bound to the mesh and follow. Because the spectrum doubles as a basis for modal analysis, external forces get physically sensible responses on the fly. A new four-dimensional training dataset accompanies the framework, which the authors present as the first feed-forward route to long, interactive motion for real captured trees.
arxiv-2510-22713:
A faint background of gravitational waves at very low frequencies was recently reported by pulsar timing teams. Mengshen Wang, Zuocheng Zhang, and Hua Xu present a Bayesian framework in 2025 to test three possible origins for that nanohertz background using pulsar timing array data.

The candidates are merging supermassive black hole pairs, an early universe phase transition, and a network of cosmic strings. Their analysis models pulsar noise and the expected angular correlation pattern, then compares evidence for each scenario. The signal fits the black hole origin well, but cosmic strings and phase transitions remain possible within allowed ranges, and no scenario wins decisively yet.
arxiv-2510-23113:
Longhua Qin leads a team of twelve researchers revisiting how very high energy gamma rays fade as they cross the cosmos. Background light should absorb such rays by making electron-positron pairs. Yet a recent bright burst showed photons up to very high energies, including a reported event near three hundred teraelectronvolts, far more than expected.

Neither Lorentz violation nor axion-like particles alone explained the transparency. The team studies both effects together, asking whether their combination fits the data. The answer tests two kinds of new physics at once using the most extreme light ever seen from a burst.
arxiv-2510-23313:
Yaokai Feng and Kouichi Sakurai survey network intrusion detection from classic methods to collaboration with large language models. Signature-based and neural network detectors each have known strengths and limits. Recent work adds language models to the mix, promising better reading of logs and alerts.

The survey summarizes current status and limits, then reviews language model integrations across conventional networks, autonomous vehicles, and Internet of Things settings. It also flags emerging risks that the models themselves bring. Security teams get a concise map of where AI help is real and where it creates new exposure.
arxiv-2510-23413:
Alessandro Di Giorgio, Pawel Sobocinski, and Niels Voorneveld study a habit shared by many algorithms. Each is written around a fixed value that is never named in advance. In cryptography that value is often a security parameter, such as the length in bits of a secret key. The trio seek, in their 2025 work, a general theory for this pattern.

They work inside resource theories, general systems for reasoning about processes, drawn as string diagrams. Within that setting, they build a general construction for repeating a process as many times as the parameter sets. They then place the construction inside the Markov category of random Boolean circuits and add a distance measure. In that home, the construction captures negligibility through closeness in the limit, step by step. Diagram proofs then yield simple cryptography results, such as showing that a guess at a random key almost never succeeds.
arxiv-2510-23613:
José Gregorio Rodríguez-Nieto and three co-authors study maps called derivations on algebras built by joining two systems through a tensor product. One part is a perm algebra and the other a unital associative algebra, and the joined objects are dialgebras, which carry two products instead of one. A derivation is a map that splits across sums and products in a Leibniz-style way, and such maps expose how an algebra is put together.

The team proves theorems: each derivation of the joined algebra breaks into derivations of the two parts plus maps that multiply inside the factors. They also give coordinate formulas, so a reader can write out what these maps do on a basis. The work extends classic results beyond the associative case, where most earlier work stayed. It also shows how perm algebras fit the wider world of non-associative algebra.
arxiv-2510-23813:
Jonathan Clivio describes the Goresky-Hingston coproduct on the free loop space of a manifold using Morse homology with differential graded coefficients. The coproduct is a string topology operation that splits loop-space classes, and computing it directly is usually hard. Clivio's route passes through a quasi-isomorphism linking chains on the free loop space to chains on the manifold with coefficients in the based loop space.

With that bridge in place, the coproduct on the Leray-Serre spectral sequence separates cleanly into two pieces: the diagonal of the manifold and the coproduct on the based loop space. That description is concrete enough to compute with. Clivio carries it out, over the real numbers, for manifolds shaped like a sphere divided by a group action. An appendix supplies the needed results on inverting morphisms of A-infinity modules, the algebraic plumbing that makes the main computation run.
arxiv-2510-24113:
Arnav Shukla and four co-authors design networks that link chiplets inside advanced AI accelerators without creating long delays. Chiplet systems split CPUs, GPUs, and memory onto separate pieces on one package, which helps scaling but adds a network on the interposer. Large model inference moves huge, bursty flows to and from memory, jamming that network.

Tail delays then break service promises on standard layouts. The team defines an interference score for worst case slowdown under contention and sets layout design as a multi goal optimization. Their generator, PARL, uses reinforcement learning with awareness of how work is split, and balances speed, delay, and power in the layouts it produces.
arxiv-2510-24213:
Haoxin Yang and six co-authors present a diffusion framework for face anonymization that separates identity from other facial traits during training. Anonymization should hide who a person is while keeping expression, pose, and other useful details. Mainstream diffusion models instead intervene at inference time with guidance tricks, which can shift the output and tangle identity with other traits.

Their method, ID squared Face, learns a structured latent space where identity and non identity information are explicitly split apart. Anonymization then becomes direct and controllable, with no optimization needed at inference. The authors report better visual quality and data utility than intervention based approaches.
arxiv-2510-24713:
Lei Gioia, Sanjay Moudgalya, and Olexei I Motrunich sort the kinds of parent rules that can hold a set quantum state as an exact state. Such parent rules are laws whose ground or special states match a state a team wants to study. Some states act as scars, odd states that stand out in a sea of mixed ones.

The trio set out three types of parent law, split by how their local terms are built. They work through the W state in full as the lead case, and draw its full set of local parent laws. That case yields signs in the acts of the system that set the three types apart.
arxiv-2510-24913:
P Chang, S Ramezanpour, and A Helmy study mixed light waves in a guide that can reach a point where two modes merge. Big light chips need small, low power parts that do more than old stuff based plans. At that merge point, the split between the low loss mode and the high loss mode grows sharp.

Their guide holds both weak and strong pair zones between its metal bound and plain wave modes. Careful size picks let it hit the merge point by design. That hit gives fresh grip on how the part acts as a whole. The team frames the find as a path to very small shifters and to on chip talk links that sip power.
arxiv-2510-25013:
Rabin Adhikari, the sole author, trains tiny attention only models from scratch and finds the least parts that can solve a known core task. The task asks a model to pick the right name for a phrase that points back in a line of text. Big trained models solve it, but their bulk hides how they do it.

A one layer model with just two heads got the task fully right, with no feed nets or norm steps at all. The two heads split into an add part and a contrast part that join to settle the pick. A two layer, one head form passed facts by its ask and key ties. Task built training gave clean, least parts.
arxiv-2510-25213:
Shane A Caldwell leads a team with twenty nine co-authors who set NVQLink, a plan to tie big compute hubs tight to quantum chip gear. Quantum runs need fast help from classic hubs, with waits capped at a span of mere millionths of a second. Their plan aims to serve each kind of quantum part and each kind of its control gear.

The link runs on plain web grade wires that shops can adopt with ease. A round trip read came in at a few millionths of a second at most, with room to cut it more. A code add on lets a coder call hub, graph chip, and gate parts in one tongue. Call backs in real time are part of the plan.
arxiv-2510-25313:
Jingyan Liu, Yue Sun, Jianwei Xu, and Ming-Jing Zhao study imaginarity. Their 2025 quantum physics paper concerns complex numbers in mechanics. Complex numbers are essential in quantum theory. A resource theory of imaginarity has grown recently. It treats imaginary parts as a usable resource. The four authors propose new measures for it.

They construct measures using real part states. One measure is defined in terms of fidelity. Fidelity gauges how close two quantum states are. They explore properties of that proposed measure. For qubit systems, they give an analytic expression. Qubits are the basic units of quantum information. They derive links to several other imaginarity measures. Those include geometric and trace norm versions. They also provide complementarity relations across unbiased bases. The work highlights the role of real part states.
arxiv-2510-25413:
Shakib Yazdani, Yasser Hamidullah, Cristina Espana-Bonet, and Josef van Genabith build sign language data. Their 2025 paper uses vision-language models for curation. Sign language translation datasets are limited in scale. Multilingual coverage is often lacking in current sets. Expert annotation and controlled recording make curation costly. Social media could supply larger, natural data sources.

Their pipeline annotates and filters videos automatically. Face visibility finding is the first pipeline step. Sign activity recognition follows in their approach. Text extraction pulls content from video material. A judgment step validates matching between video and text. The method was applied to TikTok videos. Eight sign languages are covered in that corpus. The resulting corpus is called TikTok-SL-8 here. They also tested on a German YouTube dataset. Two off-the-shelf translation models were assessed for rivals. German and American sign languages supplied test cases. The work enables scalable weakly supervised pretraining.
arxiv-2510-25613:
Dibyendu Chakraborty, Arindam Chatterjee, Ayushi Kaushik, and Kenji Nishiwaki probe extra dimensions. Their 2025 physics paper uses muon beam dump tests. A five-dimensional gauge effect is their target theory. It distinguishes muon and tau lepton numbers. Present and future muon dump tests are investigated. NA64, Mu-cubed, and MuSIC are among them.

Tests classify into two complementary categories here. Some probe feebly interacting particles decaying invisibly. Others probe states decaying into muon pairs visibly. Multiple massive gauge bosons appear as Kaluza-Klein particles. Their presence enhances signal events versus four dimensions. Decay into muon pairs enables parent mass reconstruction. That could show multiple Kaluza-Klein particles directly. Clear evidence for five-dimensional origin could result. Muon magnetic moment now agrees with Standard Model. That agreement excludes certain new particle setting regions. Nonzero kinetic mixing effects are discussed carefully too. Beam dump tests offer sensitive probes of hidden sectors.
arxiv-2510-25713:
Boshi An, Chenyu Yang, and Robert Katzschmann adapt vision-language-action models for collaboration. Their 2025 paper builds a robotic assistant for shared tasks. A pretrained Open-VLA model is adapted with minimal prompting. Dexterous human-robot collaboration is the target setting. Three additions improve it.

FiLM conditioning makes visual backbones task-aware in perception. An auxiliary intent head predicts collaborator hand poses. Target cues are also predicted by that head. Action post-processing predicts compact position and rotation deltas. Principal components reduce finger joint commands before mapping. A teleoperated dataset trains it, augmented with hand poses. Four principal components explain most hand-joint variance. Ablations identify action post-processing as primary driver. Auxiliary intent helps, while FiLM results are mixed. A directional motion loss proved detrimental overall. Real-time pick-up and pass behaviors compose long-horizon tasks. Trainer overfitting to demonstrators is key limitation.
arxiv-2510-25913:
Gilbert Bahati, Ryan M. Bena, Meg Wilkinson, Pol Mestres, Ryan K. Cosner, and Aaron D. Ames design safety filters for robots that weigh how risky each obstacle is. A safety filter overrides a planned action when it would lead to danger. Their method first solves Poisson equation, a classic partial differential equation, on the scene to build a safety function whose positive region marks safe states.

Bahati and the team then solve Laplace equation, a related equation, to build a guidance field that encodes graded caution around obstacles. A tunable boundary rule sets how strongly each obstacle repels the robot. Combined, the filter guarantees safety while steering the robot to avoid higher risk features first, as shown in simulation.
arxiv-2510-26013:
Tomohiro Kawakami and Hiroshi Tanaka prove a structure result for definable open sets in a weak form of tame geometry. Their setting is a weakly o-minimal expansion of a real closed field, a framework that keeps sets definable by formulas from becoming too wild. A strong cell is a basic building block set with a simple, layered shape.

Kawakami and Tanaka show that every bounded definable open set can be written as a union of finitely many open strong cells. They also prove another theorem of a similar kind. The result is a cell decomposition style statement, which lets complicated definable sets be understood through a finite list of simple pieces.
arxiv-2510-27313:
Philipp Davydov, Ameya Prabhu, and three other co-authors ask how new AI-written text really is, in a 2025 study. A language model may echo its training text or coin fresh wording. Word-by-word checks miss echoes that swap in synonyms. Judging against the full training set is also a huge task.

The team reframes newness as a search task based on meaning. Their three-step method finds near matches, re-ranks them by chunk length, then scales scores against human ratings. Run on the SmolLM model family, it found echoes across far longer spans than once thought. Some task types push models toward or away from fresh text. Extra tuning for chat raised newness too, not just style. Their data and index are public.
arxiv-2511-00013:
Daria Tyurina, Sergey Stasenko, and Konstantin Lushnikov predict cognitive age from psychophysiological tests using machine learning. Subjects complete tasks measuring reaction time, cognitive conflict, short-term memory, verbal functions, and color and spatial perception. Features include average completion time, share of correct answers, color campimetry differences, and words guessed in a search matrix.

Models trained on those features estimate how old the cognitive profile looks, which may differ from calendar age. Health and psychology readers get a compact battery approach to cognitive aging. Such estimates could flag faster or slower cognitive aging for follow-up, using tests that are cheap to administer.
arxiv-2511-00513:
Hans Baehr, Ken Rice, Chao-Chin Yang, and Cassandra Hall explore whether planets can start forming earlier than once thought. At that stage the disk around a young star is still massive and unstable under its own gravity. Dust grains may gather in the disk's spiral arms and collapse into planetary embryos, shortcutting slow growth. The team simulates self-gravitating gas with grains even smaller than earlier studies used.

For tiny grains with very short stopping times, a metal richness above a modest threshold overcomes the spreading effect of dust diffusion. In the outer disk the models correspond to millimeter grains and yield embryos between a tenth and one full Earth mass. Forming seeds that early could cut planet assembly time sharply, above all in outer regions where growth by sticking is slow.
arxiv-2511-00613:
Yating Yu and eight co-authors introduce CueBench, a benchmark for context-aware video anomaly understanding. Real-world anomalies hinge on context: climbing a cliff with safety gear is sport, without it is danger. Existing tests mostly reward spotting odd events or describing them shallowly, missing the principles and subtle cues that separate abnormal from normal. CueBench is the first benchmark built around that context.

An event-centered taxonomy anchors two families, conditional and absolute anomalies, refined across many scenes and attributes. Unified tasks span recognition, temporal grounding, detection, and anticipation. Leading vision-language models fell well short of satisfactory performance, while the authors' Cue-R1, tuned with reinforcement learning and verifiable, hierarchy-aware rewards, beat them by a wide average margin. The suite gives the field a fair, rigorous probe of real-world understanding.
arxiv-2511-00713:
John Campbell and Spencer Daugherty generalize a family of combinatorial tableaux. Standard immaculate tableaux of a given composition shape are known to match, in exact count, the set partitions of a number range into blocks, counted by Stirling numbers of the second kind. The authors define lexical tableaux, which replace block structure with cycle structure: standard lexical tableaux of the same shape now match permutations with a given number of disjoint cycles.

A row's reading word must be the lexicographically smallest among its own cyclic rotations, a rule that includes the weakly increasing words of the older theory. Lexical tableaux then define a pair of dual bases for the Hopf algebras of quasisymmetric and noncommutative symmetric functions. Expansions into monomial and fundamental bases, and their duals, follow through Kostka-like coefficients.
arxiv-2511-00813:
Maximilian Mangold and colleagues examine the Josephson diode effect in all metal junctions, where current flows more easily one way than the other. Their devices place iron platinum or copper platinum links between niobium leads, and the metal interfaces break inversion symmetry, producing Rashba spin orbit coupling.

In an in plane magnetic field, both link types show a diode effect whose pattern matches the symmetry expected from that coupling. A plain copper control link behaves differently, showing an axis symmetric effect instead. The team also explains a puzzling reversed hysteresis in the interference patterns: stray fields from vortices pinned in the niobium contacts account for it, separating real diode physics from a measurement artifact.
arxiv-2511-01013:
Mohammad Amanour Rahman proposes HyFormer-Net, a neural network for breast ultrasound that finds lesions and classifies them at the same time, while showing its reasons. Ultrasound diagnosis is hampered by speckle noise, operator dependence, and fuzzy lesion borders. Earlier deep learning systems often did one task. They missed global context or local detail, and they acted as black boxes.

The design joins a convolutional branch for local features with a transformer branch for global context, fused across scales, with an attention gated decoder. Interpretability comes from attention checks and from Grad-CAM heat maps for the classification side. On the BUSI data set it beat standard baselines on overlap and accuracy, with strong recall on malignant cases, and an ensemble version performed better still.
arxiv-2511-01113:
Sebastian Kempf and Frank Puppe propose S2Doc, a data format for documents and tables that keeps spatial and semantic structure together. Research on documents has no shared model: each project invents its own structure, formats clash, and most models capture either where things sit on the page or what they mean, not both.

S2Doc is designed to be flexible and extendable to new tasks, to support most existing modeling approaches for documents and tables, and to handle multi page documents. The authors describe it as, to their knowledge, the first format to combine all of these aspects in one structure. For document processing research, a common format could end the repeated cost of translating between incompatible representations.
arxiv-2511-01213:
Riddhi Jain and colleagues improve visual question answering about Indian food, a cuisine whose diversity exposes how Western centric most food question answering systems are. Answering well needs multi step reasoning about ingredients, dishes, and how items on a plate relate, not a guess followed by an explanation.

The team builds reasoning chains onto an existing Indian food question answering set, with minimal human intervention. It then fine tunes smaller language and vision language models on those auto validated chains. Training continues with reinforcement learning on more data. Adding the chains raised accuracy by an average of ten percentage points over the baseline. The paper also analyzes where the chains help, giving a detailed account for the Indian food task.
arxiv-2511-01613:
Tomáš Krsička and Tibor Kubík work on classifying three-dimensional anatomical shapes, a task held back by the complexity of mesh data and the lack of standard benchmarks. They approach it with self-supervised learning: teach a model the structure of organs from unlabeled surface meshes, then use what it learned for classification.

Their key piece is Precomputed Structural Pooling. It is a fixed, non-learned way to coarsen a mesh. It groups nodes by geometric proximity and stays reversible. It avoids the sparsity problems of selection-based pooling and the slowness of edge contraction. Built into a graph autoencoder, it improved reconstruction fidelity and class separation. To make results comparable, the authors also release MedShapeNet19, a curated benchmark of 19 anatomical classes with standard splits.
arxiv-2511-01713:
Rodrigo Avalos, Eric Ling, and Annachiara Piubello revisit a pillar of mathematical relativity: the positive energy theorems, which say an isolated gravitating system cannot have negative total energy. The classic proofs assume the system fades into flat Minkowski space at infinity, but real astrophysical objects sit inside an expanding universe, not empty stillness.

The authors take de Sitter space as the background. It is written in flat expanding coordinates. Each time slice there is a flat space, stretched with a special, umbilic second fundamental form. Because de Sitter space has a cosmological horizon, no global energy exists, so they define a quasi-local energy by adapting the Liu-Yau energy to this setting. They then establish that the energy is positive for bounded values. The values lie in the regime they analyze. This extends the spirit of the classical theorems to an expanding cosmos.
arxiv-2511-01813:
Hao Zhu and Joschka Boedecker make a class of hard optimization problems easier to specify. Biconvex problems, where the objective is convex in each of two blocks of variables separately but not jointly, appear across machine learning, signal processing, and control. Solving them usually means hand-building an alternating solver that optimizes one block at a time, tedious and error-prone work.

Their framework, disciplined biconvex programming, extends the rule-based style of disciplined convex programming. State the problem following a small set of syntax rules. The system then splits it into convex subproblems. It generates a customized alternating convex search solver automatically. Users can experiment with formulations without optimization expertise. The framework ships as the open-source Python package dbcp, built on the widely used CVXPY modeling language.
arxiv-2511-02113:
Hai-Dang Kieu, Min Xu, Thanh Trung Huynh, and Dung Le improve recommender systems that use both product images and text. Many existing methods extract coarse visual features and merge them with text in naive ways, producing redundant or mismatched item descriptions. Their framework, VIRAL, starts from an information theory view: good fusion should keep what each source uniquely says, what they share, and avoid double-counting.

One module uses a vision-language model to write fine-grained, title-guided descriptions of product images. A second module, inspired by partial information decomposition, separates and recombines the complementary signals. On three Amazon datasets VIRAL consistently beat strong multimodal baselines, and the authors report it substantially raised how much the visual features contribute to recommendations.
arxiv-2511-02213:
Kangyu Qiao, Shaolei Zhang, and Yang Feng make large language models cheaper to run by removing whole layers, but with a twist: which layers get removed depends on the input. Fixed pruning masks serve every request identically, which wastes capacity on easy inputs and starves hard ones. Their method, IG-Pruning, selects a layer mask dynamically at inference time.

Candidate masks are first discovered offline by clustering inputs by meaning and optimising which blocks to cut. At run time the system picks a suitable mask without expensive extra training. In experiments the approach consistently beat leading static depth-pruning methods. The authors pitch it at deployment settings where computing resources are tight and input difficulty varies from request to request.
arxiv-2511-02713:
Release notes tell users what changed in software, but writing them by hand is slow and error prone. Qianru Meng, Zhaochun Ren, and Joost Visser built ReleaseEval, a 2025 benchmark for testing language models at that task. It gathers nearly ninety-five thousand release notes from over three thousand code projects in six programming languages, all openly licensed.

The benchmark sets three tasks with growing detail: from commit messages alone, from commit trees, and from full code diffs. Large language models beat older baselines at all three, with the biggest gains when given the tree structure. They still struggled to sum up long diffs, though. The gap shows where automated release writing needs the most work next.
arxiv-2511-03113:
Jiameng Chen and six colleagues design antibodies with a generative model that obeys physics while it draws. Antibody design tools often produce shapes that look plausible but break physical rules, and scarce data hurts their reach. Their 2025 model, FP-AbDiff, is the first antibody generator to enforce the Fokker-Planck equation along the whole generation path, keeping the probability flow globally coherent.

The physics loss is woven into a state-of-the-art diffusion framework that respects three-dimensional symmetry, alongside deep biological priors. On the RAbD benchmark, the model set new marks. Its key binding loop designs landed within about one angstrom of the target shape. That is a 25 percent gain over the prior best, with the highest contact recovery reported. Harder six-loop co-design also improved on both shape and sequence recovery.
arxiv-2511-03613:
Sk Anisur, Kartik Singh, and Sayan Choudhury trace how two bosons wander a lattice where hopping is easier one way than the other. That one-way bias, called non-reciprocity, breaks the usual Hermitian rules of quantum motion. Their pair spreads into a lopsided density cone, and the slant can be dialed by the bias strength.

Under a steady outside force, the pair's Bloch swings also turn lopsided. Strong interaction between the bosons carves an inner hourglass pattern inside the main cone, which itself slants under the bias. Pair correlations carry further signatures of the interplay. Directional quantum walks like this could route particles in engineered lattices where symmetric hopping wastes the design.
arxiv-2511-03713:
Sorin Dumitrescu and colleagues prove a local Lorentzian version of the Ferrand-Obata theorem for conformal symmetries. A conformal vector field generates motions that stretch a spacetime metric evenly without tearing its angles. On a closed, real-analytic Lorentzian space, their result says each such flow is either locally just an isometry in disguise, or the metric is conformally flat everywhere.

The statement serves as a local form of a famous Lichnerowicz-style conjecture for Lorentzian geometry. Progress hinges on sharper local normal forms near the field's singular points, especially the linearizable kind earlier work set aside. Global arguments using compactness complete the proof. Rigidity of conformal motion constrains what exotic spacetimes can exist.
arxiv-2511-03813:
Kaushil Patel, writing alone, studies a simple rule for consumer choice between two goods: a shopper only notices goods priced below her personal threshold, then picks her favourite among those noticed. People share the same preference ranking in the model but differ in their thresholds.

Patel fully characterizes this behaviour and shows that ordinary choice data alone can identify what a price change does to welfare. The behaviour overlaps with a major class of random utility models, yet the welfare answers differ in a meaningful way. Equivalent variation under the attention model first-order stochastically dominates the random utility answer, so the choice of model changes policy conclusions.
arxiv-2511-04013:
Binbin Nie is the lead author among nine authors developing a theory of Raman-induced frequency shift for solitons in microresonators, a limit on broadband soliton microcombs. As spectra widen toward an octave and pulses shorten, the Raman shift cuts conversion efficiency, restricts span, and can even prevent steady operation.

Their complementary theory stays valid when soliton duration falls below the Raman response timescale. In that regime the shift depends more weakly on duration than older theory suggests, and the range where solitons can exist grows. Numerical simulations and experiments on silicon nitride microresonators support the predictions. Practical guidance follows for building efficient, broadband combs for spectroscopy and timekeeping.
arxiv-2511-04213:
Markus Herklotz, Niklas Ippisch, and Anna-Carolina Haensch evaluate language-model feedback on statistics exam answers, asking whether automated comments are good enough to trust with students. Large classes leave instructors little time for individual feedback, so a Munich lecture course trialled a platform that returns model-generated comments on a mock exam.

Students received overall and personalised feedback generated from lecturer-supplied solutions. Across two thousand three hundred eighty-nine feedback instances, about seven percent contained errors, from small technical slips to conceptually misleading explanations, the analysis found. That error share, documented systematically, sets a concrete caution level for deploying model feedback in teaching without review.
arxiv-2511-04413:
Jianfeng Lu and two colleagues analyze mean square error for stochastic gradient samplers. The samplers run on underdamped Langevin dynamics under a global convexity assumption. A discrete Poisson equation framework anchors their bounds on time-averaged error.

For the SG-UBU sampler, they derive an explicit error bound with first-order bias in step size. The leading error term scales with the variance of the stochastic gradient. They extend the study to variance-reduced methods for finite sums, including SVRG-UBU and SAGA-UBU. There, a phase transition changes the convergence rate, a warning for anyone tuning such samplers.
arxiv-2511-04813:
Ian Addison-Smith and three colleagues compress reduced-order models of turbulent flow using the model's own output. Galerkin models of turbulence often need too many modes to stay accurate. Getting those modes from simulation data is itself expensive.

Starting from linearized Navier-Stokes modes built without prior data, they go further. The time series of modal coefficients reveals which modes truly matter in motion. Pruning by that evidence yields a self-compressed model with far fewer degrees of freedom. First-order accuracy is maintained, they report, offering cheaper flow models for control and design loops.
arxiv-2511-05313:
Jatin Prakash and co-authors propose language models whose cost and recall can be tuned at run time, not fixed in training. Cheap mixers like sparse attention and convolutions cut inference cost, but often lose in-context recall, the skill of using long prompts well.

Fixing that trade-off in advance means some uses get too little memory and others pay for speed they do not need. Their controllable design lets one model shift its balance per task. That flex could let a single model serve both quick chat and deep document work.
arxiv-2511-05613:
Anka Reuel leads a large team mapping who checks the social effects of foundation AI models. Governments now lean on evaluations to judge risks like bias, privacy harm, and labor impact. Yet reporting on those social effects is uneven, and no one had charted the full picture before.

The team studied hundreds of company release reports and outside evaluation sources, and interviewed developers. Company reporting proved sparse and shrinking in areas like environmental cost and bias. Outside evaluators covered bias and harmful content more deeply.
