The paper frames a classic missing-data pattern as a covariate shift problem, which points to fixes beyond imputation.
arxiv-2602-06813:
Xiaojun Huang and Song-Ying Li study when a Stein manifold, a complex space with strong function-theoretic structure, can be told apart by its holomorphic functions. The Bergman space collects all square-integrable holomorphic functions, and it is said to separate points when for any two distinct points some function takes different values there. The paper connects this property to the curvature of the Bergman metric.

The authors prove separation holds whenever the Bergman metric is well defined and has nonpositive constant holomorphic sectional curvature. They then build counterexamples where the curvature is positive, or where the scalar curvature takes any sign, yet separation fails. Combined with earlier work, this shows a flat Bergman metric is impossible, and a negative-curvature one occurs exactly for the unit ball, possibly minus a negligible set.
arxiv-2602-06913:
Marcell D. Kovács and two co-authors build a clean algebra model for quantum systems that never settle down. Finding workable models of ergodicity breaking in interacting systems is a standing hard problem. Their model uses repeating unitary circuits with local cause rules, built from three-part gates they call walls, which halt the spread of local operators for good.

The shape of the resulting split parts is read off from symmetries of embedded operator algebras, which also name the local conserved quantities and carry over to time-varying circuits. Group theory then gives the general form of gates with causal splitting, with links to quantum error-correcting codes. The theory proves an entanglement area law from cause rules alone, checks its hold under local measurements, and compares spectral patterns with random matrix theory.
arxiv-2602-07013:
Jiaxi Yang and three co-authors make refusal in vision-language models adjustable to the user and the context. Fixed refusal rules miss in both directions: they refuse too little for some needs and too much for others. Their method, CR-VLM, steers activations to tune refusal instead of fixing one rule for all.

Three parts work together. First, a teacher-forced step pulls out a refusal vector that can be tuned, boosting the refusal signal. Second, a gate keeps acceptance for in-scope queries, curbing over-refusal. Third, a vision module built on counterfactuals lines up visual features with refusal needs. Tests on many data sets and models show refusals that are effective, efficient, and robust, pointing toward safety that adapts to the user.
arxiv-2602-07213:
Language models often reason badly in specialized domains because their knowledge is frozen, so retrieval seems like an obvious fix.  Srijan Shakya and three co-authors test an adaptive setup where the model itself decides when to consult an external knowledge base while thinking, against plain chain-of-thought and static retrieval on math benchmarks.

Static retrieval does worse than chain-of-thought, and traces that use retrieved text do slightly worse too.  The surprise is that traces where the model considers retrieval but does not use it do better than chain-of-thought alone.  The paper's title states the lesson plainly: adaptive retrieval helps thinking mostly when it is not used, a finding that should change how retrieval is wired into thinking systems.
arxiv-2602-07313:
Curvature settings often force a manifold into a short list of shapes, and this paper adds a sharp entry to that list.  Haiping Fu and one co-author prove a rigidity result for compact Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least eight. With harmonic Weyl curvature and a fully nonnegative curvature operator of the second kind, the manifold must be either a space of positive constant curvature, up to overall shape, or flat.

A four-dimensional classification under a cone setting follows as well, generalizing earlier work.  The payoff is a clean rigidity theorem: under these curvature hypotheses, the shape has almost no room to be exotic.
arxiv-2602-07613:
Rerandomization lifts randomized tests by drawing new treatment assignments until covariate balance meets a threshold, but rejection sampling becomes prohibitively slow under strict thresholds. Jiuyao Lu and two co-authors build a fast method on Metropolis-Hastings sampling.

The method preserves uniformity over the allowed assignment space, keeping the theoretical guarantees of the classic method, while dodging the inefficiency that forces users into suboptimal thresholds. Experimental builders get strong balance without the wait, and results that remain valid under the accelerated scheme. The method keeps the balance that justifies inference by resampling, rather than trading theory for speed.
arxiv-2602-07813:
Electrical impedance tomography images flow inside a body from edge readings, but sparse data harms the imaging. Ke Chen and two co-authors tackle the shortage by filling partly seen reading data with a conditional diffusion model, a generative method that learns the spread of full readings.

The filled data plug into ready solvers and support flexible sensor layouts, and theory bounds the gap between filled and true readings for a class of polygonal conductivities. Coupled with a deep-learning inverse solver, diffusion completion yields reconstructions comparable to using full data. The paper offers medical and industrial imaging a usable preprocessing step when sensors are limited.
arxiv-2602-08213:
Tuning drug compounds means lifting traits like uptake and harm while keeping power, but language models struggle with the hidden link between structure and drug science and the lack of labeled cases. Haoran Liu and four co-authors propose DrugR, which injects plain step-by-step drug thought into tuning.

The method mixes domain steady prep, guided fine-tuning via reverse data building, and self-even multi-granular reinforcement learning. Tests show comprehensive improvement across key ADMET traits without sacrificing the compound's core power or shape similarity. Medicinal chemists and AI drug-discovery teams gain a thought-first approach that makes the tuning path legible, not just its endpoint.
arxiv-2602-08713:
Vision-language models pair a vision encoder with a language model, but how the language backbone learns to see remains murky. Lachin Naghashyar and six co-authors present the first mechanistic analysis of that adaptation. Their arXiv paper uses stage-wise model diffing to isolate representational changes introduced during multimodal fine-tuning.

Vision-preferring features emerge or reorient during tuning, and a selective subset reliably codes spatial links, shown by controlled changes to spatial prompts. Tracing causal activation leads to a small group of attention heads. Readers learn when and where spatially grounded features arise, and how visual grounding reshapes previously text-only features. The method offers a foundation for refining multimodal training.
arxiv-2602-08813:
Mahdi Sabbaghi and three co-authors tackle a weak spot in how large language models are trained. Models often go through several rounds of tuning, first for safety and helpfulness, then for new tasks. Even small later changes can undo earlier lessons, a flaw called catastrophic forgetting. The team argues the fix should come before later tuning, not during it.

They propose a training method called FRPO that rewards a model not just for its current answers, but for answers that stay good after nearby changes. Built by adjusting an existing method called GRPO, it adds no extra computing cost. Tests across several models and tuning styles show far less loss of safe behavior, while new-task scores hold steady. Math-focused trials point the same way.
arxiv-2602-08913:
When many different feature sets predict equally well, handing an expert just one answer hides the real uncertainty. Kateřina Henclová and one co-author present GEMSS, a variational method that returns a menu of sparse solutions at once. A single mixture model approximates the multimodal posterior, and its training objective pushes the components apart so they stay distinct.

Tested on a new benchmark where the true solution set is known by construction, GEMSS beats enumeration, sampling, and masking rivals, and the lead grows as solutions overlap more. Real data sets yield several distinct yet highly predictive solutions, the practical goal other methods miss. An open-source Python package is available.
arxiv-2602-09113:
Speculative decoding speeds up language-model inference by drafting tokens cheaply and verifying them in bulk. Its energy cost, however, has drawn little attention. Rohit Dutta and seven co-authors survey the energy requirements of speculative decoding strategies in detail. They fill a gap in a literature focused on latency and inference cost alone.

The survey traces how energy savings depend on model size and family, on the choice of decoding strategy, and on the traits of the data set being processed. For teams deploying large models at scale, where electricity bills and carbon costs matter as much as speed, the analysis offers a map of which strategies save energy and under what conditions.
arxiv-2602-09313:
Lewis Ghrist and Robert Ghrist use mathematics to organize visual paradoxes, from the Penrose triangle and staircase to the Necker cube, into a graded ladder. Their 2026 paper treats each paradox as a clash between locally sensible readings that cannot be joined into one global reading. The clash is measured with cohomology, a tool that tracks where local agreement breaks down around a loop.

The key step is to limit attention to bistable parts, pieces with just two local states. Examples include a cube face seen forward or back, a gear turning one way or the other, and a tiling corner read as convex or concave. With only two states, the obstruction arithmetic becomes a matter of parity, and paradoxes sort into levels from ambiguity through impossibility to inaccessibility. A discrete Stokes theorem links each level to the next, and a new animation method makes the hidden looping structure visible.
arxiv-2602-09613:
Tobias Wöhrer and Christian Kuehn study finite-time Lyapunov rates of deep networks viewed as smooth-depth neural diff rules. These rates measure how fast input nudges spread fast, sorting input-output moves in ways that aid clarity and let distinct designs be set beside each other. Their 2026 paper links rates straight to attack weakness.

The authors offer a training method that lifts toughness through rate control, with a key economy: suppress rates far from zero only in the early stage of input moves. That early-stage focus lifts toughness while cutting compute against full-span rate control, which would require a full double back-pass. Finite-time rates thus serve both as diagnostic sorters and as a usable lever for armoring neural diff rules.
arxiv-2602-10013:
Handling fragile everyday objects, such as potato chips, demands fine force control that most commercial grippers cannot offer. A 2026 paper led by Xuhui Kang, with five co-authors, introduces TF-Gripper, a low-cost parallel-jaw gripper with tactile feedback, priced near a hundred and fifty dollars. Its force range runs from under half a newton to forty-five newtons, and it fits varied robot arms.

A paired teleoperation device records human grasping forces for training. Standard low-frequency policies learn from that data but stay unreliable, since force control is reactive and contact-dependent. The team's RETAF framework splits force control from pose prediction, regulating force at high frequency from wrist images and touch. Across six real-world tasks, direct force control improved grasp stability and overall performance over position control.
arxiv-2602-10213:
Spider binaries, millisecond pulsars that heat and wear away low-mass companions, show a rich spread of signals from radio eclipses to GeV light curves. A 2026 paper led by Christo Venter, with four co-authors, predicts their expected TeV signals as they vary around the orbit. It includes the effect of shock shape between the two stars. Fast leptons sped up in the pulsar magnetosphere and near the shock, plus a hot partner star, make a good setting for inverse Compton fluxes within reach of Cherenkov telescopes.

The code gains an updated synchrotron kernel, varied input spectra, and several shock shapes. Updated spectra that vary with phase and light curves that vary with energy may help pin down particle energies, wind traits, shock shapes, and system tilt across these systems.
arxiv-2602-10613:
Mingxun Wang and three co-authors make a strong nonparametric fitting method computationally useful in a 2026 paper. The Highly Adaptive Lasso achieves near size-free settling under minimal smoothness assumptions, but its huge design matrix makes large use prohibitive. A ridge-regularized cousin, the Highly Adaptive Ridge, offers a related path.

Building on both, the authors present principal-part versions of each estimator. An outcome-blind principal-part reduction of the basis slashes runs while matching the tested results of the originals. An early-stopped slope descent variant adds smooth spectral regularization without choosing a hard cutoff. The work turns a theoretically strong method into one builders can run.
arxiv-2602-10713:
Q. Guo and five co-authors maximize forward arcs in Hamiltonian cycles of tournament-like digraphs in a 2026 paper. A recent conjecture generalizing Dirac's theorem, proved by Freschi and Lo, promises a Hamiltonian oriented cycle with many forward arcs when minimum degree is high. The present paper asks for the exact maximum.

The authors portray the maximum number of forward arcs in semicomplete multipartite digraphs and locally semicomplete digraphs. Those characterizations yield formula-time recipes for computing the maxima. The results are sharp in an interesting way. For other generalizations of tournaments, the same problems are NP-hard even though finding a Hamiltonian cycle is easy. Maximizing direction, it turns out, is harder than merely finding a cycle.
arxiv-2602-10813:
Pradyumna Kumar Bishoyi and three co-authors manage interference between terrestrial and satellite networks in a 2026 paper. Coexistence in the upper mid-band raises concerns because dense terrestrial deployments can severely degrade non-terrestrial downlink results. Current fixes demand exact channel information and static coordination, unsuited to dynamic satellite scenarios.

The authors develop an tuning system that jointly controls terrestrial downlink power, uplink power, and antenna downtilt to protect satellite links while keeping terrestrial results. The non-convex coupling between network settings is handled by a proximal policy tuning reward-based learning method that learns adaptive power and tilt plans. Simulations show the approach protects satellite service without surrendering terrestrial quality.
arxiv-2602-11013:
Mean-field methods for coupled nuclei and electrons live or die by their first guess. Denis G. Artiukhin, writing alone, tests old first guesses for quantum nuclei and builds new ones from exact solutions of the 3D quantum harmonic oscillator. No full head-to-head check of this kind had been made before.

His isotropic guess beats old options in nuclear-electronic orbital density runs under a joint convergence protocol. Its partial Hessians, though extra work, can be found cheaply without harming the resulting proton densities. The paper offers a robust, fast start that may ease convergence troubles in mean-field nuclear-electronic work.
arxiv-2602-11213:
Backdoors in code models must both transfer and hide, a hard pair to satisfy. Shuyu Chang and five co-authors propose STAB, an attack that seeks both at once without needing full victim data. Static triggers transfer well but are easy to spot; moving triggers hide better but transfer poorly.

STAB trains a surrogate with sharpness-aware minimization, steering settings toward flat loss regions where perturbations transfer better. Differentiable search over trigger tokens then builds context-aware triggers. Across data sets and code models, STAB beat prior attacks on transfer and stealth, keeping a high success rate after defences and clean-input results intact. The paper is a warning for code-model supply chains.
arxiv-2602-11513:
Running large language models on weak devices forces queries to remote servers, raising privacy risks. Yujie Gu and four co-authors propose DEL, a frame for differentially private and communication-fast split inference. An code projection module plus differentially private random rounding cuts communication while preserving privacy.

No local model is needed for denoising: a soft prompt adapted at the server side compensates for utility loss from privacy protection. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first use of soft prompts to improve the privacy-utility trade-off in language model inference. Tests on making and grasp benchmarks show effectiveness, offering a practical path to private inference on limited devices.
arxiv-2602-11713:
Matter governed by quantum chromodynamics behaves differently under a magnetic field and at nonzero chemical potential. Modeling both effects together is hard. Zhi-Ying Qin and six co-authors build a hybrid equation of state. It smoothly joins a hadron resonance gas at low heat to an ideal parton gas at high heat. They set aside anomalous magnetic moment effects for charged and neutral particles alike.

Heat, pressure, energy density, trace anomaly, and specific heat all respond to both knobs. Raising chemical potential lifts them in both hadronic and quark-gluon plasma phases. A magnetic field suppresses them at low heat but enhances them at high heat. Both effects raise the squared speed of sound near the critical point while lowering it below. The model matches lattice data well at zero and modest field strength. At stronger fields it underestimates magnitudes while keeping the overall trend.
arxiv-2602-12413:
Benchmark scores are meant to measure how well a model generalises, but training data may already contain test-like material. Ari Spiesberger led this work with six co-authors, studying soft contamination: semantic duplicates of benchmark items that slip past n-gram filters because their wording differs while their content matches. Standard decontamination misses those near-copies.

Embedding the Olmo3 training corpus, the team finds semantic duplicates for 78 percent of CodeForces items and exact duplicates for 50 percent of ZebraLogic problems. Training on such duplicates lifts benchmark scores, and fine-tuning on duplicates also lifts scores on truly held-out items from the same benchmark. Recent benchmark gains, the paper argues, thus mix genuine progress with accumulated test-like data in growing corpora.
arxiv-2602-12513:
Finding a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum matrix games from noisy feedback is a core problem in game theory and learning. Jiashuo Jiang led this work with one co-author, Mengxiao Zhang, proposing an algorithm that repeatedly solves linear programs to estimate an equilibrium with bias at most epsilon. Its sample complexity depends on game dimensions and problem constants, giving the first instance-dependent bound for general-dimension games with noisy feedback and possibly non-unique equilibria.

The algorithm builds on recent online resource allocation advances and runs in two stages: first identifying the support set of an equilibrium, then computing the unique equilibrium restricted to that support. Both stages rest on careful analysis of linear program solutions from noisy samples. Readers get a practical, theoretically grounded route to equilibrium estimation where feedback is noisy and equilibria need not be unique.
arxiv-2602-12613:
Time graph neural nets process changing graphs, but most target one-off forecasts for a given span, while many uses need frequent forecasts over time. Zulun Zhu led this work with one co-author, Siqiang Luo, revisiting ongoing forecast in time graph nets. Straight fitting of existing models to ongoing forecast brings either heavy compute cost or quality problems, mainly for large graphs.

Their model, Coden, is designed for fast, good learning on changing graphs, beating a key hard part in existing time graph nets while keeping similar forecast hit rate. Theory checks support its goodness and speed, and clarify its two-way link with both RNN-based and focus-based models. Tests across five changing data sets show Coden beating old rivals in both speed and goodness, making it a better answer for ongoing forecast in changing settings.
arxiv-2602-12713:
Some random maps keep inputs independent: feed in separate inputs and the outputs stay separate, a rare and useful trait. Gérard Letac, Mauro Piccioni, and Jacek Wesołowski study a family of such maps linked to generalised inverse Gaussian laws, building on an older case known as the Matsumoto-Yor property. Their focus is the matrix version, where the values are special square arrays rather than single numbers.

The authors prove two results. First, matrix generalised inverse Gaussian laws are fully pinned down by the independence trait under their extended map. Second, the extended map itself obeys the Yang-Baxter equation, the consistency rule that makes such maps useful in integrable models. Together, the results tie a chance property to an algebraic structure.
arxiv-2602-13413:
Training large models under heavy-tailed noise is a daily reality, and two stabilizers compete: clipping gradients and normalizing them. This paper builds a worst-case complexity theory for stochastically preconditioned gradient descent. It covers adaptive methods such as Adam, RMSProp, and Shampoo, under noise with a finite p-th moment for p between one and two. The headline is a sharp split between the two stabilizers.

Normalization provably converges to a stationary point at optimal rates, whether problem parameters are known or not. Clipping, by contrast, can fail outright in the worst case, because the random preconditioner correlates with gradient estimates. A new vector-valued Burkholder-type inequality powers the analysis and explains the field's preference for normalization. Yuchen Fang leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13513:
Routines such as gradient descent, Newton's method, and ADAM trace smooth paths, but following those paths costs repeated calls to the objective and its gradient. This paper learns those paths directly from path data with data-driven equation discovery, then solves the discovered gradient flows as stand-ins for the original problem. The resulting Learned Gradient Flow optimizer builds stand-in models of variable order, in full or reduced dimensions, at user-chosen intervals.

Tests span engineering mechanics and machine learning, including inverse problems, structural shape optimization, and forward solves with different grids. Learned flows sped convergence markedly by capturing key path features while skipping expensive calls. Grant Norman leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14113:
Hiroyuki Tajima and three co-authors explore a 2026 arXiv puzzle in dense matter physics. Neutron star data point to a smooth crossover from hadron matter to quark matter, marked by a peak in the speed of sound. Yet the microscopic mechanism behind that crossover has stayed elusive.

The paper draws an analogy with the BEC-BCS crossover seen in ultracold atoms. In a simplified field-theory model, a tripling fluctuation effect explains both the sound-speed peak and the baryon momentum-shell structure predicted by quarkyonic matter. The authors also derive the quarkyonic model microscopically within their framework, offering a unified picture of the hadron-quark crossover.
arxiv-2602-14613:
Spins lose their quantum order through contact with nearby spins and vibrations. Conor Ryan, with Alessandro Lunghi as co-author, looks at a neglected low-temperature path: relaxation driven by dipolar forces between spins. Standard models often treat those forces as pure dephasing only.

The paper tests a method called generalized cluster-correlation expansion, which should track energy flow from a central spin into its bath. Ryan and Lunghi show the standard form fails even at a rough qualitative level. They take the theory apart to find where it breaks. That diagnosis gives a starting point for a fixed method.
arxiv-2602-14813:
Gian Pietro Bellocca and others test whether Bai's old PC spread can stand in for the spread of stepwise least-squares factors in multi-level factor models. Mock runs show that, for broad noise shapes, the finite-sample spread of global and group factors tracks the PC spread well.

Other gauges of mean squared error are also tried, and one gauge wins the tests. Economists thus gain a trusted short cut: a known spread can serve where a new, layered spread is hard to pin down. Factor work gains a checked bridge from old to new.
arxiv-2602-15013:
Liu and Koehn tackle text style transfer without parallel corpora. Rewriting a sentence in a new style while keeping its meaning is naturally a supervised task, yet paired examples exist for only a few style domains. A common fix normalizes text into a style-free middle form and then restyles it, but the normalizer is usually a small paraphraser used only at test time, feeding a correspondingly small stylizer.

The team observes that a large-scale normalizer already exists: neural translation systems trained on hundreds of millions of sentence pairs keep content while drifting toward generic phrasing. Roundtrip translation through a pivot language thus strips style with no task-specific training. Translating a monolingual in-style corpus roundtrip yields a pseudo-parallel set for fine-tuning a stylizer, called RT-SFT, which beats few-shot baselines across four style domains by wide margins.
arxiv-2602-15113:
Nguyen and Linden show the Sun can strongly constrain spin-dependent dark matter nucleon scattering below the usual evaporation limit. The Sun gathers dark matter particles through scattering and can catalyze their self-annihilation. At low masses, however, particles may evaporate after collisions with hot solar plasma. Past modeling weighed evaporation against annihilation, but observational work often assumed a fixed 4 GeV evaporation limit, below which particles escape before annihilating.

The team weighs both competing effects on spin-dependent cross-section limits. They find solar observations can beat terrestrial limits by 1 to 5 orders of magnitude for masses between 2 and 4 GeV. Solar data can even lead the world below one fifth of a GeV, where direct detection struggles. The fixed evaporation limit, the paper argues, understates what solar observations can do.
arxiv-2602-15213:
Lahiri and colleagues study the diode effect in microwave-exposed Josephson junctions hosting Yu-Shiba-Rusinov states from magnetic defects. Two rules matter: particle-hole symmetry must break through non-zero scattering, and inversion symmetry must break through unequal sizes or moments. Under irradiation, those breaks induce an extra phase-free current term.

That term makes critical currents asymmetric for opposite current sides, an effect absent without it. The imbalance is highly tunable through microwave strength and tone, and can even reach the ideal, where current dies for one polarity, like a perfect diode. While Yu-Shiba-Rusinov states give an ideal platform for a strong imbalance, the plan need not depend on them, if both hold.
arxiv-2602-15313:
Tang and colleagues propose Mnemis, a recall setup joining System-1 likeness search with a partner System-2 route called Global Selection. AI recall, how models arrange and fetch old texts, grows more and more useful to large language models. Yet current tools like RAG and Graph-RAG mainly fetch recall through likeness routes. While fast, such System-1-style fetching fails with cases needing wide thinking or full reach of all needed info.

Mnemis arranges recall into a base graph for likeness fetching and a layered graph enabling top-down, careful walk over meaning layers. By joining partner powers from both fetching paths, Mnemis fetches recall bits that are both meaning and shape relevant. Mnemis hits state-of-the-art scores across all tested tools on long-term recall tests, hitting about 94 on LoCoMo and about 92 on LongMemEval-S using GPT-4.1-mini.
arxiv-2602-15413:
Oppenlaender studies a pocket, battery-run e-ink device showing school cite counts. The StatCounter puts numbers into the stream of day-to-day life rather than a desk setting. The work leans on a first-person, long-run self-study probing how numbers shape drive, focus, thought, and moods across work and non-work scenes.

The nearness and constant presence of numbers sparks micro-checks, quiet breaks, but also brings flashes of second-guessing when numbers drop or stall. Toting the device sparks stories about school self, like a sense of company during travel and spells away from the desk. Over time, the being there of the device shifts numbers from a now-and-then touchstone into a backdrop of life. The work adds light into how bodied numbers recast their sense, and opens chances for making tools that work with school judging in quiet ways.
arxiv-2602-16113:
Qi Sun leads a team of four researchers teaching language models new skills without retraining them. Models often fail to turn relevant text into usable knowledge after deployment, and retrieval-augmented generation, which surfaces similar documents at inference time, frequently misses context that actually improves task performance. Their method, Evolutionary Context Search, searches combinations of context using accuracy on a small development set, needing only inference calls and no weight updates.

By moving beyond semantic similarity, the search finds non-obvious context pairings that lift performance markedly on benchmark tasks. Gains appear on BackendBench and on an airline task, and contexts evolved with one model transfer well to other leading models. That transfer suggests the discovered contexts capture something general about the task rather than quirks of one model. The paper positions evolutionary context search as an efficient alternative to manual prompt engineering and costly fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-16413:
Ipsita Bar, Aditi Thakar, and B. Prasanna Venkatesh propose a measurement-based route to dark steady states. Preparing such states for jointly emitting quantum two-level systems is hindered by their dark, weakly coupled nature, and existing methods rely on patterned driving, local control, or structured settings. The authors instead offer a platform-free protocol built on projective measurement on a single emitter.

For permutation-symmetric ensembles, one measurement already yields a large share of singly excited dark states. For generic arrays, repeated measurement on one emitter drives the other emitters into a nearly pure state with large overlap with the subradiant Dicke subspace. It therefore reaches dark states through measurement alone, without tailored driving or engineered setups.
arxiv-2602-16513:
Rajendra Bhati leads two coauthors on port-based teleportation under pure-dephasing decoherence. The paper studies deterministic teleportation when noise hits both the entangled resource state and the measurement process. Each Bell pair in the resource meets an identical local environment, giving independently distributed entangled links.

Two noisy cases are analyzed: decoherence on the resource alone with ideal readings, and noisy readings adapted to the noise model. In the first case the authors derive a lower bound and then a closed-form expression for the entanglement fidelity, with its long-run behavior. Surprisingly, noise-adapted readings perform worse than noiseless ones. Embedding the protocol in a spin-boson model shows how bath memory and temperature shape fidelity across environments.
arxiv-2602-16613:
Zofia Borowska and co-authors show quantum teleportation over Deutsche Telekom's city fiber testbed in Berlin, using off-the-shelf parts at a telecom data hub. The goal is to prove quantum links on real telecom kit, joining quantum computers, sensors, and clocks. A local Bell-state check joins photons from a weak coherent source with photons from a warm-atom entangled source.

The transfer lands on an O-band photon sent through a thirty-kilometer field fiber loop in real-world weather and noise. State checks after travel give an average teleport fidelity of ninety percent. Scores hold with and without live classical C-band traffic in the same fiber, showing it fits wavelength-division links that carry live data. Telecom firms get a real-world teleport milestone.
arxiv-2602-16813:
Chanhyuk Lee and co-authors present Flow Map Language Models, a one-step language modeling route via continuous denoising. Discrete diffusion language models promise faster generation than autoregressive models, yet their sample quality degrades sharply in the few-step regime, blocking dramatic speedups in practice. Continuous flows over one-hot token embeddings offer a different path.

The continuous form defines a unique flow map that can be learned directly for efficient few-step inference, a structure discrete methods lack. Both flow and flow map are learned with simple cross-entropy objectives respecting simplex geometry, and three flow map distillation choices are compared. A flow language model matches state-of-the-art discrete diffusion baselines on two large corpora, and its distilled one-step version beats the eight-step quality of recent few-step diffusion models.
arxiv-2602-17013:
Kevin Oden links pathwise and score-function gradient estimators, showing both arise from the Malliavin integration-by-parts identity. Building on that equivalence, the paper introduces a unified hybrid estimator combining pathwise and Malliavin gradients using their covariance structure.

This gives a sound account of stochastic backpropagation and achieves minimum variance among all unbiased linear mixes, with closed-form finite-sample convergence bounds. Cuts of nine percent are shown on variational autoencoders on CIFAR-10, and up to thirty-five percent on strongly-coupled synthetic problems. Early policy gradient tests reveal non-stationary optimization landscapes present challenges for the hybrid approach, pointing to directions for future work. The work casts Malliavin calculus as a single clear framework for stochastic gradient estimation. Readers get a clear map of when hybrid methods help.
arxiv-2602-17113:
Parinya Karndumri led a two-author paper in string theory, finding a large family of holographic solutions for D4-branes wrapped on curved four-dimensional spaces. The wrapped branes yield gravity duals of supersymmetric quantum mechanics in the low-energy limit, reached through twisted compactifications. The spaces studied include spheres, hyperbolic spaces, products of two Riemann surfaces, and Kahler four-cycles.

The solutions come from maximal gauged supergravity in six dimensions with two families of gauge groups, and they embed into type IIA theory through consistent truncations. They take the form of domain walls sliced by the four-manifold, running from locally flat walls to singular low-energy geometries. Many uplifted solutions carry physical singularities, making them candidate holographic descriptions of supersymmetric quantum mechanics from wrapped D4-branes.
arxiv-2602-17313:
Guillem Masdemont led a three-author team on heat flow in cylindrical cavities where Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation breaks down. Breaking that law opens one-way thermal transport and circuits. Using a specular ray-tracing method, the team studies the far-field regime in cylindrical cavities and what follows.

At thermal equilibrium, breaking Kirchhoff's law yields nonzero heat rectification values across cavity sections. Those values are tunable for perfect one-way flow and looping. Internal single-color currents vanish due to coupling between emission and uptake at mirror walls. Away from balance, spinning heat fluxes inside the cavity can be steered exactly by combining ordinary and one-way materials. The findings offer design rules for thermal control and nonreciprocal light devices.
arxiv-2602-17513:
Baris Karacan led a three-author team on clinical section segmentation from MIMIC-III to obstetrics, comparing supervised and zero-shot approaches. Clinical free-text notes hold vital patient facts in labelled sections, and spotting them aids decisions and language work.

The paper advances section segmentation in three ways. First, it builds a new section-labeled, de-identified obstetrics notes set, widening public corpora like MIMIC-III, where most current tools are trained. Second, it tests supervised transformer models in-domain on MIMIC-III and out-of-domain on the new obstetrics set. Third, it first compares supervised against zero-shot large language models head-to-head. Supervised models shine in-domain but fade out-of-domain. Zero-shot models adapt out-of-domain once hallucinated headers are fixed. The findings press the case for domain-specific clinical resources and mark zero-shot segmentation as hopeful beyond well-studied corpora.
arxiv-2602-18113:
Leslie Molag and two co-authors study random point patterns that come from a family of math tools called orthogonal polynomials. Their 2026 paper looks near a hard edge, a sharp boundary the points cannot cross, after the pattern is thinned in a way that depends on place. Thinning here means each point survives with a chance set by where it sits.

Under a fine zoom at that edge, the team proves the thinned pattern settles to a single universal limit, which they name and write out in full. The limit is tied to a system of linked equations with one tuning knob, a system seen before in related work on multiplied point counts. The result extends a classic link between the plain edge pattern and the Painlevé V equation, now for the thinned case as well.
arxiv-2602-18313:
Jan Pavšek and three co-authors build thermodynamics-aware neural networks for vapor-liquid equilibria of single substances. Their 2026 paper notes that machine learning predicts molecular properties well for process design, but scarce lab data and broken thermodynamic consistency limit it. The team moves thermodynamics-informed graph networks from the Gibbs-Duhem relation to the Clapeyron equation.

The multi-task model predicts vapor pressure, liquid and vapor molar volumes, and enthalpy of vaporization together. It beats single-task learning on accuracy and beats purely data-driven multi-task learning on honoring the Clapeyron equation. Gains are largest where data are scarcest, the properties with fewest measurements. The model promises practical help for chemical engineers working with thin data.
arxiv-2602-18813:
A robot that works fast for an hour is a different challenge from one that succeeds once under careful resets, and current tests rarely capture that difference. Jesoon Kang, with twenty-two co-authors, introduces Habilis-beta in 2026, a fast-motion, long-lasting on-device vision-language-action model for real-world deployment, presented under the Tommoro Robotics banner.

Evaluation uses a Productivity-Reliability Plane that scores tasks per hour and mean time between interventions under continuous runs, demanding both speed and stamina. Habilis-beta combines language-free pretraining on large play data with post-training on cyclic demonstrations that capture drift across repeated tasks, plus phase-adaptive motion shaping and rectified-flow distillation for fast on-device control. In hour-long runs it far outpaces a leading baseline in both simulation and a real humanoid logistics workflow, and tops the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard.
arxiv-2602-19513:
Yasutaka Shimizu and Atsushi Yamanobe propose a stats-based framework for live win odds and player ratings in team sports decided by score. It works from minute-by-minute running box-score totals, tracking how games evolve rather than judging them only at the final whistle. A steady dominance gauge, the T-score, turns final scores into real values matching win and loss outcomes.

That gauge becomes a time-evolving random process, the T-process, driven by standard scores, allowing step-by-step updates of in-game win odds. Competitive edge splits into clear parts. A hidden player-impact index, STATS X, then measures a player's role in good dominance spells, splitting team base strength from single-game swings.
arxiv-2602-19713:
Spintronics usually relies on spin-orbit coupling, which favours heavy elements. A 2026 arXiv paper by Shantanu Pathak and Saswata Bhattacharya shows that twisting two atom-thin magnetic layers can split electron spins without that coupling, using theory and symmetry checks.

In symmetric two-dimensional antiferromagnets, combined space-time symmetry forbids spin-polarized transport. Twisting layers of several candidate materials breaks key symmetries and yields spin patterns that vary with momentum. An electric field adds a further Zeeman-type splitting, while strain tunes the size of the effect and can flip its wave pattern, switching on a real spin current. The work extends altermagnetism to twisted bilayers and offers a route to spin currents by symmetry design alone.
arxiv-2602-20013:
Molecular magnets could host quantum information processing at realistic temperatures, if their nonclassical correlations survive warmth and magnetic fields. A 2026 arXiv paper by S. Bhuvaneswari and two co-authors studies thermal entanglement, measurement-induced nonlocality, and coherence in a nickel-based radical magnet.

Using coupling values estimated from experiment within a Heisenberg picture of spin-spin links, the authors compute the thermal state and track how quantum assets vary with heat and field. They persist even at room temperature. While entanglement, measured by negativity, fades quickly as heat and field rise, non-local effects and coherence hold up better and survive where it is gone. The results highlight correlations of other kinds as the hardier resource in thermally activated spin systems.
arxiv-2602-20213:
Code-generating language models are only as good as their test cases. Existing benchmarks often miss subtle corner cases, letting wrong answers pass. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jingwei Shi and four co-authors proposes CodeHacker, an agent framework that makes targeted hostile test cases to expose hidden weaknesses in program entries.

CodeHacker mimics the hack trick in contest programming. It uses stress testing, anti-hash attacks, and aiming at specific program logic to break entries. Before judging rival code, the agent refines its own Validator and Checker through a Tuning Phase, probing itself with self-generated hostile cases. Tests show CodeHacker greatly improves the true negative rate of current datasets, weeding out wrong answers that weaker test suites would pass.
arxiv-2602-20413:
Finding the laws of chaotic and complex dynamic systems is hard for both sparse regression and neural networks. Kevin Slote and two co-authors offer KANDy, a zero-depth, wide Kolmogorov-Arnold network for dynamics that learns governing laws itself. It replaces sparse regression with such a network, fixing limits on both sides: finding equations with such networks, and cases where sparse methods stall.

Applied to the Hopf fibration, the model finds topological structure, improving fit with attractor traits. The authors also test it on discrete and flowing dynamic systems and on chaotic partial differential equations. KANDy thus offers a clear and strong option for data-driven models of nonlinear dynamic systems.
arxiv-2602-20513:
Task success alone does not show whether a language model fits real use, above all in high-stakes applied settings. Gavin Levinson and Keith Feldman argue that value depends on wider human drivers beyond usual score tests, yet current metrics are rarely ordered for steady judging. They offer the Language Model Utility Taxonomy, a setup structuring utility judging across four domains: scores, use, running, and rules.

Within each domain, the map is ordered in layers into theme-aligned sides and parts, each grounded in metrics that let numbered contrast and fit of model choice with planned use happen. An outside dynamic web tool supports browsing by linking each part to a store of apt metrics for applied judging. The work gives users a shared structure for weighing models by fitness, not just scores.
arxiv-2602-21113:
Heterogeneous computing needs compilers that handle many device types from one source. Huy Trinh surveys recent SYCL compiler implementations in this 2026 arXiv paper, a key part of compiler construction for such systems. The survey traces a shift from single-source multiple compiler passes to a single-source single compiler pass.

Multiple papers built on the single-pass approach are analyzed for how they improve performance and tackle separate challenges. Readers get a map of where SYCL compilation stands and which design choices matter most. The survey serves compiler builders weighing how to structure passes for accelerators and mixed hardware.
arxiv-2602-21213:
Data-store schema design hides shape structure that hole-counting can expose. Bilge Senturk and Faruk Alpay build that lens in this 2026 arXiv paper, coding working links as triangles of a triangle complex. Betti numbers of the link complex spot cyclic link structure, and Simplicial Normal Form is defined as hole-count no-loop state in higher sizes.

For splits, the classic binary no-loss-join test gets a shape recast: under link keeping, no-loss holds exactly when overlap fields key at least one part, yielding a strong morphing pull-back. For many-way splits, a loop in the nerve of a cover blocks join-tree structure. Betti numbers thus offer a light check to pin down mystery link loops.
arxiv-2602-22013:
Vision-based retrieval systems answer questions by pulling up relevant pictures and documents, but blur, noise, dim light, and shadows can throw them off. I-Hsiang Chen and five co-authors trace the failure to visual encoders that tangle what a picture shows with how it is degraded. They propose RobustVisRAG, a two-path design that separates damage signals from clean meaning before answering.

One path captures degradation cues through one-way attention, while the other learns purified meaning guided by those cues, trained with two new objectives that keep the two strands apart. The split keeps retrieval and answer quality steadier under harsh visual conditions, without giving up speed or zero-shot skill. The result is a retrieval system that holds up when the pictures it reads are far from perfect.
arxiv-2602-22113:
Simulating quantum lattice systems at finite temperature often means writing the time-evolution operator as a tensor network. Sander De Meyer and four co-authors extend the cluster-expansion route to two-dimensional fermionic systems, an alternative to the usual Suzuki-Trotter splitting. The cluster approach preserves internal and lattice symmetries and extends more easily to higher orders and longer-range forces.

They use it to build projected entangled-pair operator approximations of thermal Gibbs states, and test different truncation schemes for multiplying layers of these operators. The framework is then applied to a two-dimensional fermionic model as a benchmark. The work gives finite-temperature simulation a symmetry-friendly tool beyond the standard splitting method.
arxiv-2602-22313:
Putting the standard model of particle physics on a quantum computer starts with simpler fermionic field theories. Bojko N. Bakalov and four co-authors tackle the massive Thirring and Gross-Neveu models with any number of fermion flavors, discretized on a one-dimensional lattice. They compute gate complexity with two leading methods in the limit of many flavors and large lattices.

Ground states of both models are prepared with excellent fidelity on systems up to twenty qubits, for one through four flavors, using an adaptive variational imaginary-time algorithm. The authors also classify the models' dynamical Lie algebras, showing both belong to the same isomorphism class. The work is a concrete step toward simulating real-time dynamics of fermionic theories.
arxiv-2602-22513:
Phase control of parameter tuning lets coupled oscillator networks reach chosen space-time symmetries, but Floquet-based predictions were proven mainly for linear systems. Scott Lambert and two co-authors establish non-linear chiral steady states in a ring of three coupled oscillators, with phases chosen to amplify a circulating mode in the linear system. A cubic non-linear effect caps the amplified mode's runaway growth, producing steady motion circling the same way.

Using space-time symmetry, the team reduces the motion to a single averaged equation. It predicts non-linear paths, steady sizes, and typical timescales of the full three-body system. The chiral states hold finite basins of attraction and are reachable from wide starting conditions and parameters. Finite-element simulations of elastic plate resonators reproduce these features, showing linear time-modulated virtues like one-way spin and one-way amplification persist into strongly non-linear regimes.
arxiv-2602-22613:
Minh Kha Do and seven co-authors bring vision-language models to satellite imagery without demanding full multi-spectral input. Operational satellites often lack complete spectral coverage, so RGB-only inference matters for scale, yet two hurdles block adoption: spectral bands are redundant and misaligned, and CLIP-style text encoders blunt fine-grained meaning.

Their system, SATtxt, learns spectral cues in training but needs only RGB at inference. A distillation stage moves spectral knowledge from a frozen multi-spectral teacher into an RGB student through a light projector. A second alignment stage then bridges that visual space to an expressive language-model embedding space. On EuroSAT, BigEarthNet, and ForestNet, SATtxt lifted zero-shot classification about four percent, retrieval about six percent, and linear probing about three percent over baselines.
arxiv-2602-22713:
Xiang Yin offers a newcomer-friendly tour of opacity in discrete event systems, a confidentiality idea for information-flow security. Opacity demands that an outside watcher never learn for certain whether a system is, was, or will be in a secret state. The article centres on core definitions and one unifying lens: estimation.

Readers meet the main verification techniques and see how different observation models reshape both the problem and its algorithms. Enforcement styles range from supervisory control that guards opacity to sensor activation, information-release tuning, and obfuscation or editing tricks. Richer models get their due too, from stochastic and timed systems to Petri nets and hybrid dynamics, plus uses in robotics, location privacy, and information services, ending with open challenges.
arxiv-2602-22813:
Cong Ye and three co-authors design machine-made music rewards that stay safe and checkable for touchy listeners. In autism, hearing varies widely person to person, so keeping interest without risking safety is hard. Past music systems bury safety inside direct input-output mappings, keeping novelty but hiding conduct from guessing or audit.

Their constraint-first Input-Envelope-Output setup makes safety open and checkable while keeping action-output cause links intact. A low-risk cover layer sits between input and audio output, stating safe bounds, holding them strictly, and logging step-ins for audit. Four checkable rules follow, shown in MusiBubbles, a web demo, with a rerun package for use in autism and other touchy domains.
arxiv-2602-23013:
Camile Lendering and two co-authors ask whether few-shot anomaly detection needs its usual complexity. Industrial inspection often has only a few normal images per category, and recent methods lean on memory banks, auxiliary datasets, or multi-modal tuning of vision-language models. SubspaceAD instead works training-free in two simple stages.

Patch-level features come from a small set of normal images through a frozen DINOv2 backbone, then a principal component analysis model fits the low-dimensional subspace of normal variation. At inference, anomalies score by reconstruction residual against that subspace, giving interpretable, statistically grounded scores. One-shot results reach about ninety-seven percent image- and pixel-level AUROC on MVTec-AD. On VisA they reach about ninety-three and ninety-eight percent, surpassing prior state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2602-23413:
Shu Liu and 16 co-authors introduce EvoX, an adaptive method that tunes its own search process for automated discovery. Combining language-model search with evolution-style search has improved programs, prompts, and algorithms, as AlphaEvolve showed. But success rests on search plans, how past answers are picked and changed. Most methods use fixed plans with set knobs that cannot shift across tasks or even within one task as the search space shifts.

EvoX jointly evolves candidate answers and the search plans that generate them, steadily updating picks and changes as it learns. The system can thus switch plans mid-run as the search goes on. Across nearly 200 real-world tasks, EvoX beats existing AI-driven search methods, including AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve, GEPA, and ShinkaEvolve, on the majority of tasks, showing that evolving the evolver pays off.
arxiv-2602-23713:
Michael Krivelevich and two co-authors give sufficient conditions for graph rigidity, with applications to random graphs. A graph is d-rigid if, for an embedding of its vertices in d-dimensional space, every edge-length preserving motion preserves distances between non-adjacent pairs.

The team shows a constant c exists such that, for p at least two log n over n, the binomial random graph is with high probability floor of c n p-rigid. That is sharp up to the constant c, complementing Peled and Peleg and Jordan, Liu, and Villanyi. For d at least 2 and r at least 501 d, an r-regular graph is with high probability d-rigid. For p between 100 over n and two log n over n, the random graph holds with high probability a floor of n p over 251-rigid subgraph. A sufficient condition for rigidity via codegree generalizes Whiteley's splitting lemmas.
arxiv-2602-24013:
Gustav Schmidt and two co-authors present an ordinal diffusion model for generating color fundus images that respects the ordered stages of diabetic retinopathy. The 2026 paper notes that most conditional diffusion models treat disease stages as unrelated classes, ignoring that retinopathy progresses continuously.

Instead of categorical conditioning, the model uses a scalar disease representation, enabling smooth transitions between neighboring stages. Tests on a large eye-image dataset use visual realism metrics and classification-based clinical consistency checks. Compared with a standard conditional model, the ordinal model improves image realism for most disease stages and raises agreement between generated images and their intended stage. Put plainly, the model treats the disease as one slow shift, not a set of boxes. That view matches how the disease moves in real eyes.
arxiv-2602-24213:
Indranil Biswas and two co-authors prove results on finite-energy equivariant minimal immersions in complex hyperbolic two-space, with cusp ends of a fixed-lift proper type. The 2026 paper studies equivariant harmonic maps from a finite-type hyperbolic Riemann surface, asking when such maps eventually leave every compact set of the target near each puncture.

The answer is clean: fixed-lift properness at every puncture holds exactly when holonomy is parabolic. For conformal immersions, parabolic holonomy at every puncture also implies completeness of the induced metric. The authors further show that for polystable parabolic Higgs bundles with local data and weakly conformal harmonic maps, the ends are unbranched, complete, and finite-energy. Stability for mixed conformal data equals two parabolic slope inequalities. Explicit constructions for higher puncture counts yield mixed unbranched examples.
arxiv-2603-00013: Hillebrecht's team takes a first step linking input-to-state stability of endless-space systems to their finite approximations. Code-based methods need that link, but rigour had not shown it. They focus on linear boundary control systems whose growth follows an analytic semigroup. For those systems they show those gains can be worked out from stand-ins. A one-dimensional heat equation with Dirichlet edge control, whose reference gains are known, shows the findings.
arxiv-2603-00113: Li and Tao argue language-model agents alone are not yet enough for social simulation. Role-play plausibility does not guarantee faithful human behaviour, and group outcomes often hinge on agent-environment interplay rather than agent-to-agent messages alone. Results can also be swayed by interaction rules, scheduling and starting information. The authors recast social simulation with agents as a Markov game set in an environment, with open exposure and scheduling machinery, yielding concrete guidance for design, evaluation and interpretation.
arxiv-2603-00413: Li and five colleagues rebuild transparent objects from multi view photos, a hard task because light bends and scatters in complex ways. Their DiffTrans framework first shapes a rough geometry from object silhouettes with a flexible surface model, then recovers scene lighting. A recursive ray tracer then refines shape, refraction, and absorption together in one end to end pass, running fast on graphics hardware. Tests on several benchmarks beat rival methods, most clearly in tangled scenes with varied shapes and textures.
arxiv-2603-00513: Verma, Kumar, and Arya steer underactuated surface vessels along any smooth path with one integrated guidance and control law, replacing the usual two loop split. Their pursuit style method treats the path as a stream of moving virtual targets and aligns the vessel velocity with the line of sight to the target ahead, creating a tail chase. The design respects asymmetric actuator limits, and sliding mode control within a nonlinear framework widens the operating envelope. The paper also analyses stability of the proposed law.
arxiv-2603-00713: Fabini, Pascucci, and Rondelli model home energy trading with storage as a kinetic mean field control problem for a coordinator of many home batteries. The coordinator pays households for direct battery control, aiming to cut local supply demand gaps and profit from intraday price swings. Charge level plays the role of position, charging power of speed, and control of speeding up, encoding ramp limits and smooth power paths. The resulting McKean-Vlasov Langevin system lets drift and goals depend on the group law, capturing interaction effects and stabilisation payoffs.
arxiv-2603-01013: Hauptmann and Kramer debias surveys without wrecking already-representative variables, a flaw of methods that reshape the whole sample for a few skewed features. Their feature-weighted subsampling down-weights highly biased features when computing sample weights, keeping more cases for later analysis. On eight artificially biased tabular sets and one real social-science set, it matches rivals on downstream generalization with no significant loss.
arxiv-2603-01213: Berdoz, Rugli, and Wattenhofer test whether language-model agents can agree in adversarial consensus games over numbers. In a no-stake setting where agents hold no preferences about the final value, valid agreement proves unreliable even without attackers and worsens as groups grow. Adding a few Byzantine agents cuts success further, with failures coming from timeouts and stalled convergence, not from quiet value tampering, warning against deployments that assume robust coordination.
arxiv-2603-01313: Distler and eleven colleagues age-date KELT-20, a young A-type star hosting a well-aligned ultra-hot Jupiter, using Gaia DR3 data. They spot 77 stars with proper motions matching KELT-20, including 19 with seen radial speeds giving full 3D motion proof. Using age-curve checks, spin-age, light shifts, and stellar action signs, they converge on an age of 58 plus or minus 5 million years. That constraint clarifies hot Jupiter birth and early drift paths.
arxiv-2603-02013:
Matthias Aschenbrenner, Lou van den Dries, and Joris van der Hoeven revisit a class of equations in this 2026 mathematics paper. The equations are second-order linear ones with rates of change as terms. Their input functions come from Hardy fields, which force very calm long-term growth. Such inputs cannot wiggle wildly, yet solutions can still swing up and down.

The authors prove a guess made by Boshernitzan in 1982 about those swinging solutions. Each swing can be split into a size part and a phase part. Both parts live in a larger Hardy field, so the swings stay highly regular. They give sharp rules for when those parts are unique. They also trace the swings' long-term path, zeros, and peak points.
arxiv-2603-02913:
Julianna Piskorz, Katarzyna Kobalczyk, and Mihaela van der Schaar ask whether a language model's number forecasts can be read from its insides. Language models now tackle regression tasks like forecasting, but sampling their word-by-word output many times to build a distribution is slow and costly. Their 2026 paper looks for a shortcut.

Small probes trained on the model's internal signals predict summary values of its output distribution directly, such as the mean, median, and quantiles. The signals carried real information about those summaries, including the model's own uncertainty. The finding suggests cheap, sampling-free uncertainty estimates may be feasible for numerical predictions. It also raises fresh questions about how models quietly encode doubt about numbers.
arxiv-2603-03313:
Minghua Wu and three colleagues probe a weakness of large language models called the embodiment gap. Models learn from text, so their sense of how words feel, move, or sound often drifts from human bodily experience. The 2026 study asks whether focused fine-tuning with human ratings can pull those internal representations closer to human ones.

Using similarity analysis across concepts, the team finds fine-tuning reorganizes the model's semantic space in a targeted way rather than lifting everything evenly. Which base model started best barely predicts which tuned model ends best. Gains carry across languages and related senses, yet fail to transfer when the task format changes sharply. The results show model representations stay surprisingly flexible under the right supervision.
arxiv-2603-03413:
Giorgio Ottaviani's lecture notes tour classical invariant theory from musical ratios to tilings. Expanded from lectures at a 2025 summer school in Tromsø, Norway, the notes connect binary quartics and ternary cubics through their harmonic and equianharmonic invariants. They then carry the analogy onward to modular forms. Harmonic quadruples, the opening topic, reach back to Pythagorean tuning and the cross-ratio.

Triangle groups appear in both elliptic and hyperbolic settings, together with their associated tilings. A short Hilbert paper on polynomials that are powers gets a full discussion, originally set as work for the school's participants. The appendix collects exercises with sketched solutions, plus a section on Pfaffians edited by Vincenzo Galgano. The notes serve readers meeting invariant theory's classical roots with modern eyes.
arxiv-2603-03813:
Aaron L Galper and seven colleagues study the flaws in a crystal made of beads squeezed between plates. Confined to a gap barely wider than one particle, colloids buckle into up or down states, and neighbors prefer opposite states, like antiferromagnetic spins. On the nearly triangular lattice, trios of neighbors frustrate each other: no arrangement satisfies everyone. Their 2026 paper catalogs the topological defects of this two-level order.

Two orders coexist, the positions of the triangular lattice and the up-down spin pattern above it, and each grows its own defects. Both kinds shape grain boundaries and the coarsening of spin domains. The team classifies the spin defects, writes basic rules for their motion, watches dislocations interact with spin defects, and maps which defects drive the coarsening dynamics. The buckled monolayer becomes a laboratory for frustrated, self-assembled matter.
arxiv-2603-04013: Damiani and colleagues propose a core calculus for type-safe product lines of C programs. They define Lightweight C, a core calculus formalizing a proper subset of ANSI C without preprocessor directives, and Colored LC, which adds those directives. They then define a type system for Colored LC guaranteeing every program generated by the C preprocessor is a well-typed C program. The simple formalization may also serve teaching purposes. The paper fits Berardi's research and teaching profile, spanning logical foundations, type-based analysis, and C courses.
arxiv-2603-04113: Avci and others study demographic predictability in brain MRI via disentangled anatomy and acquisition. Medical images allow demographic output, raising bias concerns, and X-ray acquisition contributes substantially, yet brain MRI was unclear. Across three data, predictability is driven primarily by anatomy, with contrast embeddings holding a weaker signal that does not extend.
arxiv-2603-04213: Tenzler and others design a monolithic source of photon pairs with a semiconductor laser and a Bragg reflection waveguide. They propose a monolithic, power-driven photon-pair source built around a non-linear AlGaAs Bragg reflection waveguide with a laser structure stacked on top. Since the Bragg reflection waveguide needs no doping in this vertically coupled design, free-carrier absorption losses and parasitic luminescence disappear.
arxiv-2603-04413: Perez and colleagues judge meaning in language model summaries with ICR. Meaning is relational and emergent from sign systems, not fixed word to concept maps. The paper reviews signs in static and contextual embeddings and gaps between statistics and human reading. ICR uses inductive content analysis and reflexive thematic analysis to score semantic accuracy beyond word overlap. Across five sets, models match humans on word similarity but lag on semantic accuracy, above all for grounded meanings.
arxiv-2603-04513: Joseph and colleagues tighten supernova bounds for Higgs-mixed CP-even scalars. Supernovae probe weakly coupled MeV particles beyond lab reach. An updated production rate improves the cooling bound by over an order of magnitude, joined by decay constraints from galactic positron flux and low energy Type II-P supernova energy deposition. Together they probe mixing angles as small as 10^-9, over five orders below collider bounds. A hadrophilic model constrains Yukawa couplings near 10^-10, and combined probes cover over nine orders of magnitude in coupling.
arxiv-2603-04613: So and colleagues rethink interface metaphors for language models beyond anthropomorphism. People naturally humanize chat tech, and interfaces make large language models most human. Human-like interfaces stress likeness while hiding key gaps, so users take the metaphor as fact. Users then treat models as truly human, breeding delusion and harm with few safeguards. The paper treats anthropomorphism as a design knob, with a spectrum from transparency-driven anti-anthropomorphism to uncanny hyper-anthropomorphism. The spectrum exposes models as sociotechnical systems shaped by labor, infrastructure, and data.
arxiv-2603-04713: Cardoso and colleagues present AstroInspect, a web-based system to inspect astronomical objects. Growth in imaging and spectra surveys raises the need for checks. Old tools often demand many platforms and complex workflows. AstroInspect offers access to astronomical resources through a GUI for adding lists by sky coords. It adds to lists with imaging, spectra, and photo data from SDSS, the Legacy Surveys, and S-PLUS. As an example, AstroInspect identified H-alpha emission-line galaxies in a 7 deg radius toward the Hydra I cluster, giving 80 proven galaxies from 981 picks.
arxiv-2603-05213: Marvin Lavechin and team build BabAR, a cross-linguistic phoneme recognizer for young children's speech, trained on TinyVox, their corpus of over half a million transcribed child vocalizations in five languages. Training first on multilingual child-centered daylong recordings beats alternatives by far, and adding twenty seconds of nearby audio during fine-tuning raises scores further. Errors fall mostly in the same broad phonetic categories, suggesting the system suits coarse-grained developmental analysis. Its auto speech-maturity measures match figures from the literature, validating BabAR for studying speech at scale.
arxiv-2603-05313: Saurav Kantha and Nicolas Laflorencie study strong zero modes in Ising-Majorana chains, using trueness for zero-mode operators mapping the spectrum between parity sectors. In clean systems trueness is unity topologically, zero trivially, and wide at Ising criticality. Quenched disorder modifies this picture. In microcanonical and canonical ensembles, zero modes persist in the phase, including the Griffiths regime, nearing unity. At the fixed point, trueness turns ensemble dependent: one ensemble bimodal, the other triple-peaked. Trueness is thus a robust sign of localization-protected order, revealing distinctive features.
arxiv-2603-05813: Sun and colleagues treat accent variation as an interpretable subspace inside hidden representations of speech recognition models. Most adaptation methods fine-tune parameters without locating where accent information lives. The authors extract encoder activations layer by layer and estimate mean-shift directions for accent-induced shifts. Injecting those directions layer by layer shows accent information clustering in middle encoder layers. Building on that structure, they introduce parameter-free steering that reshapes representations during inference without updating weights. Tests across eight accents show steady word error rate cuts.
arxiv-2603-06613: Mastromichalakis presents OptiRoulette, a meta-optimizer picking update rules during training instead of fixing one. It combines locking, random sampling from a pool, learning-rate scaling during swaps, and swap-out. Built as a torch-ready component packaged for setup, it reports seed results on five suites: SVHN, Tiny ImageNet, Caltech-256, CIFAR-100, and CIFAR-100-C. Against an AdamW baseline, It improves test accuracy on all five suites, with advantage in closing reliability at higher targets. It reaches targets in all runs while the rival reaches none.
arxiv-2603-06713: Karan Gupta and colleagues present ATLAS, a reinforcement fine-tuning frame that lets small language models work with very large tool sets. Instead of loading all tools at once, the model learns when to load tools step by step. It also learns to chain them in code, which bounds context growth and steadies long tasks. Success is split into rubric criteria scored by small judge models, and a 4B model nears frontier-agent scores.
arxiv-2603-06813: Malenfant connects decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning to ongoing learning: peer updates change each focal agent's rewards and dynamics even when the joint game stays fixed. A stable core captures abstract patterns shared by many successful runs, while survival tracks a pattern's coverage, not an unchanged frontier. A conditioning limit caps coverage loss in terms of run-law drift and reference success share. Combined with peer-policy movement, that limit proves survival under bounded peer updates with positive coverage margin. An effective-conflict rule yields a first-exit law.
arxiv-2603-07013: Wei and Zhang study whether answers exist and behave for a wide-range parabolic MEMS rule with Dirichlet edge rules. Using tool groups and a shrinking map rule, they prove being with a cutoff test. Under small size rules on power and first data, being and fast settling to the state follow. If the answer stays clear of the break point, the system forms a slope system. Showing smoothness of the energy and a Łojasiewicz-Simon bound, they prove settling to a steady state at a fast or power rate.
arxiv-2603-07213: Grasselli and colleagues build a random macro-money model joining debt price falls and Ponzi-type unrest with a jump-spread stock market. The economic block feeds on a stochastic interest rate tied to asset returns. The market block carries endogenous, state-dependent jump intensities driven by speculative credit flows. Together they formalize a feedback loop among credit expansion, crash risk, perceived returns, and bank lending spreads. Under suitable setting limits, the coupled system exists as a whole without blowup, and models span stable growth to repeat boom-bust regimes.
arxiv-2603-07513: Ashraf and colleagues build Bolbosh, the first special open-source neural text-to-speech system for Kashmiri. Zero-shot multilingual rivals fail on the language, largely mishandling Perso-Arabic diacritics and local sound patterns. Bolbosh adapts cross-lingually with script-aware flow matching, expands its vocabulary for Kashmiri graphemes, and cleans varied speech through echo removal, trimming and loudness control. It clearly beats the baselines and sets a new benchmark for the language.
arxiv-2603-07613: Bozorgnia and Eshkobilov study an inverse spectral problem for the p-Laplacian with Robin and mixed boundary data. The unknown coefficient sits on a hidden Robin patch, while data are the main eigenvalue and nonlinear flux on an open Dirichlet patch. For a thin coating they prove convergence to an effective Robin problem, with bounds, a single answer, stability and smoothness of the value map. Other cases are identified under linkage and smoothness rules.
arxiv-2603-08013: Chai and colleagues move GUI agents from reactive to proactive, a smart assistant should foresee user intents from continuous visual input and offer timely tips without explicit prompting. Current agents wait for orders, yet real screen activity runs long, noisy, and multithreaded. Their PIRA-Bench evaluates multimodal large language models on continuous, weakly supervised visual inputs, featuring complex trajectories with interleaved intents and noisy segments. The PIRF baseline helps general models manage multiple task threads and handle misleading visual inputs.
arxiv-2603-08213: Rabefihavanana and colleagues introduce a new family of stabilizer quantum LDPC codes built from the classical linear codes L_k and L_k^+, defined via sub-exceding functions. In earlier work these codes showed strong minimum distance, fast decoding, and simple structure. By joining the hypergraph product with a generalized Shor construction, the authors obtain a growing class of quantum codes with parameters [[6k^2, k^2, d]]. The new codes show rich combinatorial structure and promise for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2603-08513: Nikhil Bisht and David Collins train a gradient-boosted model to guess which gas parcels in stormy, magnetized clouds will form stars. Fed snapshots from cloud runs of place, speed, density, and field strength, it tracks parcels well and ranks collapse risk with high skill. Yet the point-wise view lacks the local context real collapse checks need, so the authors call for spatial designs.
arxiv-2603-08613: Alex Myhill and David Al-Attar code synthetic quake records for round, self-gravitating planets that do not spin. Past direct-solution codes used a potential form in fluid zones, but their displacement form runs throughout, letting gravity and any fluid layering be handled in full. Their DSpecM1D code matches the MINEOS and YSpec codes closely on both elastic and anelastic models.
arxiv-2603-08813: Kivokurtseva studies axion-neutrino couplings in mass models with two seesaw types, Type-I and inverse. The effective coupling ties to the axion scale and can be bounded by star limits on axion-electron couplings. In the allowed range, axion-driven scattering barely dents neutrino travel, leaving no visible signs at today's reach.
arxiv-2603-08913: Alexander Nemecek and colleagues gauge how genome models recall their training DNA. Models trained on private cohorts risk leaking exact strings, yet genome recall had few careful checks. Their multi-vector audit blends surprise detection, canary extraction, and membership guessing into one worst-case score, finding real recall that varies by design and training regime.
arxiv-2603-09313: Shivam Raval and colleagues question linear steering of language model behavior, arguing activation spaces are not globally linear. Measuring distortion as the ratio of geodesic to Euclidean distance, they find large, concept-dependent warping. Their Curveball steering instead acts in a polynomial kernel PCA feature space that better fits the learned geometry. It beats linear PCA-based steering across the board, most clearly where distortion is strongest, offering a geometry-aware path for control.
arxiv-2603-09713: Subhadip Mondal, Atul Kumar and Srihari Keshavamurthy study whether light in an optical cavity can steer chemical product choice. Their model treats reactions that split after a transition state, where two products compete. Classical and quantum calculations show strong vibrational coupling can nearly double one branching share. Which cavity frequency works best shifts when the shape of the energy surface changes.
arxiv-2603-09813: Joseph O'Rourke revisits whether prismatoids can be cut along their edges and laid flat without overlap, a case of Dürer's open problem. Nested prismatoids were settled recently by mixing two natural unfoldings. Band unfolding alone fails on one known counterexample. He characterises when band unfolding works for nested shapes and shows that example is, in a sense, the only possible failure.
arxiv-2603-09913: Carlos Ortega-Taberner, Eoin O'Neill and Paul Eastham show that shaping a qubit's link to its environment can reset the qubit very fast. Reset speed and quality are normally capped by entanglement built up with that environment. Exact tensor network simulations trace the cap to a polaron state that forms during reset. A time dependent coupling can undo that state, reaching tiny leftover excitation in ten nanoseconds.
arxiv-2603-10113: Joseph DeRose and coauthors ask how sparse weak lensing source samples can be without losing cosmological power. Combining lensing and clustering in three by two point analyses, they model redshift uncertainty, intrinsic alignments and baryonic physics flexibly. With current baryon uncertainty, information saturates on quasi linear scales, so much thinner source samples suffice if redshift means are calibrated tightly. That sparseness opens direct redshift calibration with wide field spectroscopy.
arxiv-2603-10213: Laitz and coauthors present Sabiá-4 and Sabiazinho-4, a new set of Portuguese language models centred on Brazilian Portuguese. Training runs in four stages: more pre training on Portuguese corpora and Brazilian legal texts, long context growth, fine tuning on taught data, and preference alignment. Tests span chat, Brazilian law, long context reading, taught task following, exams and agentic tool use. The pair offer a good cost to score balance against rival models.
