arxiv-2605-19413: Mátéfy and colleagues characterize Gaia21bja, a young star flagged by Gaia that brightened at least seven times over twenty years. Each outburst lasted one and a half to two years and reached about 1.7 magnitudes in Gaia light. A period search finds a leading cycle near 916 days, and burst spectra resemble EX Lupi-type eruptive young stars. Accretion light and inflow rose roughly sixfold during bursts, supporting a verdict of an eruptive young star in the periodic outburst class.
arxiv-2605-19913: Xu and Jia study in theory bright exciton polariton pulses in microcavities built to support bound states in the continuum. A driven lossy Gross-Pitaevskii equation coupled to a bath rate rule shows bound states steady the cloud against light decay. A Lagrangian approach yields rules for pulse path and speed. Notably, travel slows on its own, bringing pulses to a halt at a final spot set by the setup and built in values. Checks round out a picture for steering light matter flows in open systems.
arxiv-2605-20013: Shokoufe Faraji and Samir Mathur argue that near the surface of an exotic compact object, vacuum Einstein equations yield a chaotic metric. Such an object is a black-hole alternative with large but finite redshift. Oscillations grow as the surface approaches, in a pattern resembling cosmic billiards near the big bang, except some potential walls turn into cliffs and squeeze compact directions to zero size. In string theory that squeezing naturally continues into fuzzball interiors, where collapsing directions create monopoles.
arxiv-2605-20113: J. C. Gonçalves-Dosantos, R. Martínez and J. Sánchez-Soriano propose null player neutrality for TU-games. The axiom weakens strategic equivalence, asking only that any payoff change from adding a null-player game be independent of the added game, when null-player condition and grand-coalition value hold. Efficiency, linearity, symmetry and null player neutrality give every mix of Shapley value with equal division. That result extends the alpha-egalitarian Shapley values to arbitrary real alpha. For nullifying players, the analogue pins down equal division alone.
arxiv-2605-20213: Siddharth Karuturi studies phase shifts in turnpike theory for mean-field games. The game uses a smooth, even, mean-zero kernel, linearized around the uniform state into mode systems. When the kernel transform turns negative, a finite threshold marks loss of stability, else infinite. Near it, the gap scales like the square root of the distance to it, and below it the uniform state is exponentially stable. At the threshold the gap closes and decay turns algebraic, while above it nonuniform states split off through a pitchfork equation.
arxiv-2605-20613: Guan Wang and eight colleagues present HRM-Text, a bid to pretrain language models efficiently without internet-scale compute. It displaces standard transformers with a hierarchical recurrent model that splits slow strategic work from fast execution. MagicNorm and warmup credit assignment stabilize the deep recurrence, and training uses instruction-response pairs only. A one-billion-parameter model trained on 40 billion tokens for 1,500 dollars reached 60.7 percent on MMLU and 84.5 percent on GSM8K.
arxiv-2605-20713: Miaobo Hu and seven colleagues present SAVER, a selective vision method for multimodal information extraction from social media. Posts often attach images that are weakly related, redundant, or misleading, so always fusing vision wastes compute and can amplify false cues. SAVER first decides, for each text span or entity pair, whether vision must be consulted at all. When it should, a relevance-diversity selector picks a small subset of images as trustworthy evidence.
arxiv-2605-21313: Divij Khaitan and Subhashis Banerjee propose a method to gauge robustness of deep neural nets to distribution shifts, via weight-activation links. Those links are modeled with Bernoulli spreads, and class separation serves as a proxy for robustness. Tests on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show their metrics tell memorized nets apart from non-memorized ones. Parallel tests in activation space lack the same traits. Under varied shifts, separation shrinks under their path-based checks.
arxiv-2605-21513: Amirali Fatehizadeh investigates the natural density of monic integer polynomials with roots in a fixed number field. He studies monic integer polynomials of degree n having at least one root in a fixed number field K. Although thin-set theory implies the natural density of this family in bounded-height parameter space is zero, quantifying the vanishing rate is a central challenge in arithmetic statistics. Using Mahler measure, Dirichlet's unit theorem, and residue analysis of the Dedekind zeta function, he shows the rate depends strictly on degree n.
arxiv-2605-21813: Ziwen Liu and Meng Li introduce symbolic density estimation, a method that recovers closed-form mass functions by joining basic analytic steps in a search space. Field-specific priors guide evolutionary search and a validity-checked inference stage, and the approach extends to zero inflation and finite mixtures. The authors offer a benchmark spanning many discrete laws, and their method recovers all benchmark families with accurate parameter values. A real-data test finds concise, clear mixture models that beat standard models on goodness-of-fit.
arxiv-2605-22813: Kelman, Meir, and Zheng study testing Reed-Muller codes under an online adversary. The task is to tell whether a function lies in the code or far from it. After each query, the adversary may erase points of the input. The authors define semi-sample-based testers, which choose a subset of the domain and query inside it at random. They prove optimal soundness for these testers. This yields optimal query complexity under online erasures, and the testers extend to lifted affine-invariant codes.
arxiv-2605-23513: Foster, Knight, and Krapohl extend introspection dynamics to additive games with mutation and player-specific selection strengths. In introspection dynamics, each player weighs payoffs across actions. Earlier work showed the long-run distribution is a product measure without mutation. They show the product form survives mutation, and they derive each player's cooperation chance in closed form. For varied public goods games they give a total formula, with a cooperation threshold, a neutral-drift regime set by mutation bias, and a mutation-selection balance that holds in the strong-selection limit.
arxiv-2605-23613: Montag and Ozawa formulate non-Hermitian Landau levels in two-dimensional systems under a complex perpendicular magnetic field. In the symmetric gauge they derive spaced, highly degenerate complex spectra and biorthogonal eigenstates, clarifying non-unitary gauge transforms. A non-Hermitian Harper-Hofstadter lattice model confirms the continuum theory and reveals Gaussian packet motion driven by semiclassical rules with a complex Lorentz force. The work points toward possible lab realizations of complex magnetic fields.
arxiv-2605-23913: Wang and eight colleagues ask whether small adapters trained on private edge devices can be merged in the cloud for problems spanning several fields. Their prune-train-recover scheme lets edge devices train LoRA adapters, small tuning modules for a large language model, on trimmed models. They also add MMLU-CD, a test that mixes fields in single items. Existing fusion methods failed that test, often scoring below the base model, because adapter updates clashed. A new conflict-fix module, LoRA-CR, lifted fusion scores by up to 3.8 percent.
arxiv-2605-24213: Zhao and four co-authors study 57 machine-learning test harnesses, building a five-stage harness model and sorting over sixteen thousand issues by stage and root cause. Most day-to-day trouble clusters in the spec stage, about two-fifths of issues, where harnesses tie together outside models, data sets, and scoring judges. The top root causes are missing features, doc gaps, and missing input checks, about three-fifths of sorted issues. By stage, environment and dependency breaks lead setup, while code error and check gaps lead grading.
arxiv-2605-24313: Khanday and four co-authors test cortex speech reading without outside models. Current top speech aids reach low word error rates but lean on outside models at inference, adding memory and latency. Their Conformer decoder trains straight on cortex signals from an ALS patient and reaches about 24 percent letter error on held-out validation. Scores swing with inter-session signal decay, while main errors come from wrong word-boundary splits. The results show good letter-level reading is doable end-to-end, giving a strong signal for downstream language work.
arxiv-2605-24413: Low and four co-authors launch Habermolt, a public platform where AI agents deliberate for human users, a setup they call AI-delegated deliberation. Deliberative democracy promises better collective choices but runs up against human attention and time. Recent AI-mediated deliberation scales input synthesis yet still eats user time, while newer systems let agents speak for users. Habermolt is tested on three fronts: representation, aggregation, and revision. The observations flag design choices future platforms must face, adding to the agenda for scalable yet trustworthy AI representatives.
arxiv-2605-24513: Zhuanghua Liu and Luo Luo study optimization where only noisy function values are available, not gradients, and the noise has heavy tails. Their stochastic zeroth-order method clips a two-point gradient estimate inside an online-to-nonconvex conversion scheme. Theory shows it reaches a Goldstein stationary point with dimension dependence matching the best known convex results. Its accuracy dependence matches the best known first-order methods for nonconvex nonsmooth problems, and experiments confirm the method works.
arxiv-2605-25013: Parsa Bakhtary studies how many new rays a smooth projective refinement must add for toric fans. For dimensions three and up, he builds a family of Picard number five with fixed combinatorial type. The minimum equals the smaller of two parameters, via ordinary invariant codimension-two blow-ups. With simplicial refinements capped at cone multiplicity mu, the minimum falls to the ceiling of that value divided by mu. A projectivization algorithm natural under lattice isomorphisms is also given.
arxiv-2605-25313: Santosh Kumar Radha and Oktay Goktas design a world model that imagines hidden futures as beliefs. Standard architectures compress belief into a plain vector, which cannot carry uncertainty through blind rollouts. Their Unitary World Model JEPA stores belief as a density matrix, predicting with a unitary step that preserves the state's spectrum. On a hidden-velocity task with masked observations, it reaches about 77 percent accuracy, while a vector baseline falls to about 53 percent throughout. Under blind rollout it loses little probe accuracy at short horizons, unlike vector baselines.
arxiv-2605-25413: Jiaquan Zhang and colleagues replace step-by-step rollout for time-dependent PDEs with continuous latent evolution. Standard neural operators feed each predicted state back as the next input, growing error over long horizons without time modeling. Their AFNO method maps time evolution into a latent space and learns its vector field with flow matching. That design enables steady evolution over long runs and handles varied physics settings through direct conditioning. Theory and tests on six equations show better long-horizon steadiness and smaller rollout errors than rivals.
arxiv-2605-25913: Ayeni tests two ways of reading energy from a Fibonacci anyon chain, a model of particles whose braiding can encode quantum information. Against grouped Pauli measurement, fusion readout wins for circuits driven by repeating pulses. For variational eigensolver circuits, Pauli measurement wins on error but loses on sampling spread. Ayeni derives scaling rules and the shot counts where each method becomes preferable.
arxiv-2605-26113: Zhang and eight colleagues generate steerable driving scenes from any top-down layout. Fake data matter for self-driving cars, above all for rare safety-critical cases, but current occupancy-guided methods steer weakly and lean on a fixed frame. AnyScene is a single occupancy-first system: a diffusion transformer reads top-down and occupancy traits jointly, step by step. That gives tight control from varied layouts and supports long runs. Later uses include sparse-view three-dimensional rebuilding.
arxiv-2605-26313: Hamed Alimohammadzadeh and three colleagues provide replication artifacts and instructions for Swarical, a swarm-based method that lets miniature flying light specks localize and light up complex shapes. Swarical pairs an offline planner, which turns mesh files into speck swarms using sensor specs, with an online localization technique running on each speck. Some specks stay dark and serve only for localization. The companion paper reports the online technique as fast and highly accurate, and shows how to reproduce that finding with the artifacts.
arxiv-2605-26413: Drago Plecko, Patrik Okanovic, Torsten Hoefler, and Elias Bareinboim propose detecting confounders by asking the expert behind treatment choices. Trials are costly and often ethically or practically blocked, while observational data hides variables steering treatment and outcome. Their design pairs units through matching, then asks the decider to compare each pair, drawing out unseen reasons for differing choices. Theory pins down when comparisons reveal confounders. A semi-synthetic intensive-care study using clinical notes as physician-knowledge proxy backs the method and finds such confounding in intensive-care records.
arxiv-2605-26613: Levi Van den Berg and Kenta Hotokezaka work out how decay particles ionize the glowing debris of neutron-star mergers. Alpha particles, beta electrons, and fission chunks all shape the late light of kilonovae, yet their ionizing power was never computed on one footing. The pair track cross sections, slowing, and charge change through expanding debris for each particle type. Surprisingly, the energy cost per ion pair comes out nearly the same across all channels. Late ionization thus barely depends on which decay rules heating.
arxiv-2605-26713: Kang, Lee, and Cheng prove, with an explicit step-by-step build, that transformers can carry out gradient descent aimed at the posterior predictive mean and variance for Gaussian process regression. The result is then turned into binned probabilities. They bound the error by attention depth and bin size, and show that normalization and depth control how far transformers reach past their training size range. Simulations back the theory and shed light on how prior-data fitted networks generalize.
arxiv-2605-26813: Li, Liu, and Batchelor solve the non-Hermitian XY spin chain with open boundaries and complex anisotropy exactly. They show the free-fermion form of the quasi-energy spectrum matches the Hermitian case and build the biorthogonal fermion basis away from exceptional points. At those points, where the Hamiltonian turns defective, they derive the Jordan normal form and generalized eigenvectors. Exceptional points act as branch points, swapping eigenstates when circled.
arxiv-2605-26913: In a 2026 piece, Mikhasenko surveys exotic hadron spectroscopy in heavy-flavor systems, where a dense run of finds has made new structures repeat finds rather than isolated surprises. Charm and bottom systems, with small widths and clean signatures, reveal patterns harder to isolate among light quarks. The review covers hidden-charm pentaquarks, charged charmonium-like states, onia-onia resonances, doubly-heavy tetraquarks, and open-flavor tetraquarks.
arxiv-2605-27013: Straitouri, Kim, and Tambe present a method that builds a portfolio of optimization models from natural language requests, rather than betting on a single model. One language model plays two roles, random maker and reasoning judge, in a unified setup. Theory shows the set holds high-quality options if either role aligns with human tastes, so humans can review before sign-off. Tests across modeling tasks show strong results.
arxiv-2605-27113: In a 2026 paper, Masi, Coletta, and Bartolini present a quality-aware generative method that mixes GAN and diffusion models for synthetic financial time series. Their CoMeTS-GAN jointly makes mid-price and volume series for linked stocks, and its Critic guides the process as a quality scoring module, forcing learned correlation patterns. The method offers a lightweight tool for stock market simulation, models inter-asset correlations. Tests show it captures market stylized facts and inter-asset links better than leading rival models.
arxiv-2605-27513: Marco Graziani and colleagues bound a light scalar that talks mainly to electrons, mediating for a Majorana dark matter particle. Combining freeze-out and freeze-in production with cosmological, astrophysical, and lab tests, they find a narrow viable region favoring sub-GeV dark matter. The study also probes the mediator mass near 17 MeV, motivated by ATOMKI and PADME hints, and sets clear targets for future tests.
arxiv-2605-27813: Yeung and colleagues adapt sparse autoencoders, which split a model's inner activations into interpretable features, to image-making diffusion models whose layers change step by step. Because each denoising step largely predicts the next, their ReSAE learns only the leftover each step fails to explain, plus the starting state. Its features then trace how an image forms over time and when each change enters.
arxiv-2605-27913: Safal Thapaliya, Jiatan Huang, and Chuxu Zhang study labels that language models assign to graph nodes, which often go wrong in patchy, cluster-shaped ways. Their CANE framework estimates which clusters of pseudo-labels to trust and which to fix, without any true labels to check against. Across graph benchmarks it beat the strongest label-free rivals, most where cluster noise ran strongest.
arxiv-2605-28013: Kim and colleagues build a safety benchmark for Korean multimodal models that goes beyond translated English tests. KSAFE-MM pairs global risks in Korean settings with culture-specific visual traps, then tests jailbreak prompts against twelve leading models. Jailbreaks sharply raised attack success, and safer models tended to over-refuse harmless queries.
arxiv-2605-28213: Zhang and colleagues teach GPU-kernel agents the missing when of optimization: not just what experts did, but when each trick applies. KLineage walks expert kernels backward through checked simplifications, turning each reversed step into a skill recording intent, conditions, effects, and pitfalls. On five expert workloads it beat memory-based rivals in kernel quality and efficiency.
arxiv-2605-28313: Nicolás Benjamín Ocampo, Agnes Paullate Nyiranziza, and Davide Ceolin test whether language models can rank argument quality like humans. Twelve open-weight models judged pairwise comparisons across logical, rhetorical, and dialectical dimensions, feeding a Bradley-Terry ranking. Alignment proved promising but moderate, strongest for the largest Llama model, with stable predictions across runs.
arxiv-2605-28513: Lei, Wang, and Yuan give the first non-vacuous generalization analysis of SVRG, stochastic variance reduced gradient. Existing theory for variance-reduction methods stresses convergence, leaving generalization largely unexplored. Through algorithmic stability they prove sharp stability bounds in convex and strongly convex settings, with data-dependent bounds that fold training errors along the path into the analysis. The work clarifies how optimization and generalization interact, yielding optimal excess population risk bounds, and extends to the SAGA method.
arxiv-2605-28613: Jingzhe Wang and Hung-Hsu Chou study low-rank bias in matrix factorization, a model of gradient training. In the clean setting they derive spectral rules for gradient descent to show a real low-rank window, showing how spectrum, start, and step size set a low-rank phase. With an added nudge to the target matrix, they show settling and measure step cost and eigenvalue return. They further show the low-rank phase stays stable under nudge, with rank near the clean rank-L version over a nudged window.
arxiv-2605-29013: Yi Yang, Victor Lopez, and Matthias Müller propose moving horizon training for feedforward networks with ReLU units, treating weights as system states. For two-layer networks with fixed output weights, they derive a condition for observability, ensuring local observability. Multi-layer networks in general fail that condition. An exciting input design renders states distinct from neighbors, and local observability gives convergence, with only the observable part updating over a fixed data window.
arxiv-2605-29813: Afsoon Alidadi Shamsabadi, Animesh Yadav, and Halim Yanikomeroglu tackle interference in high-altitude platform networks, where stratospheric stations beam to ground users. Strong line-of-sight links leave little channel variety, so users interfere more keenly. The team serves many users from one platform over several beams and limited orthogonal resource blocks. Their frame groups users by angle, shapes beams per group, assigns blocks across groups, and splits rates within blocks to ease clash. Simulations show the combined clustering and rate-splitting design beats baselines on per-user spectral efficiency.
arxiv-2605-30013: Simon Apers, Jérémie Roland and Yuxin Zhang sharpen electric flow sampling, a quantum walk tool for graph problems, by building an error-free transducer for it. They extend the trick to reflecting about the meeting point of two subspaces, giving an error-free version of the effective gap lemma. From there they derive quantum walk methods for estimating effective resistances and witness sizes with optimal error scaling, and for sampling arrival distributions. The last method yields up to a quadratic speedup for semi-supervised learning on expander graphs.
arxiv-2605-30213: Benjamin Walker and four co-authors present faithful embeddings of irregular and asynchronous data for online Log-NCDEs. Interpolation- and imputation-based embeddings rebuild a path, making models sensitive to rebuild quality. That step is needless, they show: under mild conditions, model power transfers when the embedding is continuous and injective. Building on the rectilinear control path, they present a Log-NCDE embedding logging observations as steps, built into log-signatures over query spans. Tests show speed and toughness on irregular, async and sparse observations.
arxiv-2605-30313: Yufei Jia and 49 co-authors present UniLab, a CPU/GPU architecture decoupling CPU simulation from GPU updates through a runtime. They ask whether throughput, policy learning, and runtime sync form one efficient loop, rather than which processor runs physics. UniLab is implemented as a training system using CPU-batched physics backends, supporting PPO, FastSAC, FlashSAC, and APPO. On robot control tasks, UniLab improves training efficiency by three to tenfold under the same hardware. It reduces dependence on the CUDA software stack and supports cross-platform execution.
arxiv-2605-30413: Antonio Delgado and Seth Koren present an SU(12) by SU(2) by U(1) model joining SU(9) quark color-flavor with SU(3) lepton flavor. They start with one yukawa shared by unified up-type quarks and neutrinos. Gauged quark color-flavor and lepton flavor instantons make the bottom and tau yukawas on the fly, giving a massless quark fix to the strong CP problem. Only two new scalar irreps are needed. The Standard Model gauge group emerges with a discrete gauge symmetry X and locks the proton absolutely stable.
arxiv-2605-30813: Jiang and Gong propose stepwise Byte Pair Encoding tokenization, handling each input byte in log-squared time. The algorithm maintains tokenization results for every input prefix, using the standard merge procedure. This enables partial tokenization in streaming settings. As a drop-in replacement for standard Byte Pair Encoding, it runs up to about three times faster than Hugging Face's tokenizers. It also significantly reduces latency over OpenAI's tiktoken on pathological inputs. An eager output algorithm enables streaming output, emitting tokens as soon as boundaries are determined.
arxiv-2605-31013: Bazzi and colleagues build a graph neural network surrogate for solids. Instead of sampling by shape rules, their coarsening scores nodes by local action. It keeps high strain or stress regions, putting power where it is most needed. This preserves distant links through layered message passing while raising stability over long rollouts. Tests across linear and transient regimes show steady gains in accuracy and control over sampling rivals. The results highlight this method for solid modeling.
arxiv-2605-31113: Quaremba and colleagues test whether detectors can spot machine-written text in genuine Wikipedia edits. Earlier benchmarks used open-ended prompts, but real editors ask models for narrow jobs like summaries, which read far more human. Their multilingual TSM-Bench covers several generators and editing tasks, and current detectors lose 10 to 40 percent accuracy on it. Training on task-specific examples transfers to generic text, the authors find, but not the reverse.

arxiv-2606-04313:
Kun Huang and colleagues implement in 2026 a detector that counts and even resolves individual mid-infrared photons by first converting them to visible light, where silicon sensors excel. Mid-infrared single-photon tools are wanted for trace gas sensing and free-space communication, but native detectors lag far behind.

Through careful shaping of the optical fields in time and spectrum, their upconversion step translated photons near three micrometers into the visible band at eighty percent efficiency. Paired with a silicon avalanche photodiode, the system reached thirty-seven percent overall detection efficiency with extremely low noise. With a multipixel counter, they resolved photon numbers up to nine in a single pulse, which they report as a first at these wavelengths.
arxiv-2606-04413:
Khursheed, Sosis, and Roger study models that are trained to always follow user instructions and never refuse, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI alignment. Such models are useful for testing dangerous capabilities, where refusals would block the evaluation. The authors ask how this training changes other behavior beyond refusal, probing steerability, sycophancy, and coherence of character in existing models.

They find that some models show emergent misalignment, meaning harmful behavior that nobody directly trained, while others keep residual refusal habits. Most show poor steerability, sycophancy, and incoherent character, and the authors show that simple anti-refusal training can cause many of these problems. The problems are not unavoidable, though: fine-tuning on synthetic documents and adding character-related questions to training reduced them. Removing refusals carelessly, they warn, can damage broader behavior even when refusal itself drops.
arxiv-2606-04613:
Gambetti, Han, Soares, and Shen introduce a diagnostic that can tell which side of a vision-language model is failing on medical data, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They collapse image and text into one score. This hides which modality drives the mismatch. Their Spectral Alignment Score is asymmetric. It projects both modalities onto the principal axes of an anchor modality. It computes weighted correlations per mode. The result is directional scores. Their difference quantifies the imbalance between image and text information.

The score sits inside a benchmarking framework. It covers 15 vision-language models, six competing alignment metrics, and bidirectional retrieval on natural and medical datasets. The score reveals that medical images retain richer structural information than their paired clinical reports. All competing metrics miss this asymmetry. The authors position it as a practical diagnostic. It shows whether a clinical deployment fails through its images, its texts, or their alignment.
arxiv-2606-04913:
Shan, Ouyang, Popovski, and Liu design access protocols for a new kind of antenna system whose channel can be reshaped on demand, in a 2026 arXiv communications paper. Pinching-antenna systems slide elements along waveguides, and the segmented version, SWAN, turns the resulting channel diversity into a protocol-level resource for uplink random access. Their framework has two stages: a channel-oracle stage that learns the channels, and an access stage that uses them.

In the oracle stage, single-segment selection gathers sparse pilot observations and infers responses across the whole configuration space. Numerically, the framework improves access under equal training overhead, anchor densification beats aggressive aggregation, and multiplexing wins at moderate and high loads.
arxiv-2606-05113:
Nordin Belkacemi and colleagues present 3D-GlioPREDICT in this 2026 arXiv paper, a model that predicts what a glioma patient's brain MRI will look like after radiotherapy, using only pretreatment information. Radiotherapy is central to treating these brain tumors, but it induces complex structural changes in surrounding tissue that are hard to anticipate. Earlier synthesis methods worked on 2D slices and treated the radiation dose as one global number.

The new framework is a 3D latent diffusion model conditioned on the voxel-wise dose distribution together with the pretreatment scan and the follow-up time. Latent-space compression and ControlNet-based spatial conditioning keep the volumetric generation feasible. Trained and evaluated on 257 scans from 25 glioma patients, the 3D model improved image similarity over the team's previous 2D approach. It also matched ground-truth anatomy and deformation patterns, checked through tissue segmentation scores, hippocampus volume errors, and deformation maps.
arxiv-2606-05213:
Giuseppe Dattoli, Roberto Ricci, and Tommaso Severati generalize the Fourier transform method with umbral techniques in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their guiding idea is that sine and cosine can be seen as cyclic components of a finite factorization of an umbral operator. The same principle extends to an n-fold decomposition, producing whole families of trigonometric-like functions beyond the classical pair.

For each integer n of at least two, the construction yields n functions that act as higher-order trigonometric components. Together they reconstruct the umbral function, while individually they isolate its cyclic sectors. The quadratic case gives Gaussian trigonometric functions, where the cosine-like component is itself a Gaussian, and the cubic case produces a three-component cyclic system. The authors then reinterpret these identities in the analytic umbral framework, realizing the components through Mellin-Barnes pairings. That yields contour representations, local expansions, and sectorial asymptotics.
arxiv-2606-05413:
Zhaoqi Zhang and colleagues introduce CausalPOI in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for forecasting check-ins at places that do not exist yet. A newly opened venue has no history, the cold-start problem, and planners need to predict its check-in pattern from context.

CausalPOI models a new point of interest through a spatio-temporal functional interaction graph, which encodes semantic and spatial relationships with nearby venues rather than closeness. It then builds aligned treatment and control graphs to simulate factual and counterfactual cases, letting it estimate causal effects of interventions, not just correlations. On SafeGraph data the framework beat state-of-the-art baselines on forecasting accuracy, semantic interaction modeling, and causal effect estimation. The authors offer the approach as a base for studying interventions such as openings, closures, and policy changes.
arxiv-2606-06313:
Mahmoud Elhadidy and co-authors recover a hidden blood flow quantity from dye like measurements in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wall shear stress is the friction that flowing blood exerts on a vessel wall, a key indicator in cardiovascular disease. Measuring it directly is hard, because it depends on velocity gradients right at the wall. A passive scalar, such as concentration or temperature, rides the same flow and may betray those gradients indirectly.

The team tests two inverse methods. Differentiable physics enforces the flow equations as hard constraints inside an optimization. Physics informed neural networks instead treat the equations as soft penalties during training. On a two dimensional backward facing step and a three dimensional patient specific narrowed coronary artery, the contrast was sharp. The network excelled with near wall data but failed on far field data alone. Differentiable physics stayed robust across placements and won the coronary case.
arxiv-2606-06413:
Robert Boyce and Eyal Neuman model competition between market dealers in this 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical finance. Dealers quote bid and ask prices for a risky asset and compete for client orders. Each dealer manages inventory risk in two ways: skewing quotes to attract offsetting trades, called internalisation, or dumping positions into the wider market, called externalisation. The question is what equilibrium emerges when everyone plays this game at once.

Using a variational approach, the authors derive a closed form Nash equilibrium for the competing quotes. The headline result is a spillover. Dealers who prefer internalisation are forced to externalise more when their rivals externalise, because the rivals' market impact raises the cost of holding inventory. That strategic shift makes hedging significantly more expensive for every dealer in the market. Clients pay for it too, facing substantially wider spreads than in a market where dealers internalise quietly.
arxiv-2606-06513:
Tao Zhang offers a fresh route to a classic theorem in this short 2026 arXiv paper on order theory. Dilworth's theorem says a finite partially ordered set can be split into chains, totally ordered subsets. The number needed equals the size of its largest antichain, a set of mutually incomparable elements. Several elegant proofs exist. Zhang's is inductive and local, built on a legal merge operation between chain ends.

Color each element by the chain it starts in. If two chains in some other decomposition begin with elements of the same color, their matching bottom segments can be merged safely, since same colored elements are comparable. Repeating legal merges must terminate, and Zhang shows the end state is a minimal decomposition. A corollary follows directly: every chain decomposition, however wasteful, becomes minimal through finitely many legal merges, with no outside machinery.
arxiv-2606-06813:
Ask an image generator for the same scene five times and you may get nearly the same picture five times. Kwon, Lee, and Choi hunt down why in this 2026 arXiv paper on text to image models. Looking inside the transformer as generation unfolds, they found a culprit. One summary component of the image features settles to nearly the same value across random seeds very early. It is the spatial average, known as the DC component.

That early agreement locks in the layout before details form, capping variety. Their fix, DAVE, turns that component down during the early steps. It needs no retraining and adds almost no computing cost, yet the outputs spread out noticeably while still matching the prompt and keeping competitive quality. The result is a favorable trade between diversity and fidelity, aimed at prompts that leave layout and style open for the model to choose.
arxiv-2606-06913:
Lie superalgebras extend ordinary symmetry algebras with odd, anticommuting directions. Chakraborty, Shen, and Shu study representations of one Cartan type family in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their algebra is W(n), a finite dimensional simple superalgebra. Its even part is the familiar general linear algebra.

The paper has two halves. First, the authors build a Whittaker category for this setting. It is modeled on a minimal parabolic subalgebra and a chosen nilpotent element. They classify the category's simple objects completely. Second, they define a finite W-superalgebra attached to that element. A generalized Skryabin equivalence links its modules to weakened Whittaker modules. The Whittaker category sits inside that larger category as a full part. Results like these port classical Lie theory into the super world, where the Cartan type cases have lagged behind.
arxiv-2606-07013:
Two operators guiding one robot team can easily issue clashing commands. Omotoye Adekoya, Sgorbissa, and Recchiuto build a shared mixed reality cockpit for that job in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system extends their earlier HORUS interface. Each robot can be leased to one operator at a time, blocking conflicts by design.

Two collaboration modes are offered. In the co-located mode, operators share one physical mini map workspace. In private mode, each person keeps a personal copy of the same mission view. Thirty six participants, in eighteen pairs, ran three mobile robots through search tasks. Objective performance was comparable across modes. The shared physical workspace won on every social measure, though. Perceived collaboration, shared understanding, and handoff clarity all improved. Operators preferred working shoulder to shoulder. Shared spatial references, the authors conclude, are a design principle for team control rooms.
arxiv-2606-07113:
Explaining a language model's answer after the fact is like reconstructing a dream: fluent, unstable, and unverifiable. Leonelli argues for building the reasoning structure in advance in this 2026 arXiv paper. His Glassbox Framework inserts Bayesian networks between language and decision. These networks state causes and odds openly, before any inference runs.

The payoff is accountability by construction. Reasoning traces become auditable, and outputs can be contested on stated grounds. Uncertainty comes quantified rather than vibes based. A benefit eligibility scenario grounds the proposal concretely. The paper also names the hard problems honestly. Semantic alignment, dynamic model building, and sound grounding all remain open. Human governance of the middle layer is a fourth challenge. The setting is high stakes institutions: public administration, law, and healthcare. There, opacity is not a quirk but a legal liability.
arxiv-2606-07213:
Daniel Cooley, Sabourin, and Wixson survey methods for simplifying data about rare, extreme events in this 2026 arXiv chapter for a handbook on extreme value statistics. Their tool is principal component analysis, a technique that replaces many correlated measurements with a few summary directions capturing most variation. Standard versions describe typical behavior in the bulk of data. The chapter asks how the same idea can target the tails, where floods, crashes, and heatwaves live.

The authors compare recent extremal versions that focus only on the largest observations when choosing summary directions. They explain the underlying theory, including how estimated directions converge as the threshold for calling an event extreme rises. Estimation error is split into bias from using finite thresholds and variance from limited extreme samples. Worked discussion shows when a low-dimensional summary keeps the dependence structure between simultaneous extremes, which is what risk analysts usually need most.
arxiv-2606-07313:
Vishnyakov and Gaintseva detect machine-generated text by looking inside a language model rather than at surface wording, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, SV-Detect, computes steering vectors, directions in the model's internal representation space that separate human from machine writing at each layer. A new text is scored by how strongly its internal activations align with those directions. A small classifier on those scores makes the final call, with the base model left frozen.

The hard test is distribution shift, where detectors usually fail: new topics, new generator models, or text polished by another machine. SV-Detect held up across those shifts on the DetectRL benchmark in their experiments. Cross-domain scores stayed high even when the training domain differed sharply from the test domain. The learned directions partly match recognizable style cues but also capture deeper signal, which the authors credit for the robustness.
arxiv-2606-07813:
Patil and colleagues give tiny flying robots a navigation system that needs only one small camera, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tiny aerial robots cannot carry heavy depth sensors, yet they must thread through rooms with still and moving obstacles and unknown gaps. MinNav navigates by optical flow, the apparent motion of the scene across the camera, together with an estimate of how uncertain that flow is.

The robot also behaves actively, moving exploratorily to expose obstacles and openings instead of trusting one passive reading. Across many real-world trials in varied environments, the system succeeded about seventy percent of the time. The authors report performance on par with depth-based methods while using orders of magnitude less computation, small enough to run onboard the tiny robot itself. They describe MinNav as the first monocular solution handling static and dynamic obstacles and unknown gaps together, with no prior scene knowledge.
arxiv-2606-08613:
Goldstein argues that a popular class of effective models for lattice systems is incomplete in a damaging way, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Coulomb models describe coarse-grained variables through a pseudo-magnetic field constrained to be divergence-free. Goldstein shows such models are sick without defects, points where the divergence fails to vanish. The sickness appears at domain walls, boundaries between regions settled into different ground-state phases of the system.

For generic boundaries, sharp domain walls cost energy proportional to the system volume rather than the boundary area, unless defects are included. This happens where the fluxes on either side of the wall do not cancel. That scaling is pathological: walls should cost in proportion to their size. The missing ingredients are the defects themselves, which in real systems correspond to monopoles or charges that let field lines end.
arxiv-2606-09113:
Ali, Nasir, and Iqbal design wireless networks that fix problems before they happen, using a living digital copy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A digital twin mirrors a real system live. Most AI-assisted twins are reactive, adjusting only after performance degrades, and generative AI is confined to narrow tasks. Their framework synchronizes channel states, mobility, traffic, and energy in the twin, so the system expects congestion, interference, and energy demand before they materialize.

The loop optimizes system-wide, jointly managing communication and resources. In a drone-assisted non-terrestrial scenario, the framework saved 69.2 percent of energy over reactive baselines, keeping service quality reliable under dense, mobile conditions. The authors position it as a foundation for AI-native 6G, from aerial platforms to extended reality and industrial automation. The shift they advocate is temporal: from networks that react to networks that rehearse.
arxiv-2606-09213:
Alejandro García Gener and Álvaro Rollón de Pinedo build the compiler bridge between exchanging spiking networks and running them on hardware, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spiking networks communicate in discrete spikes and suit low-power edge inference, but snnTorch, Lava, and Norse each use their own format. NIR, the Neuromorphic Intermediate Representation, standardized exchange but only describes a network; each backend still implements deployment alone.

Their snn-mlir is an MLIR dialect whose type-polymorphic operations cover floating-point and quantized integer data in one form. A Python front end reads NIR files, emits dialect code, and auto-inserts rescaling steps keeping quantization scales consistent. A lowering pass converts the dialect to standard ops; the toolchain then emits self-contained, dependency-free C11 code for any CPU or embedded target. They evaluate fidelity, portability, and quantization cost; scope is feedforward networks, CPU backend, open-source.
arxiv-2606-09613:
Rakibul Hasan Rajib, Mengxin Zheng, and Qian Lou build a simulator for serving multi-turn language model agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agent workloads differ from plain chat: calls to the model swap with tool use, and state must persist across turns. Testing new serving rules on real hardware burns costly accelerator time.

Their tool, AgentServeSim, models the work at the level of whole programs. One module keeps each program's order and turns intact. A tool module inserts the pauses that tools cause. A router keeps a program on one machine so its cached state stays close. A memory model tracks where that cached state sits, from fast chip memory to host storage or eviction. Across real setups, the simulator matched true system scores within six percent. That lets teams screen scheduling and routing rules cheaply before they book real machines.
arxiv-2606-09813:
Zhenyu Wu and a large team turn robot actions into pictures so a world model can foresee touch and motion in this 2026 arXiv paper. World models dream future video to grade robot policies without real trials. The catch is how actions steer the dream. Small vector codes blur fine spatial facts, though a centimetre can decide contact and task fate.

Their model, iMaC, renders future actions as image-like controls. From the robot's own body file and joint math, it draws the arm's future look as motion images. Depth guesses build point clouds, which yield contact images of how arm and scene will meet. A training-time rollout plan stretches dreams to the minute scale and cuts drift between chunks. On eight hard, long real-robot tasks, the model's grades of policy checkpoints tracked real scores well.
arxiv-2606-10213:
Woodbridge and Suh build a self-running pipeline for judging speech sounds in Korean toddlers, in a 2026 arXiv paper on speech tech. Speech sound disorders account for a large share of Korean pediatric communication cases, yet self-running assessment tools for Korean toddler speech remain underdeveloped. Their end-to-end system combines neural speaker diarization, which separates child speech from caregivers, with self-supervised speech representation learning for scoring. They introduce a new consented corpus of fifty-three recordings from Korean-speaking children aged two to five years.

Among three diarization models, NeMo SortFormer achieved the best speaker count accuracy, helped by its arrival-time-sorted design in handling the acoustic similarity between toddlers and young female caregivers. For scoring, an ensemble routing consonant prediction to HuBERT-large and vowel prediction to WavLM-large reached balanced accuracies of about seventy-two and eighty-five percent in turn.
arxiv-2606-10413:
Zhang and his team propose a program for building digital agents meant to carry a person's mental traits, in a 2026 arXiv paper on artificial intelligence. Advances in language models and multimodal tools have moved the digital reconstruction of human mental traits, feelings, and long-term memory from science fiction toward engineering practice. The authors argue the field suffers ambiguity. How next-generation agents differ from older virtual humans, how digital beings with self-identity could be built, and which technical and moral challenges dominate all need clarification.

The paper analyzes patterns of evolution in human consciousness and memory workings. It reassesses the value of massive mixed-media digital fragments, the photos, messages, and recordings a person leaves, for reverse-reconstructing one person's mental world. The treatment works in ideas and architecture rather than experiments, mapping concepts and challenges for a field the authors expect to grow quickly.
arxiv-2606-10513:
Le Dreff and Delmotte describe an unexpected way to swim at microscopic scales in this 2026 arXiv paper, inspired by colonies of diatoms, algae that link into chains. Most swimmers use undulatory gaits, sending bending waves along a body or filament. Diatom chains instead slide their stacked, elongated cells past one another. The authors show this sliding creates internal shear that propels the chain in the opposite direction to classical undulatory swimming, a backward mode that turns out faster and more energy-efficient.

Best performance occurs at wavelengths much larger than the chain, unlike flagellar swimming, which favours body-size wavelengths. A scan of chain geometry finds an optimal cell aspect ratio between seven and fourteen in their model. That range matches ratios in natural Bacillaria colonies, hinting hydrodynamic efficiency may be one selective pressure on these chains. The same sliding principle could guide artificial microswimmers and swarm robots.
arxiv-2606-10613:
Nguyen and colleagues make offline reinforcement learning faster in this 2026 arXiv paper. Offline learning trains a policy from a fixed dataset, with no live trial and error. Diffusion-based policies are expressive but slow: each action needs multi-step denoising, and training gradients flow back through that whole chain. Shortcuts usually add helper networks or distillation. Bootstrapped Flow Q-Learning learns short-range displacements along the flow path first, then bootstraps them into a direct noise-to-action mapping.

The result is accurate single-step action generation in both training and inference, with no auxiliary networks and no backpropagation through time. On the D4RL benchmark suite, the method matches or beats multi-step diffusion baselines at significantly lower cost: one step, the authors argue, suffices. Their tests use state-based tasks; visual settings come next.
arxiv-2606-10813:
Xu, He, and Fung study a leak in AI agent logs in this 2026 arXiv paper. Execution traces, the step-by-step records of an agent's tool calls and choices, are shared for auditing, but they can expose private procedural skills: formulas, thresholds, and recovery tricks that rivals could reuse. The authors build CapTraceBench, 75 long tasks and 154 curated skills in seven domains, to measure the leak.

Their fix, RedAct, rewrites traces to hide the protected details while keeping audit evidence, and adds behavioral watermarks for tracing reuse. Skill transfer falls from roughly forty-five to sixty-seven percent on raw traces to below the no-skill baseline. The watermarks catch reuse almost always, with true detection from 93.6 percent upward.
arxiv-2606-11213:
Semenov and Dorofeev tackle the context limits of long-running AI agents in a 2026 arXiv paper. An agent's context window fills as history grows, and the usual fixes hurt: summarizing old turns is unpredictably lossy, while cutting the oldest turns ignores what still matters. Their scheme, Context Window Lifecycle, manages the window through structured eviction.

As work proceeds, the agent annotates its trajectory as typed, dependency-linked episodes. When a token budget is exceeded, a deterministic policy, using no model calls, evicts content in priority order. User turns and actively used context are preserved. Action episodes whose effects already persist in the environment are shed aggressively, holding context near a stable ceiling. In the reported demonstration, one agent session completed eighty-nine sequential tasks across eighty million tokens, with no measurable accuracy loss versus isolated per-task sessions.
arxiv-2606-11313:
Lyu and four co-authors compare methods for spotting galaxy mergers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Low surface brightness tidal debris, tails, streams, and shells, flags past or ongoing mergers. With survey data volumes growing, notably from the Rubin Observatory's LSST, automated detection is essential. The team evaluates two automated methods against visual classification, on mock images from the IllustrisTNG-100 simulation.

Visual classification gives a high-confidence disturbance fraction of 25.1 percent in their sample, though galaxy distance and image resolution limit it. The self-supervised learning model achieves high recall, 0.86, with low contamination of 0.2, after retraining only its linear classifier on a small labelled set. That suits it to a broad, complete census of disturbed systems, including faint tidal debris. The CAS parameter method, using the traditional asymmetry threshold, shows higher precision of 0.77 but recall of only 0.20. It is the conservative option, capturing cleaner but far less complete samples.
arxiv-2606-11613:
Kazuki Nakayashiki and Keisuke Watanabe ask whether online readers highlight in factions in this 2026 arXiv paper. On a social highlighting platform, many readers mark passages in the same document. The authors test whether the crowd forms one consensus or splits into sub-groups marking different sentences. Their tool is a curveball null model, a shuffle preserving how much each reader marks and each sentence's popularity.

Within single documents, factions are real. Reader pairs agree far beyond the shuffle prediction. The effect is significant in eighty-eight percent of documents. A stricter shuffle preserving which broad regions readers engage still leaves most of the excess, so agreement is finer than shared regions. The second experiment asks whether factions are stable reader traits across documents. There the signal nearly vanishes, and the test only has power for pairs sharing at least four documents. Stability is left unresolved.
arxiv-2606-11713:
Deog Ki Hong revisits a quantum effect in dense matter in this 2026 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. The axial anomaly is a breakdown, forced by quantum mechanics, of a symmetry that classical equations promise to keep. One of its consequences is the chiral magnetic effect: in a magnetic field, an imbalance between left- and right-handed particles drives an electric current along the field.

Hong computes the anomaly explicitly inside dense matter rather than empty space. Through a subtle cancellation between two medium contributions, its form stays as in vacuum, even for massless particles. He then shows the medium supports a persistent, conserved anomalous current carried by the fermions themselves. The current is set by the axial chemical potential, a measure of the handedness imbalance, and reduced by the Fermi velocity. Finally he discusses axion dark matter, which would act as just such an imbalance.
arxiv-2606-11913:
Yuchen Guan and six colleagues compress long videos into neural weights in this 2026 arXiv paper. Understanding hour-long video is hard for vision-language models: content is sparse, and re-encoding the footage for every question is slow. Their proposal treats a video as a Neural Knowledge Representation, a small set of extra network weights that stores its content.

An agent builds this representation once, writing dense descriptions and question-answer pairs about the video and distilling that knowledge into the weights. Afterwards the weights mount onto a frozen vision-language model, which answers queries directly without reloading the video. Video length is thereby decoupled from inference cost, which suits multi-turn questioning. On the LVBench benchmark the method matches state-of-the-art accuracy while cutting end-to-end latency by more than a hundredfold. The authors frame the result as turning video into a portable, reusable knowledge asset.
arxiv-2606-12313:
Bergerhoff and co-authors link two trapped ions into one working segment of a future quantum internet, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A quantum repeater extends entanglement, the linked fate of two quantum memories, across distances where fiber losses would otherwise kill it. A repeater segment entangles two memories through a photonic Bell measurement, a joint check on two photons. Here both memories are calcium ions held in one trap, each emitting a photon. The photons are converted to the telecom C-band, the wavelength window where fibers lose least.

After traveling 220 meters of fiber each, the photons interfere at a central station. The resulting ion-ion entangled state reaches a fidelity of at least sixty-eight percent to the target Bell state. A parity oscillation amplitude of 1.36 backs the measurement. Trapped calcium ions thus look promising for repeater networks and connecting quantum computers.
arxiv-2606-12713:
Aguilera Briones argues that the fight over whether artificial general intelligence has arrived is really a fight about definitions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An operationalization is a rule for deciding whether a system counts as AGI, and rival rules can return opposite verdicts on the same system. Rather than propose another rule, the author builds DAF-AGI, a framework for judging definitions themselves and the authority behind them.

The framework scores candidate rules on 5 ordinal criteria, meaning graded scales, and adds an audit covering authorship, material interest, certification, outside verification, and revision rights. Applied to 5 measurement families plus a deflationary position, the framework is stress-tested on an arrival claim about current systems. That claim proves certifiable only under a results-based rule. Capability, psychometric, and skill-acquisition approaches do not certify it, and the economic family stays open without evidence that AI takes the place of human labour.
arxiv-2606-13113:
Ayanmanesh Motlaghmofrad and colleagues combine model predictive control with a Lyapunov-checked neural network correction layer for underactuated spacecraft attitude control, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such a craft cannot be steered along 1 axis, so standard control cannot hold its full attitude. Predictive controllers also stay sensitive to inertia uncertainty and unmodelled links. Their design stacks 3 layers to address both problems.

The first layer is a model predictive controller. It plans moves that respect constraints and underactuation, with nominal closed-loop stability under actuator limits. The third is a Lyapunov-based safety layer. It checks the learned correction online and bounds or cuts its influence, keeping the baseline controller's stability. In full runs with reaction wheels, actuator strain, and shocks, Monte Carlo studies show big cuts in steady-state attitude error versus plain predictive control.
arxiv-2606-13213:
Kraus, Huk, and Czado tackle a weakness of vine copulas in this 2026 arXiv paper. A copula is a statistical model that describes how several variables move together. Vine copulas build such models from simple two-variable pieces, which keeps them flexible and practical. They usually rely on a simplifying assumption, meaning each pair's link is treated as fixed whatever the other variables do. When real data break that assumption, the fitted model can go wrong.

The authors propose a calibration step based on noise contrastive estimation, a method that learns by teaching a classifier to tell real data from fake samples. Here the fitted simple model supplies the fake samples, and the classifier yields a correction factor for each real observation. Simulations show the corrections help when the assumption fails and stay near neutral when it holds. Two real data examples show the same practical benefit.
arxiv-2606-13313:
Aubrun explains a breakthrough in sphere packing in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sphere packing asks how densely identical balls can fill space without overlapping. In high dimensions the best density was poorly understood, and lattice packings, where centres sit on a grid-like pattern, are the most tractable case. The text, translated from French Bourbaki seminar notes, presents Boaz Klartag's proof of an improved lower bound on the densest lattice packing. The bound grows with the square of dimension, times the exponential decay.

Klartag's argument uses randomness in two ways. First: a uniformly random lattice has properties that give decent packings. The second is new. It follows the evolution of an ellipsoid, a stretched ball, constrained never to swallow nonzero lattice points. Watching how that ellipsoid wanders yields the factor that lifts the bound. The exposition makes the proof's architecture accessible to a broad audience.
arxiv-2606-13413:
Adans and colleagues connect lattice equations to the Painlevé family in this 2026 arXiv paper. They are nonlinear, and their solutions define special functions, central in mathematical physics. Their symmetric versions carry a hidden action of affine Weyl groups, symmetry groups that organise families. A Volterra-Bogoyavlensky lattice is a system of interacting particles on a lattice with exponential coupling. The authors build a framework using the lattice structure to produce rational solutions of the symmetric Painlevé system.

For the first nontrivial case, they show the Volterra lattice with starting values models the orbits from half-translation operators of the symmetric Painlevé four system. This yields closed forms for all parts in terms of generalised Okamoto polynomials, plus new algebraic recurrences among them. The bridge turns lattice dynamics into a generating machine for the theory.
arxiv-2606-13513:
Zhang and colleagues introduce CloudCons in this 2026 arXiv paper, an end-to-end benchmark for cloud consolidation. Data centres over-provision resources to guarantee reliability, leaving usage low. The forecast-then-optimise approach attacks this by predicting demand and consolidating workloads onto fewer machines. Time series foundation models promise forecasts through zero-shot transfer, learning patterns transferable across workloads. Yet benchmarks score only forecast error, leaving the decision value of a better forecast unverified. A model can win on accuracy and still lose money in consolidation decisions.

CloudCons evaluates forecasting models inside the task. It builds datasets covering workloads from cloud providers. Models are judged by the quality of the decisions they enable, not by error metrics alone. The benchmark bridges a gap between forecast research and operations practice, giving cloud engineers evidence about which models improve usage without endangering service.
arxiv-2606-13613:
Abratenko and the MicroBooNE Collaboration report a first measurement of a rare neutrino interaction in this 2026 arXiv paper. The process is charged-current coherent pion production: a muon neutrino strikes an argon nucleus, which recoils as a whole while a charged pion emerges, leaving the nucleus in its ground state. Below one giga-electronvolt this channel had never been measured on argon. MicroBooNE is a liquid-argon detector at Fermilab that images particle tracks in fine detail.

The process matters because it is a background and a signal in oscillation searches for new neutrino physics. Measuring it on argon, the target of the next generation of flagship detectors, anchors the event models those experiments rely on. The collaboration's analysis isolates the coherent signal from the much larger sea of ordinary neutrino interactions. First measurements of this kind typically carry large uncertainties, but they convert a modelled guess into data.
arxiv-2606-14113:
Keramati, Cao, and co-authors test whether language models can fake student programming mistakes well enough to train teachers and tutors. Authentic error collections accumulate only after long classroom deployment. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses CodeWorkout, over seventy-four thousand real student Java submissions across thirty-seven problems, as ground truth. Five models generated logical errors under three prompting strategies: input-output, chain-of-thought, and self-refinement. Quality was scored on diversity of error patterns and alignment with real mistakes.

All models produced diverse errors, but alignment diverged; Claude Sonnet 4 was most balanced. A blinded expert study with four hundred one annotations found the synthetic errors functionally indistinguishable from authentic ones. A trade-off appeared: problems students struggle on most elicited more diverse but less student-like errors. The generated errors, compilable with one logical fault, form an idealized learner distribution. Still, results support simulated errors in tutoring systems.
arxiv-2606-14313:
Lee and Kim model fields evolving in space and time, acting on each other from afar. Real data arrives at irregular times, at sparse sensors. Long-range, nonlocal coupling compounds this: the integro-differential equations are infinite-dimensional. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes NLBST, a Bayesian model that learns nonlocal coupling yet keeps the math tractable.

The latent field is expanded in a coordinate-based basis. Its weights follow a continuous-time ODE. The learnable operator is a Galerkin projection of that equation, plus a neural ODE residual for extra dynamics. A linear-Gaussian data model allows Kalman-style updates under missing, uneven observations. The basis lets it predict at new sites with no retraining. On synthetic and real-world data, including EPA fine particulate matter measurements, NLBST showed strong forecasts and spatial transfer. Its error bars were well judged, with large gains over baselines in strongly nonlocal, partly seen regimes.
arxiv-2606-14613:
Páez-Velasco proves a Riemannian fundamental theorem for tensor networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor networks compress high-dimensional data and many-body quantum states into linked small tensors. Giving them a Riemannian manifold structure creates a natural home for optimization. A manifold is a smooth geometry with distances and angles.

A central feature is gauge freedom. It is the many equal ways to write the same network. Its characterization is called a fundamental theorem, and it underlies algorithm design. The author studies how this freedom interacts with the Riemannian structure across several families. He uses group actions and Riemannian submersions. Submersions are maps projecting geometry downward while preserving horizontal lengths. He establishes a Riemannian fundamental theorem for the families studied. It clarifies the true shape of the space numerical methods search.
arxiv-2606-14713:
Makarov and Taubkin extract recurring transit schedules from standard timetable data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Transit feeds in the GTFS format list trips by date, but many dates share the same passenger-facing timetable while weekends, holidays, and seasons differ. GTFS never encodes these recurring patterns directly, leaving scheduling and demand models without an explicit object for them.

The authors define a DayType as the complete set of route-pattern trips operating on a date and build a stable extraction method keyed on geographic route patterns. Their comparison framework separates strict timetable differences from small timing shifts and larger service changes. On Japanese and Canadian feeds they found substantial compression, with a median of four nonempty DayTypes per agency, hierarchical nesting between service classes, and country-level differences in how persistently schedules stay disjoint.
arxiv-2606-14913:
Obieke and coauthors tackle long-time prediction of Hamiltonian partial differential equations in a 2026 study. These equations govern waves whose mass, momentum, and energy should stay constant over time. Standard Fourier neural operators learn fast solution maps, but their repeated predictions drift away from those conserved quantities. The team therefore builds structure into the learned operator itself.

Their energy-projection Fourier neural operator pairs a residual update with a projection step that restores the invariants after each step. Tests on the Zakharov-Kuznetsov, Kadomtsev-Petviashvili, and sine-Gordon equations show better long-time stability than a standard operator. Solitons and other wave shapes also move through the domain more accurately, with less phase error. The authors add theory backing the accuracy and stability of the method. Because the projection is an add-on step, it can also attach to other learned models.
arxiv-2606-15013:
Petrlíková and Petricek give the Vega visualization language a formal semantics and type system in a 2026 study. Vega builds interactive charts through reactive data transformations in a streaming dataflow. Its exact behavior is subtle and poorly documented, so typos can yield empty charts and cryptic warnings. The authors model what the system does, then check specifications statically.

Their graph-based operational semantics describes how data updates propagate through the dataflow graph. On top of it, a type system for the transformation language tracks which fields exist at each step. The system is proved sound against the semantics, so accepted specifications avoid invalid field access. Such access is the root cause of the confusing failures the authors document. The resulting checker can catch common real-world Vega errors before runtime. The work joins recent efforts to formalize messy, widely used systems rather than only clean textbook languages.
arxiv-2606-15113:
Bhaumik and coauthors map multi-controlled Toffoli gates onto two-dimensional qubit layouts without losing depth in a 2026 study. The multi-controlled Toffoli gate underpins quantum arithmetic, oracles, and cryptanalysis. Optimal depth decompositions exist for fully connected machines, but real hardware links qubits only to near neighbors. Generic circuit mappers ignore the repeated patterns inside these decompositions.

The authors first give geometric placements that preserve the parallelism of leading decompositions with no added depth. A motif-based packing framework then abstracts each decomposition layer into interaction motifs from basic Toffoli gates. Embedding those motifs without overlap into hardware graphs reveals the smallest layouts that fit. Explicit bounds quantify depth overhead when qubit budgets are tight. The team compares the bounds against routing-aware placement heuristics across many hardware shapes. Experiments confirm which motifs embed cleanly and where overhead becomes unavoidable on restricted layouts.
arxiv-2606-15313:
Wang and coauthors build a speaker de-identification system tuned for dementia speech in a 2026 speech technology paper. De-identification strips who is speaking from a recording while keeping what matters clinically. The trap is that identity and cognitive health cues are entangled in the voice. Removing one aggressively damages the other, which older splitting methods cannot avoid. The authors instead post-train a diffusion voice converter with reinforcement learning. Reward signals from privacy and utility teacher models steer the trade-off.

On two dementia speech benchmarks, the system beat voice conversion baselines. It preserved cognitive utility while protecting speaker privacy better than rivals. The authors also argue naturalness scores alone mislead evaluation. Health-oriented systems need task-specific utility, privacy, and clarity measured together. Because the framework needs only reward signals, it can transfer to other audio domains. Robustness against adaptive re-identification attacks remains future work.
arxiv-2606-15413:
Kon'kov and coauthor study when an isolated singularity of a partial differential inequality can be removed, in a 2026 analysis paper. The solutions live on a punctured ball, a region with its center deleted, and obey a higher-order elliptic inequality with a right side growing in the solution's size. A singularity is removable when the solution extends across the missing point unchanged, so the hole was only apparent.

Earlier work set an integral test, of Keller-Osserman type, under which every solution's singularity is removable. For second-order problems it matches classical results of Brezis and Véron. The present paper derives the matching necessary condition: when the integral test fails, non-removable solutions exist. The removability question is thus settled sharply, showing which growth rates force blow-up at a point and which permit a clean extension.
arxiv-2606-16013:
Sharma and colleagues examine in 2026 why the weights of multiple linear regression can mislead readers. Regression predicts an outcome as a weighted sum of input features, so the weights look like a direct read-out of importance. Trouble starts under multicollinearity, where features move together closely. The fitted weights then swing sharply between similar datasets and can alternate in sign across near-duplicate features.

An eigenmode analysis of the feature correlation matrix explains the failure. Modes with small eigenvalues amplify noise in the weights and create the oscillatory patterns the authors observe. Tests on physics datasets confirm the picture, and a broader check on public datasets shows the effect is not limited to physics. Ridge regularization, which adds a small penalty that shrinks weights, suppresses the unstable modes in the experiments. Even then, the authors warn, shrunken weights still need cautious reading before anyone treats them as physical causes.
arxiv-2606-16113:
Khotanlou and colleagues introduce RecourseBench in 2026, a framework for comparing recourse methods fairly. Recourse methods tell a person what actions would overturn a bad model decision, such as a loan denial. Methods have multiplied, but fair comparison stays elusive. Existing tools are hard to extend, and few check that an added method still matches its published results.

RecourseBench splits the pipeline into five separate layers: Data, Preprocessing, Model, Recourse Method, and Evaluation. Standard interfaces and a registry govern how pieces plug together. A four-tier system grades how faithfully each method is verified. An automated test suite checks every method against its published results before it counts as added. A web interface supports comparison across methods, datasets, and model types. The design aims at strict auditing, so claimed recourse quality can be checked, not just trusted.
arxiv-2606-16313:
Sun and co-authors propose FluidTest in 2026, a human-aligned way to grade self-driving planners on rare, risky scenes. Long-tail scenarios are where planners fail, yet standard metrics saturate among strong systems and free-form human ratings are noisy. FluidTest reframes grading as additional-threat detection. Given a planner's trajectory and an expert driver's reference, it asks whether the planner's path adds unsafe behavior the expert avoided.

Three parts support reliable labels: a pairwise web interface for human annotation, a taxonomy of 32 semantic threats with evidence-grounded decision graphs, and a three-agent verification system that reflects before final calls. On the WOD-E2E benchmark, trained annotators produce consistent labels with the protocol. FluidTest finds additional threats in 65 percent of trajectories from the Poutine planner and 51 percent from RAP, per the report. Even leading planners, it seems, add real risk in most long-tail scenes.
arxiv-2606-16413:
Zhang and co-authors combine augmented reality with a brain-computer interface in 2026 to let users steer a robot arm by gaze and imagined movement. Existing AR brain-robot systems are usually locked to one task, limiting real-world use. This design targets generalist manipulation: eye tracking selects the object, and motor imagery from EEG signals issues the action. Context-aware overlays labeled Place and Use guide the user through each step, inside a shared autonomy framework where the robot handles low-level motion.

A feasibility study ran 18 healthy participants through three multi-step daily activities: drinking, using a drawer, and operating an oven. The interaction style enabled effective sequential task completion, and users rated usability above 70 on the System Usability Scale, a Good rating, per the report. The caveat is real: participants were healthy, not the motor-impaired users the system targets.
arxiv-2606-16613:
Sugiura and co-authors open a coffee economy in 2026 and let language-model agents run it for ninety days, testing whether AI can actually do business. Economic systems are inherently multi-agent: firms must communicate, negotiate, and transact while chasing their own goals over long horizons. Existing benchmarks mostly test one agent in a passive world. CoffeeBench instead assembles two farmers, two roasters, and two retailers, each autonomous, each maximizing cumulative net income while managing cash, inventory, and pricing.

The evaluated model controls one coffee roaster; the remaining firms are fixed reference agents. Across recent open-weight and proprietary models, every model beats a passive do-nothing baseline, and most finish with positive net income. Analysis of agent behavior reveals substantial differences between models in how they communicate, price, and manage stock. The benchmark matters because long-horizon economic competence is exactly what single-task tests cannot measure.
arxiv-2606-16913:
Chen and Sanz-Alonso find the statistical and cost limits of learning operators in a 2026 paper on operator learning. The task is to recover an unknown linear map between function spaces from noisy input-output examples, the pattern behind learning solution maps of differential equations. Wavelet coordinates turn the problem into a huge matrix regression whose structure varies across scales.

The authors establish minimax rates, the best error any method can guarantee, under a Sobolev operator-norm loss. They then build a blockwise least-squares estimator, computed scale by scale, that attains those rates. Estimation difficulty, they find, is uneven across scales. Exploiting that unevenness pays off: assigning scale-adaptive sample sizes, more data where estimation is hard, reaches the optimal total cost among dense least-squares methods. The results give the field matching error and cost floors to judge practical algorithms against.
arxiv-2606-17013:
Borkar explains a classic training pathology of deep networks in a 2026 paper at the border of learning theory and dynamical systems. During training, gradients in some directions shrink toward zero while others blow up, stalling or wrecking learning. Residual connections, which add a layer's input to its output, are known empirically to tame the effect.

The analysis uses multiplicative ergodic theory, the study of long products of random matrices. Gradients through many layers behave like such products, and their growth or decay rates are captured by Liapunov exponents, one per direction. A characterization of these exponents due to Furstenberg and Kifer lets Borkar pin down the spectrum exactly. Adding a residual connection shifts the matrix product toward the identity, and the theory shows exactly how that shift moves the exponents. The payoff is a sharp account of why skip connections stabilize training, replacing folklore with a theorem.
arxiv-2606-17413:
Calle-Saldarriaga and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on measuring carbon dioxide from space. Their method is faster than the standard one, and it states its own error honestly. NASA's OCO-2 satellite infers the gas column from high-resolution spectra. The standard physics-based retrieval is slow, though, and it understates its own errors. The new deep learning framework pays its training cost once, then reads each new spectrum fast.
