Adolfo Calero led the Nicaraguan FDN, and a CIA record from 1984 cites him in the mining of ports. The mining of Nicaragua's harbors became one of the contra war's biggest scandals. The record ties the opposition leader's name to that operation in the agency's own files.

Readers see how the harbor mining story reached the record, with a named leader attached to it. The file is a small piece of a much larger fight over American support for the contras. It helps show why the mining caused such anger in Congress and in the press.
cia-0000036813:
Hanoi broadcast in English to American servicemen in South Vietnam, and a CIA record dated September 1, 1967 kept the item. The broadcast material names John Sydney McCain among its subjects. Radio aimed at enemy troops was a standard weapon of the war.

Broadcasts like this tried to weaken morale by speaking straight to soldiers in the field. Naming a captured pilot made the message personal for men who knew the risks. The file preserves one piece of that radio war, filed by the monitors who listened daily. Broadcasts were beamed at night, when lonely troops were most likely to be listening to the radio.
cia-0000045913:
In November 1956, CIA analysts finished an estimate asking what would follow if the United States joined the Baghdad Pact or stayed out of it. The pact was a defense alliance linking Turkey, Iraq, Britain, Pakistan, and Iran against Soviet pressure. Washington backed the alliance but had never signed as a full member.

The paper weighs both branches of the choice: what joining might gain, what it might cost, and how allies and rivals would react. Papers of this kind show how the agency gamed out big alliance decisions before presidents made them. The question faded within a few years, when Iraq quit the pact after its 1958 revolution.
cia-0000046513: A spokesman deflated the summer's big sensation in 1991: the supposed prisoner pilot in the famous photograph was, he said, a farmer. A CIA item dated September 1, 1991, kept the correction. The claim had raised the hopes of hundreds of families, which made its collapse a hard public moment. Few corrections in the whole affair traveled as fast.
cia-0000049013: A CIA item from 1981 reports the civilian extreme right in El Salvador as disorganized and short on armed activity at that moment. The lull surprised watchers used to steady death-squad violence. Reports of quiet mattered as much as reports of attacks, since each side's strength was guessed from just such signs.
cia-0000049113: President Duarte instructed his minister of justice in 1985 to open an investigation, and a CIA item preserves the instructions. A president ordering a probe was the easy half; courts and police doing the work was the other. The item survives among the Truth Commission records, a marker of intent filed before the outcome.
cia-0000049213: El Salvador's Foreign Ministry worried over the Jesuit case in 1991, and a CIA item preserves the concern, including the foreign minister's own belief about it. Diplomats carried the case's cost abroad: every capital they visited raised the murders, and asked what would be done. The item survives among the Truth Commission records.
cia-0000049413: A statement on El Salvador and certification issues before the Senate committee is preserved as declassified CIA document 0000049413, dated July 1, 1982. The heading is cut short in the catalog but names the setting plainly. Readers find a short record of a formal statement, tied to the certification debate that runs through several Salvadoran files.
cia-0000098713: Police officers spot UFO; rapid reaction force alerted is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098713, dated May 3, 1996. A semicolon joins the sighting to the alert in one breathless title. Readers find a short incident record unlike any neighbor, its subject an unidentified object sighting preserved in the agency's declassified files.
cia-0000109013: Soviet Forced Labor: an Update is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000109013, dated November 1, 1985. The title marks a revisiting: an update on Soviet forced labor, not a first report. A system update with a near matching name shares the same date in the files. The brief record is a system update item from the autumn of 1985.
cia-0000112813: Untitled Supplmentary Report is the heading, with supplementary misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000112813, dated January 1, 1945. The catalog marks the file untitled, then gives this short label. A supplementary report adds to a file already open, by its own name. The brief record preserves the misspelling exactly as released in the wartime files as filed there.
cia-0000119213: Notice of Priority Change no. 6 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000119213, dated November 5, 1982. The title marks a numbered notice: the sixth change of a priority, in the heading's terms. What priority changed is not stated in the title itself at all. The brief record is an administrative notice item, filed in the autumn of 1982 as released.
cia-0000119713: A May 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Indonesia. The young republic faced revolts in its regions and disorder in its parliament. Washington counted the islands a Cold War prize, and the paper weighs where the country might turn. The republic was only a few years old, and its hold on the outer islands was still being tested when the forecast was written.
cia-0000124313: Dated July 1951, this CIA document addresses Communist treatment of United Nations prisoners, with the word treatment misspelled in the original heading. The error survived into the released file along with the substance. The paper records that treatment as the agency understood it then. Treatment reports fed the public argument over the war at home, where stories from the camps shaped how Americans judged both the enemy and the armistice talks.
cia-0000132213: From January 1991, situation report 530 covers political developments including a Baghdad radio call, the heading breaking off. Iraqi state radio served as Saddam's mouthpiece to the world during the crisis. The report notes what the broadcast said that day. Baghdad radio was heard worldwide through monitoring services, and a call noted in a sitrep usually meant a message aimed at Iraqis and enemies at once.
cia-0000132413:
A break in relations between the Castro government and the United States is weighed in a CIA report dated October 3, 1959. The report treats the rupture as a real possibility. The open question was when it might come, not whether feelings were souring.

Inside, analysts weigh the signs pointing toward a formal break. Relations did in fact end in January 1961, little more than a year later. For readers, the report is an early marker of how soon the agency saw the end coming. It shows the split being forecast while public ties between the two countries still held.
cia-0000132513:
Fallout for the United States from a failed attack on the Castro regime fills a CIA document dated April 5, 1961. Its headline calls the findings preliminary, and the title breaks off before finishing that word. The failed attack it names already lay in the past when analysts wrote.

The document assesses what the attempt cost and what it changed. Coming twelve days before the Bay of Pigs landing, it reads as a warning from a smaller failure. For readers, it shows the agency studying defeat in Cuba once already. The larger defeat that followed that month would echo many of the same lessons.
cia-0000132613: Haiti seeking closer ties with Cuba fills item 4 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 5, 1960. The pairing was an odd one: a harsh dictatorship courting a young revolution. Duvalier's Haiti was hunting for friends wherever they could be found that year. The short item reports the outreach and what Haiti hoped it might bring.
cia-0000135613: Brigade 2506's declassified Spanish files hold this document, dated 5 March 1961. The exile brigade was then in its last weeks of preparation for the April landing in Cuba. Nothing in the catalog record states what this document covers, who wrote it, or which unit it came from. It stands as a dated primary source in the original Spanish, released by the CIA, and any account of its contents must come from reading it rather than from its file title.
cia-0000135713: This Spanish text, dated 2 February 1961, belongs to the 2506 Brigade document set released by the CIA. The brigade was then in final training for the invasion of Cuba. The catalog title is generic, offering no subject, author, or unit. The document is kept in Spanish as a primary source. Its date places it among the last records of the training period, weeks before the brigade sailed.
cia-0000135813: The declassified CIA document dated 1 February 1954 takes up political action talks and debriefings, with the names in the heading deleted by the censors. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000135913: Filed on 4 May 1954, this CIA meeting record concerns a report of meetings with undisclosed persons, written as the situation began to change. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136113: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 4 April 1954, covers a review of a report that urged playing the waiting game, patience weighed against speed. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136313: Radio material from 1400 to 2300 hours is summarized in this 26 June 1954 LINCOLN cable. Castillo asked that Chajon attack Zacapa at 0800 the next day in a synchronized action, and that planes find and bomb enemy artillery near Cumbre Ingeniero. A delayed message from another operator called the situation very bad, with enemy units reported at Entre Rios, Morales, and Champona. The summary captures the confused final days of the Arbenz government.
cia-0000136613: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 January 1961, filed with the 2506 Brigade documents released by the CIA. It shares its date with companion items in the same stretch of the file. The exile brigade was in winter training for the April landing. The catalog names no subject for this document. Preserved in Spanish, it is part of the dense early-January layer of the brigade's surviving paperwork.
cia-0000136713: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, cataloged under an estimated date of 5 January 1960. That is strikingly early for this file, since the brigade was formed during 1960; the estimated flag in the title is part of the record and worth noting. No subject is named for the document. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, dated by estimate to the brigade's first days or before them.
cia-0000137313: NSC Briefing — Cuba, dated 1960, is a declassified CIA briefing for the National Security Council, the body that advises the president on security policy. Cuba dominated that council's agenda in 1960 as Castro's government turned toward Moscow and against Washington. A group of near-identical Cuba briefings from 1960 survives in these files, and the catalog does not set this one's contents apart from theirs. It is best read as part of that run: the steady flow of Cuba papers reaching the top of the U.S. government that year.
cia-06146213: CIA IN KOREA 1946 - 1965 VOLUME III, a CIA history. The Korea history. This file preserves that declassified volume. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
cia-06859713: What if Charles Taylor left Liberia's scene? The agency gamed out the strongman's departure. The West African question. It retains its place in time. This file preserves that declassified assessment. Its contents inform the historical record.
cieza-war-of-quito-markham-1913:
The War of Quito, in Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society translation of 1913, is Pedro Cieza de León's account of civil war among Peru's conquerors. After the Inca empire fell, the Pizarro and Almagro factions turned their swords on each other. Cieza, who knew Peru from years of travel in 1532 to 1550, wrote the record of that fratricidal struggle.

His narrative follows plots, marches, and battles around Quito with a chronicler's care for names and dates. Cieza stands out among the conquerors' writers for fairness: he blames greed on every side. The work shows the conquest eating its own children within a few years of triumph. It is documentary history of the first order.
commons-labor-and-administration-1913:
Commons gathered his papers as Labor and Administration in 1913. The pieces came out of his double life as a university scholar and a working reformer in Wisconsin. That state was then famous as a laboratory of democracy, testing new laws on work, safety, and insurance.

The essays treat the day-to-day problems of reform: joblessness, the arrival of immigrants, and the hard task of making labor laws work in practice. Commons writes about administration with respect, arguing that a good law badly run is a bad law. His high theory is tested here in committee rooms and factory inspections. The book shows the institutional school of economics at its most practical, and it helps explain how Wisconsin's experiments spread to the whole country.
commons-races-immigrants-america-1913:
Commons published Races and Immigrants in America in 1913, when immigration to the United States stood near its historic peak. An earlier version had appeared in 1907, and he revised it as the debate over new arrivals grew hotter. Commons studied the newcomers as an economist: who came, what work they found, and what they earned.

The book sorts immigrant groups by the terms his age used and asks how each fared in American industry and city life. Commons writes as a liberal of his time, sympathetic to the newcomers yet sharing some of the era's assumptions about race and fitness. That tension is part of the book's value now. It stands as a pioneering work of immigration history and a record of how a thoughtful reformer wrestled with the questions of his day.
conrad-chance-1913:
Chance, published in 1913, was the novel that finally made Conrad famous and sold in large numbers. His narrator Marlow returns, this time piecing together the fate of Flora de Barral from the talk of others.

Flora's father, a swindler whose crash ruined thousands, leaves her to the mercy of fortune hunters and a sinister captain husband. Marlow follows her through danger toward an unlikely rescue. The telling is layered, ironic, and full of Conrad's doubts about chance, gender, and respectability. Its success freed him from money worries for the first time in his writing life.
constitution-austria-2013:
Austria's Federal Constitutional Law dates from 1920, was restored after the Second World War, and is hosted with amendments through 2013. It makes Austria a democratic republic and a federal state of nine provinces, called Laender. German is the state language. The opening articles cover general provisions, then federal legislation in detail.

A federal president is head of state, while a federal chancellor leads the government. Parliament has two chambers, the National Council, elected by the people, and the Federal Council, sent by the provinces. Other parts handle lawmaking in the Laender, self-administration by towns, audit of public funds, and the Constitutional Court. The 1920 draft, shaped by jurist Hans Kelsen, still anchors Austrian law.
constitution-croatia-2013:
Croatia adopted its constitution in 1990, on the eve of leaving Yugoslavia, and the hosted text carries changes through 2013, the year Croatia joined the European Union. The opening parts set out the history and the bases of state power. Croatia is a unitary, democratic republic. A long part then protects human rights and basic freedoms.

A president is head of state and shares some powers with the government. Day-to-day rule sits with a prime minister and cabinet answerable to the Sabor, the single-chamber parliament. Later parts cover the courts, the Constitutional Court, local and regional self-rule, and foreign ties. Changes in 2000 and 2001 cut the president's wide early powers and made the system fully parliamentary.
constitution-cyprus-2013:
Cyprus gained this constitution at independence from Britain in 1960, and the hosted text includes changes through 2013. Part one gives general provisions. The republic was built as a shared state of Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots, and both Greek and Turkish are official languages. Part two protects basic rights and liberties, from life and liberty to speech, faith, and property.

A president leads the executive, chosen by the Greek Cypriot side, with a Turkish Cypriot vice-president under the original plan. The House of Representatives makes laws. Later parts cover the courts, the public service, and finance. The shared system broke down in the 1960s, and the text has since been applied in the south alone.
constitution-fiji-2013:
Fiji adopted this constitution in 2013, the fourth since independence, after years of coups and a military-backed government. Chapter one covers the state. Fiji is a republic and, by the text's own terms, a secular state, which sets it apart from earlier drafts shaped by church pressure. Chapter two is a full bill of rights, covering life, liberty, speech, and fair trials.

A president is head of state, while a prime minister leads the government. Parliament is a single chamber, chosen by one nationwide vote under the 2013 rules. Later chapters cover the courts, elections, land, public finance, and the armed forces. The text also made all citizens Fijians by name, ending older ethnic labels in law.
constitution-honduras-2013:
Honduras works under a constitution adopted in 1982, as elected rule returned after military governments, and the hosted text carries changes through 2013. Early titles cover the state, its land, and nationality. Later titles give the rights, duties, and promises of the Honduran people, from life and free speech to health, schooling, and work.

A president leads the executive for one term; the text famously bars re-election in strong terms and even strips citizenship from those who push to change that rule. The National Congress is a single chamber. Other titles cover the courts, a constitutional chamber, elections, local towns, and public finance. In 2009 a president's push for a vote on changing the charter sparked a coup.
constitution-iceland-2013:
Iceland adopted this constitution in 1944, when the island cut its last tie to the Danish crown and became a republic. The text is short and spare. Early chapters cover the republic and the president, then the Althing, the parliament Iceland has kept in some form since the year 930. Later chapters cover the government, the courts, and taxes.

A president is head of state, chosen by direct vote, while a prime minister leads the government and must hold the Althing's trust. One chapter protects human rights, including speech, faith, and equality. The text names the Evangelical Lutheran Church the national church, backed by the state. Repeated efforts to replace the 1944 charter with a new one have so far failed.
constitution-israel-2013:
Israel has no single constitution. Instead, the hosted text gathers its Basic Laws, passed one by one since 1958, in a version through 2013. The first Basic Law covers the Knesset, the parliament: what it is, where it sits, how its members are chosen, and who may vote. Later Basic Laws cover Israel Lands, the President of the State, and the Government.

Other laws in the set cover the judiciary, the state economy, the military, Jerusalem as capital, and human dignity and liberty, which courts use much like a bill of rights. A prime minister leads the government, chosen through the Knesset. A president serves as head of state in a largely ceremonial post. Courts treat the Basic Laws as the closest thing Israel has to a constitution.
constitution-montenegro-2013:
Montenegro adopted this constitution in 2007, a year after voting to leave its union with Serbia, and the hosted text includes changes through 2013. Early parts give basic provisions: a republic founded on the rule of law, with Montenegrin as the official language and other tongues guarded in use. A long part protects human rights and liberties, including the rights of minority peoples.

A president heads the state, while a prime minister leads the government. The Assembly is the single lawmaking chamber. Later parts cover how power is arranged, the economy, the courts, a Constitutional Court, the army, and local self-rule. At 158 articles the text is thorough. Its writing drew close advice from European legal experts.
croce-philosophy-vico-1913:
The Philosophy of Giambattista Vico, published in English in 1913 in R. G. Collingwood's translation, is Croce's study of the Neapolitan thinker who first saw history as man's own creation. The translator was the young Collingwood, later a philosopher himself.

Croce presents Vico's new science: nations passing through ages of gods, heroes, and men, with poetry as the first form of thought. He credits Vico with founding the philosophy of history and of spirit. The study launched serious Vico studies in English almost single-handedly. It is also a meeting of minds: Croce finding his own system anticipated two centuries early.
crowley-book-4-part-2-1913:
Part two of Book Four, printed in 1913, turns from stillness to the tools of rite. Book 4, Part II: Magick gives the first theory of Crowley's ceremonial system in full. Mary D'Este Sturges again worked with him on the text.

The temple, the circle, the triangle, and the wand, cup, sword, and pantacle are each defined and placed. Crowley tells what each tool means and why the plan of the rite takes its shape. The book made his magic a teachable craft with clear rules and reasons. It is the working mate to part one's mystic training.
crowley-book-of-lies-1913:
Ninety-three short chapters make up Crowley's Book of Lies, printed in 1913. Each chapter is a paradox, a jest, a riddle, or a brief shock of prose or verse. The book is also called, in jest, Breaks, and its full title warns the reader not to trust it.

Crowley said each chapter held a truth that flat statement would spoil. Thelemites have read the squibs as doctrine, as humor, and as traps for the too-literal mind. Few of his books have drawn so much commentary line by line. It remains the central Thelemic book of wit and contradiction.
dawson-woodward-piltdown-1913:
Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward presented the Piltdown finds to the Geological Society in 1913. Gravel pits at Piltdown in Sussex had produced skull pieces and a jaw. They named the supposed creature Eoanthropus dawsoni, Dawson's dawn man.

The authors describe a big-brained skull paired with an ape-like jaw. Britain celebrated a first Englishman of great antiquity. Forty years later, tests exposed the bones as a planted forgery. The paper remains history's most famous scientific fraud, read now as a warning about wishful thinking. Schoolbooks repeated the dawn-man story for the next forty years.
deleuze-histoire-critique-magnetisme-181:
J. P. F. Deleuze published his Critical History of Animal Magnetism in 1813. By then the quarrel over Mesmer's fluid had run for thirty years. Deleuze set out to survey every tract written for and against, and to weigh the whole affair with care.

He was a believer, but a judicious one, and his history reads fair to both sides. Mesmerism's rise, its royal trials, and its fall all find their place. Deleuze then traces its quieter afterlife in medical practice. His book remains the pivotal history of the debate. Anyone studying the episode starts with his summing-up of the evidence.
devisser-dragon-in-china-and-japan-1913:
Marinus Willem de Visser was a Dutch sage of the East. His The Dragon in China and Japan came out in 1913. The book is a full study of the dragon in the faith and tales of both lands. De Visser worked from the old texts in their own tongues.

In China the dragon brings rain, rules seas, and marks the throne of kings. In Japan the beast takes new forms from the lore of India and China. Tales of dragon kings, gems, and maids fill the rich text. The book is the great store of dragon lore of the East in English.
doe-osti-3013553-neutrinoless-double-bet: Xe-136 got double-beta-decayed, and this DOE final studies neutrinoless structure. The pages detail the scientific findings. The physicists get their closeout. The decay was double beta. The closeout was physicist. The isotope was Xe-136. The studies were nuclear.
doyle-poison-belt-1913:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Poison Belt in 1913. Professor Challenger calls his old crew to his home with tanks of air in hand. Earth, he says, is about to cross a belt of bad ether in space. The crew of The Lost World meets once more at his side.

One by one, the folk of the world fall in a death like sleep. Cars crash, trains halt, and towns stand still as the hours pass. The crew watch from a sealed room as the hush takes all lands. The tale is a stark end of world piece in the Challenger line.
dunbar-complete-poems-1913:
Paul Laurence Dunbar's complete poems were gathered in 1913, after his early death. Dunbar wrote both in standard English and in Black dialect, as it was then called. The volume includes Lyrics of Lowly Life, his best-known early book. An introduction by W. D. Howells, who championed Dunbar, opens the collection.

The poems cover love, nature, faith, work, and the pain of slavery's memory. Some are light songs, while others carry grief and protest. Dunbar was the first Black American poet to win wide national fame. This full collection lets readers judge his whole range. It remains the standard way to read him.
edgar-great-pyramid-passages-vol2-1913:
John Edgar and his brother Morton measured the Great Pyramid passage by passage. Volume two of Great Pyramid Passages and Chambers appeared in 1913. The first volume, from 1910, began their survey of the monument. The brothers worked in the years when Charles Taze Russell's movement prized such measures.

Their records give lengths, angles, and chambers in dense detail. Photographs and plans support the text of the survey. The set became the measurement canon of the Russell era pyramid studies. Believers read prophecy in its numbers; engineers checked its care. Volume two completes the set as planned. It preserves a strange, devoted piece of fieldwork.
elias-artista-redivivus-oder-das-buch-vo: Elias Artista redivivus, 1913. The revived Elias. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-13:
Michel de Montaigne defends two favorite Roman authors in Volume 13 of his Essays, given here in Charles Cotton's translation. Montaigne (1533-1592) built his book from reading, memory, and close study of his own mind. Seneca the philosopher and Plutarch the biographer fed that study for years. Their honor, he argues, needs guarding against careless critics.

After the long defense, shorter chapters follow a young Roman named Spurina who scarred his own beauty. War chapters borrow Julius Caesar's methods for moving and feeding an army. Portraits of three good women and a ranking of excellent men show Montaigne judging lives from Plutarch's pages. A final piece asks why children resemble their fathers in body and temper. History lovers come for the Roman material. Essay readers come for the sharp, personal judgments mixed through it.
europmc-pmc10021213: Mulchandani and co-authors chart global trends in the use of antibiotics and similar drugs in farm animals from 2020 to 2030. Their study maps how much of these drugs food production uses now and where use is heading. The work speaks to worries that heavy farm use feeds drug resistance that can reach people.
europmc-pmc10129313:
Ruffolo, Chu, Mahajan, and Gray present a deep learning method that predicts antibody structures fast and accurately, in a 2023 study. Antibodies are proteins that bind targets with great precision, and they have become key drugs and lab tools. Their grip comes from six flexible loops whose shapes are hard to predict.

The team trained their model on a huge set of natural antibody sequences and shapes. The method predicts loop shapes quickly for new antibodies. Faster, reliable shapes help scientists design better antibody drugs without slow lab work for every candidate.
europmc-pmc10211313:
Lv and colleagues review obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in a 2023 paper, covering its mechanisms and treatment approaches. In this disorder, the airway narrows or closes during sleep, so breathing stops again and again through the night. It is increasingly common worldwide, above all in middle-aged and older adults, and it strains the heart and brain.

The review explains why airways collapse and what the broken sleep does to the body. It surveys treatments, from air pressure masks to surgery and oral devices. The paper is a full guide to a common, under-treated disorder.
europmc-pmc10356613:
Lake and a huge team built a cell atlas of the human kidney in 2023. The KPMP Consortium was among the groups behind the work. The team tested over 400,000 cells and cell cores from 45 healthy donors and 48 patients. Tests read gene activity in single cells and mapped cells in place inside tissue.

The atlas names 51 main cell types, some rare and some never seen before. It also names 28 cell states seen across kidney parts. Those states cover growth, good repair, poor repair, change, and decline after injury. Lake tied some repair signs to a later drop in kidney function. Maps of about 1.2 million tissue zones linked the states to immune activity nearby.
europmc-pmc10481913:
Dijkstra led a five-year check of the RAPIDO trial in 2023, with Collaborative Investigators across many centres. The trial tested two care paths for rectal cancer before surgery. One path used short radiation, then chemo, then surgery. The standard path used long radiation with chemo, then surgery. In all, 920 patients joined the trial.

At a median of 5.6 years, local failure split the paths. Dijkstra reports failure in 12% of the short-path group and 8% of the standard group. Return of cancer near the first site hit 10% versus 6%. Survival after such failure was much the same in both arms. The short path still cut spread to distant sites, so the team urges finer tuning of it.
europmc-pmc10730913:
Janesick and co-authors joined three gene mapping tools in 2023, with the 10x Development Teams, to read a tumour in fine detail. Each tool alone gives one view: single-cell genes, spatial genes, or targeted reads in place. The team ran all three on large human breast cancer sections kept in wax. The joint view aimed to catch how regions of a tumour differ.

Merged data split tumour zones by their gene marks. Janesick found signs tied to the step toward invasive cancer, the point where it breaks its bounds. Rare cells sat at the muscle-like border that pens the tumour in. Those border cells may hold the key to spread. Each tool alone gave part of the tale; the merge gave the depth.
europmc-pmc10963913:
Riesco and Trujillo update the rules for naming microbes from their genome data in this 2024 paper. Prokaryotes are single-celled life forms without a nucleus, such as bacteria. Naming them once rested on looks and traits, which gave a poor view of their true variety. DNA reading changed that, and genome-based naming now defines species and higher ranks too.

The paper revises the minimal standards set in 2018 for using genome data in this naming work. It adapts measures such as average amino acid identity, which compares proteins between two genomes, and the share of proteins two genomes hold in common. Data and code behind the checks are posted openly online. The authors say fresh standards are vital as sequencing tools and databases keep growing. Outdated rules, they warn, would let naming drift out of step with the data.
europmc-pmc12159213:
Xu, Pang, and Fan reviewed mitochondria in stress, swelling, and aging in 2025. Mitochondria are the energy centers inside cells. They carry their own small set of DNA. When they fail, cells face deep trouble.

Failure sparks excess reactive oxygen, a form of chemical stress. It also triggers swelling responses and cell death signals. Similar changes build up as tissues age. Xu casts mitochondria as hubs linking stress, inflammation, and aging. Fixing their function could open new treatment paths. The review spans mechanisms to early therapy ideas. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1297513:
Patwardhan, Warude, Pushpangadan, and Bhatt compared two ancient medical systems in 2005. Ayurveda is Indian medicine, and TCM is Chinese medicine. Both remain living traditions with global interest rising. Herbal drug monitoring and regulation efforts are underway.

China has promoted its therapies with stronger research backing. Ayurveda still needs a wider scientific evidence base, they argue. Shared principles and differences are laid out side by side. Success factors for global markets get direct discussion. Patwardhan urges evidence building without losing traditional foundations. Side effects and drug cost drive much of the new interest. Both schools of care are still in wide use in Asia and in the West. Old texts sit at the root of both of them.
europmc-pmc1679813:
Fungi get their own family tree built from whole genomes. Fitzpatrick and co-authors constructed it in 2006 from 42 complete fungal genomes, covering 345,829 genes. Older trees rested on one or a few genes.

Two methods agreed closely: a supertree merging 4,805 single-gene trees, and a joined alignment of 153 universal genes. One merging method suffered long-branch attraction, a known artifact; the other stayed immune. Within the largest fungal phylum, the tree resolved two great sub-groups and placed the Leotiomycetes as closest kin to the Sordariomycetes. Fitzpatrick offers the tree as scaffolding for comparative genomics.
europmc-pmc1796613:
Lartillot, Brinkmann and Philippe showed in 2007 how a better evolution model can fix a known tree-building error. The error is long-branch attraction, where fast-evolving species get wrongly grouped together. In animal family trees, fast-changing nematodes and flatworms had been placed either at the base of other bilaterians or inside the protostomes, depending on the outgroup used.

The team compared a standard model, called WAG, which treats all sites in a protein alike, with a mixture model called CAT. CAT lets each site favor its own set of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. With CAT, the false grouping largely vanished. Cross-checks showed CAT also fit the data better and matched the true level of repeated change. Site differences, they argue, must be modeled for reliable trees.
europmc-pmc1867813:
Rosenberg and colleagues reviewed malignant hyperthermia in 2007, a dangerous inherited reaction to common anesthetics. In susceptible people, gases such as halothane and sevoflurane, or the relaxant succinylcholine, trigger runaway muscle metabolism. Reactions strike between one in 5,000 and one in 100,000 anesthesias, while the underlying gene faults may affect one in 3,000 people.

The classic signs are steep fever, racing heart and breathing, excess carbon dioxide, acid buildup, rigid muscles, and muscle breakdown. Untreated, the syndrome is often fatal. The root fault is uncontrolled calcium release inside muscle cells, which burns through energy stores and ruptures the cell membrane. A rise in exhaled carbon dioxide is the earliest clinical clue. Inheritance in humans follows a dominant pattern, so one faulty copy suffices.
europmc-pmc1885213:
Ayoub, Hayashi and co-authors read in 2007 the first complete genes for spider dragline silk. Dragline silk beats nearly all natural and manmade materials for combined strength and toughness. Making it artificially is a major goal, yet earlier designs used only short, partial gene copies.

The team sequenced the full genes for the two proteins, MaSp1 and MaSp2, that form the black widow's dragline. Each gene carries one enormous coding stretch over 9,000 letters long, translated into a highly repetitive protein. Comparing the repeats showed that selection plus recombination within and between genes shapes these modular proteins. The flanking non-coding regions were strikingly conserved between the two genes and held candidate control elements. The full blueprint now exists for anyone engineering true spider silk.
europmc-pmc1978513:
Parekkadan and colleagues tested a new approach in 2007 for fulminant hepatic failure, a sudden and deadly loss of liver function. They used molecules released by mesenchymal stem cells, which are bone marrow cells that calm immune activity. Instead of transplanting cells, they gave only the liquid the cells had grown in. Rats with liver failure received that liquid, or blood filtered through a device holding the cells.

Both forms gave a clear survival benefit in the rats. Benefit depended on cell number, and too many cells removed the gain. Treated livers showed far less immune cell invasion and cell death. Tracking studies showed immune cells were diverted away from the liver. The active part bound to heparin, pointing to chemokines, signals that guide immune cells.
europmc-pmc2043013:
Cragg and co-workers traced in 2007 how the lung cancer drug gefitinib kills tumour cells. Gefitinib blocks EGFR, a growth signal receptor that is mutated in some non-small cell lung cancers. How blocking it causes tumours to shrink was unclear. The team used biochemical and genetic studies in human lung cancer cell lines, including gene silencing to test each step.

Gefitinib triggered the intrinsic death pathway, centred on mitochondria, the cell's energy centres. It activated BAX and released cytochrome c, starting the caspase enzyme cascade. The drug rapidly raised BIM, a pro-death protein, through gene activity and protein stabilising. Blocking the MEK-ERK signal path prevented that rise. Silencing BIM stopped the killing, and a BH3-mimicking drug, ABT-737, made gefitinib kill more strongly.
europmc-pmc2124913: A medical paper on the cultivation of tissue in plasma from alien species. The foreign-grown flesh. This article preserves that tissue culture. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2125213: A medical paper on the relation of bacteriolysis to proteolysis in ferment action. The germs dissolved. This article preserves that biochemistry. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125513: A medical paper on the digitalized dog's heart as affected by amyl nitrite or atropine. The drugged dog heart. This article preserves that cardiology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2125813: A medical paper on identity of the toxins of different strains of Bacillus welchii. The gas gangrene toxins. This article preserves that bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
europmc-pmc2131213: A medical paper with studies on immunity to pneumococcus mucosus, antibody response. The type III defense. This article preserves that immunology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2140313: A biology paper on rate of recovery from the action of fluorite rays. The UV recovery. This article preserves that photobiology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2141013: A biology paper on how arthropods sense gravity, Malacosoma larvae. The caterpillars' gravity sense. This article keeps that bug study. Future scholars will find it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
europmc-pmc2202913:
Coll, Farooqi and O'Rahilly reviewed in 2007 how hormones control food intake. Body weight stays remarkably steady over years despite daily swings in eating and activity. That stability implies precise matching of intake to energy use. Circulating peptides and steroids act on the hypothalamus, brain stem and autonomic nerves to adjust appetite. The review synthesises recent evidence on those signals.

The hormones come from three main sites: fat cells, the gut and the pancreas. Early rat experiments showed the hypothalamus is essential, since damage there caused overeating or refusal to eat. Joined-animal experiments proved a blood-borne satiety factor exists and needs an intact hypothalamus. The molecules behind those classic observations took over forty years to identify. Leptin, the fat-cell hormone, leads the modern account.
europmc-pmc2214813:
Hromádka, Deweese and Zador recorded brain activity in awake rats in 2008 to learn how the auditory cortex represents sounds. Earlier work used anaesthetised animals, where responses looked mainly brief. The team used cell-attached recording, a method that samples neurons regardless of their activity. Rats heard tones, frequency sweeps, noise bursts and natural sounds while recordings were taken from primary auditory cortex.

The population response proved sparse, meaning only a few neurons fire strongly at any moment. Stimuli typically drove high firing rates, over 20 spikes per second, in under five percent of neurons. Some neurons stayed almost silent, below 0.01 spikes per second. Others exceeded 50 spikes per second. Overall firing followed a lognormal distribution. The results support a model where most neurons rest while small, shifting subsets carry the representation.
europmc-pmc2234413:
Hallez and colleagues reviewed methods in 2007 for solving the EEG forward problem in source analysis. Electroencephalography records brain waves at the scalp, and researchers want to locate their sources. The forward problem calculates electrode voltages from a known brain source. Solving it is required before the inverse problem, finding sources from measurements, can be attempted. The review is aimed at newcomers to the field.

Brain signals arise from post-synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons, modelled by Poisson's equation. Simple three-shell spherical head models allow exact solutions. Realistic head shapes from 3D medical images need numerical methods: boundary element, finite element and finite difference approaches are compared. The last two handle direction-dependent tissue conductivity easily. Reciprocity tricks and iterative solvers speed the large calculations involved.
europmc-pmc2323613:
Alonso-Magdalena and colleagues studied in 2008 how the hormone estrogen affects insulin-making cells in the pancreas. These beta cells make and release insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. Two estrogen receptors, named ER alpha and ER beta, sit in these cells, but their roles were unclear.

The team showed both receptors are present in beta cells. Long exposure to natural estrogen raised insulin content, insulin gene activity, and insulin release, without adding new cells. The plastic chemical bisphenol-A, a widespread pollutant that mimics estrogen, did the same at low doses. Tests in mice lacking each receptor pointed to ER alpha as the one responsible. Its effect ran through a signal pathway called ERK1/2.
europmc-pmc2394813:
Long, Vagin, Young, and Murshudov presented an automated crystallography pipeline in 2008. Crystallographers work out protein shapes from X-ray patterns, and one standard trick is molecular replacement: using a known similar structure as a starting model. The archive of known structures then held over 40,000 entries and grew by thousands a year.

Their pipeline, BALBES, searches that archive through a rebuilt database organised by protein domains and by how pieces assemble into multi-part units. Given only the X-ray data and the protein's letter sequence, it picks candidate models and solves the replacement problem with no human steering. Older domain libraries, built for general biology, had proved awkward for this job, so the team redesigned the hierarchy for it. They offered BALBES as a fully automatic route from raw data to a starting structure.
europmc-pmc2410013:
Satagopan and colleagues explained a trap in survival statistics in 2004. The trap is competing risks: a patient may meet a different event first, which removes any chance of the event being studied. Treating that patient as merely censored, the standard Kaplan-Meier habit, distorts the answer.

Their paper shows how to estimate cumulative incidence, the chance of the event by a given time, while handling rival events properly. They work through two published data sets, computing incidence both ways. The Kaplan-Meier figures overshot the true incidence, because they pretend rival-event patients could still have the studied event later. The corrected method counts them as permanently out of the running. The authors addressed the note to clinical researchers, stressing that the choice of method changes reported risks in real studies.
europmc-pmc2584113:
Hulsen, de Vlieg, and Alkema built a web application called BioVenn in 2008 for drawing area-proportional Venn diagrams from biological lists. Genomics projects produce many lists of gene or protein identifiers, and researchers want to see overlaps at a glance. In a proper Venn diagram the circle and overlap sizes match the list sizes, but no existing tool tied that to biological databases.

A user pastes two or three lists and presses submit. The result is a diagram whose areas are proportional to the overlaps. Colours and text size adjust through the page, labels drag into place, and the picture exports as SVG or PNG image files. BioVenn also lists the identifiers in each subset. It links recognised ones to their source databases. It converts between Affymetrix, EntrezGene, and Ensembl identifiers.
europmc-pmc2702413:
Peng and colleagues published a United States study in 2009 on which parts of fine particle pollution send people to hospital. Fine particles are a mix of chemicals from traffic, diesel, wood smoke, and other sources. The question was whether some parts of that mix are more harmful than others.

They used daily hospital and air data from 2000 to 2006 for 119 urban areas and 12 million older adults on Medicare, which is public health cover for older people. Elemental carbon, a soot-like part, was linked to same-day heart admissions. Organic carbon matter was linked to same-day lung admissions, while other parts showed no clear link.
europmc-pmc2772813:
Comas, Homolka, Niemann, and Gagneux tested in 2009 how well standard genotyping methods reconstruct the family tree of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a pathogen with very little DNA diversity. Such monomorphic bacteria are usually typed by mobile or repeated elements: spoligotyping and MIRU-VNTR typing in this case. Using full sequences of eighty-nine genes from a global strain collection as the gold standard, they compared the trees each method produced.

Sequence-based trees were highly consistent and strongly supported, with almost no conflicting signal. Trees from spoligotyping and fifteen-locus MIRU-VNTR clashed with them, distorted by convergent evolution, where unrelated strains gain look-alike patterns. The twenty-four-locus version did better but still missed some lineages, and its power varied by lineage. They advise defining lineages by robust sequence markers and tailoring repeat-based typing to each lineage.
europmc-pmc2777313:
Capra and co-authors introduced in 2009 ConCavity, an algorithm that predicts where small molecules bind on a protein by combining evolutionary conservation with three-dimensional structure. Knowing a protein's functional sites is a key step toward knowing what it does. Earlier methods used sequence or structure alone. Their direct comparison showed the two approaches carry largely complementary information.

ConCavity merges conservation scores with a search for pockets on the protein surface. In large tests on diverse single- and multi-chain structures, it beat existing methods at finding both whole binding pockets and the individual residues that line them. It also reached top performance on catalytic sites and drug binding pockets. Blending the two evidence types, they conclude, improves on either alone and sharpens the link between conservation and function.
europmc-pmc2781113:
Schnoes, Brown, Dodevski, and Babbitt measured in 2009 how often public protein databases mislabel what an enzyme does. Most sequences in these databases were never tested in a lab; computers assign their functions by similarity, and errors can spread. The team audited four major databases using thirty-seven enzyme families with strong experimental records, grouped into six superfamilies.

The hand-curated Swiss-Prot database showed almost no errors. The other databases, including GenBank NR and TrEMBL, averaged error rates from five to sixty-three percent across the superfamilies. In ten families, over eighty percent of entries in some database were wrong. Errors grew in one database between 1993 and 2005, and most came from overpredicting, assigning a specific job the protein does not have. The authors suggest fixes for the systematic causes they found.
europmc-pmc2807913:
Nishimura and colleagues hunted in 2010 for plant proteins that work with ABI1, a brake on signaling by the drought hormone abscisic acid, called ABA. ABA helps plants survive dry spells and keeps seeds dormant. Because backup copies hide many signals from gene studies, the team fished out ABI1's partners directly from Arabidopsis plants.

Nine of the fourteen members of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family, the plant's ABA sensors, bound ABI1 most strongly in living tissue. The grip between one sensor, PYR1, and ABI1 tightened within five minutes of ABA treatment. Plants missing four sensor genes barely closed their leaf pores in response to ABA, hard proof the sensors matter for water saving.
europmc-pmc2826413:
Krebiehl and colleagues showed in 2010 that losing a protein called DJ-1, a rare cause of inherited Parkinson disease, gums up both the cell's power units and its recycling system. DJ-1 was known to guard cells against oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive oxygen. The team used cells from knockout mice and from human carriers of a faulty DJ-1 version.

Without DJ-1, mitochondria breathed poorly, leaked more reactive oxygen, and changed shape in set ways. Recycling through lysosomes, the cell's digestion sacs, ran slowly at baseline, so defective mitochondria piled up instead of being cleared. A signaling protein called ERK2 was also underactive. The work ties DJ-1 directly to keeping mitochondria sound through steady housekeeping.
europmc-pmc2831913:
Clougherty reviewed the evidence in 2010 on whether air pollution hits male and female lungs differently, and whether the split is social or biological. Studies repeatedly find effects differing by sex, but the pattern is patchy and the reasons tangled: men and women differ in jobs, chores, and hormones, all at once.

Across adult studies, stronger effects more often appeared in women, especially in older groups and in studies using home-based exposure measures. Among children, boys looked more affected early in life and girls later in childhood. The author offers a framework borrowed from gender analysis, which separates social roles from body traits, to help future studies pull the two apart.
europmc-pmc2852313:
Emsley, Lohkamp, Scott, and Cowtan presented Coot in 2010, the graphics program crystallographers use to build and check molecular models by hand. Automated builders can draft a protein chain into an electron-density map, but scientists must inspect, fix, and validate the result interactively, especially at low resolution where errors creep in.

Coot displays atomic models, contoured density maps, and helper objects in a rotatable three-dimensional view built for ease of learning. Its tools cover model building, real-space refinement, and validation checks, with scripting access to nearly everything underneath. The paper surveys the program's features and design choices, including its library foundations, and traces how development has shifted emphasis toward validation as automatic building has improved.
europmc-pmc2855713:
Wang, Henning, and Heber showed in 2010 that two of the most popular lab tests for cell growth quietly misread green tea's star compound. Laboratories reported wildly varying potency for EGCG against cancer cells, and the team suspected the measurement method itself. They compared five assays on prostate and breast cancer cells treated with the compound.

Tests counting DNA or energy molecules agreed closely with direct counting. The dye tests MTT and MTS, which read mitochondrial activity, overestimated surviving cells and made EGCG look about half as potent as it truly was. A different plant compound, apigenin, showed no such distortion. The authors warn that assay choice must match a compound's chemistry when judging botanical extracts.
europmc-pmc2891813:
Oliveira-Ferreira and colleagues overviewed in 2010 the state of malaria in Brazil, a country that cut the disease hugely yet cannot finish it. Annual cases fell from around six million in the early 1940s to about three hundred six thousand registered in 2009. The main mosquito carrier lives across most of the country, but transmission now clings almost entirely to the Amazon Basin.

Disorderly settlement of the Amazon from the 1960s onward pushed cases back up and keeps them there. The milder parasite Plasmodium vivax causes over four fifths of cases and most of the economic burden, while the dangerous falciparum causes most of the rest. Worryingly, vivax has begun producing unusual severe complications in recent years, challenging its benign reputation.
europmc-pmc2930213:
Summers and colleagues reviewed neutrophil kinetics, the birth, movement, and removal of the most common white blood cells, in a 2010 article. Neutrophils kill germs but live only hours in the blood, so the body must replace them at a huge daily rate.

The review covers release from bone marrow, guided in part by signals acting through the CXCR4 receptor, and the split between freely flowing cells and a slower marginated pool. It also covers how aged cells are cleared and how stress or inflammation disturbs the balance. Too much neutrophil activity can injure healthy tissue.
europmc-pmc2936113:
Aggleton and co-authors reviewed the linked pathways between the hippocampus and the front part of the thalamus in 2010. These brain areas connect through several routes, and together they seem central to remembering past events.

Evidence from brain studies, patient work, and electrical tests shows parallel direct and indirect streams, the indirect ones passing through the mammillary bodies. The streams often push activity in opposite directions while staying partly separate. Damage at one site can disturb distant partners across the network. The system matters most for vivid recollection rather than simple feelings of familiarity.
europmc-pmc2936313:
Cole reviewed the biology of human chorionic gonadotropin, better known as hCG, in a 2010 article. The name covers four separate molecules, each made by different cells and each doing distinct work.

Standard hCG from placental tissue supports progesterone output, blood vessel growth in the womb, and quieting of the mother's immune response near the placenta. A sugar-heavy form drives growth and invasion of placental cells during implantation. A free fragment appears in many cancers outside the placenta, while a pituitary form comes from hormone cells in the brain. Each variant gets its own account.
europmc-pmc3000813:
Fiehn and co-authors profiled blood chemicals in obese African-American women with and without type 2 diabetes in a 2010 study. Insulin resistance disturbs the handling of many fuels at once, and mapping that disturbance may expose early markers.

Measuring several hundred fasting metabolites, they extracted components tracking closely with a long-term blood sugar score. Diabetes samples ran high in certain amino acids and their by-products, a hydroxy acid, long-chain fats, and sugar derivatives. Two amino acids climbed steadily with worse sugar control and matched a marker of fuel burning. The pattern hints the cell's central furnace runs inefficiently.
europmc-pmc3017113:
Gao led a large team sequencing two Metarhizium fungi used as living insecticides in a 2011 comparative genome study. One species attacks many insects while its cousin targets only grasshoppers and locusts, a contrast written somewhere in their genes.

The two genomes proved highly aligned in structure, with signs the genus descends from plant-associated fungi. Both devote an unusually large share of genes to secreted proteins, many with no known match. The broad attacker carries expanded families for cutting insect armour, detoxifying, and making toxins, matching its wider menu, while the specialist shows a genome defence trick the generalist lacks.
europmc-pmc3053313:
Izawa and Shadmehr asked in 2011 whether the brain learns movements from two kinds of error at once. One kind is sensory errors, where a movement feels different than predicted. The other is reward errors, where an outcome is worse than hoped. Volunteers adapted their reaching while the quality of visual feedback was varied. The team watched how learning spread to nearby movements and whether predictions themselves changed.

With crisp feedback, learning ran almost entirely on sensory errors. That learning rewrote the brain's predictions and spread broadly to neighboring movements. As feedback grew fuzzy, reward errors took a larger share. Reward driven learning changed the movement just as much, but left predictions untouched and spread only narrowly. The two signatures were so distinct that a person's learning style could be read from them. The work suggests rehabilitation and training should match feedback quality to the learning route they want.
europmc-pmc3156713:
Juliette Stehlé and colleagues recorded every close contact in a French primary school in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. How children mix drives how respiratory infections spread, yet hard numbers were scarce. Pupils and teachers wore radio badges for two days, logging tens of thousands of face-to-face encounters among more than two hundred people.

Each child averaged several hundred contacts a day with dozens of others, totalling nearly three hours of close time, though most single contacts were brief. Contact concentrated inside each class, with children spending about three times longer with classmates than with other classes. The resulting contact matrix, split by class and age, gives disease modellers a realistic alternative to assuming everyone mixes evenly, and helps rank measures such as class closure.
europmc-pmc3228813:
A. P. Jason de Koning and colleagues argued that far more of the human genome is repetitive than textbooks say, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. The standard way to find transposable elements, matching DNA against known element sequences, had credited repeats with about half the genome. Their alternative method hunts for clusters of abundant short fragments related to one another.

The new approach predicted hundreds of millions of additional repetitive bases, pushing the estimate to roughly two-thirds of the genome. Detailed checks on two common element families showed the standard tool misses even moderately long fragments, while the new method stays sensitive down to small pieces. They also identified large amounts of previously unannotated element sequence. The message is that genome annotation needs combined, probability-aware methods.
europmc-pmc3270013:
Ravi Patel and Mukesh Jain introduced the NGS QC Toolkit, software for cleaning next-generation sequencing data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Modern sequencers pour out enormous datasets, and bad reads can poison every downstream result, so quality control is essential. Fast, efficient tools were needed to handle the volume.

The toolkit is written in Perl as a free, standalone, open-source application. It checks quality and filters for high-grade data. It serves the two dominant platforms of the day, Roche 454 and Illumina machines. Extra utilities convert between sequence formats, trim reads, and compute statistics. Users can set their own thresholds at each step rather than accepting defaults. The authors expect the toolkit to improve the reliability of analyses built on sequencing data across many laboratories.
europmc-pmc3356313:
Agustí and the ECLIPSE investigators asked whether lasting inflammation throughout the body marks out a distinct group of people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The large ECLIPSE cohort followed patients for three years with repeated blood measurements, letting the team separate persistent inflammation from temporary spikes.

Of 1,755 patients, about thirty percent showed no systemic inflammation while sixteen percent stayed inflamed, based on a panel of six blood biomarkers. Despite similar lung damage, the persistently inflamed group died at far higher rates and suffered more exacerbations. The authors identify this as a distinct COPD phenotype that might benefit from targeted anti-inflammatory treatment.
europmc-pmc3418213:
Steinsbekk and co-authors pooled trials in 2012 on group-based self-management education for type 2 diabetes, compared with routine care. Group courses are popular because they cost less and let patients learn from each other. The review gathered twenty-one randomized trials with several thousand participants followed for at least six months.

Blood sugar control improved in the group courses at six months, a year, and two years, and fasting glucose fell too. Knowledge of diabetes and self-management skills rose clearly, and patients felt more empowered early on. Satisfaction and body weight improved at one year, while death rates, blood pressure, and blood fats did not differ. Quality of life results were too mixed to judge. Group teaching, they conclude, earns its place.
europmc-pmc3473013:
Kim and co-authors tested how a high-fat diet stirs inflammation through gut bacteria, in a 2012 PLoS ONE mouse study. Obesity travels with low-grade inflammation, but where that inflammation starts was unknown. Mice ate a high-fat or low-fat diet for eight weeks, and the team tracked gut microbes, gut leakiness, and inflammatory signals in body and colon.

The high-fat diet shifted gut microbes, raised a bacterial toxin called endotoxin in blood and stool, and loosened the gut wall's seals. Mice bred without the toxin sensor TLR4 still gained weight on the diet, but gained far less fat and showed no rise in inflammatory signals. Kim's group concludes the diet drives inflammation by raising endotoxin that acts through that sensor.

file-no-113: File No. 113, Émile Gaboriau's detective novel. The numbered file. This book preserves that mystery. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
frobenius-the-voice-of-africa-1913:
Leo Frobenius led an expedition across the Western Sudan in 1910 to 1912 and told it in The Voice of Africa, published in 1913. The German ethnologist sought the roots of African civilization among Yoruba, Nupe, and Jukun peoples. Sacred art, bronzes, and temples amazed him, and he carried word of them to Europe.

Frobenius argued that Africa held high cultures of great age, a claim Europe resisted hearing. His finds and photographs changed how the West saw African art forever. The book stands as both travel record and manifesto, the voice of a continent speaking through its shrines.
frost-boys-will-1913:
Robert Frost published A Boy's Will in 1913, his first book of poems. Frost was an American farmer and teacher who had moved to England. The poems speak in a young man's voice about nature, love, and finding his own path. Into My Own and Storm Fear are among the best-known pieces.

Many poems pair a plain scene with a quiet doubt or hope. Frost uses traditional forms but a fresh, spoken tone. The book won notice in England and helped launch his career back home. Readers can hear his later themes starting here: work, weather, isolation, and choice. It is a modest and lovely debut.
frus-1861-d113:
Mr. Jones wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 July 1861. The dispatch is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Jones wrote on the eve of Bull Run, the war's first great battle. His July report is the second of his two papers in this file. Read with his April note, it brackets the season in which the short war became a long one. His two reports, spring and summer, frame the war's first season from one post. One post, two seasons: the frame shows how much the war had changed by July.
frus-1861-d13:
Norman Judd, the American minister to Prussia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 July 1861. The dispatch is document 13 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd was a friend of Lincoln's from Illinois politics, sent to Berlin that spring. Prussia was rising as the strong power of north Germany, and its stance mattered. Judd's reports told Washington how the Berlin court read the American war in its first summer. Berlin watched the war through the lens of its own struggle with Austria and France. Berlin's cool tone suited the Union, which asked no more than strict fairness.
frus-1861-d213:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Marsh on 21 June 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 213 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d113:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 31 July 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 113 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d13:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 February 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 13 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d213:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 5 April 1862, in a note printed as Document 213 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, received it at the legation.

Early April 1862 brought the great battle of Shiloh in Tennessee and the start of the campaign against Richmond. Each swing of the war changed the odds that Europe might step in, so envoys traded paper at a fast rate. A note from this week sits in the file as part of that quick, watchful exchange. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d313:
On 20 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton another dispatch, printed as Document 313 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark the post-battle rush.

Seward wrote on the eve of Lincoln's emancipation announcement, which he had helped shape and knew was coming. The proclamation would give the war a cause that European publics could cheer. His letters to Paris in these days prepared his envoy for the new ground, on which defending the Union also meant defending freedom. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d413:
From Madrid on 9 November 1861, Carl Schurz sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 413 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message.

Schurz wrote in the weeks when Britain, France, and Spain had just agreed to act together in Mexico, a move that worried Washington deeply. As minister in Madrid he could watch Spanish motives at close range. His reports home fed the Union's effort to keep the European powers separate and neutral. The dispatch is part of the first season of that long campaign, before Schurz left Spain for army service.
frus-1862-d513:
Two days after Pike's latest report was dated, on 8 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 513 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The crossed dates are the Atlantic mail at work: each man wrote from news the other had not seen. Seward's August orders to The Hague kept up the standing themes of Dutch neutrality and colonial ports. They also kept up the Union's refusal to treat the rebellion as a nation. Pike's replies, arriving a month later, show how those themes landed. The pair of files, order and report interleaved, is the true shape of the record the volume preserves. It is a slow conversation. Two governments carried it on in good faith across an ocean.
frus-1862-d613:
The Danish file opens on 22 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen. It is Document 613 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Denmark was a small maritime kingdom. Its ports and its Sound dues touched Baltic trade. Wood, a New York lawyer, held the post through the war. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Copenhagen court. The Baltic was far from the fighting, but its states' goodwill counted in the general European balance the Department tracked. The letter begins a quiet, regular file in the volume's northern tier.
frus-1862-d713:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington, a lawyer who had long handled his land's affairs in the United States. The letter is document 713 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Foreign envoys in Washington wrote to Seward on the business between their lands and the United States. For Costa Rica, trade and the transit routes of Central America were never far from the talks. Molina's letter is part of that formal exchange, in which small republics dealt with a great power then fighting for its life. The file that follows shows the talk run both ways.
frus-1863p1-d113:
On 11 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of three letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 113 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three letters in a day, a week after a batch of twelve, show a desk that never let the London file cool. Seward split his points across the sheets so Adams could use each on its own. This one opens the day's set. It is part of the spring press on Britain, kept up sheet by sheet from Washington.
frus-1863p1-d13:
On 13 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 13 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote on the day of the battle of Fredericksburg, though its news had not yet reached London.

Letters crossed the Atlantic in about ten days by steamer, so each side wrote in the dark about the other's last moves. Seward's mail set the claims Adams was to press on Britain. They were fair dealing, a tight rein on warships built for the South, and no aid to the rebellion. This letter is one link in that chain of orders.
frus-1863p1-d213:
The mail from London dated 11 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 213 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d313:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 313 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d413: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 March 1863. It is document 413 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d513:
A dispatch dated 14 May 1863 went from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d613:
Document 613, dated 14 August 1863, records a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d113: On November 10, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and his message is Document 113 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two leaders wrote almost daily that week, even with a meeting a fortnight ahead, because the plans for two conferences still had loose ends. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series' pre-departure papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d13: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on June 28, 1943, and the message stands as Document 13 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The same day produced a Churchill note in return, a sign of how fast the exchange moved that week. The record lists the parties and the date only. In the State Department's published series, the letter belongs to the build-up toward the Quebec talks of August and the summits that closed the year.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d213:
The Joint Staff Planners sent report J.C.S. 600 to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 11 November 1943. Its subject is airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area, tying the question to the decisions taken at the Quebec conference that August.

The planners say B-29s could be ready early in 1944, and that attacks on Japan could start sooner if fields were built in time. They call for at least four fields near Calcutta and five near Chengtu in China, built with British and Chinese help. Their recommendation is that all nine be authorized and finished, as far as possible, by May 1944.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d313:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 410 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, an examination of how weather limits any postponement of Operation Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion of France. It was ammunition in the Anglo-American argument over the invasion's date.

The assault needs a quiet spell of four days with winds of force three or less. Counting ten years of weather, such spells came eighteen times in April and twenty-one in May. They came nineteen times in June, and still seventeen in September. On the assault alone, the operation could slip to September. The build-up after landing needs about three months of workable weather. Tides confine each attempt to two short windows a month, and missing the full-moon window, needed for the air lift, costs twenty-four days.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d413:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent Ambassador Harriman a confidential telegram, numbers 1342 to 1344, from Washington at midnight on 4 December 1943. It reports the uproar in the American press over Moscow's early announcement of the Tehran Conference.
