Horace Hayman Wilson translated Kalidasa's Meghaduta into English verse in 1813, at the College of Fort William in Calcutta. His Cloud Messenger was the first English rendering of the poem. An exiled yaksha, a minor spirit of the god of wealth, pines for his wife in the far north of India.

When the monsoon cloud rises, he begs it to carry his message across India to her. The cloud's route becomes a tour of rivers, cities, and temples in Kalidasa's glowing verse. Wilson, a surgeon turned Sanskrit scholar, opened much of Sanskrit poetry to English readers. His version, with notes, stayed standard for a century. The poem itself remains Kalidasa's lyric masterpiece.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-13: Etext 3563, released in December 2002, is volume thirteen. Its author is Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary in his rising years. Gutenberg's head note marks the file with the year 1815. That head note, plus the license that trails it, is the whole sample. Not a single paragraph of the memoir is included in the held portion. Reporting must therefore rest on the series, author, and file facts, and go no further.
mitchell-business-cycles-1913:
Wesley Clair Mitchell published Business Cycles in 1913, the fruit of years spent gathering facts about booms and slumps. Mitchell, a Columbia economist, distrusted theories built without evidence. He set out to describe the business cycle exactly as it happens before daring to explain it.

The book follows prices, wages, interest, and profits through prosperity, crisis, depression, and revival, using long runs of statistics. Mitchell shows the cycle as a process in which each phase breeds the next. The facts-first program made the treatise the founding work of the empirical study of cycles. It also launched the research institute Mitchell later led, where measuring the economy became an organized national task.
montgomery-aramaic-incantation-texts-nip:
James A. Montgomery published his edition of Aramaic incantation texts from Nippur in 1913. Excavators had found clay bowls inked with spells under house floors there. Families buried the bowls to trap demons beneath their homes.

Montgomery's volume was the first scholarly publication of these Jewish Babylonian bowls. He transliterated, translated, and explained the spiraling Aramaic inscriptions. The spells name angels and demons and quote scripture for protection. Everyday magic of late antiquity comes alive in these household objects. The edition founded a whole field of bowl studies. Archaeology and linguistics meet on every page of Montgomery's work.
munro-prehistoric-britain-1913: Robert Munro wrote this short survey of the deep past of Britain for the Home University Library in 1913. The set was made to put sound learning in the hands of plain readers. Munro was a Scots doctor who had dug much of his own proof in the field. In a small compass he sets out the stone age case for the isles, from flint tools to cave finds. It is the clear word on the deep past as its age knew it.
nasa-tm-19680027791-experimental-perform:
Samuel M. Futral Jr. and Donald E. Boleski of Lewis Research Center tested a small axial-flow turbine across Reynolds numbers in this 1968 report. The five-inch, single-stage turbine was designed for a Brayton cycle power application. Argon served as the working fluid during the tests.

Inlet pressures varied widely, giving Reynolds numbers from high to quite low. Efficiency and equivalent mass flow both fell as Reynolds number dropped. Torque fell notably across the test range as well. Exit diffuser effectiveness stayed high throughout the tests. Performance losses were greater than those of a radial-inflow turbine designed for the same job. The data warn designers that small turbines suffer at low Reynolds numbers.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, gathers Chrysostom's homilies on eight of Paul's letters: Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. The volume came out in 1886 under Philip Schaff. It is the Chrysostom volume of short courses.

His commentary on Galatians runs whole, one of the few complete ancient ones we have. The prison letters get warm, pastoral treatment, full of praise for Paul's chains. The talks to Timothy and Titus turn to the duties of clergy and household. Taken together, the volume is a school of Pauline preaching. It also shows how the early church read nearly the whole of Paul in public worship.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, holds more of Gregory the Great, then turns east: Ephraim Syrus and Aphrahat, the Persian sage. Schaff and Wace edited the series. The Syriac fathers here wrote in the language of Jesus's own country.

Gregory's later letters and his book of dialogues, full of Italian saints and wonders, open the volume. Ephraim, the fourth-century deacon of Edessa, then sings the faith in hymns of unmatched imagery; the English here is prose, but the music shows through. Aphrahat's demonstrations, written under Persian rule, are the earliest Syriac theology we have. The volume is the series' window on the eastern church.
nukariya-religion-of-the-samurai-1913:
Kaiten Nukariya, a Japanese Zen scholar of the Soto school, wrote for Western readers in 1913. The Religion of the Samurai sets out Zen thought and training as it grew in China and Japan. No earlier English book by a Japanese Zen teacher had reached so far.

Nukariya tells the rise of Zen, its view of mind and world, and the hard drill of sitting and koan work. He shows how the warrior class of Japan took Zen as its inner rule of life. His tone is calm, clear, and free of mystic fog. The book first opened Zen to the English-speaking world.
odd-charges-odd-craft-part-13:
William Wymark Jacobs wrote the comic sea tale Odd Charges. It is part thirteen of his book Odd Craft. The scene opens in the Cauliflower inn tap room. A stranger eats and drinks in quiet comfort. An old man nearby longs for beer and tobacco.

The old man wishes a conjurer could fill his mug. The stranger then raps his pipe on the table. Beer and tobacco appear as if by magic. Talk turns to a conjurer who once performed in Claybury. Jacobs builds humor from talk, timing, and surprise. The tale shows his gift for inn talk and quiet trickery.
openalex-w146743813:
Betty Abelev and the ALICE Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in August 2012. The team studied a particle called J/psi in lead collisions. Collisions ran at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN. They compared lead results with proton collision results.

The team found fewer J/psi particles than scaling predicted. That shortfall is called suppression in the report. The shortfall showed no strong link to collision centrality. Results differed from those at lower collision energies. Models with charm quarks in hot, free matter fit. Such matter is called quark-gluon plasma by physicists. The work probes matter formed just after the Big Bang.
openalex-w1648382113:
Viviana Fanti and the NA48 Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physics Letters B in October 1999. The team worked at CERN and partner institutes across Europe. Their subject is direct CP violation in kaon decays. A neutral kaon can decay into two pions.

CP violation means matter and antimatter behave slightly differently. Direct forms of it are rare and hard to measure. The paper presents a new measurement of that effect. The hosted sample preserves the long author and institute lists. It gives no abstract text stating the numeric result. Readers can confirm the team, venue, and topic from the sample.
openalex-w2023422813:
Marcelo Samsa, Juan Mondotte, Nestor Iglesias and colleagues studied how dengue virus builds new copies of itself. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2009. Dengue causes high rates of illness worldwide. Vaccines and antivirals were urgently needed. How the virus packs its genome was poorly known.

The team watched the virus capsid protein inside infected cells. The protein gathered on fat droplets inside the cell. Small changes to the protein broke that targeting. Those changes also blocked new virus particle formation. Changing droplet amounts in cells changed virus growth. The authors propose the droplets hold the capsid early on. They may then serve as a platform for packing the genome.
openalex-w2054504313:
Stefan Monecke, Geoffrey Coombs, Anna Shore and colleagues compiled a field guide to resistant staph bacteria. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2011. MRSA bacteria resist common antibiotics. They have become a global health challenge. New strains now appear outside hospitals too. Some strains produce a toxin that raises concern.

The team typed over three thousand bacterial isolates. Samples came from clinics and animal sources worldwide. A DNA microarray identified each strain's type. The guide sorts strains into pandemic, epidemic and sporadic groups. It describes where each major clone occurs. Tracking clones helps hospitals spot outbreaks early. It also guides infection control across countries.
openalex-w2062462813:
Miriam Scheel, Mario Rohrer, Christian Huggel and colleagues tested satellite rainfall estimates in the Central Andes. Their paper appeared in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences in 2011. Mountain regions often lack good rain gauges. Climate projects still need solid rainfall records. Satellite products could fill the gaps.

The team compared a satellite rainfall product with gauges. Study areas covered Cuzco in Peru and La Paz in Bolivia. Daily satellite amounts showed large biases. The product caught strong rain events well. It still underestimated how heavy they were. Near La Paz it raised many false alarms. Averaging over longer periods improved agreement strongly. The results guide careful use of satellite rain data.
openalex-w2138831913:
Catrine Tudor-Locke, Cora Craig, Wendy Brown, and colleagues published this review in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2011. They ask a simple public question: how many steps per day are enough for adults? Step counters make the question practical, but published step targets varied widely.

Healthy adults typically take between four thousand and eighteen thousand steps a day. The authors judge ten thousand steps a reasonable target for this group. Programs that add walking usually raise counts by about two thousand to twenty-five hundred steps. Studies also tie walking pace to effort: about one hundred steps per minute marks the floor of moderate intensity walking.
openalex-w2154052713:
Humberto Lara, Elsa Garza-Treviño, Liliana Ixtepan-Turrent, and Dinesh Singh published this review in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2011. They survey silver nanoparticles as broad killers of bacteria and viruses. Silver has served medicine since ancient times, and shrinking it to nanoscale size has opened new uses in wound care and infection control.

The review explains how the particles attack microbes, with HIV as the best-studied virus case. The particles bind the outer coat of enveloped viruses and block them from entering cells. Work on HIV showed blocked transmission in human cervix tissue culture. The authors argue such nanosystems could strengthen infection prevention and antiviral therapy, while much about virus interactions remains unexplored.
openalex-w2164613013:
Catrine Tudor-Locke, Cora Craig, Yukitoshi Aoyagi, and colleagues published this review in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2011. They translate activity guidelines into daily step counts for older adults and special populations. These groups, including people with disabilities or chronic illness, gain from moving more, but adult step targets may not fit them.

Healthy older adults average roughly two thousand to nine thousand steps a day. Special populations average somewhat lower, from about twelve hundred up. Walking programs added modest gains in older adults and larger gains in special groups. No firm pace threshold exists for older adults yet. The authors offer guiding values built from adult pace data, taken above daily living activity.
openalex-w2780728213:
The International Helminth Genomes Consortium reported this study in Nature Genetics in 2018, with Avril Coghlan and James Anthony Cotton among its authors. It compares genomes of the major parasitic worms: roundworms and flatworms. These parasites infect over a quarter of humanity for years on end. They also stunt crops and livestock, and slow growth in poor regions.

The team analyzed eighty-one worm genomes, from parasites and free-living kinds alike. They found gene families born and expanded at key points in worm evolution. Some help parasites dodge host immunity, move through tissues, or feed. Core metabolism differed widely between lineages, including in families long targeted by drugs. A computer screen then ranked fresh drug targets and candidate compounds. The resource gives worm researchers a shared basis for fighting these neglected parasites.
openalex-w3084362113:
Valentina Zavala, Paige Bracci, John Carethers, and colleagues wrote this review in the British Journal of Cancer in 2020. It summarizes cancer health disparities among racial and ethnic minorities in the United States. Gaps in cancer rates and outcomes by race are well established.

Those gaps grow from an interplay of structural, economic, social-environmental, behavioral, and biological factors. Yet most large studies of cancer causes have drawn mainly on people of European origin. Data and tissue samples from diverse groups remain scarce, which deepens the knowledge gap and risks widening the disparities themselves. The review covers the most common cancers, plus stomach, liver, pancreas, and blood cancers, to show how complex the pattern is.
openalex-w4385691013:
Unai Pascual, Patricia Balvanera, Christopher Anderson, and colleagues argue that nature's many values must guide sustainability choices, in Nature in 2023. Twenty-five years after landmark work on valuing ecosystem services, the biodiversity crisis deepens. Decisions still rest on a narrow slice of what nature means to people. Property rights and current norms decide whose values count, and many are simply ignored.

The authors organise values in layers, from worldviews down to measurable indicators. People value nature as a means to human ends, for its own sake, and through relationships of care and reciprocity. Broad values like justice and stewardship often support sustainability. Bringing these diverse values into policy, they argue, is essential if decisions are to protect both nature and human wellbeing.
openalex-w4406161213:
Catherine Overed-Sayer, Eresha Fernando, Randall Jiménez, and colleagues present the first full global assessment of freshwater animals. Their paper appeared in Nature in 2025. Rivers and lakes hold rich wildlife and support billions of people's livelihoods. Yet conservation policy has relied on data from land animals.

The team assessed extinction risk for freshwater fishes and invertebrates using the IUCN Red List. Their headline result is stark: one quarter of freshwater fauna faces extinction. Land species turn out to be poor stand-ins for freshwater ones. The findings give governments, for the first time, direct evidence for protecting freshwater life rather than guessing from other habitats.
openalex-w7205009213:
Pedro Santos Silva Azevedo led a Portuguese-language study, in Brazil in 2026. Of 548 mining engineering graduates of the Federal University of Ouro Preto from 2013 to 2023, drawing on 125 alumni responses and faculty curricula. New graduates face disproportionate demands, the authors find: prior practice, software skills, and English, with networking decisive, since nearly half of jobs came through referrals. About three quarters of graduates now work in the field, while nearly a quarter moved to other sectors.

Complementary activities during the degree were thin: most students did no extension work, about half skipped research initiation, and most never joined teaching projects. Faculty involvement was uneven too, with most research initiations concentrated in few professors. The authors urge stronger market integration, more practical training, and balanced faculty contributions.
openalex-w7205013813:
Nina de Azevedo Aragao Viana and five colleagues review current strategies for handling septic shock in its first hours, in a 2026 article from Brazil. Septic shock is the most severe form of sepsis, a runaway infection that disrupts circulation and metabolism and still kills many patients. The team searched medical databases for studies published between 2021 and 2026, including trials, observational work, and earlier reviews.

Across those studies, the same early moves kept saving lives: fast recognition, blood markers that help confirm the diagnosis, and antibiotics started without delay. Controlling the source of infection and restoring circulation under set protocols also lowered deaths and improved recovery. The authors argue that care built on this evidence can be both earlier and better fitted to each patient, rather than improvised under pressure.
openalex-w7207867013:
Vitor Martins Alves and three colleagues test whether practice consultations with a standardized patient can raise medical students' empathy. Empathy is tied to better outcomes and happier patients, so schools look for ways to teach it. Students from the eighth semester onward at a medical school in western Parana took theory classes, then held three simulated consultations, each followed by structured feedback. Empathy was measured before and after with a standard scale.

Only six of the ten volunteers finished both measurements, and their scores rose slightly, a shift too small to count as proven. The authors report an encouraging but unconfirmed trend, and they blame the tiny sample for the weak result. Their practical message is aimed at researchers as much as teachers: run the same design with far more students before judging the method.
openalex-w7208815613: Lays Batista Fitaroni leads a team of authors in a study of the internship market in Mato Grosso, Brazil, published in 2026 in the journal Research, Society and Development. The sample available for this entry gives the title, authors, and journal only, without an abstract. The work's stated scope is the conditions of internship openings in the state, how attractive they are to candidates, and how organizations compete for interns.
openalex-w7208828113:
Samira Sbardelatti Regis Pereira and Jaqueline Ronconi Borba track leprosy in Rolim de Moura, a town in the interior of Rondonia state in Brazil's Legal Amazon. Leprosy, caused by a slow-growing bacterium, attacks mainly the skin and peripheral nerves, and Brazil remains among the three countries with the most new cases worldwide. The authors reviewed official notifications recorded in the national reporting system over six recent years, from 2020 to 2025.

Across those years the town notified just under two hundred cases, a steady presence rather than a fading one. The study ties that persistence directly to the region's health conditions: distance, poverty, and hard access to services keep the chain of transmission alive. For local health teams, the message is that leprosy in the Amazon interior is a standing public health problem shaped by social conditions, not a leftover of the past.
openalex-w7212017413:
Maria Fernanda Goncalves Pereira, Emilly Paschoal de Oliveira, and Valeria de Lima Kaminski review how one group of immune cells helps colorectal cancer grow. The cells are called myeloid-derived suppressor cells. They calm the immune attack that should fight the tumor. The team read studies from 2020 to 2025 in two databases. Their aim was to map the tricks these cells use.

The cells starve immune cells of nutrients they need. They release harsh molecules that blunt lymphocytes, the white cells that kill tumors. They also pour out signals that damp the whole response. Gut microbes, above all one common species, feed their growth and keep the tumor zone inflamed. The authors see the cells as a prime drug target. But the cells vary a lot, and labs still lack one standard way to spot them.
openalex-w7213272813: Weber de Santana Teles leads a large team on the path from strain to fire in the brain. Their study traces how hardships of social life — want, strain, and loss — can stir the body's guard, and how that stir can reach the brain itself. The lens joins three fields: the study of the nerves, of the guard, and of the mind's health.
openalex-w7213777613:
Catarina Fontana Gomes leads a scoping review, written in English, on changeable risk factors for cognitive decline. Their 2026 review follows PRISMA scoping guidance and searches four databases between March and April 2026. Ten studies from the last five years were selected, with emphasis on Brazil.

Decline proved many-sided, spanning clinical, behaviour, psychosocial, and social factors. Low schooling, high blood pressure, and diabetes stood among the main factors. Physical inactivity, depressive symptoms, and social isolation also appeared. Poor social conditions raised exposure to those risks and weakened protection. Since many factors can be changed, the authors frame prevention as a social task, not only a medical one.
openalex-w7213951513:
Veronica Souza de Oliveira and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva analyse digital technology in early childhood schooling. Their 2026 library study uses thematic analysis of academic work and official documents. A historical-cultural view treats technology as a cultural tool whose value depends on teaching intent.

Digital tools can widen children's languages, support creativity, and enrich interaction and learning, they find. Such gains hold when technology is tied to play and face-to-face experience. Teacher training gaps remain a central challenge, alongside excessive screen use. Integration therefore demands critical, ethical, and carefully mediated practice, the authors conclude. The child's full development, not the device, must direct classroom choices.
openalex-w7214361913:
Wandrya Karolina de Oliveira Macedo, Davi Abiner Soares Amaral, and Delner do Carmo Azevedo wrote a 2026 Brazilian legal article on children exposed on social media. Parents who post their children's lives online, sometimes for money, raise hard questions about privacy and image rights. The authors ask where civil liability falls: on parents, on legal guardians, or on the digital platforms that host the posts.

Reading constitutional protections, child law, data protection law, and internet rules, they find parent liability lacks clear, settled standards in court decisions. Platform rules, long tied to court orders for removing content, are judged too slow for cases involving children. A new 2025 digital child statute now makes careful moderation a legal duty for platforms, though courts still must settle how it applies.
openalex-w7215129713:
Dennis Soares Leite led a 2026 study of what quilombola women in Itacuruçá, Abaetetuba, Brazil, know about cervical cancer and its prevention. Quilombola communities, founded by descendants of escaped enslaved people, face weak public policy and poor access to health care, including preventive exams. One hundred women filled in a semi-structured questionnaire in a study carried out in 2017 and reported here.

The women knew least about syphilis, condom use, and the right age for the exam, gaps the team checked directly. The women described public health policy for their population as precarious despite government efforts. Few studies exist on this theme, the authors note. Their conclusion is a call for more health education research with traditional peoples, so information reaches these women well and health risks shrink.
openalex-w7220980513:
Francisco Rafael Bispo dos Santos and five co-authors reviewed studies on physical training for sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with aging. Their 2026 integrative review searched health databases for work published between 2019 and 2025 on older adults, exercise, and daily functioning.

From an initial pool of well over a hundred studies, four met all their criteria. Those studies found that resistance training and its variants raised muscle mass and strength, cut body fat, and improved functional capacity. The gains point toward fewer falls, more independence, and better quality of life. The review supports regular strength work as a practical defense against frailty in old age.
original-short-stories-volume-13:
Volume thirteen closes the English set of Maupassant's Original Short Stories with seventeen pieces, among them A Mother of Monsters, The Little Cask, Boitelle, The Englishmen of Étretat, and Madame Hermet. The range runs from grotesque comedy to some of the darkest inventions of his later years.

Old Judas opens the book on a landscape of almost religious grandeur and sinister desolation: a wild lake of stagnant black water ringed by naked hills. One small house stands on its bank, home to Uncle Joseph, an old boatman who fishes the lake and carries his catch to the villages once a week. Out of such stillness Maupassant habitually draws cruelty, greed, or grace, and the volume ends the collection in that key.
ouspensky-symbolism-of-the-tarot-1913:
P. D. Ouspensky wrote The Symbolism of the Tarot in 1913. Ouspensky was a Russian thinker drawn to hid lore and higher space. The book reads the tarot pack as a scheme of signs. Its heart is the set of two and twenty great cards, the Major Arcana.

Card by card, he draws out the sense of the Fool, the Magus, and the World. Each card, he holds, holds a key truth on man and the cosmos. The tone is that of thought, not of fate tells for pay. The book is a chief text of the tarot as a path of the mind.
pirke-avot-gorfinkle-1913:
Joseph I. Gorfinkle translated Pirke Avot into English in 1913, with an introduction and notes. Pirke Avot, the Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, is a tractate of the Mishnah, gathered between about 200 BCE and 200 CE. It holds no law; instead, the rabbis of the early centuries hand down maxims on study, humility, and conduct.

Sayings ascribed to Hillel, Shammai, and their successors fill its six short chapters. If I am not for myself, who will be for me, is among its most quoted lines. Gorfinkle, a Cincinnati rabbi, made the little book handy for English readers and students. The Gutenberg text is ebook 8548. Jews still study Pirke Avot on spring Sabbaths.
plaw-112-239-2013:
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2013 is Public Law 112-239, approved on January 2, 2013. Congress used it to authorize fiscal year 2013 funding for the military activities of the Department of Defense and for military construction. It also authorizes defense work at the Department of Energy and sets the size of the armed forces for the year.

Four divisions organize the act. Division A holds the Defense Department authorizations, starting with procurement. Division B holds military construction authorizations, and Division C holds Energy Department national security authorizations and other authorizations. Division D holds the funding tables that list the money in detail.
plaw-112-240-2013:
The American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-240, approved on January 2, 2013. It is the tax deal Congress passed at the start of 2013, and most of its changes amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Title I is headed General Extensions. Its sections make the 2001 tax relief and the 2003 tax relief permanent, with changes, extend the 2009 tax relief, and give permanent relief from the alternative minimum tax. Title II extends single tax breaks, including the deduction for teachers' expenses, the exclusion for canceled home mortgage debt, and the deduction for state and local sales taxes.
plaw-112-241-2013:
Public Law 112-241, approved on January 10, 2013, designates the City of Salem, Massachusetts, as the Birthplace of the National Guard of the United States. The findings start in 1629. In that year Captain John Endicott organized the first militia in the Massachusetts Bay Colony at Salem. The system required all males aged 16 to 60 to keep arms.

In 1636 the colony's General Court ordered three militia regiments. The East Regiment, the forerunner of the 101st Engineer Battalion, mustered as a regiment for the first time in 1637 on Salem Common. Congress finds that this marked the beginning of the Massachusetts National Guard and of the National Guard of the United States.
plaw-112-242-2013:
The Medicare IVIG Access and Strengthening Medicare and Repaying Taxpayers Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-242, approved on January 10, 2013. It also amends title XVIII of the Social Security Act on how Medicare secondary payer rules apply to certain claims.

Title I orders a demonstration project under Medicare Part B. The Secretary must test paying for the items and services needed to give intravenous immune globulin at home to treat primary immune deficiency diseases. The project starts within one year of enactment and runs for three years. No more than 4,000 Medicare patients with that diagnosis may enroll, and taking part is voluntary.
plaw-112-243-2013: Public Law 112-243, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office in Cocoa, Florida. The Postal Service facility at 600 Florida Avenue is to be known as the Harry T. and Harriette Moore Post Office. The references clause says any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Harry T. and Harriette Moore Post Office.
plaw-112-244-2013: The Lake Thunderbird Efficient Use Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-244, approved on January 10, 2013. It lets the Secretary of the Interior allow storage of nonproject water at the Norman project. If the Secretary finds enough excess capacity in Lake Thunderbird, contracts with the Central Oklahoma Master Conservancy District may be amended or newly made. The water would add to city and industrial supplies for district towns. New works are paid for by the non-federal party, and nothing in the act allows the lake's storage capacity to grow.
plaw-112-245-2013:
The Pinnacles National Park Act is Public Law 112-245, approved on January 10, 2013. It establishes Pinnacles National Park in California as a unit of the National Park System, raising the old monument to park rank.

The findings recall that Pinnacles National Monument was set up by presidential proclamation on January 16, 1908 to guard its rock formations, and grew under later proclamations and laws. The monument shelters plant and animal life of the central California coast, including 32 species with special federal or state status, within 14,500 acres of designated wilderness. Its heritage runs from Native Americans and Spanish arrivals to miners, cowboys, ranchers, and homesteaders.
plaw-112-246-2013: Public Law 112-246, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office building in Little Rock, Arkansas. The Postal Service facility at 600 East Capitol Avenue is to be known as the Sidney 'Sid' Sanders McMath Post Office Building. The references clause says any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of that building name.
plaw-112-247-2013: Public Law 112-247, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office in Roseville, California for a lance corporal. The Postal Service facility at 8771 Auburn Folsom Road is to be known as the Lance Corporal Victor A. Dew Post Office. Under the references clause, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Lance Corporal Victor A. Dew Post Office.
plaw-112-248-2013:
The Improper Payments Elimination and Recovery Improvement Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-248, approved on January 10, 2013. Its purpose is to step up efforts to find, prevent, and recover payment error, waste, fraud, and abuse in federal spending.

Section 3 works on how agencies pin down improper payments. It amends the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002, renumbering its subsections and adding a new duty. Each year, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget must name a list of high-priority federal programs that will gain greater levels of oversight and review. The definitions in the act reach states, the District of Columbia, territories, and federally recognized Indian tribes.
plaw-112-249-2013:
Public Law 112-249, approved on January 10, 2013, bears the heading Comprehensive Veterans Education Information Policy. It adds section 3698 to chapter 36 of title 38. The Secretary of Veterans Affairs must build a full policy to improve outreach and openness to veterans and service members, by giving them better facts on colleges and other schools.

The policy must include ways to tell students about the education and job counseling the law already offers. It must set up one central system for tracking and publishing feedback from students and state approving agencies on teaching quality, recruiting practices, and job placement after graduation. Schools may check facts in feedback before it posts, and student names stay private.
plaw-112-250-2013: Public Law 112-250, approved on January 10, 2013, lets the Secretary of Agriculture accept a railroad's gift back of a right of way in Colorado. The Manitou and Pikes Peak Railway Company, successor to the Mt. Manitou Park and Incline Railway Company, may hand back its right of way in Pike National Forest, El Paso County. The grant dates to the Act of March 3, 1875. The land is traced on a map filed at the Pueblo land office in 1914. Land the company holds in fee title is untouched.
plaw-112-251-2013: Public Law 112-251, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office in Fowler, California. The Postal Service facility at 19 East Merced Street is to be known as the Cecil E. Bolt Post Office. The references clause makes any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record count as a mention of the Cecil E. Bolt Post Office.
plaw-112-252-2013: Public Law 112-252, approved on January 10, 2013, repeals a dated rule on car insurance costs. Subsection (c) of section 32302 of title 49 is repealed, and any rules made under it lose all force. In its place, the act orders a study. The Secretary of Transportation must study the question and report to Congress within two years. The study follows public comment. It covers the most useful data, format, and method for giving buyers simple, clear facts on how easily a vehicle is damaged.
plaw-112-253-2013:
The Katie Sepich Enhanced DNA Collection Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-253, approved on January 10, 2013. It authorizes the Attorney General to award grants to states that set up DNA arrestee collection processes.

The act defines that process in detail. A state collects DNA profiles or data, for the National DNA Index System, from adults arrested for or charged with named state crimes. The list shown covers homicide, offenses with a sexual act or contact element carrying over a year in prison, kidnapping or abduction, burglary, and aggravated assault on the same penalty terms.
plaw-112-254-2013: Public Law 112-254, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office in Mountain View, California as a memorial. The Postal Service facility at 211 Hope Street is to be known as the Lieutenant Kenneth M. Ballard Memorial Post Office. The references clause adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of that memorial name.
plaw-112-255-2013: Public Law 112-255, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office in Ravenel, South Carolina for a representative. The Postal Service facility at 6239 Savannah Highway is to be known as the Representative Curtis B. Inabinett, Sr. Post Office. Its references clause makes any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record count as a mention of that post office name.
plaw-112-256-2013: Public Law 112-256, approved on January 10, 2013, names a post office building in Simi Valley, California for a postal inspector. The Postal Service facility at 225 Simi Village Drive is to be known as the Postal Inspector Terry Asbury Post Office Building. The references clause says any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of that building name.
plaw-112-257-2013: The Former Presidents Protection Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-257, approved on January 10, 2013. It amends section 3056 of title 18 to remove certain limits on how long Secret Service protection lasts. For former presidents, a long clause that began "unless the former President did not" is struck from subsection (a)(3). For children of former presidents, subsection (a)(4) loses the words that set a time period ending at the earlier of two events. The deletions are the act's whole content.
plaw-112-258-2013: The Video Privacy Protection Act Amendments Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-258, approved on January 10, 2013. It clarifies how a video service provider may gain consent to share viewing records. Consent must be informed, written, and may come online. The consent form must stand apart from forms on other legal or money duties. Consent may be given at disclosure time, or ahead for a set span of no more than two years, or until it is withdrawn. Providers must offer a clear way to withdraw from sharing.
plaw-112-259-2013:
The Mt. Andrea Lawrence Designation Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-259, approved on January 10, 2013. It designates a mountain for Andrea Mead Lawrence, the skier and conservationist, and its findings tell her story.

Born in Rutland County, Vermont, on April 19, 1932, Lawrence raced at the 1948 and 1956 Winter Olympics and lit the torch at the 1960 Squaw Valley games. At Oslo in 1952 she won both the special and giant slalom, the only American double gold medalist in alpine skiing. She moved to Mammoth Lakes, California in 1968, founded the Friends of Mammoth, and served 16 years on the Mono County Board of Supervisors guarding Mono Lake.
plaw-112-260-2013:
The Dignified Burial and Other Veterans' Benefits Improvement Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-260, approved on January 10, 2013. Its first aim is to ensure that veterans who die with no known next of kin can gain a dignified burial.

Title I covers cemetery matters. Its sections provide caskets and urns for such veterans, guard freedom of conscience, and improve talks between the Veterans Affairs Department and medical examiners and funeral directors. Other sections cover the finding and burial of unclaimed remains, and bar persons convicted of certain sex offenses from burial or honors in veterans' cemeteries. Title II, on health care, opens with an open burn pit registry.
plaw-112-261-2013: Public Law 112-261, approved on January 10, 2013, changes one definition in the Animal Welfare Act. Section 2(h), the definition of "exhibitor", gains added words after "stores". The new words cover an owner of a common, domesticated household pet. The owner gains less than a substantial portion of income from a nonprimary source, as the Secretary decides. The words concern showing an animal that lives only at the pet owner's home. Read in the definition, the insertion takes such a pet owner out of the exhibitor class.
plaw-112-262-2013: Public Law 112-262 is a joint resolution, approved on January 10, 2013, that names a new Smithsonian regent. Under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, a vacancy sat on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. Alan Spoon's term ended on May 5, 2012, and the resolution fills that seat with Barbara Barrett of Arizona. Spoon, of Massachusetts, sat in the class of regents who are not members of Congress. Barrett's term is six years, starting on the later of May 5, 2012 or the day this resolution was enacted.
plaw-112-263-2013: Public Law 112-263, approved on January 14, 2013, orders a Kotzebue, Alaska land transfer. Within 180 days, the Secretary of Health and Human Services must convey all federal title in three sites to the Maniilaq Association, for its health and social services programs. The sites are the Kotzebue hospital and land, at 8.10 acres, and two quarters sites of 5.229 acres and 1.29 acres. The deed is a warranty deed, without payment, added terms, or a federal reversionary interest, replacing any earlier quitclaim deed.
plaw-112-264-2013:
The North Korean Child Welfare Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-264, approved on January 14, 2013. It states the sense of Congress on North Korean children and on children of one North Korean parent. It also requires the State Department to brief the named House and Senate committees on work to help these children.

Congress states that hundreds of thousands of North Korean children suffer from malnutrition at home. Those living outside North Korea may face statelessness in nearby countries. The Secretary of State should press for their best interests, seeking quick protection through family reunification or, where fitting and allowed, adoption at home or abroad.
plaw-112-265-2013:
The Investigative Assistance for Violent Crimes Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-265, approved on January 14, 2013. It clarifies the legal basis for a long-standing practice: the Justice Department helping state and local officers, when asked, with certain serious violent crimes.

One edit raises a funding figure in section 530C of title 28 from $2,000,000 to $3,000,000. A new clause lets the Attorney General help with certain cases, at the request of a state or local law officer. The help covers probes of violent acts and shootings in a place of public use, and mass killings or attempted mass killings. Mass killings means three or more killings in a single incident. Help given counts as within federal office.
plaw-112-266-2013:
The Drywall Safety Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-266, approved on January 14, 2013. Its aims are to keep unsafe drywall out of commerce, and to make the maker of drywall easy to identify. A third aim is to see that bad drywall taken out of homes is not used again.

The sense of Congress addresses the Chinese-made drywall that harmed American homes. Congress urges the Secretary of Commerce to insist that China's government press the makers to meet United States officials, remedy homeowners, and submit to United States federal courts. A labeling section then treats the gypsum board labeling rules of standard ASTM C1264-11 as a safety rule of the Consumer Product Safety Commission, from 180 days after enactment.
plaw-112-267-2013: Public Law 112-267, approved on January 14, 2013, makes clear that Thrift Savings Fund accounts can be reached by federal tax collectors. It amends section 8437(e)(3) of title 5 to add that the accounts shall be subject to a federal tax levy under section 6331 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. A second section handles the money side. Any revenue gain from the act goes to the Treasury's general fund. The Congressional Budget Office Director finds the gain. The money may be used only for cutting the deficit.
plaw-112-268-2013: Public Law 112-268, approved on January 14, 2013, authorizes right-of-way permits for natural gas pipelines inside Glacier National Park. The Secretary of the Interior may issue a permit for each pipeline that lay within the park boundary as of March 1, 2012, with its fittings. Each permit acts as a renewal, under the laws for utility rights-of-way in National Park System units. The right-of-way may be no wider than 25 feet on either side of the pipeline's centerline, and the Secretary may add any terms found needful.
plaw-112-269-2013:
The Foreign and Economic Espionage Penalty Enhancement Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-269, approved on January 14, 2013. It raises penalties in section 1831 of title 18 for espionage that aids a foreign power and harms American trade secrets.

For individuals, the top fine rises from $500,000 to $5,000,000. For organizations, the cap becomes the greater of $10,000,000 or three times the value of the stolen trade secret, counting research and design costs the thief thereby avoided. The act also orders the United States Sentencing Commission to review its guidelines for such offenses, so penalties match their seriousness and harm and deter them well.
plaw-112-270-2013:
The Endangered Fish Recovery Programs Extension Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-270, approved on January 14, 2013. It amends Public Law 106-392 to keep yearly base funding for the Upper Colorado and San Juan fish recovery programs through fiscal year 2019.

The dates move in step: 2011 becomes 2019, and 2008 becomes 2018. A required report must now also tell what the recovery programs have done, and the status of the endangered fish. It must give the projected dates for downlisting and delisting under the Endangered Species Act. It must also tell how power revenues fund the work. A new cap holds indirect cost recovery on funds sent to the Fish and Wildlife Service to three percent.
plaw-112-271-2013: The Clothe a Homeless Hero Act is Public Law 112-271, approved on January 14, 2013. It amends section 44945 of title 49, on unclaimed items at airport security checkpoints. The head of the Transportation Security Administration must make every reasonable effort to pass the clothing to the local airport authority or other local authorities. The effort is made in consultation with the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. They donate it to charity, including local veterans groups, for homeless or needy veterans and veteran families. The handoff must create no cost to the government.
plaw-112-272-2013:
The World War I Centennial Commission Act is Public Law 112-272, approved on January 14, 2013. It establishes a commission to ensure a suitable observance of the one hundredth anniversary of World War I. The commission also provides for memorials to the service of American armed forces members in that war.

The table of contents lists the commission's establishment, duties, and powers, its personnel rules, its termination, and a bar on obligating federal funds. The findings note that from 2014 through 2018 the world will mark the centennial, including America's entry in April 1917. They call that entry the first time American soldiers went abroad in defense of liberty against foreign aggression.
plaw-112-273-2013:
The Space Exploration Sustainability Act is Public Law 112-273, approved on January 14, 2013. Its purpose line says it extends certain space launch liability provisions through 2014, though the operative section in the sample sets the date at December 31, 2013.

Section 2 voices the sense of Congress on human space flight. The NASA head should carry forward use of the space station, and technology work. Follow-on systems should move ahead too, such as the Space Launch System, the multi-purpose crew vehicle, and commercial crew and cargo craft, in a balanced way. Resources for one set of systems should not be found by cutting the other. A later section grants an exemption from a nonproliferation law named by its initials, INKSNA.
plaw-112-274-2013:
Public Law 112-274, approved on January 14, 2013, carries the heading Leahy-Smith America Invents Technical Corrections. It repairs and improves parts of the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act and of title 35, the patent code.

The items shown are small and precise. The advice of counsel rule, section 298, applies to civil suits begun on or after enactment. Wording is fixed in the transitional program for covered business method patents and in the joinder of parties rule. Dead zones are closed in inter partes review, so one timing rule does not reach patents outside a named class, and a reissue phrase is struck. A grammar fix turns "correct inventors" into "correct inventor".
plaw-112-275-2013:
The Protect our Kids Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-275, approved on January 14, 2013. It establishes a commission to build a national strategy, with recommendations, for cutting the number of children who die from abuse and neglect.

The findings are stark. Such deaths are preventable, greatly underreported, and tracked under no national standard. The Child Maltreatment Report of 2011 counted 1,545 children dead from abuse and neglect in fiscal year 2011, and experts think the true count is higher. Over 42 percent of the children who die this way are under age 1, and almost 82 percent are under age 4. Neglect played a part in 70 percent of the deaths, physical abuse in 48 percent.
plaw-112-276-2013:
The Intercountry Adoption Universal Accreditation Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-276, approved on January 14, 2013. It spreads one set of accreditation standards across nearly all adoptions of children from other countries.

Title II and section 404 of the Intercountry Adoption Act of 2000 now apply, with their rules, to a wide class of cases. They reach anyone offering adoption services for a child classed under the Immigration and Nationality Act's orphan clause. They apply just as they do for a Convention adoption, whether or not the case is a Convention case. The Secretaries of State and of Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the accrediting bodies hold the same duties. The change takes effect 18 months after enactment, with a transition rule for cases already under way.
plaw-112-277-2013:
The Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2013 is Public Law 112-277, approved on January 14, 2013. It authorizes spending for fiscal year 2013 for intelligence work across the government and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and for the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I covers budget and personnel authorizations, with a classified schedule and personnel ceiling adjustments. Title II funds the CIA retirement system. Title III lists general intelligence community matters in the contents. They include limits on intelligence acts, pay rises, and non-reimbursable details of staff. They also include an automated insider threat detection program, software licensing, and a strategy for sharing security clearances across agencies.
plaw-112-278-2013:
The Uninterrupted Scholars Act, or USA, is Public Law 112-278, approved on January 14, 2013. It improves the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, the law that guards student education records.

A new subparagraph lets schools share records with a caseworker or other agent of a state or local child welfare agency, or a tribal organization. The agent must hold the right to see a student's case plan. The agency must be legally in charge of the student's care and protection. Shared facts may pass on only to persons working on the student's education needs, under state or tribal privacy law. A second change carves out cases where a parent is a party to a child abuse, neglect, or dependency court case.
plaw-112-279-2013: Public Law 112-279, approved on January 14, 2013, names a post office in Waterford, Wisconsin for a captain. The Postal Service facility at 218 North Milwaukee Street is to be known as the Captain Rhett W. Schiller Post Office. The references clause makes any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record count as a mention of the Captain Rhett W. Schiller Post Office.
plaw-112-280-2013:
The Lieutenant Ryan Patrick Jones Post Office Designation Act is Public Law 112-280, approved on January 14, 2013. It names the Postal Service facility at 6 Nichols Street in Westminster, Massachusetts, as the Lieutenant Ryan Patrick Jones Post Office Building.

The findings honor Jones. He volunteered for the Army and earned the Army Achievement Medal, the Purple Heart, the Bronze Star, and the Combat Action Badge. He took a science degree with honors in civil and environmental engineering at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, on a Reserve Officers' Training Corps scholarship. As a platoon leader with the First Infantry Division in Iraq, he was killed in action by an improvised explosive device on May 2, 2007.
plaw-112-281-2013: Public Law 112-281, approved on January 14, 2013, makes a one-word technical correction to the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973. In section 102(d)(1)(A), the word "residential" is inserted before "improved real estate", each place that phrase appears. Nothing else in the act changes. The edit narrows the clause it touches to homes rather than to all improved property.
plaw-112-282-2013: Public Law 112-282 is a joint resolution, approved on January 14, 2013. It grants the consent of Congress to the State and Province Emergency Management Assistance pact. The parties are ten states and four provinces of Canada. The states are Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, New York, and Wisconsin. The provinces are Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, and Saskatchewan. Under the pact, the parties may help each other in a crisis or disaster when the stricken party asks.
plaw-112-283-2013:
The Department of State Rewards Program Update and Technical Corrections Act of 2012 is Public Law 112-283, approved on January 15, 2013. It authorizes the Secretary of State to pay rewards in the fight against transnational organized crime, and for facts about foreign nationals wanted by international criminal tribunals.

The findings describe the older rewards work. Existing programs pay for facts leading to the arrest or conviction of persons behind international terrorism or narcotics crimes, or indicted by world tribunals. Since the program began in 1984, over 60 people have been paid for facts that stopped attacks or helped convict attackers. The arrest of Ramzi Yousef, convicted in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, is named as one success.
plaw-113-1-2013: Flood insurance borrowing room grows under Public Law 113-1, the first act of the 113th Congress, approved on January 6, 2013. The act briefly raises how much the Federal Emergency Management Agency may borrow. The borrowing funds the National Flood Insurance Program. Section 1309 of the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 had set the cap at $20,725,000,000. The act strikes that sum and inserts $30,425,000,000. Congress marks the added sum as an emergency need under two budget laws.
plaw-113-10-2013: Coin blank wording is fixed by Public Law 113-10 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. The rule sits in the National Baseball Hall of Fame Commemorative Coin Act, Public Law 112-152. It sets the size of the precious-metal blanks used to strike the coins. In two places, the old text said the coins shall have a stated size. The new text says they shall be struck on a planchet having that size. A planchet is the blank disc a coin is struck from.
plaw-113-11-2013:
Four girls killed in a 1963 church bombing are honored after death by Public Law 113-11 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. They are Addie Mae Collins, Denise McNair, Carole Robertson, and Cynthia Wesley. A bomb killed them at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama. The medal marks 50 years since their deaths.

Congress finds that September 15, 2013, marks 50 years since the bomb took their lives. The four were getting ready for Sunday School that morning in 1963. Their deaths shocked the conscience of the world, the findings say. The loss spurred the Civil Rights Movement and helped it gain force.
plaw-113-12-2013:
Public Law 113-12, the Stolen Valor Act of 2013, targets false claims of military honors. The 113th Congress amended title 18 of the United States Code. Section 704 covers fraud about having won a decoration or medal. The act strikes the word wears from one part of that section. It then rewrites the fraud part in full.

The new text sets the crime in plain terms. A person must act with intent to gain money, property, or a like benefit. The person must also falsely hold himself out as a medal holder. The penalty is a fine, up to one year in prison, or both.
plaw-113-13-2013: Public Law 113-13, the Freedom to Fish Act, was passed by the 113th Congress in 2013. It bars the Corps of Engineers from blocking public access to waters below a dam through a restricted area. A restricted area means the zones for hazardous waters at dams in the Cumberland River basin. The term rests on a Corps rule book from November 29, 1996. The act then turns to zones set between August 1, 2012, and the day before the act passed. The sample ends at that point.
plaw-113-14-2013:
Two user fee programs for animal drugs are renewed by Public Law 113-14 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. Its full short title adds the words Animal Generic Drug User Fee Reauthorization. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. User fees are charges paid by drug makers that help fund federal review of their products.

Title I covers fees for new animal drugs. Its sections set the power to charge and use the fees, plus reports and sunset dates. Title II covers fees for generic new animal drugs in the same way. Each title has its own short title, finding, and start date.
plaw-113-15-2013: Flu shots join a tax list in the Internal Revenue Code under Public Law 113-15 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. Section 4132 names taxable vaccines. The act inserts the words or any other vaccine against seasonal influenza into one item of that list. A start rule then sets two dates and takes the later one. One date turns on the month that follows passage by more than four weeks. The other turns on a vaccine listing by the Health and Human Services Secretary.
plaw-113-16-2013:
The First Special Service Force receives the Congressional Gold Medal as a group under Public Law 113-16 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. The medal marks the unit's fine service in World War II. Section 1 gives the unit's story. The Force drew volunteers from the United States and Canada. It was activated in July 1942 at Fort Harrison, near Helena, Montana.

The Force was first meant to strike plants that fed the German war effort. Power plants that made key war goods were prime targets. Its combat arm held 1,800 soldiers, half from each country. A service battalion of 800 United States members backed them.
plaw-113-17-2013: The Secretary of State must plan for Taiwan under Public Law 113-17 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. The goal is observer status for Taiwan at the assembly of the International Civil Aviation Organization. That body meets every three years. Findings call safe, secure, and low-cost world air travel a good for all. Safe skies rest on shared flight standards, the findings say. They also rest on shared security steps and fast sharing of new rules. Direct seats in world flight forums help all lands, Congress finds.
plaw-113-18-2013: A new bridge over the Mississippi River is named by Public Law 113-18 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. The bridge carries Interstate Route 70. It links St. Louis, Missouri, with southwestern Illinois. The bridge must be known as the Stan Musial Veterans Memorial Bridge. Any mention of the bridge in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of that name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-113-19-2013: Public Law 113-19, the South Utah Valley Electric Conveyance Act, was passed by the 113th Congress in 2013. It tells the Interior Secretary to convey federal parts of an electric distribution system. The buyer is the South Utah Valley Electric Service District, a Utah body. The system means power poles, wires, insulators, and like gear. It also means substations built with Strawberry Valley Project funds. The gear in scope is rated at 12.5 kilovolts and sits on federal land.
plaw-113-2-2013:
Public Law 113-2, approved by the 113th Congress on January 29, 2013, grants extra funds for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2013. Its heading is Disaster Relief Appropriations Act, 2013. The stated aim is better and smoother disaster aid for Hurricane Sandy. Division A holds the sums, starting with the Department of Agriculture.

Title I covers domestic food programs. The Food and Nutrition Service gets $6,000,000 more for the Commodity Assistance Program. That money serves the emergency food assistance program. The Secretary may also shift foods and funds for office costs from sums granted for that end.
plaw-113-20-2013: Public Law 113-20, the Bonneville Unit Clean Hydropower Facilitation Act, helps hydropower grow on a Utah water system. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. The Interior Secretary gains room to aid power work on the Diamond Fork System of the Central Utah Project. A 2004 plan report for the Bonneville Unit defines that system. Section 3 then fixes cost shares. Sums charged to project power in that report count as final costs for power built above the system.
plaw-113-21-2013: Public Law 113-21, the Vietnam Veterans Donor Acknowledgment Act of 2013, lets donors be thanked at a memorial center. The 113th Congress amended Public Law 96-297, the law for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Visitor Center. One edit moves a date from 2014 to 2018. A new part then sets the donor rule. The Interior Secretary must let the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund show thanks inside the center. A fit statement or credit may name the gift that a donor gave.
plaw-113-22-2013: One part of the tax code is renamed by Public Law 113-22 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. Section 219(c) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 covers spousal retirement accounts. Its heading had read Special Rules for Certain Married Individuals. The act strikes that heading in full. The words Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA take its place. No rule in the section changes, only its name.
plaw-113-23-2013:
Public Law 113-23, the Hydropower Regulatory Efficiency Act of 2013, seeks to grow water power with less red tape. The 113th Congress passed it in August 2013. Findings say the hydropower trade employs about 300,000 workers across the United States. Hydropower is the largest source of clean, renewable electric power in the country, Congress finds.

The sections that follow promote growth in set lanes. They back small hydroelectric projects and conduit hydropower projects. They let the energy regulator stretch early permit spans. They back power at dams with no power plant and at closed loop pumped storage sites. One section orders an Energy Department study.
plaw-113-24-2013: Small conduit hydropower at reclamation sites is backed by Public Law 113-24 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. It clears all Bureau of Reclamation conduit sites for hydropower growth under federal reclamation law. A conduit is a canal or pipe that carries water. Section 2 amends section 9(c) of the Reclamation Project Act of 1939. Most early edits renumber the parts. A later edit touches terms for sales of electric power and leases of power rights.
plaw-113-25-2013: An air traffic control center in Nashua, New Hampshire, is named by Public Law 113-25 of the 113th Congress, passed in 2013. The air route traffic control center at Nashua must be known as the Patricia Clark Boston Air Route Traffic Control Center. Any later center at the same site takes the name as well. Any mention of the center in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the full name.
plaw-113-26-2013: Veterans groups gain wider access to federal surplus goods under Public Law 113-26 of the 113th Congress, the FOR VETS Act of 2013. It amends title 40 to widen veterans groups' access to federal surplus goods. Section 549 gains a new class of takers. A group whose members are in the main veterans may take surplus goods. Its spokesmen must be known to the Veterans Affairs Secretary under title 38. The goods must serve veterans.
plaw-113-27-2013:
Air travel can be hard for troops and veterans with severe wounds, and Public Law 113-27, the Helping Heroes Fly Act, speaks to that problem. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. It amends title 49 of the United States Code and directs the head of the Transportation Security Administration to act.

The act orders a process that helps severely injured or disabled service members and veterans get through airport screening with ease, with fast screening where possible. Screening should be private to the fullest extent that can be done. The agency must also run an operations center that helps these travelers move through screening before they board a plane. The plan is built with the Defense and Veterans Affairs departments and with groups that speak for these travelers.
plaw-113-28-2013:
Student loan rates for new federal loans are reset by Public Law 113-28, the Bipartisan Student Loan Certainty Act of 2013. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013, amending the Higher Education Act of 1965. It covers loans first paid out on or after July 1, 2013.

The act ends the old fixed rate setup for new loans and writes new rate terms into the law, starting with Federal Direct Stafford Loans and unsubsidized loans for undergraduates. Rates are set for loans paid out in each 12-month period. The act also tells the Secretary of Education to call together an advisory group to study how to make federal data on colleges clearer and more open.
plaw-113-29-2013: Public Law 113-29, the Reverse Mortgage Stabilization Act of 2013, gives one grant of power. Passed by the 113th Congress, it lets the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development set added rules for the home equity conversion mortgage insurance program, the federal reverse mortgage plan. The Secretary may issue the rules by notice or mortgagee letter, and they take effect at once, to make the program safer and sounder in its finances.
plaw-113-3-2013:
Public Law 113-3, the No Budget, No Pay Act of 2013, pairs a short pause in the debt limit with a push for Congress to pass a budget. The 113th Congress passed it early in 2013. Its heading says its aim is to make sure the debts of the United States Government are paid in full and on time until May 19, 2013.

Section 2 lifts the debt limit set in title 31 from the day the act passed through May 18, 2013. On May 19 the limit snaps back, raised by the amount of new debt issued in the pause that was needed to pay bills due before that date. Section 3 holds the pay of members of a house of Congress in escrow if that house has not agreed to a budget plan for fiscal year 2014 by April 15, 2013.
plaw-113-30-2013: Public Law 113-30 makes three word-level changes to pipeline safety law. Passed by the 113th Congress in 2013, it amends section 60102(p) of title 49 of the United States Code. That clause deals with how pipeline safety rule papers are made open to the public. The act swaps 3 years for 1 year, strikes the words guidance or, and strikes the phrase that tied the duty to an Internet web site.
plaw-113-31-2013: Congress named the Coast Guard headquarters building in Public Law 113-31, passed in 2013. The Washington, District of Columbia site at 2701 Martin Luther King Jr Avenue Southeast is now the Douglas A Munro Coast Guard Headquarters Building. Federal laws and records use the new name whenever the building comes up. The whole law is that naming, plus a rule that later references follow the new name.
plaw-113-32-2013:
A shooting range in Wyoming sits at the heart of Public Law 113-32, the Powell Shooting Range Land Conveyance Act. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. It orders the Secretary of the Interior to hand a tract of federal land to the Powell Recreation District in Wyoming, keeping any valid rights others already hold.

The tract is about 322 acres run by the Bureau of Land Management in its Wind River District, shown on a 2011 map as Powell Gun Club. The United States gives up all right, title, and claim to the land for no payment. The Secretary must settle the exact legal lines of the parcel and may fix small flaws in the map or the lines. Both must stay on file where the public can see them.
plaw-113-33-2013:
Public Law 113-33, the Denali National Park Improvement Act, brings set upgrades to Denali National Park and Preserve in Alaska. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. Its second section joins two tools: a small water-power project in the Kantishna Hills and a land swap.

The act defines a microhydro project as a power plant that can make no more than 100 kilowatts. The project takes in intake pipes, among them one on Eureka Creek about half a mile above the Park Road. It also takes in power lines, signs, buried phone lines, and access routes needed to build and run it. The Kantishna Hills area is the part of the park within two miles of Moose Creek, as shown on the act's map.
plaw-113-34-2013: Public Law 113-34 puts the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands on equal terms with Guam, the Virgin Islands, and American Samoa under an older land law. Passed by the 113th Congress in 2013, it adds the islands' name after Guam in Public Law 93-435 wherever it appears. The act also adjusts planned wage rises in the islands under the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2007, adding the years 2013 and 2015 to the schedule in that law.
plaw-113-35-2013:
Two surplus parcels along a famed parkway change hands under Public Law 113-35, the Natchez Trace Parkway Land Conveyance Act of 2013. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. It tells the Secretary of the Interior to pass the land to the State of Mississippi by quitclaim deed, for no payment, giving up all federal right, title, and claim.

The two parcels total about 67 acres inside the edge of the Natchez Trace Parkway, as shown on a November 2010 map. One parcel, southeast of US Route 61/84 and known as the bean field property, comes with a catch. Its deed keeps an easement for the United States that limits the land to uses that fit with the parkway.
plaw-113-36-2013:
Public Law 113-36 redraws the edge of the Minuteman Missile National Historic Site in South Dakota. The full name of the law is the Minuteman Missile National Historic Site Boundary Modification Act, and the 113th Congress passed it in 2013. It amends the 1999 law that set the site up.

The change adds a visitor center and office site to the historic site. That land is about 25 acres in the Buffalo Gap National Grassland, north of exit 131 on Interstate 90 in Jackson County, as shown on a January 2011 map. The act also adds about 3.65 acres at the Delta 1 Launch Control Facility, meant for a parking lot and other office uses.
plaw-113-37-2013:
Public Law 113-37, the Department of Veterans Affairs Expiring Authorities Act of 2013, keeps a set of veterans programs from lapsing. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013, amending title 38 of the United States Code. Its stated aim is to extend set powers that were set to end and that touch veterans and their families.

The first items in the text fund sport for veterans with disabilities. One adds 500,000 dollars for monthly aid payments to veterans invited by the United States Olympic Committee, for the span from October 1 to December 31, 2013. The next adds 2,000,000 dollars for aid to the committee itself over the same span, and bars such aid after December 31, 2013. Both clauses swap in the committee's name where the law once named United States Paralympics Inc.
plaw-113-38-2013:
Missing children are the focus of Public Law 113-38, named the E Clay Shaw Jr Missing Children's Assistance Reauthorization Act of 2013. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013, amending the Missing Children's Assistance Act. The law funds and guides the federal work that helps find lost children and guard them from harm.

The changes start with the findings: a new line states that many missing children are runaways. The act then reworks the duties of the official who runs the program. One new duty is to work with the United States Interagency Council on Homelessness. Staff who serve homeless people are to know the learning tools and aid the center gives on child sexual exploitation. Other edits widen the list of Congress panels that get word of the work.
plaw-113-39-2013:
Public Law 113-39, the Pay Our Military Act, was passed by the 113th Congress on September 30, 2013, on the edge of a government shutdown. Its heading calls it a law making continuing appropriations for military pay in the event of a shutdown. It covers fiscal year 2014, for any span when normal funding laws are not in effect.

The act sets aside such sums as are needed to pay members of the Armed Forces, reserve parts included, who serve on active duty in such a span. It also pays the civilian staff of the Defense Department, and of Homeland Security for the Coast Guard, whom the Secretary finds are backing those troops. The same cover reaches contractors in that support role. The money stays open until a set end point, the first of which is a funding law for the same ends.
plaw-113-4-2013:
Public Law 113-4 renews the main federal law against abuse of women: the Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013 to reauthorize the Violence Against Women Act of 1994. It opens with shared definitions and grant terms that run through the whole act.

Title I strengthens tools for judges and police. Its sections cover STOP grants, grants that back arrest policies and the enforcement of protection orders, legal aid for victims, sex offender management, and a crime clause on stalking that includes cyberstalking. It also funds outreach to groups that get too little service and services shaped to fit set cultures. Title II turns to care for victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking, starting with a sexual assault services program and rural aid.
plaw-113-40-2013:
Helium is scarce and vital, and Public Law 113-40, the Helium Stewardship Act of 2013, sets the end of the federal role in its supply. The 113th Congress passed it to amend the Helium Act. Its stated aim is to finish the move of the federal helium reserve into private hands in a fair market way that keeps helium markets steady and guards the interests of taxpayers.

The act rewrites the definitions in the Helium Act. It names the Cliffside Field, the storage site that holds the reserve, and the federal helium pipeline that moves the gas. The federal helium system takes in the reserve, the field, the pipeline, and all other gear the Secretary owns, leases, or runs for storing, moving, and cleaning helium. A federal user is an agency or a grant holder who uses helium in research.
plaw-113-41-2013:
Public Law 113-41, the Organization of American States Revitalization and Reform Act of 2013, backs change inside the main body that joins the nations of the Americas. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. Its findings quote the body's charter: representative democracy is a must for stability, peace, and growth in the Western Hemisphere. One aim of the body is to spread and firm up that form of rule while honoring nonintervention.

The findings say the United States backs the charter, the Inter-American Democratic Charter, and the American Declaration on the Rights and Duties of Man. They also back the body in its work with member states to meet those pledges. The policy section then states the stance of the United States, opening with the spread of democracy and the rule of law across the hemisphere.
plaw-113-42-2013:
Iraqis who worked for the United States Government in Iraq get more time under Public Law 113-42, passed by the 113th Congress in 2013. The act stretches the span in which such workers may gain special immigrant status. That status is a path to live in the United States, offered to people whose service put them at risk.

For the first three months of fiscal year 2014, the cap on new grants is the count of pending cases on September 30, 2013, plus 2,000 more. The work span runs from March 20, 2003 to September 30, 2013, and the last day to apply is December 31, 2013. A second section briefly raises the fee or surcharge for machine-readable nonimmigrant visas, with the rise due by January 1, 2014.
plaw-113-43-2013: Public Law 113-43, the Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act of 2013, keeps a youth honors program alive with a single date swap. Passed by the 113th Congress, it amends section 108 of the Congressional Award Act. The end date moves from October 1, 2013 to October 1, 2018. The change counts as if it took effect on October 1, 2013, so the program never lapses.
plaw-113-44-2013:
Public Law 113-44 is a joint resolution that pays death benefits to the families of fallen troops during a funding gap. Its full name is the Department of Defense Survivor Benefits Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2014. The 113th Congress passed it on October 10, 2013, in the midst of a government shutdown fight.

The resolution sets aside the sums needed, at fiscal year 2013 rates, from the Operation and Maintenance and Military Personnel accounts. The money pays the death gratuity owed when a service member dies. It also pays or repays funeral and burial costs, travel for funerals and for the dignified transfer of remains, and unit memorial services. One clause keeps a housing allowance going for a time for dependents of members who die on active duty.
plaw-113-45-2013: Public Law 113-45 ties the hands of transport officials on one point: sleep testing for truck and bus drivers. Passed by the 113th Congress in 2013, it says the Secretary of Transportation may act on sleep disorders for drivers of commercial motor vehicles only through a full rulemaking process. Such a rule may cover screening, testing, or treating drivers. The term sleep disorders includes obstructive sleep apnea. Rules already in force before September 1, 2013 are not touched.
plaw-113-46-2013:
Public Law 113-46, the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2014, is the law that reopened the federal government in the fall of 2013. The 113th Congress passed it on October 17, 2013. It makes continuing appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2014, funding departments, agencies, and other units of government.

Division A keeps work going at the pace set by the fiscal year 2013 funding laws. It names those laws one by one: agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration, commerce and justice and science, defense, homeland security, and military building and veterans affairs, among others. Projects and work run under the same terms as in 2013, with the rate trimmed to match the cuts the text requires.
plaw-113-47-2013:
Public Law 113-47, the United States Parole Commission Extension Act of 2013, keeps the federal parole board at work. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013. Its stated aim is to provide for the continued performance of the functions of the United States Parole Commission, the body that rules on parole for older federal cases.

The act works by a swap in the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984. Each mention of 26 years or a 26-year period, where that law speaks of the commission, is to be read as 31 years or a 31-year period. The act also orders the commission to report to the judiciary panels of both houses within 180 days. The report must give, for fiscal years 2012 and 2013, counts of cases by type, hearings held, record reviews, and warrants issued and carried out.
plaw-113-48-2013:
A severe allergic attack at school can kill in minutes, and Public Law 113-48, the School Access to Emergency Epinephrine Act, pushes states to let school staff act fast. The 113th Congress passed it in 2013, amending the Public Health Service Act. It raises the preference given to set states when asthma-related grants are handed out.

A state gains the added edge by certifying that it meets set terms.
