Cryo-electron microscopy then caught spermine sitting inside the open pore, stretched along its axis through the central cavity and selectivity filter. Mutations and simulations confirmed the main binding site in the filter and suggested spermine passes two further, temporary sites on its way in. The authors offer the stepwise blocking mechanism as a template for designing TRPV6 inhibitors.
pmc-13216713:
Julianna L. Barbaro and co-authors present a 2026 case report and literature review of a Wilms tumour growing outside the kidney, in the soft tissue beside a newborn's spine. Such extrarenal tumours are vanishingly rare and can only be identified under the microscope.

The mass was spotted on prenatal ultrasound at twenty weeks, beside the lower spine, while both kidneys looked normal. Removed days after birth, it showed the classic three-part Wilms pattern of blastemal, stromal, and primitive epithelial tissue. Counting their case, the authors find sixteen reports of spinal or paraspinal tumours of this kind. Surgery followed by chemotherapy is the usual approach, and they call for a standardized regimen and wider awareness of the diagnosis.
pmc-13217913:
Laila I. Sakhnini and colleagues present a 2026 computational study on predicting when therapeutic antibodies will bind to things they should not. Such non-specific binding can undermine a drug candidate, so developers want an early warning from the antibody's amino acid sequence alone. The team tested two routes to that prediction.

One route used embeddings from protein language models, which capture sequence context. The other used a set of plain physical descriptors that humans can read directly. Models were trained on published human and mouse antibody data and checked against three public datasets. The heavy chain, especially its third hypervariable loop, carried most of the predictive signal, and the best model reached about 71 percent accuracy in cross-validation. The isoelectric point stood out among the physical descriptors, and combining both approaches made the scores more reliable for early screening.
pmc-13219813:
Xiaoqian Lan, Hongyan Zhuang, and Pengfei Li report a negative result on a prescribing workaround for antipsychotic side effects in a 2026 study. The antipsychotic amisulpride raises prolactin, a hormone whose excess can disrupt periods, fertility, and bone health. Clinicians add aripiprazole, a drug with an opposite grip on the dopamine system, hoping it will pull prolactin back down, but proof for amisulpride specifically was missing.

The average change was small and insignificant, and splitting the patients by sex or diagnosis changed nothing. Removing any patient from the analysis, one at a time, never altered the conclusion, so no outlier was driving the result. Until evidence arrives, the authors advise caution about expecting this combination to rescue patients from prolactin elevation.
pmc-13221113:
Jinghui Zhai and co-authors test a ginseng compound alongside cisplatin in a 2026 lung cancer study. Cisplatin works well against tumors, yet it harms kidneys and tumors often resist it. Ginsenoside Rg3, drawn from ginseng, has shown anticancer effects and possible protection for healthy tissue.

Transporter changes may explain both kidney protection and reduced drug resistance. The compound looks promising as a chemotherapy partner.
pmc-13221513:
Nisith Kumar and colleagues convene patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy to rank what matters in treatment, in a 2026 multinational advisory board study. The disease stiffens the heart as misfolded protein builds up, often ending in heart failure. Thirteen patients from five countries completed a pre-meeting survey, then discussed priorities together.

Tiredness and fatigue bothered participants most among side effects, while injection site pain bothered them least. Lowering death risk ranked as the top benefit, though quality of life and time for enjoyed activities mattered deeply too. Once-daily pills were the preferred format on average. Preferences varied between individuals, which the authors say trial designers and prescribers should respect.
pmc-13222013:
Chunhong Shi and co-authors interview family caregivers of people in hospital with HIV/AIDS in Hunan, China, in a 2026 interview study. Seventeen caregivers, aged twenty-two to seventy-four, spoke in depth between August 2024 and January 2025 at a hospital infectious disease ward. Family members carry most caregiving duties in China, yet their hospital experiences were little studied.

Three themes emerged. Caregivers described personal growth, stronger family bonds, and new resilience alongside the strain. They advocated for mental-health support, better HIV education, easier access, respectful care, and financial relief. Views on death mixed anticipatory grief with wishes for a dignified end. The authors recommend structured family-centered support.
pmc-13222213:
Nina Hadzimustafic, Tyler Safran, and Joshua Vorstenbosch comment on a bibliometric review of capsular contracture research, in a 2026 piece. Contracture, a tightening scar shell around breast implants, remains common and poorly understood. The reviewed analysis counted 2,065 English articles and mapped growth, leading countries, institutions, journals, and cited authors over the past decade.

Hot keywords included biofilm, contamination, dermal matrices, and implant placement, pointing at current theories for prevention. The commentators praise the map of collaboration gaps, yet note a sting: the highest-impact studies rest largely on low-level evidence. They call for randomized trials and systematic reviews to firm up guidance on reducing contracture.
pmc-13222513:
Miroslav Zashev and Nevrie Niyazi report two cases of Buschke–Lowenstein tumour, a giant wart-like growth around the anus, in a 2026 surgical report. The lesion links to human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 and grows aggressively in place despite benign cells. Both patients had large circumferential growths that had enlarged progressively.

pmc-13222613:

The index combines lymphocyte counts and serum albumin into one number. Fang and Ding value the work, yet warn that acute infections can distort both halves of the score in opposite directions depending on severity and timing.

Albumin also reflects inflammation more than nutrition, guidelines now caution, so infected participants could skew the index away from baseline status. Cleaner participant selection is their main request.
pmc-13222913:
Johan Gustafsson and co-authors improve digital patient models used to test nuclear medicine imaging accuracy, in a 2026 simulation study. Three body phantoms received tumors copied from real patient scans, placed at realistic sites, and set moving with breathing. Activity levels were drawn from patient distributions, and organs such as liver and spleen got uneven internal patterns.

Full models looked much more like real patients than standard spherical-lesion versions. Estimated tumor activity ran more negatively biased in the realistic models for both PET and SPECT imaging, showing that motion and background texture change the errors researchers must expect. Realistic phantoms, the authors conclude, give fairer tests of correction methods.
pmc-13226713:
Mohamed Zaki Khedr and colleagues investigate a 2026 geological survey of Egypt's black sands, beach deposits rich in heavy minerals along the Mediterranean coast and in southern Sinai. pmc-13230313:
Meltem Kaya and colleagues trial in 2026 expiratory muscle training, which strengthens the muscles used to breathe out, in children with asthma. pmc-13231013:
Chengcheng Zhang and colleagues compare in 2026 industrial ways to dry cabbage while keeping quality and nutrition high. Nearly one hundred scent compounds were found, and the combined method widened both their range and their total amount over plain hot air. pmc-13232613:
Roddy M Grieves and colleagues ask in 2026 whether the brain maps of rats hug the ground surface when land rises and falls. Place cells in the hippocampus fire at set spots and anchor the mental map of a space. Rats foraged over flat and ridged floors while the team recorded those cells.

A boundary-based model reproduced the pattern, tying map shape to the lay of the land.
pmc-13233013:
Yongbo Yang and colleagues published a 2026 prospective cohort study on alcohol drinking and esophageal cancer risk across age groups in China. The country carries more than 40 percent of the world's new cases of this cancer. pmc-13233513:
Mengna Xu and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study mapping where the invasive plant Nicotiana glauca could spread. Suitable territory already spans large parts of the Americas, Africa, Europe, Asia, and Oceania, with the highest threat in southern regions. Future scenarios enlarged the total threatened area and shifted its center. The authors offer the maps as a planning reference for prevention programs.
pmc-13234713:

The authors present the tuned antibody as a candidate for wider filovirus therapy.
pmc-13236513:

pmc-13236613:

pmc-13236913:

pmc-13237013: Shuya Li and team issued a correction in 2026 to their Scientific Reports study comparing natural and artificial musk. The notice is a correction only, with no new study content. pmc-13239413:

pmc-13239713:

pmc-13240013:

pmc-13240213:

pmc-13241013:

pmc-13241413:

pmc-13241513:

pmc-13241713:

pmc-13243013:

pmc-13244513:

pmc-13245513:

pmc-13246613:

pmc-13246713:

pmc-13247313:

pmc-13247913:

pmc-13248113:

pmc-13248313:

pmc-13249113:

pmc-13249713:
Alperen Aksakal and colleagues report a 2026 lung study of young smokers who feel perfectly healthy. Standard breathing tests can look normal early in smoking, even while the smallest airways are already changing, so the team used a gentler sound-wave test that is more sensitive to those airways.

Both groups had similar standard test results, but smokers showed higher airway resistance and stiffer small airways. Smokers also walked less far and had lower oxygen levels in their leg muscles. The authors say the sound-wave test could flag early smoking harm sooner.
pmc-13250213:
Tuyisenge and colleagues reflect on a six-year partnership that worked to improve care for mothers and newborns in Rwanda. Their 2026 BMJ Paediatrics Open paper describes work by British and Rwandan pediatric bodies with UNICEF and Rwanda's health ministry. From 2017 to 2023, the program ran across many hospitals and selected health centers.

The authors report measurable gains in care quality and patient outcomes over the program years. Even so, preventable newborn deaths persisted, which they link to deeper system limits and community-level health factors. They argue that the numbers are only part of the program's value. pmc-13250613:
Zhongzheng Zhang and three colleagues present a 2026 revision of Iris series Tenuifoliae, a group of irises spread across Central and East Asia. About ten species were recognized, but their boundaries and relationships stayed unclear from appearance alone. The team combined full chloroplast genome sequences with plant morphology to settle the group's structure.

One branch is marked by a flipped segment in a specific region of its chloroplast genome, a rare structural clue. The authors also name three species new to science, all collected in central-western China. The work gives growers and conservationists a firmer map of a group adapted to dry country.
pmc-13253713:
Lasse Bohlen and colleagues test machine learning for intensive care in a 2026 study across two health systems. Models were built with data from a German university hospital and the MIMIC-IV database from the United States. The tasks were to predict death, length of stay, and return to hospital for ICU patients.

Models trained on local data beat models brought in from outside when enough local data existed. Simpler and mid-level models, such as additive models, traveled better across hospitals than complex ones. They also needed far less local data, and tools that explain model choices helped show where data gaps hurt results.
pmc-13253813:
Shakila Umer and a large team study plant DNA barcodes in a 2026 paper on the western Himalayas. The region holds many plants found nowhere else, yet its local flora is little studied at the DNA level. The team tested eight barcode regions in 32 endemic and threatened species from Pakistan's western Himalayas.

One marker, rbcL, worked best, with full copying success and 96% sequencing success. Another marker reached full copying but 80% sequencing, while ITS2 lagged at 52%. Database matches were at least 97% alike for most species, supporting barcodes as a tool to name and group these plants.
pmc-13254113:
Sadia Munawar and colleagues build an AI tool for lung tissue diagnosis in a 2026 study. The system uses CLIP, a model that links images with text, to sort lung samples into benign tissue, adenocarcinoma, or squamous cell carcinoma. Tailored text prompts and a loss method that handles uneven class sizes guided training.

Training used thousands of images per class, split for training, checking, and testing. The best check accuracy reached 95.20 percent, with strong curve scores near 0.987. Training stopped early at epoch 23, a full pass through the data, after steady gains. The authors see promise for digital pathology systems.
pmc-13254713:
Yuhan Wang and Peiling Li investigate a long non-coding RNA that accelerates ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. The molecule, ITGB2-AS1, does not code for a protein but regulates other genes, and it was found abnormally expressed in ovarian tumors. Ovarian cancer spreads aggressively and its five-year survival remains low, so its molecular drivers are prized targets.

The authors show the RNA's production is switched on by a super-enhancer, an unusually powerful cluster of gene-activating elements that cancers often hijack for growth genes. Inside the cell, ITGB2-AS1 physically binds a scaffold protein called IQGAP1. That binding switches on the Wnt and beta-catenin signaling pathway, a classic engine of cell growth and movement. The authors present the super-enhancer, the RNA, and its protein partner as connected points where future drugs might intervene.
pmc-13255213:
Jan Stein and colleagues track body temperature in major trauma in a 2026 registry study. Low body temperature is part of a deadly triad in severe injury, but how it changes during early care is less known. The team analyzed 34,877 patients from a German trauma registry between 2015 and 2023.

Low temperature affected 10.7 percent of patients on arrival and 9.7 percent at intensive care transfer. Staying cold throughout carried the highest death rate at 43.5 percent, plus the most clotting problems and transfusions. New cold at transfer also fared badly, with 31.9 percent deaths. The authors urge active temperature tracking and control.
pmc-13255713:
Zuoliang Liu and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of gut microbes in colorectal cancer, with a regional focus on Sichuan, China. The gut community influences inflammation, metabolism, immune defense, and the gut lining, all of which can feed or restrain tumor growth. Because diet and environment shape that community, place matters in this story.

Sichuan's distinctive spicy, oily food culture may mold microbial patterns that differ from those in Western cohorts. The review moves from mechanisms to clinical ideas, including prevention, earlier detection, and treatment tailored to a patient's microbes. The authors argue that regional studies keep global conclusions honest, since a microbiome finding in one population may not travel unchanged to another.
pmc-13256313:
Cheng He and a large team report a 2026 battery study tuning zinc-based catalysts. Their target is lithium-sulfur batteries' biggest flaw: sulfur intermediates that dissolve and wander, draining capacity. The team embedded zinc compounds with three different partner elements, oxygen, sulfur, or selenium, inside nitrogen-doped porous carbon, and compared how each handled the wandering polysulfides.

Selenium's version balanced gripping the intermediates and converting them fastest, an effect the authors trace to its electronic structure sitting closest to the ideal energy level. Cells with the selenium catalyst started at a very high capacity and kept strong performance even in pouch cells with heavy sulfur loading and lean electrolyte. The authors present anion choice as a design lever for catalysts, and their results as support for the d-band theory guiding such choices.
pmc-13256613:
Shevchenko and a local team surveyed drug residues in beef, pork, and animal feed across Kazakhstan's Kostanay region, and tested meat bacteria for drug resistance. Traces were common in all three materials, though every level stayed below legal maximum limits. Levels differed sharply by feed type.

The authors warn that even trace residues moving through the feed-to-food chain may sustain selective pressure and spread resistant microbes. They call for thorough checks of feed and animal products.
pmc-13256813:
Katharina Gelles and colleagues report in 2026 a mouse study of baricitinib, a JAK inhibitor used for inflammatory diseases, asking whether its cytokine suppression also helps bones weakened by aging. They used SAMP8 mice, a strain that ages quickly, since age-related osteoporosis still lacks enough treatment options.

The drug clearly lowered several inflammatory cytokines from T cells. Bone results were mixed: one measurement method showed higher bone volume while high-resolution scans showed no clear difference. The authors conclude that aged bone responds sluggishly even when inflammation is controlled.
pmc-13257913:
Mohammad Saberian surveys new cement materials in a 2026 review. Plain Portland cement brings heavy carbon cost and resource use, which pushes work toward lower-impact binders. Three paths frame the field: waste-based add-ons, strength boosters, and print-ready mixes for layer-built work.

Plant ash, steel slag, sludge ash, and crushed old concrete can swap part of the clinker and recycle waste streams. Nano bits, fibers, and mix aids lift strength and life in set ways. Three-dimensional printing adds fresh needs on flow, stack hold, and early strength. Links among recipe, set chemistry, inner build, and long life are traced across studies. Trial-and-model design now grows beside bench work. Civil builders gain a fair map, with long-life proof and shared rules named as brakes.
pmc-13258713:
Veronika Huntošová and colleagues build a virus like nanoparticle aimed at a cell entry receptor in a 2026 study. The base particle is a porous metal organic framework widely used in delivery research. Surface steps added cysteine, flexible linkers, and the binding part of a coronavirus spike protein.

Treated particles kept their crystal structure and light based properties. Cells carrying the target receptor took up the decorated particles more than plain ones. Imaging placed most particles inside recycling and cleanup compartments of the cell. Both surface versions were tolerated well by the test cells. The platform offers a proof of concept for receptor guided delivery and imaging tools.
pmc-13260013:
Jeongkuk Park and colleagues compared in 2026 the genomes of methane-making archaea collected from many habitats. These microbes live in seas, fresh water, soil, animal guts, and the rumen, where their methane adds to farm emissions. The team rebuilt family trees from two marker genes and mapped the full gene sets of 71 genomes.

Trees from the two markers mostly disagreed, since one marker changes slowly and the other moves between species more freely. Shared core genes covered basic tasks like protein building, while many outer genes remain poorly described. Rumen types lacked some genes of one methane pathway, and gut types lacked several cofactor-making modules. pmc-13260213:
Zhenbing Ma and colleagues compare starch from zhiqu wheat, grown for liquor starter, with bread wheat starch. The two wheats feed very different crafts, yet their starch architecture was barely contrasted. Their 2026 analysis measures granules, crystals, and cooking behavior side by side.

Zhiqu starch carried slightly less amylose and somewhat larger mid-sized granules. Its crystals packed more orderly, and its pastes thickened higher at peak, trough, and finish. Branching ran lower in the liquor wheat's starch chains. Statistical mapping showed zhiqu quality traits holding unusually steady across samples. Growers choosing varieties for fermentation now have firmer guidance.
pmc-13260713:
Maria Margarida Teixeira and colleagues charted in 2026 the real-world cost in Portugal of treating locally advanced head and neck cancer. About six in ten patients with this cancer are found at an advanced local stage, where combined care is demanding. Their TRACE2 study followed 150 patients across four hospitals from their medical records.

Most patients were men aged fifty to seventy-nine, with very high rates of tobacco and heavy alcohol use. Combined drug therapy with radiotherapy was the most common treatment path. Nearly nine in ten patients needed outpatient visits and exams, and three quarters were hospitalized at some point. The median yearly cost per patient came to roughly seventy-seven hundred euros, driven mainly by combined therapy and hospital stays. The authors offer the figures as a baseline for planning follow-up care and resources.
pmc-13260813:
Mohamed M Shabib and colleagues present a 2026 numerical study of tuned mass dampers for earthquake protection in twelve-story steel buildings. A tuned mass damper is a heavy mass that sways against a building's motion to cut shaking, without external power. Using nonlinear time-history simulations under scaled earthquake records, the team compared a single damper with multi-damper layouts spread vertically, horizontally, and around the perimeter, in regular and irregular building plans.

For the regular building, a four-corner horizontal layout was tested for mistuning, and a frequency deviation of plus or minus four percent gave the lowest top displacement. For irregular plans shaped like T, C, L, and a stadium, a perimeter multi-damper layout cut maximum top displacement by between 18.3 percent and 52.3 percent, depending on the plan. Torsional rotation fell by between 25.4 percent and 68.0 percent, a large drop in twist, with base shear and acceleration also reduced.
pmc-13262613:
Xiaoxiao Sun and colleagues present a shared resource for studying cancer cells that survive targeted drugs in a 2026 journal article. These persister cells lack stable genetic resistance yet can seed relapse. The resource, called ResMap, offers a standard test setup and a data set so results from different labs can be compared fairly.

The team tested 94 compounds against 57 candidate targets in four lung cancer models, under normal and low oxygen. A first screen found 12 targets with activity across cancer types and oxygen levels, and follow-up work confirmed 9 of them. Some targets worked only in certain settings, including combinations tied to KRAS-driven cancer. Mouse and human cell data added a safety check for ranking targets.
pmc-13262713:
Cornelia M Weyand and Jörg J Goronzy review how ageing reshapes the immune system in a 2026 journal article. The immune network defends against infection and cancer, but stress over a lifetime wears down its structure. The authors trace changes in blood stem cells and in T and B cells, the white blood cells that learn to target specific threats.

Ageing stem cells renew themselves less well and produce skewed mixes of cells, they explain. Learner immune cells lose their fresh, untrained pool, their variety shrinks, and their internal power and stress systems falter. The result is a paradox: weaker defense alongside more chronic inflammation and self-attack. They illustrate this with rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis, two diseases of older adults.
pmc-13263013:
Annie Reid and co-authors evaluate action planning inside a digital program to cut sugary drink intake in Appalachian adults in a 2026 journal article. In most modules, users set goals, name barriers, and pick strategies, then update plans as feedback arrives.

The 119 participants completed most of their drink action plans, and 80 percent finished all five. About half rated carrying out their plans as hard or impossible, a share that stayed steady. pmc-13263213:
Shejil Kumar and co-authors evaluate a risk-targeted bone fracture service in Sydney in a 2026 journal article. pmc-13264113:
Chenyang Xianyu and colleagues review competition for amino acids inside tumors in a 2026 article. pmc-13264313:

pmc-13264613:

pmc-13264913:

pmc-13265013:

pmc-13265213:

pmc-13266213:

pmc-13266413:

pmc-13266613:

pmc-13267413:

pmc-13267513:

pmc-13268913:

pmc-13269113:

pmc-13270413:

pmc-13270913:

pmc-13272013:

pmc-13272213:

pmc-13272313:

pmc-13272413:

pmc-13272513:

pmc-13272613:

pmc-13272913:

pmc-13273013:

pmc-13273213:

pmc-13274913:

pmc-13275613:
Agata Burzawa, Katarzyna Potera, and Aleksandra Walczyńska present a 2026 journal article testing whether diet changes how tiny animals shrink as temperatures rise. Many cold-blooded animals mature smaller when warm, a pattern called the temperature-size rule. The team raised three clones of a rotifer, a microscopic water animal, with different heat preferences, each at four temperatures on three laboratory diets.

Diet changed the pattern, but unevenly across its parts. The lower temperature limit, where growth switches from negative to positive, shifted most with diet. The upper optimum temperature barely moved. The strength of the shrinking response also varied by food. The authors conclude that nutrition can bend thermal growth rules in different directions for different traits, so temperature effects cannot be read off without knowing what the animal eats.
pmc-13276313:
Kai Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on cleaning cadmium from rice paddy soil with charred rice husks. Cadmium, a toxic metal, builds up in farm soils and ends up in rice, threatening food safety. Biochar, a charcoal-like material, can lock metals in place, and chemical treatments may improve it.

The team incubated contaminated soil for one hundred twenty days at four cadmium levels. They compared raw husk biochar with three modified versions, treated with acid, alkali, or an oxidizing agent. The oxidant-treated char held the most acid groups and trapped cadmium best at low to moderate pollution. The alkali-treated char, strongly alkaline, stabilized soil best under severe pollution. Both also shifted soil humus, the dark organic matter tied to fertility. The authors map which char suits which contamination level.
pmc-13276413:
Amanda Morris and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how two bacteria interact in the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis. The thick mucus of this disease hosts chronic infections, often with both Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus together. Patients with both fare worse, but how the species affect each other was unclear.

The three-year study followed forty-five patients with chronic Pseudomonas infection. Microscopy of sputum at flare-ups, after antibiotics, and at recovery mapped both bacteria and a staph protein they release. During flare-ups in children, Pseudomonas volume and cluster count rose, and the two species sat farther apart. Antibiotics shrank small Pseudomonas clusters far more than large ones, which persisted. More staph protein tracked with more Pseudomonas in children. The authors say the species occupy separate niches yet still influence each other.
pmc-13276513:
Mari-Vorgan Louyer and colleagues present a 2026 lab method for measuring glyphosate in human urine. Glyphosate is among the most widely used weedkillers worldwide, and its health effects remain debated. Trustworthy exposure data depend on methods that stay accurate at very low levels.

Their approach dilutes urine and injects it directly into an ion chromatography system linked to a tandem mass spectrometer. A labelled internal standard corrects for losses and urine matrix effects during each run. The method reliably measured levels from very low levels upward. Full validation covered accuracy and precision under global standards.
pmc-13276713:
Szymon Andrusiów and colleagues examine gut and spinal fluid microbes in a nerve disease called CIDP, in a 2026 study. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy damages the insulation around nerves through immune attack. Its triggers are unknown and no confirmed biomarker exists.

Thirty-two untreated patients were compared with fifteen healthy controls using stool, blood, and spinal fluid samples. Patients' gut bacteria were more diverse, with clear shifts in community makeup. Greater diversity tracked worse nerve conduction results, an unexpected direction. Short-chain fatty acids and one immune gene's variants each matched distinct microbial patterns. Spinal fluid carried only a faint bacterial signal, and fungal communities showed no firm case-control gap.
pmc-13276813:
Yueying Zhang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study linking plant-based diets to throat tissue microbes and disease in China. They studied 236 people having upper gut screening in Linzhou, an area with high rates of esophageal cancer, meaning cancer of the food pipe. Food surveys sorted diets by how healthful the plant foods were.

Healthful plant diets were tied to less severe esophageal disease, while unhealthful plant diets were tied to worse disease. Swabs from the throat lining showed different microbe patterns for each diet type. Adding diet and microbe data improved risk grouping a little beyond basic factors. The authors treat the link as a lead for screening, not proof that diet caused the changes.
pmc-13277113:
Chon-Kit Chou and colleagues review immune receptors that control regulatory T cells in a 2026 article. Transplant patients face graft-versus-host disease, where donor cells attack the recipient, plus rejection of the graft itself. Regulatory T cells can calm both, yet growing stable batches for therapy is difficult.

The review walks through eight members of the TNF receptor superfamily found on these cells. Switching on TNFR2 or DR3 may expand the cells while sparing the graft's anti-leukaemia power. Two other receptors mark out the most suppressive cell subsets for selection. Some targets behave unpredictably, helping or harming by context, and one pathway makes cultured cells fragile.
pmc-13277213:
Guleser Akpinar leads a 2026 study of simple scores that predict outcomes for sepsis patients in an emergency department. Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection. The team compared shock indices, which combine pulse and blood pressure, with organ failure scores and lactate, a blood marker of stress, in 203 patients.

Lactate and the SOFA organ score were the most reliable guides overall. Lactate best predicted death within one month, and SOFA also predicted ward and intensive care admission. One shock index helped predict hospital admission, but the others added little. Quick lactate and organ checks, rather than shock formulas alone, should guide early calls, the authors argue.
pmc-13277413:
Yong Soo Jang leads the panel behind part three of the 2025 Korean resuscitation guidelines, published in 2026. The section sets adult basic life support steps for lay rescuers and professionals alike. Early action before hospital care largely decides whether a collapsed person survives.

Anyone finding an unresponsive person should call 119 at once and send for a defibrillator before checking breathing. Trained rescuers willing to give breaths should use standard CPR with ventilations included. Untrained or unwilling rescuers should give compression-only CPR instead. Pad placement on the side of the chest is preferred for speed. Health workers treating possibly infectious patients should use a thirty-to-two ratio with full protective equipment.
pmc-13277613:
Seong-Hyeon Cho leads a 2026 study of augmented reality glasses that help people who cannot tell some colors apart. Color vision deficiency, often red-green confusion, has no cure. Tinted lenses change the whole view, while screen tools work only on screens. The team's glasses film the real scene and add overlays only where confusion is likely.

A neural network, a computer program modeled loosely on brain circuits, tracks problem colors in real time. A special optical element built into a thin waveguide directs two colors into the view. Tests confirmed selective light coupling, and demonstrations placed overlays on target objects only. Wearable, targeted help of this kind proved feasible in principle.
pmc-13277713:
Isaac Zablah leads a 2026 letter responding to a review of large language models in health care. Large language models are computer programs trained on vast text that can draft and answer in human-like language. The letter praises the review's coverage of clinical uses and ethics, but says computing performance needs more attention, above all in low-resource settings.

Response times of several seconds may be too slow for emergency triage or surgery support, the authors argue. Top models also need large amounts of graphics memory that many hospitals, especially in poorer countries, lack. Serving hundreds of users at once adds further strain. They urge work on shrinking and trimming models so they can run on local devices.
pmc-13278813:
Yan Zhou leads a 2026 modeling study of climate change and hydropower effects on endangered plateau fishes in the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau region of China. Three Schizothorax species, protected in China, live mainly in the middle and upper Yarlung Zangbo River. The team modeled suitable habitat from species records and environmental factors, then projected futures under climate scenarios.

Water flow patterns and the coldest quarter's average temperature mattered most. Suitable habitat grew until the 2050s, then shrank by the 2070s, while shifting toward higher upper reaches. Hydropower plants, though, cause permanent local habitat loss in middle and lower reaches. Stronger protection in three named basins, plus monitoring and early warning, is recommended.
pmc-13279013:
Yangxia Wang and Ka Kit Hui published a 2026 commentary calling for health care to move from disease-centered treatment toward whole-person health. They describe how aging populations, chronic disease, rising costs, and mental health strain expose the limits of care organized around single organs or symptoms. Their discussion centers on integrated Chinese-Western medicine, which they present as one of the most developed models for combining traditional practice with modern biomedicine.

The authors trace how that integration grew from a mainly China-based experiment into an international framework, and they connect it with new tools such as artificial intelligence, systems biology, and precision medicine. Their central challenge is building models that are scientifically rigorous yet personal and affordable in real clinics. The piece speaks to clinicians and policymakers weighing how traditional systems might contribute to a wider redesign of care.
pmc-13279313:
Sara Garcia Bravo and colleagues published a 2026 study of whether two extra blood markers worsen pregnancy outlook in women within the antiphospholipid syndrome spectrum. The syndrome is an autoimmune condition tied to clots and pregnancy complications, but many patients fall short of full classification criteria. The authors studied 285 women with related obstetric problems, grouped as full syndrome, non-criteria, or seronegative cases, and tested them for antinuclear antibodies and low complement.

About 22 percent of the women tested positive for antinuclear antibodies, and they had fewer pregnancies and live births on average. Low complement, found in about 6 percent, tracked with more preeclampsia and early miscarriage, especially in the non-criteria group. Both abnormalities were also tied to greater use of antimalarial treatment during pregnancy. The authors suggest these markers flag a higher-risk subgroup that may need closer monitoring and stronger therapy, even when the classic label does not fully apply.
pmc-13279713:
Haifang Chen and colleagues published a 2026 review of in silico perturbation, a computer strategy for decoding the regulatory networks behind cancer immunity. Systems models replace the old habit of linking one gene to one trait. The models draw on genome, transcriptome, protein, and metabolite data from bulk, single-cell, and spatial sources. In a virtual knockout, researchers switch off a gene or cell type inside the model and watch the predicted system-wide response, hunting for control points in the tumor microenvironment.

Early versions relied on metabolic models and flux balance analysis. Newer deep learning systems can predict non-linear effects and perturbations never tested in labs. Uses include finding immune regulators, mapping how tumors evade attack, and ranking drug targets. The authors note hard problems in merging data layers, but present virtual perturbation as a promising engine for precision immunotherapy.
pmc-13280313:
Nicholas Norton and colleagues published a 2026 literature review and economic assessment of what timely systemic treatment of psoriatic disease could save by preventing illnesses. Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis raise the risk of cardiovascular disease, mental health disorders, type 2 diabetes, and obesity. The team gathered published data on those risks and costs, then built a lifetime cohort model from a societal perspective. The model covered three settings: Denmark, the United States, and Vietnam.

Untreated disease carried a heavy price in the model. The United States alone showed an untreated burden near 153 billion dollars for moderate-to-severe cases. Treating everyone with biologic drugs produced an offset of about 62.9 billion dollars in direct costs and 8.1 billion in social costs against an undertreated population. Results pointed the same direction in Denmark and Vietnam. The authors argue early, effective therapy pays back through avoided illness. They call for fuller cost studies to follow.
pmc-13280413:
Heba A. Fayyaz and colleagues report a 2026 study of lipid nanoparticle behaviour cell by cell. Lipid nanoparticles, or LNPs, enabled the first approved RNA drugs, yet their cellular behaviour holds unknowns. Particles matched the make up of Onpattro, an approved RNA drug. Flow cytometry read uptake, transfection and effects in thousands of single HeLa cells. Transfection means the RNA load turns on in the cell.

A subpopulation stood out: cells with uptake like peers but much lower transfection. Those cells also showed signs of stress and toxicity. The pattern held with empty particles and RNA loaded ones, and in a second formulation and other cell types. As dose rose, uptake and transfection first rose, then fell, and high uptake linked to cell death. Serum protein coats on particles were checked as a dose factor. One-size cell averages hide a stressed minority.
pmc-13282013:
William Gibson and co-authors published a 2026 study on false alarms in heart attack care at a large Canadian centre. Fast opening of blocked heart arteries saves lives, but calling out the catheter lab team, the team that threads tubes into the heart, when no procedure follows wastes staff time. The centre added Stenoa, a cloud-based phone platform that lets doctors check heart tracings and case details before the full team is called.

The team reviewed six hundred thirty-two lab activations from before and after the platform began. Needless team call-outs fell from about nine percent to about four percent. False activations also fell, though that drop was not firm by standard tests. Among false alarms, fewer led to a full call-out. The authors say structured digital checking can cut wasted mobilisation, but wider testing in more centres is still needed.
pmc-13282213:
Żabka Aneta and co-authors present a 2026 plant lab study on how a cancer drug stresses dividing cells in bean roots. The drug, methotrexate, blocks an enzyme needed to copy DNA, slowing cell growth. The team exposed root tip cells of the broad bean Vicia faba to a low dose for seventy-two hours. They then checked chromosome shape, DNA copying, cell survival, and chemical marks on DNA-packaging proteins.

Treated cells showed abnormal chromosome structure yet kept making DNA. Levels of hydrogen peroxide, a reactive oxygen chemical, rose inside the cells. One packaging mark grew more common in bright spots, while another mark's pattern shrank in key cell groups. More cells also showed marked nucleoli, the cores where cell parts are built, in an early phase. The authors read the pattern as a joint response to copying stress and oxygen stress.
pmc-13282413:
Amani A Alotaibi wrote a 2026 cross-sectional study on gender differences in attitudes toward mental illness in Jizan, Saudi Arabia. Stigma still harms people with mental illness despite improving attitudes. The survey enrolled five hundred eighty-six adults from public places between January and July 2024. A forty-item standard scale measured attitudes across four themes, including benevolence and social restrictiveness.

Men scored slightly higher overall on the attitude scale than women. Over half of all participants fell in a moderate stigma band on the study's percentile cut-offs. Women showed a more benevolent stance toward people with mental illness. Men showed stronger social restrictiveness, a wish to keep distance. No gender gap appeared on the other two themes. Among men, older age and higher education linked to more negative attitudes.
pmc-13283413:
Ahmad Mohammad led a 2026 review of calcium scoring, a heart scan that measures chalky deposits in the heart arteries, for adults with no symptoms and low-to-middle risk. The review asked whether the score predicts hard events such as heart attacks and whether it moves people into more accurate risk groups than standard factor checks alone. Eight long-term studies published between 2000 and 2025 qualified.

Across studies, higher scores tracked with higher event risk in a steady step-by-step pattern, even after standard factors were counted. A score of zero linked to very low event rates over the near term, while scores at or above one hundred carried much higher risk. Scoring also shifted many middle-risk people into truer groups. The authors see it as a useful, heart-specific add-on.
pmc-13284113:
Senyue Liu and co-authors studied in 2026 how ammonia in fish farm water wrecks the gut lining of a catfish species, Leiocassis longirostris. Ammonia builds up in intensive aquaculture and attacks organs including the intestine. Using live fish and tissue models with imaging, electrical resistance measures, and gene profiling, the team watched the barrier fail.

Ammonia drew inflammatory cells into the gut wall and broke the seal between lining cells. Oddly, the genes for seal proteins rose while the proteins themselves failed to assemble at the cell surface, a mismatch the authors call ineffective transcriptional compensation. A drug that stabilises one seal protein, ZO-1, restored its placement and barrier strength without big gene changes, and partly revived a support pathway. The authors propose ZO-1 stabilising as a farm strategy.
pmc-13284213:
Machine learning predicts groundwater oxygen-isotope values well only within its data heartland, caution Faten A Mohamed and colleagues in 2026. Isotope readings help trace recharge and salt build-up in dry regions. Sparse sampling in the mid-Nile Valley made model testing valuable.

Three ensemble methods competed on chemistry and location variables together. Random splitting flattered all models, with the forest method on top. Honest spatial testing cut accuracy roughly in half across methods. Longitude and three chemistry measures drove most predictions in the models. Without location, chemistry alone explained about forty percent of variance. Edge samples carried much wider uncertainty.
pmc-13284313:
Graded sponge-like cores strengthen sandwich panels in bending, show Hasnaa W Taha and colleagues in a 2026 simulation study. Auxetic cores deform unusually, thickening where stretched, which suits light structures. Their panels use a common printable plastic throughout for fair tests.

Computer models bent panels with uniform and graded re-entrant cores. Wall thickness grading ran vertically and horizontally across core layouts. Models were checked against published lab data before comparisons began. Graded designs spread loads better and delayed local failure in runs. Horizontal grading won, lifting peak load and energy uptake by wide margins. Progressive crushing added to the safety benefit.
pmc-13284413:
Akira Hanazono and co-authors write a letter, published in 2026, about diagnosis in functional neurological disorder, or FND. The letter responds to an editorial by Stone in Brain Communications and backs its call for caution. The authors warn that a focus on brain signs alone can miss social and lived aspects of illness.

Two problems guide the argument. First, positive signs do not cover all symptoms well, and strict labels can lead patients to give up their own story of illness. Second, a patient may not yet be ready to accept an FND label. The authors propose the idea of FND before readiness to help clinicians time talks, respect reported experience, and avoid harm while care moves forward.
pmc-13285013:
Gelan Ayana Zewdie and a team in Ethiopia asked health staff how ready the country is for an mpox outbreak. Their 2026 survey went to staff who track disease at state and local levels. Mpox may come back to the Horn of Africa. Fast spotting of new cases needs trained staff, labs, and clear lines for reports.

Forty-two staff filled in a long survey with five parts. Views were split on how well the system would cope. Most said labs were too weak. Many said there were no back-up plans, no staff trained on mpox, and no masks or gloves in store. The team calls for more training, better labs, and a fairer spread of funds.
pmc-13285713:
D Szpilman and co-authors describe a low-cost training kit for teaching CPR and defibrillator use in schools and community events, in a 2026 letter. Standard training manikins with feedback are expensive, which limits teaching in crowded or low-resource settings. Their kit, used by a Brazilian project, builds a practice dummy from recycled bottles and printed cardboard.

Learners can practice checking responsiveness, calling for help, opening the airway, placing hands for compressions, giving breaths, and positioning defibrillator pads. Early results from 857 students showed that very few knew these steps before training. The authors note that compression quality can only be judged by eye. Even so, they argue the kit's low cost spreads life-saving skills widely.
pmc-13285913:
Linling Tan and colleagues build a machine learning guide for artery-based liver cancer care in a 2026 multicenter study. Tumors that cannot be cut out are often treated through the liver's own artery, but results vary widely by patient. Their system sorts patients by risk of death within five years, using facts known before and after the first treatment round.

Data covered 5,646 patients treated at 15 hospitals between 2008 and 2022, split into training and test sets. Models fed only pre-treatment facts sorted risk fairly well, led by one gradient boosting method. Adding facts gathered after treatment sharpened sorting a great deal, with a rival method on top. The final system split patients into three risk bands with clearly apart survival curves, a guide the authors say now needs trials in live care.
pmc-13286213:
Willian da Silva and co-authors ask whether skin heat skews muscle oxygen readings during strength work in a 2026 exercise study. Light-based sensors worn on the thigh promise a window on muscle fuel use, but blood shifting in the skin above might bend the signal. Seventeen men ground through repeated sets of machine knee work while sensors tracked thigh skin heat and muscle oxygen in both legs.

Skin cooled steadily across the sets in the worked leg and the resting leg alike. Muscle oxygen climbed only in the worked leg, as heavy effort would predict. Paired readings from the two sensors showed no firm link at all across the session. Weak ties turned up only for total blood pigment in the resting leg, which the authors read as the two tools telling apart stories rather than one corrupting the other.
pmc-13286513:
Ahmed Alshehri and Asaad Abdulrahman Abduljawad explored how women in underserved Saudi communities judged a diabetes education program designed for them. Their 2026 mixed-methods study ran in two towns in the Makkah region. Interviews with 20 women came first, then a survey of 136 participants built from what the interviews surfaced.

Most women reported real changes: about seven in ten cut sugar, two thirds moved more, and similar shares drank more water and checked glucose regularly. Large majorities found the advice practical and felt it understood women's challenges. Barriers included scarce time, family duties, money limits, and poor access to care. Phone follow-up and community support, the authors suggest, could help changes last.
pmc-13287013:
Grzegorz Pajestka and Katarzyna Skałacka ask whether psychological courage, the willingness to act while afraid, predicts whether women intend to attend mammography screening. Their 2026 study surveyed 292 women aged forty-five to seventy-four with no breast cancer history. Fear-based accounts dominate screening research, yet dread alone does not decide behavior.

Courage predicted screening intention even after anxiety, cancer worry, perceived personal risk, and past screening habits were accounted for. Courage did not simply cancel out negative feelings; no interaction effects appeared. Because courage can be trained, the authors suggest, health campaigns might build it rather than only trying to soothe fear, opening a fresh lever for raising screening uptake.
pmc-13287213:
Xiaohan Sun and colleagues grew two problem bacteria together in 2026 using samples taken from people with long-lasting sinus infection. Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa sat in linked chambers that let shared chemicals pass but kept the organisms apart, so the team could measure how each changed the other's surface growth.

Pairs taken from the same patient boosted each other's growth several times over, while mixed pairs from different patients did not. The matched pairs also tolerated an antibiotic better. Liquid collected from one species reproduced much of the boost. The authors argue that treatment choices for mixed infections should account for this local adaptation.
pmc-13287413:
María Santamera-Lastras and colleagues linked weather and air pollution records in 2026 to outcomes for 336 dialysis patients treated in Madrid between 2016 and 2024. The records held 563 admissions and 90 deaths. Short spikes and longer averages were both tested.

Sulfur dioxide stood out, tracking with higher admission and death risk under both short and long views. Nitrogen dioxide predicted death only over longer periods, hinting at slow build-up. Sunlight measures linked to faster death in some models, while higher air pressure looked protective for admissions. The authors suggest adding local air measures to risk tools for kidney patients.
pmc-13288713:
Ji-Xiang Wan and colleagues weigh one-sided versus two-sided spine numbing in 2026. Their review searched three databases. The cut date was December 2024. Only randomized trials in adults were kept. All used the same local drug in both arms.

Nineteen trials with 1,191 patients made the cut. One-sided blocks started a bit slower. They also wore off sooner. Yet low blood pressure fell sharply with them. Sickness and headache after the tap also fell. Racing heart and urine hold showed no split. For picked patients and short surgery, safety wins. The authors favor the one-sided trade there.
pmc-13289013:
Philipo Joshua Loishiye and colleagues study teen pregnancy in rural Tanzania. Their 2026 study mixes surveys with talks. It ran in Korogwe District in the Tanga Region. The survey drew 418 girls aged 15 to 19. Talks added girls, parents, and local leaders.

Pregnancy had touched 16 percent of girls. Older teens faced higher odds. Leaving school raised the odds too. Early unions and money strain also mattered. Birth control use was higher after pregnancy. That likely shows late uptake, not protection. Talks blamed poverty and trade in sex. Myths about birth control also blocked use. Power gaps tied girls' hands as well.
pmc-13289113:
Georgii Alexandrov and Yiping Wu write a 2026 memorial for a fellow scientist. The piece marks the death of Academician George S. Golitsyn. He died in his ninety-first year, on May 6. He sat on the board of the journal Carbon Balance and Management. He helped found that journal in 2006.

Golitsyn was born in Moscow in 1935. He earned a physics degree there in 1958. He spent his career at one air physics institute. He led it as director from 1990. His books dealt with air flow on planets. Later work dealt with climate disasters. Top honors capped his long career.
pmc-13289313:
Robert R Zwaan and colleagues report a 2026 feasibility study of ultrafast ultrasound for heart stiffness in congenital aortic stenosis. In this birth condition the aortic valve is narrow, forcing the heart to push harder for years. Extra pressure can stiffen heart muscle, hurt filling, and lead toward heart failure over time.

Shear wave elastography uses very fast scans to time waves crossing the heart wall, giving a stiffness readout without surgery. Recordings were taken in 68 adults with the condition and 19 healthy volunteers for comparison. The method worked in most patients, though less often after valve replacement surgery. Wave speed ran higher in moderate to severe cases than in healthy hearts, suggesting the tool can flag stiffer muscle.
pmc-13289413:
Annemette Høegh Pedersen and colleagues studied a 2026 Danish registry cohort. They asked whether inflammation at treatment start predicts success of two biologic classes in axial spondyloarthritis. That disease inflames the spine and pelvis joints. The marker tested was C reactive protein, a blood sign of inflammation, split into low, middle, and high bands.

The DANBIO registry held 3387 patients starting a first IL-17 blocker or first TNF blocker between 2015 and 2024. Staying on therapy at twelve months rose slightly with higher starting inflammation for TNF blockers, but not clearly for IL-17 blockers in the models. Remission by a standard activity score was also checked by band. Sex and X-ray status did not change the broad picture.
pmc-13290613:
A boy who should not have recovered did, and Kai Fiedler and colleagues examine why in a 2026 case report from a German children's hospital. The 13-year-old drowned, needed prolonged resuscitation, and developed severe pediatric ARDS that required ECMO support.

Against several poor-outcome risk factors, he left the hospital in an age-appropriate neurologic state, matching his pre-accident condition. The team set his course beside their center's ten-year run of childhood drowning cases, from 2013 to 2023, and the published literature, hunting for the special circumstance that saved him. They found no significant difference and no starting parameter that explained the gap. Fiedler and colleagues conclude that early decisions in pediatric drowning rest on real uncertainty, and single good outcomes should not rewrite caution.
pmc-13290713:
Neighbors handing COVID tests to neighbors reached people clinics could not in a 2026 community case study from Chicago by Elizabeth Lynch and colleagues. Working with the Alive Faith Network, a coalition of academic partners and African American churches, the team let community members pass rapid antigen home tests through their own social networks.

Between October 2021 and August 2022, distributors moved 8,386 tests across high-vulnerability South and West Side neighborhoods. Survey returns covered 1,555 kits from 1,075 people, many of them young, male, and unvaccinated, groups conventional outreach often misses, and 602 test results came back. Follow-up calls showed high acceptability and willingness to test again. The authors argue trust-based, decentralized distribution deserves a permanent place in outbreak response.
pmc-13290913:
Strong COVID antibody memory does not mean twitchier airways in asthmatic children, Peter Kunc and colleagues find in a prospective study from 2026. Chronic cough is a common Long COVID complaint in children, blamed on virus-sensitized airway nerves, and the team tested whether antibody strength matches objective cough sensitivity.

Sixty-one children aged 8 to under 12 with well-controlled asthma and past infection gave antibody titers and took a capsaicin cough challenge. Splitting them at the median antibody level showed no difference in cough thresholds, and correlations between titers and nerve measures were absent. Parent-reported cough severity and quality of life also floated free of the objective thresholds. Kunc and colleagues warn against diagnosing nerve-driven Long COVID from questionnaires alone and urge objective testing instead.
pmc-13291013:
Chengjian Cao, Chaoxiang Lv, and Ali ElFar review phosphofructokinase as a drug target in cancer in a 2026 article built around cell metabolism. Cancer cells lean heavily on sugar breakdown even when oxygen is present, and this enzyme sits at a central control point in that pathway, in forms known as PFKP, PFKM, and PFKL.

Beyond basic energy control, the enzyme shapes cell growth, spread, resistance to therapy, blood vessel growth, and escape from immune attack, the authors argue. Both lab-made blockers and natural products such as curcumin are surveyed as ways to hit the target. A forward plan pairs those drugs with artificial intelligence design, tiny delivery carriers, and immune-metabolic methods, while noting the hard problems that still limit patient use.
pmc-13291113:
Copper aluminate particles that reveal hidden fingerprints are tested by Rameen Fatima and colleagues in 2026. Fingerprints anchor many crime inquiries. Prints lose contrast as they age. Tricky surfaces make them hard to see.

The particles were made by a low-cost sol-gel route. Prints were dusted on paper, ceramic, and wood. Smooth plastic, steel, and glass were also tried. Glass gave the strongest contrast in plain light. Ultraviolet light sharpened ridge detail further. Fine match features became visible under that light. Patterns stayed readable for up to thirty days. A cheap, steady powder option is the claim.
pmc-13291313:
Aligning two medical scans of soft tissue is hard. Bingxian Xie, Guimei Zhang, and Ke Xu present a 2026 network to do it better. Organs shift shape between scans in complex ways. Learned methods often lose accuracy under big shifts.

Their network, CRR-Net, rebuilds fine detail inside its features. A core module maps how points match across scans. A pyramid layout works from coarse to fine scales. Pictures of the warp field help users judge quality. Tests on brain and heart data beat rival methods. One win used far fewer parameters than a top rival. It also ran much faster in that test.
pmc-13291613:
A faster physics method can rank drug binding strength. William Sinko leads a 2026 study of ModBinddG, a simulation-based predictor. Binding strength decides if a drug candidate works. Gold-standard methods are too slow for mass screening.

Hot sampling lets rare unbinding events happen on screen. Population math then restores true room-temperature values. Hundreds of drug-protein pairs validated the method. Accuracy matched leading industry tools. Throughput rose by orders of magnitude. Large physics-based screens become feasible before synthesis. Chemists can test ideas in silico first. Costly lab work can focus on the best bets.
pmc-13291713:
Zaid Nathani and Helene Alphonso present a 2026 case report about a 46-year-old woman whose first manic episode was read at first as late-onset bipolar disorder. Her perimenopausal symptoms and a decade of stability on an antidepressant shaped that early reading. Months later she developed painless leg weakness and needed a wheelchair, yet spine imaging looked normal, so clinicians suspected conversion disorder.

Brain imaging plus a neurologic workup eventually pointed to primary progressive multiple sclerosis behind both the mania and the weakness. The authors argue that new mania in perimenopausal women calls for a brain MRI and an autoimmune blood panel before a primary psychiatric label is settled. Their case shows how a hormone-based explanation can delay the search for a hidden neurologic illness.
pmc-13291813:
Myung Jae Jin and Jaewon Shin present a 2026 case report about a fecaloma hiding above the reach of a rectal exam after hemorrhoid surgery. Their patient, a 49-year-old woman, came in 14 days after stapled hemorrhoidopexy with severe abdominal pain and obstipation. Her rectum felt empty on examination, which first pointed the team the wrong way.

A CT scan instead showed a large fecal mass in the proximal sigmoid colon, 15 cm above the staple line, which stayed intact. An enema through a rectal tube did not work, but a high enema through a flexible sigmoidoscope softened the mass partway. Flushing polyethylene glycol through a nasogastric tube then cleared it without surgery. The authors recommend early CT when blockage is suspected after this operation.
pmc-13292313:
T K Sundari Ravindran and co-authors compare a 2026 pair of lenses on gender-transformative sexual and reproductive health programs in sub-Saharan Africa: what practitioners say matters versus what published evaluations measure. The study draws on interviews with 19 African practitioners and researchers plus 44 published evaluations of 20 interventions run between 2012 and 2025.

Practitioners wanted assessments that follow change across levels, use shared design and long first-hand tracking, and record how change happens. Published studies mostly measured short-term attitude and behavior shifts in individuals, mostly men, using standard outside tools. Women's empowerment, system change, and staying power got little attention. The authors propose models that involve communities, validate men's self-reports, and keep evaluating after projects end.
pmc-13292513:
Simona Guerzoni and co-authors track a 2026 real-world money question in Modena, Italy: does starting the migraine preventive atogepant shrink how much acute triptan medicine patients need? Administrative records covered adults with chronic migraine or frequent episodic migraine who began the daily CGRP blocker between November 2023 and December 2024. The team compared dispensed triptan units across the six months on either side of the start date.

Of 95 patients, 86 percent women with a mean age of 53.5, fifty-five used triptans and entered the analysis. Use fell in 82 percent of them, dropped by at least 60 percent in about half, and stopped entirely in ten people. Median consumption slid from 76 to 24 dosage units. The cohort saved 2,591 euros in triptan spending, a statistically solid drop the authors read as clinical and economic gain.
pmc-13293513:
Siphamandla Lamula and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how widely chikungunya virus circulates in Southern Africa, where its footprint is poorly mapped. The mosquito-borne virus causes major illness in warm regions, often with fever and joint pain.

A search kept 20 studies from January 2012 to October 2025 across eight countries in the region, from Madagascar to South Africa. Past infection rates varied widely, from rare finds in Angola to steady signs in Madagascar and Tanzania. Women of working and childbearing age were hit most. Testing leaned on antibody methods, with gene confirmation mostly during outbreaks. Stronger surveillance is urged.
pmc-13294113:
George Delgado and colleagues review what happened when people took a hormone drug to try to keep a pregnancy after a first abortion pill in a 2026 chart study. Callers to a nonprofit hotline between October 13, 2021, and January 5, 2024, were screened. To count, the hormone had to start within 72 hours, before the second pill, with pregnancy under 12 weeks at first pill use.

Of 1,466 people screened, 765 qualified, and 418, or 55%, still had ongoing pregnancies two weeks after starting the hormone. Earlier first pill use lowered the chance in the reported split. Bad bleeding was rare, with no transfusions or deaths. The authors call for strict trials.
pmc-13294313:
Casey E Eaton and coauthors study what happens when engineers omit technical measures while choosing large systems in a 2026 analysis. Measures set limits or serve as goals when comparing designs, yet picking the set is uncertain and hard to validate. Two frameworks, one constraint-based and one optimization-based, were built from real measures and tested on NASA's Human Landing System with 13 alternatives.

Dropping a measure in the constraint view opened the design space and could flip the winner. Dropping one in the scoring view reordered preferences and also flipped the winner. Since contracts steer millions of dollars, careful problem framing and validation of the measure set are essential.
pmc-13294413:
Stefania Livia Ciummo and coauthors trace a two-way signal that pushes prostate cancer toward bone in a 2026 study. Tumor cells release interleukin-30, which reprograms nearby fibroblasts through IL6 receptor signaling into growth-friendly cancer helpers. Chip models linking tumor-fibroblast balls to a bone marrow-like niche tested migration and settling, with gene removal to check necessity.

Reprogrammed fibroblasts boosted tumor migration genes and bone niche colonization, and extra interleukin-30 strengthened the effect while depletion largely erased it. Oddly, fibroblasts alone muted spread genes, but interleukin-30 overrode that brake. Blocking the axis could slow metastasis and resistance, the authors propose.
pmc-13294513:
Qilu Li and coauthors reply to a critique of their leadership and AI deployment study in a 2026 response letter. Dr Bair questioned how impact was defined amid publication bias, whether models held with few negative results, and whether last authorship fairly signals leadership. The authors thank the critic and revisit their healthcare AI analysis from an organizational science angle.

They concede that causal wording needs caution and that 88% positive findings may mirror publication chances more than true benefit. Mediation by trial design and geography gets fresh attention. Expanded contributor-level data gathering is underway, and the team frames the first findings as a meaningful early step, not a verdict.
pmc-13295713:
Felix Oluoch and colleagues use satellite flood maps to judge water service resilience in coastal Kenya in a 2026 study. Repeated flooding can knock out safe water and working latrines, but community-level proof over time was scarce. Ten community health units in Kilifi County were followed across eleven survey rounds from 2017 to 2024.

Radar images set each unit's flood exposure for every round, matched against household water and latrine coverage. More frequent flooding cut latrine coverage notably harder than safe water coverage over time. Rural units trailed most on safe water, while town-fringe units ranked highest overall, shaping where flood-proofing money should go first.
pmc-13296213:
Rina Hoffmann and colleagues chart innate lymphoid cells in tissue and blood from people with chronic rhinosinusitis, in a 2026 study. These cells are strong makers of signaling proteins that steer local immune responses in the nose and sinuses. The team used flow cytometry to count cell kinds in polyp tissue, sinus tissue, and blood, sorting patients by whether polyps were present.

Natural killer cells in nasal tissue proved mixed and less mature than their blood kin. In polyps, killer cell counts ran lower, and type 2 lymphoid cells showed stronger marks of the type 2 program that feeds polyp growth. Counts of several subsets that answer to interleukin-18 ran low in polyps, hinting that this signal plays a small part there. The authors give killer cells a larger role in disease without polyps.
pmc-13296413:
Clara Musicco and colleagues assess cell-free mitochondrial DNA as a blood marker for gynaecological cancers in a 2026 review. Liquid biopsy looks for tumour clues in body fluids instead of cutting tissue. Mitochondrial DNA is attractive because each cell holds many copies, making it easier to detect in circulation.

The review gathers reported changes in this DNA fraction for ovarian and endometrial cancers, the two cancers covered in depth. Both develop in strongly inflammatory settings, and the marker ties closely to cell damage and inflammation signals. Evidence so far is promising but limited, the authors stress. They set out what standard methods and larger studies would be needed before clinical use.
pmc-13296513:
Riccardo Standish and colleagues measure how well polyethylene, the most common plastic, dissolves in a range of solvents, in a 2026 study. Melting waste plastic into a chosen liquid could clean streams that normal recycling cannot handle. Data on which liquids work, and at what heat, are still scarce.

The team tested four samples of the plastic in ten solvents at many heat levels. A maths model of molecule groups matched the measured results well for eight of the solvents. Decalin and scent-rich solvents such as toluene dissolved the most plastic at a set heat. Several plant-based solvents worked about as well, giving greener choices. How the plastic melts mattered more than the length of its chains.
pmc-13296913:
Pablo Pagano and colleagues combine low-dose isotretinoin with staged laser treatment for acne and scarring in a 2026 case series. Five patients had severe inflammatory acne together with sunken, reddened scars. Pairing the drug with lasers was long avoided over fears about wound healing.

All five reached near-complete or complete acne clearance within a month, and the result held at three months. Scar scores fell sharply on both rating scales used. No serious side effects or healing problems appeared during follow-up. The authors suggest the combination can treat active disease and old scars together, while asking for larger prospective studies to confirm safety and refine the protocol.
pmc-13297213:
Zengyun Mou and colleagues survey computational methods for finding new uses for approved drugs in a 2026 review. Repurposing skips much of the cost and risk of fresh drug discovery because safety testing already exists. Methods are grouped by their logic, from biological mechanisms through networks to data-driven text approaches.

Mechanism-based methods explain deeply but scale poorly, while network methods predict systematically across many sources. Text mining unlocks the literature, and large language models amplify that reach greatly. No single family wins outright, the authors argue. The future lies in smart combinations, with mechanism work still needed to validate and explain whatever the big prediction engines propose.
pmc-13297313:
José Luis Cortes-Altamirano and a large team review how immune imbalance, centred on the calming signal IL-10, bears on hard-to-treat depression in a 2026 survey. Depression that resists standard drugs is increasingly tied to lasting inflammation in the brain and body. Fourteen studies, from trials to cohort work, met the entry rules.

Across them, high levels of pro-inflammatory signals such as IL-6 tracked worse symptoms and weaker responses to standard drugs. Immune-calming treatments helped most in patients whose inflammation started high. IL-10, which counteracts those signals, looks like both a marker of balance and a possible target. Immune profiles may one day guide which treatment each patient gets.
pmc-13297513:
Eglė Jauniškytė, Giedrė Žulpaitė, and Jolanta Labanauskienė report a six-year-old whose broken thigh growth plate slowly shortened one leg, in a 2026 case report. The child was hit in an electric scooter crash with a motor vehicle, an unusual load of force for so young a patient. Surgeons washed the open wound, set the bone, and fixed it with crossed smooth wires the same day.

Healing looked sound at first. Yet the growth plate closed early, and the leg gap grew from just over one centimetre at ten months to six and a half centimetres over five years. Growth maths predicted a final gap above seven centimetres, so the healthy leg's growth plate was fused to let the sides even out. Long watch, not early success, decides such cases.
pmc-13297713:
Atsuko Hirabae and a large team test whether vessel-blocking drugs can wake the immune system inside gene-driven lung tumours, in a 2026 mouse study. Such tumours, carrying EGFR faults, answer poorly to immune checkpoint drugs because their surroundings stay immunologically cold. The mice modelled that cold setting before any targeted drug exposure.

The vessel drug did not switch on immune activity and did not make checkpoint treatment work better. A surprise emerged when paclitaxel chemotherapy joined the vessel drug: tumours shrank through a route that did not need T cells, with more natural killer cells moving in. Future strategies for these tumours may need to recruit immune paths beyond T cells, the authors argue.
pmc-13297813:
Kidney disease grew markedly more common among heart center patients in Brazil over a decade, report Farid Samaan and colleagues in a 2026 laboratory-based study. They tracked creatinine and urine albumin results for adults seen at a cardiologic center between 2014 and 2023.

Adjusted prevalence of chronic kidney disease rose from 20% to 31% across the period, and the share of patients in high or very high risk categories climbed from 14% to 21%. New cases over the decade reached 21.7%, concentrated among women and older patients. The authors warn that services must adapt to a sicker population, more of whom may eventually need dialysis or transplantation.
pmc-13299213:
Irena Zupanič Pajnič, Tomaž Zupanc, and Eva Podovšovnik compare DNA recovery from bones found in two Slovenian Second World War mass graves, in a 2026 forensic study. Identification of victims is hampered by decay that varies with burial conditions. Their dataset combined hundreds of samples across six skeletal element groups from both sites.

The best bone type depended on the grave. One site favoured small long bones and short bones, while the other favoured teeth and torso bones, and decay rates did not simply follow yield. Dense ear-region bone performed well at both sites. A multi-sample, site-aware strategy is recommended.
pmc-13299313:
Junling Tang and others review berberine, a natural plant alkaloid, as a candidate helper in inflamed bowel disease, in a 2026 survey. Current treatments leave incomplete responses, side effects, and relapses common. Evidence gathered through early 2026 covers the compound's pharmacology, delivery gains, and clinical use attempts.

Berberine appears to reshape gut microbial communities, calm mucosal immune reactions, and support repair of the intestinal barrier, jointly restoring gut balance. Delivery systems that respond to microbes or target the intestine may raise local exposure. Evidence is still mostly early-stage, clinical data are limited, and causal links between those effects stay unclear, the authors caution.
pmc-13299413:
Care for sugar disease in state clinics in Palestine feels mid-grade to the sick who use it. Hiba Ziad AbuZayyad and Shahenaz Najjar found that view in a 2026 survey. They asked 417 adults with type 2 sugar disease in the north, south, and mid West Bank to grade how much care bends to the sick.

Mean marks came to 2.82 in the round. The bond with the doctor scored top, at 2.90. Shared ground on care plans scored low, at 2.71. Marks swung by zone and by town, camp, or farm home. No trait of the sick, once weighed, stood on its own as a cause. The team urge set fixes where marks lag and a wider sweep of zones.
pmc-13299713:
Stem cell therapy is giving way to the particles those cells release, and Ramya Lakshmi Rajendran with Prakash Gangadaran chart the handoff in a 2026 perspective on regenerative medicine. Mesenchymal stem cells have shown benefit in graft-versus-host disease and other conditions, and a first cell product has now won FDA approval.

Yet whole cells vary from batch to batch, producing uneven trial results. Their extracellular vesicles carry much of the healing signal with greater stability and lower immune risk, but potency testing and regulation lag behind. The authors argue the field must solve manufacturing and approval hurdles to turn these vesicles into programmable nanomedicines for routine care.
pmc-13299913:
M Marino leads a team testing a dual-energy catheter for durable isolation of the left atrial appendage in persistent atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 prospective study. Blocking cuts recurrence yet often fails to last. Straight patients received pulsed field energy alone at the appendage opening, or short radiofrequency bursts at two power levels, plus pulsed treatment inside the appendage.

Every strategy achieved isolation acutely in all 182 patients. Three months later, reconnection appeared in every pulsed-only patient and most of the lower-power group, yet in none of the higher-power radiofrequency group. The authors conclude extra radiofrequency energy is necessary for lasting isolation with this catheter.
pmc-13300213:
Taomei Yang and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of TCEA1, a transcription elongation factor, in acute promyelocytic leukemia, a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. Earlier work showed that losing TCEA1 in myeloid cells speeds growth and blocks maturation, so the team tested what raising its levels does in NB-4 leukemia cells and in mouse xenograft models.

Extra TCEA1 slowed cell growth, raised cell death, and pushed cells toward differentiation, while raising two maturation regulators, C/EBP epsilon and IRF8. Restoring either regulator reversed the effects of TCEA1 loss in a second cell line. In mice, extra TCEA1 reduced leukemia spread in marrow, spleen, and liver and lengthened survival. Public patient data linked higher TCEA1 with better prognosis, which the authors offer as a possible treatment target and marker.
pmc-13300413:
O Alothman and co-authors describe a simpler pulsed field ablation workflow for pulmonary vein isolation in a 2026 single-center report. Standard heat-based ablation often needs several catheters and vein punctures. The team tested one leg vein access, one ablation catheter, and guidance from a CT scan taken beforehand, fused with live X-ray images. The series looked back at 191 patients in a row having first-time ablation for atrial fibrillation.

Isolation of all pulmonary veins succeeded in every patient, with two catheter designs used. Mean procedure time sat near one hour, and X-ray exposure stayed low. Brief weakness of the phrenic nerve hit about eleven percent of patients, and it always cleared before discharge. Major problems were rare: one case of breathing trouble, one mini-stroke, and two groin hematomas. The authors present the simpler route as a strong option over multi-catheter workflows.
pmc-13300513:
