Zhijiao Song and co-authors catalogue the NAC transcription factor family in avocado in a 2026 genome-wide study. These plant regulators steer fruit development, ripening, seed life, and stress responses, yet avocado had no full survey. Using sequence searches, family tree reconstruction, expression profiling, and co-expression network analysis, the team characterized the family and tracked its behavior across fruit development.

They found 130 NAC genes spread over all twelve avocado chromosomes, falling into eight subfamilies. Seventy of them changed activity during development, with a few showing the strongest rises or falls. Ethylene experiments singled out one gene suppressed by the ripening hormone and switched on when ethylene perception was blocked, plus three genes showing the mirror pattern. The authors offer the catalogue as a framework for probing avocado ripening and postharvest handling.
pmc-13300713:
Lola R. Nogueira and co-authors report real world use of the HER2DX genomic assay in early HER2-positive breast cancer, in a 2026 single-center study from Madrid. The twenty-seven gene test returns three scores covering response to pre-surgery therapy, long-term recurrence risk, and HER2 pathway activity. The team reviewed forty-five tested patients treated between 2023 and 2025 and asked how often the scores actually changed management.

Testing altered care in just over half the patients. The response score shifted the choice between starting with drug therapy or surgery in about eighteen percent of cases. It also supported lighter chemotherapy backbones, with ninety percent of high-score tumors clearing completely at surgery. The risk score helped pick chemotherapy foundations within stage II disease, and the activity score tracked laboratory staining intensity. The authors call the assay informative beyond standard pathology, while asking for larger prospective validation.
pmc-13300813:
Seda Busra Sarac and co-authors pair eye tracking with machine learning to forecast purchase decisions from product reviews, in a 2026 consumer research study. One hundred twenty-eight participants shopped in a simulated online store while their gaze was recorded across ten review related screen regions. The scenarios varied whether buying felt pleasurable or practical, and whether the purchase was for the shopper or for someone else.

Attention patterns lined up with motives and purposes, giving each scenario a distinct gaze signature. Twenty features built from fixation counts and durations then fed six forecasting methods. Support vector machines performed best, reaching roughly fifty-nine to sixty percent accuracy against a naive benchmark near fifty-four percent, a modest gain of about five to six points. The authors present the work as methodological evidence that objectively recorded gaze can serve as behavioral input for purchase prediction.
pmc-13301113:
A skin fungus that normally stays on the surface can burrow deep when one immune gene fails, Dipika Shaw and colleagues explain in a 2026 review of CARD9 mutations. The adaptor protein CARD9 links fungal sensors such as Dectin-1 to NF-κB and MAPK signaling, driving cytokine release and Th17 defenses against invaders.

Without working CARD9, neutrophils falter and patients, otherwise immunocompetent, suffer chronic, drug-resistant deep dermatophytosis with nodules, plaques, and ulcers, mostly on the legs. Cases cluster across Asia, North Africa, and the Middle East, often in adult men. Early genetic testing guides care, and stem cell transplantation can cure selected patients, the authors stress.
pmc-13301413:
Tiny drug carriers could find and treat inflamed heart tissue, Aikaterini-Eleftheria Karanikola and colleagues argue in a 2026 review of nanomedicine for heart and vessel disease. The survey spans clogged arteries, heart attack, and heart failure, where today's scans and drug delivery miss targets or spread medicine through the whole body.

The carriers can home to sore tissue for sharper pictures and drop drugs right at the spot, with some doing both jobs at once. Newer designs copy the body's own surfaces, and AI helps tune them. The authors weigh that promise against safety checks, factory scale-up, and proof hurdles that keep most designs out of routine care.
pmc-13301513:
A Estevez Paniagua and co-authors check whether left bundle pacing stays electrically stable over eighteen months in a 2026 follow-up study. The series covered 149 patients paced for slow heart rates with preserved pumping function, comparing twelve lead tracings at implant against those at about eighteen months. Changes in activation timing and QRS width were regressed against clinical and procedural variables.

Synchrony did not decay; it improved. Activation times to both sides of the chest shortened, and QRS duration narrowed whether measured from the pacing spike or from its onset. Higher body mass predicted worsening of right sided timings, while kidney disease, larger atria, older age, and a septal perforation at implant predicted more QRS narrowing. The pacing subtype and capture pattern at implant did not determine evolution. The authors read the stability as evidence that conduction system pacing is durable across its variants.
pmc-13301913:
V Nemeth, P K Kupo, and K J Janosi describe, in a 2026 study, how lung veins reconnect after ablation for atrial fibrillation that later returns. Isolating these veins electrically is the core of the procedure, yet reconnection is a frequent reason the rhythm comes back. The authors compared veins first treated point by point against those treated with single-shot devices.

Repeat procedures in 105 patients between 2021 and 2023 remapped every vein for restored conduction. About a quarter of patients showed no reconnection at all, pointing to triggers elsewhere in the heart. Overall reconnection rates were similar between the two original techniques. Right-sided veins, however, reconnected significantly more often after single-shot treatment, a pattern that could guide repeat procedures.
pmc-13302313:
Alishah Ahmadi and co-authors apply machine learning clustering to more than four hundred thousand hip replacement patients in a 2026 study of arthritis care. Patients arrive with very different bundles of other illnesses, which drives how long they stay and whether they go home or to a facility. The analysis used a national inpatient database covering 2015 to 2021.

Grouping by forty-nine illnesses and complications produced five distinct patient clusters, one of them holding most patients. Clusters rich in kidney disease, heart failure, anaemia, and cardiovascular disease faced up to triple the odds of non-routine discharge. Their hospital stays also ran longer, with medians up to four days against two in low-risk clusters. The authors offer the grouping for planning beds and support.
pmc-13302713:
Praise mixed with pointed caveats fills a 2026 comment by In-Suk Bae on a meta-analysis of spine fracture treatment. Lee and colleagues had compared teriparatide drug therapy against vertebroplasty for acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, crediting the drug with better long-term pain relief, bone density, and fewer new fractures. Bae congratulates them on the first such pooled comparison.

The comment then lists the soft spots: only five studies and 326 patients, heavy statistical heterogeneity, and the exclusion of kyphoplasty, a sibling cement procedure. Cost and the burden of daily injections also went unexamined. Bae calls for large multicenter trials with standardized protocols before practice shifts.
pmc-13303413:
Chienhsiu Huang, Lichen Lin, and Tiju Tang present a 2026 meta-analysis on added oxygen treatment for Fournier's gangrene, a fast-moving and often fatal tissue infection. Standard care relies on broad antibiotics and surgery to remove dead tissue, yet deaths stay common.

Pooling 14 studies with 793 patients, the authors compared people who also received hyperbaric oxygen with those who did not. Deaths were lower in the oxygen group than in the control group, and the pooled risk ratio favored added oxygen. The authors still call for careful randomized trials to settle dose, timing, and which patients gain the most.
pmc-13304613:
Sergey I. Ashitkov and colleagues watch cone-shaped damage channels grow in a thin aluminum film under repeated terahertz pulses in a 2026 physics study. Strong pulses below the single-shot damage level can still reshape surfaces shot by shot.

A 20 nanometer film on glass received bursts of 8, 20, and 100 pulses from a crystal-based source. Evenly spaced cones lengthened with each burst, aligned across the electric field direction. Current crowding at each cone tip, growing as tips sharpen, drives the stepwise growth through a heat-and-force process. Controlled patterning could serve future terahertz polarizers and sensors.
pmc-13306613:
Huize Cui added a liquid-crystal epoxy monomer into heat-conducting potting resin in a 2026 materials study. Heavy filler loads carry heat away but thicken the mix and make cured resin brittle, hurting factory handling and service life.

Rising monomer share lifted the glass transition point from 59 °C to 96 °C and thickened the room-temperature mix in reported checks. Heat flow fell from 0.95 to 0.52 W/(m·K) across the same range in the given values. A mix near ten percent gave the best strength balance, and fracture surfaces showed how the additive reshapes break patterns.
pmc-13307413:
Jamie Green and co-authors pilot in 2026 a shared care pathway for chronic kidney disease, paired with three months of teaching for primary care doctors at two health systems. Surveys before and after the teaching checked knowledge, confidence, barriers, and how happy doctors were with the pathway.

Confidence rose across many areas of finding and treating kidney disease at both sites. At one site, urine screening for kidney damage in adults with diabetes rose from 49 percent before the work to 60 percent after it ended. At the other site, use of a key diabetes drug class rose slightly. The pathway proved workable when shaped to local clinic routines.
pmc-13307913:
Codruța-Claudia Gherman-Lencu and co-authors review in 2026 chemicals that disrupt hormones, found in food, water, air, goods, and factory materials around us. Groups covered span bisphenol A and phthalates, dioxins, long lasting fluorinated compounds, farm sprays, and flame retardants in home goods.

These agents can mimic or block hormones, stir cell stress, and leave marks on genes that may pass to offspring in some cases. Linked harms span weight and heart ills, poor fertility, some cancers, thyroid upset, and harm in early life. Full escape is not real, yet joint steps by people, clinics, and rule makers can cut loads across the life course.
pmc-13308313:
Jinglan Zhang and colleagues test in 2026 whether chlorogenic acid, a plant compound in coffee and fruit, can stop a feed toxin from killing pig lung immune cells by iron-driven cell death. The toxin, deoxynivalenol, is the most common mould contaminant in world feed. Cell assays and fat oxidation profiling traced the damage pathway.

The toxin scrambled iron handling, raising uptake proteins and lowering the exporter, which loads cells with iron. It also weakened the GPX4 defence axis that normally mops up damaged fats. Oxidised fat products surged, and the cells tipped into ferroptosis, a death driven by iron and fat oxidation. Chlorogenic acid restored iron balance, revived the defence axis, and cut the fat oxidation surge. The authors present the compound as a feed additive candidate for protecting pig immunity where toxin exposure is hard to avoid.
pmc-13308713:
Mengting Niu, Quan Zou, and Lei Xu present in 2026 a deep learning tool, ASC2BF, that both predicts and breeds DNA aptamers, short strands that grip a chosen target. Some targets lack any known gripper in donor pools, so fresh strands must be built rather than found by screening.

A multi scale network scores how well a strand should bind, then a foraging style search grows new strands under body based rules. Seeds that pass the network start each search round for the best yield. As a case, the tool bred pools aimed at ASC specks, a part of the cell alarm system. Maps of what the model heeds link key strand spots to their grip role.
pmc-13309413:
Ulrike Wirth and colleagues validate in 2026 a portable home device, Streamcheck, that lets men run early urological checks without visiting a clinic. Ninety-two men aged twenty-three to eighty-nine used the device at home conditions inside a clinical study. It records urine flow curves, volume, voiding time, biomarkers, and standard questionnaires.

Results from seventy-three men could be evaluated fully. Flow volumes matched control measurements closely, and voiding times differed by under five percent at most. Biomarkers were detected with full sensitivity and specificity above ninety-five percent. Satisfaction averaged just over four on a five-point scale. Men notoriously skip screening, so the authors argue home testing with computer-supported advice could reach them where clinics fail. Whether results change doctor-visiting behaviour awaits a follow-up study.
pmc-13310613:
Katharine Creamer and co-authors argue that clinicians need carbon footprint literacy before changing practice in a 2026 article. Health care leaves a large climate footprint, and studies now estimate emissions for many care activities. Acting on those numbers without grasping their methods risks skewed, unfair decisions.

Common footprint approaches are laid out with their assumptions, blind spots, and bias risks. Clinicians are urged to ask how boundaries were drawn, which data fed the count, and what got left out. Training steps for students and practicing professionals are proposed. The authors aim for sustainable medicine that rests on evidence, not on headline numbers alone, and they sketch research needed to firm the methods.
pmc-13310813:
Rehab A Abd-elaziz and colleagues test how heat worsens ammonia harm in farmed catfish in a 2026 lab study. Ammonia builds up in fish ponds and harms health, while warmer water may lower tolerance. The team held striped catfish at two heat levels, with or without ammonia, for four weeks.

Fish in warm ammonia water showed skin erosion, muscle death, and breathing distress. Blood counts fell, stress hormones rose, and tissue harm grew in gills, liver, and kidney. Harm was worst when heat and ammonia came together. Strict water control matters more as climate warms tropical fish farms.
pmc-13311013:
Haya Aljadani led a 2026 survey on salt habits among Saudi adults through a belief model lens. Salt intake in Saudi Arabia far tops global advice and drives high blood pressure risk. Knowing the health risk may not be enough to change daily use, so beliefs and habits were mapped together.

Answers came from 522 adults on a checked questionnaire. Most linked high salt to high pressure, yet few knew the advised daily limit. Over half always added salt in cooking, and salty snacks were common. Intent, confidence, and prompts linked to better practice, while knowledge alone lagged. Programs should build skills and cues, not just facts.
pmc-13311113:
Fangqin Fei and co-authors grade chatbots for thyroid eye disease advice in a 2026 benchmark study. Patients with the chronic autoimmune eye disease increasingly ask large language models for guidance, yet quality and safety proof was thin. A bank of 35 Chinese questions from guidelines and common patient asks was posed to five chatbots.

Two blinded experts scored replies on accuracy, logic, flow, safety, and plain access against a guideline standard. Reply speed and length varied widely by model. Scores split clearly on accuracy, logic, flow, and access, but not on safety. Longer replies did not mean better replies. Risk centered grading may guide patient use.
pmc-13311213:
Adeleh Dadkhah and colleagues, in 2026, report a case-control study on bile duct width in people with bladder urothelial cancer. Scattered case reports had hinted the duct might widen in these patients, but no full study had checked.

CT scans from 63 patients were compared with scans from 63 matched controls of like age, sex, smoking, and opium use. The duct was wider on average in patients, and widest in those whose tumor had come back or spread. Return of the tumor and a raised blood marker were the main links to abnormal width. The authors call the finding early and urge larger studies.
pmc-13311813:
Tamia Ridet and co-authors report two 2026 cases of palm-side dislocation of the trapezoid wrist bone, an injury so rare that few cases exist in print. Both followed motorcycle crashes.

Each patient also had several fractures and joint dislocations around the wrist. Surgeons opened the back of the wrist, restored the bone's place, pinned it briefly, and repaired ligaments. Final checks showed the reduction held, with no sign of bone death on X-ray or CT. A literature review found eight earlier cases, mostly treated the same way. Early spotting and open repair anchor the care advice.
pmc-13311913:
Feifei Li and colleagues examine a 2026 study of bird flu patterns in Chinese poultry and the forces that drive outbreaks. Poultry are a main host, and spillover to mammals and people is a standing worry.

Outbreaks clustered from November to March, with hotspots in the southeast. The H5 subtype persisted across the study span and its center drifted east, while H9N2 produced the most reported cases. A machine learning model ranked human activity factors highest, led by road density, population density, and poultry trade points. Winter rain led the climate factors. Risk rose fast at low-to-mid levels of these drivers.
pmc-13312013:
Morteza Sanei Taheri and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a 19-year-old Afghan man whose parasitic cyst disease ended in a fatal brain hemorrhage. The infection, cystic echinococcosis, comes from the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus and usually affects the liver or lungs. In this patient, imaging also found a cyst inside the right ventricle of his heart, an uncommon site.

Doctors first found a cyst in the liver and planned heart surgery after starting the drug albendazole. Hours before the operation, the man developed weakness on his right side and lost consciousness. A brain scan showed bleeding in the left middle cerebral artery territory reaching into the ventricles, and he died despite emergency drainage. The authors argue that every patient with this infection needs a heart check, and that surgery should come early, because a heart cyst can send material to the brain with deadly results.
pmc-13314113:
Amal Hassan Abd Al_Shabbani and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, how the parasitic roundworm Toxocara canis adjusts its gene activity inside different hosts. Dogs are the worm's natural home, but larvae wandering in accidental hosts, including humans, cause visceral, eye, and brain disease. The team collected larvae and adult worms from infected dogs and from mouse models standing in for human infection, at four time points. They measured three genes tied to immune evasion, tissue invasion, and stress survival.

Larvae in the human-like host switched the first two genes on more strongly than larvae in dogs. That suggests harder immune manipulation and tissue invasion where the worm does not belong. The stress gene ran highest in those misplaced larvae. All differences reached statistical significance. The authors say these host-specific patterns expose the worm's survival playbook and could seed diagnostics or treatments for zoonotic toxocariasis.
pmc-13314413:
Ayşe Günsel and co-workers study remote leadership in spread-out product teams in work published in 2026. Leading through screens is now central to how such teams work, and product work adds time pressure, doubt, and thin social cues that strain both planning and feelings.

Drawing on social exchange and leader-member exchange ideas, the team asked whether e-leadership lifts team results directly or through the emotional skill and engagement of the team. Early interviews and group talks shaped their measures, and survey data from product teams in Türkiye were modeled with a partial least squares method. E-leadership had no direct effect on results that counted as real, but it did act through an indirect path, as the authors report. The lesson: remote leaders win by building team feeling and drive, not by pushes alone.
pmc-13315113:
Xuehui Qin and colleagues report a fungal meningitis case that wore a viral mask, in work published in 2026. Cryptococcus gattii can cause grave brain and lung disease in people with sound immune systems, unlike its kin that strikes the weak, and it is often caught late.

Their patient was a man with sound immunity whose illness was first taken for meningitis from the Epstein-Barr virus, and steroids were given, as the report relates. He also carried a lung cryptococcoma, a fungal ball, and his spinal fluid showed the virus waking again, which muddied the picture. Lung masses ride along in up to a share of 67 percent of such infections by the figure cited, and may cause no symptoms. The case urges doctors to suspect this fungus in slow meningitis with lung masses, even in healthy hosts.
pmc-13315513:
Víctor García-Milán and a multicenter team tested in 2026 a light-based sensor that might tell tumor from nearby brain during surgery for brain metastases. Such tumors were once thought to have clean edges, but tumor cells often seep into surrounding brain, and current surgical tools can miss that spread.

In a prospective study, paired samples of tumor and nearby brain were taken during operations and read outside the body with a nanostructured plasmonic sensor that picks up differences in light bending. Standard tissue checks served as the reference. The team judged whether the label-free sensor could sort the two tissue types fast enough to guide surgery.
pmc-13315613:
Georgi P Georgiev and colleagues report in 2026 a rare mixed infection after heel bone fracture surgery in a 59-year-old man. Heel fracture repair carries a high wound infection rate, and this surgical site infection included the oxygen-shunning germ Peptoniphilus olsenii among several microbes.

Care came in stages, with strong surgical cleaning of dead tissue, filling the bone cavity with bioactive glass, a silver dressing, vacuum-assisted closure, skin grafting, and targeted antibiotics. The team also lays out their treatment plan in light of published data. The case shows how layered steps can close a deep, hard-to-treat bone infection.
pmc-13316213:
Joseph Sekhar Santhappan and co-authors review in 2026 chemometric methods for finding emerging pollutants in the environment and judging their harm to people and ecosystems. Fast industrial growth and rising living standards keep releasing new pollutants that now rank among the top threats to health and ecological balance.

Recent studies pair hybrid lab detection with advanced machine learning and deep learning analysis, offering scalable, lower-cost ways to evaluate pollutants at large. Knowing each pollutant's specific health effects also guides which detection process fits. The review aims to support smarter monitoring and cleanup choices.
pmc-13316613:
Tomasz Poboży and colleagues report a 2026 real-world ultrasound study of pain where tendons and ligaments meet bone in the lower limb. Such entheseal damage is often misread as vague soft tissue pain, so the team scanned an unselected clinic population to count it properly.

Records covered 667 adults scanned at fourteen set sites around the hip, knee, and ankle or foot. Confirmed tendon or attachment problems appeared in 152 patients, a 22.8 percent share in the clinic group. The gluteal tendon and the sole band led the list, most problems sat on one side only, and age alone predicted trouble. Routine early scanning, they argue, would sharpen diagnosis and aim treatment better.
pmc-13317313:
Galina Portnova and colleagues probe, in a 2026 study, how heart rhythm and saliva antioxidant power react to mental strain in obsessive-compulsive disorder. The links among body stress systems, chemical defense, and this illness remain murky.

Thirty-one patients and twenty-nine healthy peers did a demanding eye-movement task while heart signals and saliva were sampled before and after. Patients began with lower antioxidant capacity and failed to raise it under load, unlike controls. Splitting patients by resting heart rate revealed a sharper split: the low-rate subgroup lost antioxidant ground and showed stress-system overdrive, while the high-rate subgroup coped like controls. Resting heart rate may flag a harder-hit body subtype of the disorder.
pmc-13318713:
Luchang Fan and colleagues present a 2026 retrospective study of liver cancer treated by radiofrequency ablation. They test whether the aMAP score predicts cancer returning after treatment. The score was built to forecast liver cancer risk in hepatitis patients. Its value after ablation was unclear.

The sample held 350 patients having ablation for the first time. A low score meant 63.55 or below, and 197 patients fell in that band. Low-score patients enjoyed longer recurrence-free survival. Adjusted analysis confirmed the score as an independent prognostic factor, with a hazard ratio of 1.40 reported. Adding the score to a tumour size and number model improved prediction. Reclassification gains reached 15.9 percent in their checks.
pmc-13319713:
Akari Terada and colleagues follow, in 2026, a cluster of moles on a woman's sole over nine years, a record the authors say is unmatched in detail. Such grouped moles, called acquired agminated melanocytic nevi, are rare on the palms or soles and can mimic melanoma because spots multiply and vary in colour.

The woman first noticed twelve small spots at age twelve. Their number began rising spontaneously at thirty-six, and at thirty-nine she sought care. Examination found many brown spots of a few millimetres within a small area of the right sole. Magnified skin examination showed a benign parallel furrow pattern. During follow-up to age forty-eight, some spots darkened and new ones appeared, especially around a biopsy scar, while the overall pattern stayed benign.
pmc-13320013:
Guy Paré and co-authors hear from older adults and family carers in a home heart monitoring program in Canada in a 2026 study. Home kits that send heart data to nurses can cut hospital strain, yet gains hinge on how well frail users fit the gear into daily life and care ties. Three primary care sites in Quebec ran a six month program for this work.

Talks and field notes came from 34 patients, 28 family carers, and 20 nurses. Patients used four linked devices, from a smart watch to a smart pill box, while carers used a phone app and nurses checked a data board each weekday. Ease of use, trust, and the human tie with nurses all shaped whether the kit felt like help or burden.
pmc-13320413:
Alexander Kopp and co-authors follow dissolving magnesium bone screws in mini pigs for eighteen months in a 2026 study. Magnesium gear can hold bone while it heals and then melt away, which spares a second surgery, but fast melt can break hold and puff gas pockets. A plasma coat meant to slow the melt was tested against bare gear of the same alloy in leg and arm bones.

Coated and bare screws and plates sat in non broken bones and were checked by fine scans and tissue cuts after removal. Bare gear had melted away in full, while coated gear kept part of its frame, which shows the coat worked. Coated gear also sat in richer mature bone and caused no late harm. The coat may suit load bearing fixings.
pmc-13320513:
Sarah Meng and colleagues examine, in 2026, whether travelling farther for spinal fusion surgery worsens recovery. Distance can delay review, complicate follow-up and hinder rehabilitation, and effects are documented in other surgical fields. Lumbar fusion had not been well studied from this angle.

Records covered 403 adults who had fusion of the lower spine at an academic trauma centre between 2013 and 2025. Average travel was roughly forty-four miles and about an hour of driving, with wide variation. After statistical adjustment, travel burden showed no significant link to any complication type or to length of hospital stay. The authors suggest distance alone should not be treated as an independent risk factor for poor fusion outcomes, while noting that confirmation in other settings is still needed.
pmc-13320813:
Yue Xie and co-authors track immune cells during treatment of a rare bone disorder in a 2026 study. Children with X-linked hypophosphatemia have a gene fault that raises FGF23 and weakens bone mineral growth. The antibody drug burosumab blocks FGF23 and helps patients, yet its effects on immune cells were unknown.

Single cell gene reading of blood cells at five time points, before and during treatment, covered 93,112 cells from patients and healthy children. Eleven main immune groups were mapped. Helper and regulatory T cell shares were high before treatment and settled during therapy, while another T group moved the other way. Some cell signals tied closely to bone eating cell pathways.
pmc-13321213:
Mariam Esmaeeli and her team compare, in 2026, two closely related antioxidant enzymes from the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. Superoxide dismutases cancel out a harmful oxygen radical and need a metal cofactor. During evolution, one family member changed from using only manganese to taking iron as well, a flexibility called cambialism. Whether other traits changed alongside was unknown.

Lab tests showed the flexible enzyme resists chemical and heat unfolding better than its manganese-only relative. Exchange tests, which map which protein regions stay tightly folded, found a larger and tougher protected core around the metal site in the flexible version. Two properties, metal choice and stability, therefore shifted together during recent evolution. The authors propose studying how those changes were picked together in this bacterial line.
pmc-13321313:
Joanna Palion-Gazda and co-authors tune light emitting iridium complexes in a 2026 chemistry study. The complexes pair iridium with terpyridine and benzothiazole based ligands and are candidates for light emitting devices. The team asked how a remote amine group on one ligand reshapes light output and device behaviour.

Plain model complexes glowed from a ligand centred excited state with sharp structure and little solvent shift. Adding the amine group smoothed the glow band and made it sensitive to solvent, signalling a switch to a mixed charge transfer state. Swapping in a triphenylamine group also steadied test devices built with the complexes. Wide lab methods, from voltage scans to light spectra, backed the assignments.
pmc-13322813:
Weina Ma and co-authors report a rare brain tumour case in 2026, centred on a 58-year-old woman with a lasting headache. Scans showed a cystic mass in the right temporoparietal lobe, and surgeons removed the whole growth.

Lab tests on the tissue found markers Desmin, MUC4, CD99 and ALK, while gene testing found an EWSR1::ATF1 fusion that confirmed this rare tumour type. About two years later scans showed the tumour had returned in the same area, and a second full removal followed. Full removal stays the main treatment, yet the authors note that long-term behaviour and best care remain unclear, so gene testing matters for a correct diagnosis.
pmc-13323813:
Huigan Li and team hunted for biomarkers of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy among genes tied to centrosome duplication. Their 2026 study combined differential expression analysis, co-expression networks, Mendelian randomization, and several machine learning models, then checked cell-type patterns with single-cell RNA sequencing and functional assays in cardiomyocytes. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy thickens the ventricular wall and scars heart muscle, yet the role of centrosome-related genes in it had stayed unclear.

Two candidates emerged, HBEGF and VPS8, with VPS8 standing out as a key regulator linking endosomal and lysosomal balance to immune-related remodeling. The authors propose VPS8 as both a candidate biomarker for early diagnosis and a potential therapeutic target, with HBEGF as a second lead. Because the findings rest on computational finding plus laboratory validation, they frame the next step as testing whether these markers hold up in patients and point to treatments.
pmc-13325913:
Yang Lu and colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about how a ketogenic diet may slow colorectal cancer through gut microbes. The cancer strikes about 1.93 million people a year, and advanced cases still fare poorly.

Their proposed chain starts with diet reshaping gut bacteria, cutting species that make the metabolite MMA. Less MMA means less signaling through Rap1 and the MAPK and ERK cascade in tumor macrophages. That shift holds macrophages back from the tumor-friendly M2 state. In patients, higher blood MMA matched heavier M2 presence in tumors and worse outlook. The letter ties diet, microbes, and immunity into one testable axis.
pmc-13327613:
Xiaoli Xu and co-authors identify a new resistance plasmid in a tomato pathogen in a 2026 study. Clavibacter michiganensis causes bacterial canker and spreads through seed, and streptomycin sprays remain a main control once infection sets in. Strain TX-0702 resisted the drug, and the team traced how.

Resistance sat on an uncharacterized plasmid named pCM3, which carries a gene for an enzyme called APH(3). Lab tests showed the enzyme disables streptomycin by adding a phosphate group, a route not shown before in Gram-positive plant pathogens. The plasmid also carries mobile DNA pieces, raising concern that resistance genes can move through farm and soil microbes toward wider food and health risks.
pmc-13327713:
Ondřej Fiala and team tested blood neuron-specific enolase as a fate marker in advanced castration-resistant prostate cancer treated with androgen receptor signal blockers. Their 2026 look-back study covered 120 patients with start enolase values, split at the normal top of 12.5 ng per milliliter. It tracked scan-based stall-free and overall survival with multi-factor Cox models, adjusting for age, PSA, therapy line, Gleason score, spread timing, and spread.

Start enolase above normal tracked with shorter stall-free survival: 9.4 months against 20.8 months in this group. Overall survival was shorter: 23.5 months against 38.2 months in this group. Worse results stayed linked after change. In day-28 landmark models, higher four-week enolase shifts alone foretold worse results, with hazard ratios of 4.30 for stall and 8.78 for death in this group. The team backs enolase as an add-on to clinic risk sorting, catching fate news past PSA and standard factors.
pmc-13328413:
Jiachen Zhao and co-authors sequence a rare human infection strain in a 2026 genomic study. Streptococcus parasuis, newly split from a pig pathogen group, infects people so rarely that fewer than five human case reports exist. Their strain, S62, came from the blood of a fever patient.

The genome measured 1.93 Mb with a G+C content of 39.5 percent, and family tree checks placed it firmly in the species, close to four named strains. It carried virulence genes including hasC plus possible resistance gear, yet lab testing found it sensitive to most antibiotics, with only middling response to tetracycline and clindamycin. The profile sets a baseline for watching this spillover threat.
pmc-13329513:
Jennifer Emilie Mannino and a large team map research on self-management during the move from child to adult care in a 2026 scoping review. About 1.2 million young people with long-term conditions from childhood enter adulthood each year in the United States, the authors note. Gaps in care can follow if young people cannot manage their own health.

Searches of six databases up to November 2024 yielded 640 included articles, spanning 1989 to April 2025. Most work appeared after 2014 and came from the United States. Cross-sectional and number-based designs dominated. Only 89 studies tested an intervention. Most focused on physical conditions. The review shows where evidence is thick and where trials are still scarce.
pmc-13330413:
Bhawani Shankar Verma and team mapped virulence genes among Enterococcus isolates from Central India. Their 2026 study took 106 enterococcal isolates from patients at Index Medical College Hospital in Indore between December 2021 and August 2024. It tested for cytolysin, surface protein, and gelatinase genes by RT-PCR. Enterococci, once known mainly for heart, urinary tract, and belly infections, now raise serious concern through rising antibiotic resistance genes.

The surface protein gene esp proved most common at 74.53%, then cytolysin at 55.66% and gelatinase at 45.28% of those tested. Enterococcus faecalis carried virulence genes more often than Enterococcus avium. Resistance was high to erythromycin, penicillin, chloramphenicol, and tetracycline, while most isolates stayed sensitive to linezolid and vancomycin. The team says they show strong disease-causing power, with high virulence gene rates and varied resistance patterns that muddy treatment choices.
pmc-13330613:
Sabrina Schneider and a large team arm a cancer-killing virus with a fiery cell death protein in a 2026 study. Gasdermin E can flip quiet cell death into loud, immune-stirring pyroptosis, but many tumours silence it. The team built a chimeric vesicular stomatitis virus that carries full gasdermin E into tumour cells.

The armed virus kept its growth pace yet killed with higher potency in lab tests, the authors report. Death shifted toward pyroptosis and tumour cells grew more visible to immunity. In mice, tumour control improved, survival lengthened, and dendritic cells plus killer T cells grew more active inside tumours. Pairing viral killing with loud death may widen therapy reach.
pmc-13330913:
Duval Donoso and colleagues report a rhenium complex built on a brominated pyrazole-pyridazine ligand in a 2026 article. Such ligands grip metals well, stay flat, and suit light-based uses, yet the bromo form had no solved structure before. The team reacted the ligand with a rhenium carbonyl chloride in hot toluene.

The product formed in a yield of 48 percent in the reported synthesis. Crystals held one dimethylformamide solvent molecule per complex, tied by hydrogen bonding to the ligand frame. The rhenium centre sits in an octahedral layout with three carbonyls on one face. Related metal cases are rare in the literature, the authors note. The structure anchors future light and catalysis work.
pmc-13331113:
Obidimma Ezezika and a large team set out a 2026 protocol for comparing COVID-19 vaccine uptake across 12 African countries. Uptake gaps across the region are wide, yet local drivers at service, system, and political levels are poorly mapped. Countries span Angola to Uganda and will be grouped by high, moderate, or low uptake.

Number data will come from global sources on health, economy, and governance. Talk data will come from expert interviews in all countries except Angola, where ethics delay means public reports and literature will stand in for now. Pair and trio country contrasts aim to show what helps or blocks uptake. Lessons should guide fairer pandemic planning.
pmc-13331213:
Kolos Kalman Nagy and colleagues audit head and neck vessel scans in emergency trauma care in a 2026 study. Scans hunt blunt injury to brain-feeding vessels at a level 1 trauma centre. Charts covered visits from January 2021 to December 2023 for patients over age 16 with blunt injury who received such imaging.

In total, 643 patients met the entry rules. A large share, 74.2 percent in the reported yield, had negative scans, and low yield tied strongly to skipping the modified Denver screening rules at triage. Transfer status and trauma level showed no clear link to yield. Most patients with true action-worthy findings had met the screening rules. Tighter rule use could cut radiation and delays.
pmc-13331713:
Mengyuan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 endoscopy case involving a 74-year-old woman who had part of her colon removed for cancer three years earlier. A check found a flat spreading tumor, about 4 by 3 cm, growing inside a blind loop left by her surgery, a spot that is hard to reach and see.

The team cut around the growth and lifted it with injected fluid. They finished the removal underwater, adding an internal traction clip where the tissue base was firmly stuck. The two-hour procedure took the full wall thickness at one point, and the gap was closed with clips in a folded pattern. Tissue study showed an adenoma with early cancer change and clear margins, and she went home on day three without needing more surgery.
pmc-13333313:
Natalia Cediel-Becerra and co-authors developed a framework in 2026 to grade how well One Health tools handle gender equality and social inclusion. One Health, which treats human, animal, and ecosystem health as one problem, preaches equity at policy level. Yet its everyday assessment and planning tools largely ignore gender and social difference.

Their OH GESI framework scores tools along a ladder: ignoring inequality, noticing it, responding to it, and finally transforming the root causes and structural barriers behind it. Applied to tools inventoried by the One Health High Level Expert Panel, the framework exposed major shortfalls while marking exactly where each tool could improve. The authors aim the guidance at tool builders, users, and stakeholders. They align practice with the equity promises of the One Health Joint Plan of Action and urge intersectional analysis inside real programs.
pmc-13333413:
Omar Alqaisi and colleagues surveyed bone surgery patients in Amman in a 2026 study linking how pain care feels, how well patients sleep, and how satisfied they end up. Pain after orthopedic surgery is near-universal, and the three-way relationship among these experiences is tangled.

The descriptive study enrolled 125 patients at two government hospitals, using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and a pain treatment satisfaction scale. Overall satisfaction with pain management landed at moderate, averaging 3.23 on its subscale: pain relief itself was rated kindly, while doctor-patient interaction was flagged as the weak spot. Lower income and more dependents went with lower satisfaction. Older age, higher body mass index, and longer stays went with worse sleep, with BMI correlating strongly with poor sleep scores at r = 0.72. The authors call for personal care plans, timely medication checks, and better conversations between doctors and patients.
pmc-13333513:
Muhammad N. Aslam and colleagues pilot a mineral supplement for leaky gut in ulcerative colitis in a 2026 open-label trial. Aquamin, an extract of red marine algae rich in calcium and minerals, had already raised gut barrier proteins in colon tissue, and the team tested whether that translated into tighter intestines.

Eight patients with mild or remitting colitis and eight healthy controls took Aquamin capsules supplying 800 mg of calcium daily for 90 days. They drank a mannitol solution before and after, so urine levels could reveal how much sugar leaked through the gut wall. At baseline the patients leaked 54 percent more mannitol in the first two hours than controls. After supplementation their leakage dropped by a quarter to two-fifths across collection windows, with total excretion down 29 percent, and no serious side effects appeared. The authors call the result preliminary support for a barrier therapy and want a larger trial.
pmc-13333613:
Working from hospital records, Juan Yu and co-authors examined how laparoscopic surgery for ovarian cysts affects later ovarian reserve in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Their review covered 150 patients treated for cysts on one ovary.

Hormone measures were compared before surgery and at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months afterward. AMH levels fell and FSH levels rose at every check, showing reduced reserve after surgery. Drops were largest for cysts of 7 centimeters or more and for bleeding stopped with electrocoagulation rather than stitches. Among 86 patients hoping to conceive, the pregnancy rate reached 59.3 percent during follow-up. Large cysts, endometriotic cysts, and electrocoagulation stood out as risk factors surgeons should weigh when planning care.
pmc-13334813:
Kristie L Ebi and co-authors gave a 2026 working group report for the ADVANTAGE project, mapping how climate and environmental change cross into health across the whole life course. The report takes an ecological view, weighing genes and health status alongside diet, social conditions, and physical surroundings.

Stage by stage, from before birth to old age, the authors link weather exposures such as heat stress, humidity, and poor air quality to undernutrition, overnutrition, micronutrient gaps, and priority diseases. At-risk groups get close attention where physiology makes them sensitive. Rather than a single study, the document gathers felt impacts and future risks, then names knowledge gaps and research priorities for the project's diet and adaptation agenda.
pmc-13335513:
Yu Xia and co-authors reviewed stem cell therapy for stroke in a 2026 article covering mechanisms, clinical translation, and what comes next. Clot-busting treatments help only within narrow time windows, leaving many survivors with lasting deficits that restorative therapy might address.

The review gathers evidence on mesenchymal and neural stem cells mainly, noting the field's shift from expecting transplanted cells to replace dead tissue toward having them reshape the post-stroke environment. Human trials so far show dependable safety but inconsistent benefit. A central obstacle is that most transplanted cells die quickly. The authors discuss cell-free options such as extracellular vesicles and bioengineering tricks to harden cells, and argue standardization is the gate to real clinical impact.
pmc-13335913:
Linsha Ma and co-authors mined a rat retrovirus for a better prime editing enzyme in a 2026 genome engineering study. Prime editors write precise DNA changes without cutting both strands, but their power depends heavily on the reverse transcriptase they carry, and good ones are scarce.

Screening 558 candidates surfaced 19 active new enzymes, with a Rattus norvegicus retroviral enzyme, RERV-RT, the strongest. Structure-guided engineering plus deep mutational scanning produced an optimized variant, enRERV-RT. Editors built on it beat the standard M-MLV enzyme by 1.20-fold across mammalian and plant cells, reaching 1.88-fold at stubborn loci, and handled multiplex edits of functional genes. A high-throughput testing platform, TRAP-seq-PE, let the team compare performance across many mutation types systematically.
pmc-13336413:
Zifeng Wu and co-authors showed that swallowed microplastics hasten Alzheimer's-like decline in mice by wrecking gut microbes in a 2026 brain study. The particles fill the food chain, but their brain effects were unknown.

Long oral exposure to 2-micrometer polystyrene particles in 5XFAD Alzheimer's-model mice worsened memory, amyloid buildup, brain inflammation, and synaptic loss, and stalled cellular cleanup. The plastics breached the gut barrier and grew a taurine-eating pathobiont, Bilophila, while holding back taurine-making commensals, leaving a body-wide taurine deficit that foretold the brain damage. Wiping out or swapping microbes proved the effect runs through the microbiota. Restoring taurine calmed microglia, restarted cleanup, and rescued memory, and human ADNI plasma data backed the taurine link.
pmc-13336513:
Yujin Ahn and co-authors created a wound dressing that blasts biofilms apart with tiny bubbles in a 2026 study. Treatment-resistant wounds harbor mixed-species biofilms armored in polymer slime, and even new nanoparticle, phage, and enzyme approaches struggle to clear settled mats.

The dressing, called µBLAST, layers manganese dioxide-doped diatom silica under a cellulose mesh that releases hydrogen peroxide. Catalytic oxygen bubbles form inside the biofilm and burst there, tearing the viscoelastic matrix at the tissue interface while peroxide keeps working. The confined disruption dislodges mature, antibiotic-resistant mixed biofilms that drugs alone cannot shift. Pairing physical demolition with chemical attack offers a route for chronic wounds stuck in inflammation and pain.
pmc-13336913:
Haoxuan Wu and a large team teach a swallowable camera capsule to steer itself through the stomach in a 2026 study. Capsule endoscopy is painless, yet unguided capsules miss patches of lining and navigation tricks rarely transfer between patients. Their learning system follows anatomical landmarks, fusing edge, contour, and depth cues into compact coordinates instead of raw video.

In simulations across eight patient-derived stomach models, coverage topped 97% within 50 s for the method. It beat three standard learning agents on coverage and consistency. In lab scans outside the body, mean coverage hit 87% across five scans with procedure time cut by 53% versus expert manual control in the reported setup. Cheaper, steadier autonomy could widen capsule screening.
pmc-13337413:
Xinmiao Hong leads a 2026 team linking earlier menopause to heart disease and death using national survey data plus a hospital cohort. Women with natural menopause in the NHANES database were grouped by menopause age. Those reaching menopause before 40 years faced more cardiovascular disease and higher overall and cardiovascular death risks than women with menopause at 50–51 years in the comparison.

Each one-year drop in menopause age added about 3% to disease prevalence and overall mortality risk, and 4% to cardiovascular mortality risk, in the dose-response analysis. Blood cholesterol measures, blood pressure, and blood sugar partly carried the effect in mediation models. The hospital cohort backed the pattern, tying early menopause to metabolic drift worth monitoring.
pmc-13337713:
Jonathan Diener leads a 2026 trial of a phone app meant to prevent falls in nursing homes. The BeSt Age App guides staff to give personal exercise sessions to residents. Lasting use depends on whether staff and residents accept the tool and find it workable.

Eleven homes in Southern Germany joined a 12-week cluster trial, with 37 employees and 137 residents. Staff rated ease of use, usefulness, experience, and intent to keep using the app. Residents rated motivation and their own intent to continue. Statistical models linked usefulness and usability to continued use, showing what homes must get right for digital fall prevention to stick.
pmc-13337913:
Jianfeng Huang and co-authors describe three rare uterine mesothelial cysts in a 2026 case report. These benign, fluid-filled growths arise from surface lining cells and usually appear in the belly lining. In the uterus they are uncommon and often missed or mistaken for other disease.

Cases treated at Minda Hospital over ten years are detailed, with a review of prior reports alongside. All three patients had scope exploration and did well afterward as reported. No shared standard for diagnosis or treatment exists yet. By laying out symptoms, imaging, and surgical handling, the report aims to help gynecologists recognize the condition sooner.
pmc-13338213:
Gülşah Saç and co-authors turn an invasive fish into biodiesel in a 2026 study. Gibel carp harms ecosystems where it spreads, so using its oil offers both control and value. Lipase enzyme fixed onto magnetic nanogels served as the reusable catalyst.

Conditions were tuned for enzyme amount, methanol to oil ratio, and temperature. Best output came at 4000 units of lipase with a 5 to 1 ratio at 55 degrees in the reported optimization. Yield reached 97.45 percent under those settings. The catalyst kept at least half yield across 13 reuse cycles, presenting a first case for this fish as biodiesel feedstock.
pmc-13338313:
Maryam Kohsari and colleagues studied gene variants and cardiometabolic disease in 2026 among 509 Kurdish people in Iran. Variants in the antioxidant genes Nrf2 and NQO1 may shape risk for hypertension and type 2 diabetes, but evidence in this population was thin. Genotypes were typed by PCR, diets were surveyed, and health markers were compared across genetic groups.

Carriers of recessive variants showed higher biochemical, oxidative stress, and body measures. Cox models linked homozygous recessive genotypes to much higher hypertension risk over time, with a hazard ratio of 2.82, and linked combined variants to higher diabetes risk. The findings suggest genetic screening could refine prevention in this community, pending replication in larger cohorts.
pmc-13338813:
Yan Ting Woo and colleagues weighed two front routes to chest spine surgery in 2026, small cut versus wide open cut. Files from adults treated at Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham from 2016 to 2021 were read, with harms and pain after surgery as main outcomes. Days in hospital, days in intensive care, blood loss, drain time, and op time were also tracked.

A small cut may mean less pain and a faster return home, but only if safety and access to the spine hold up. The head to head test helps spine surgeons and patients weigh a gentler route against the wide view of open surgery for varied chest spine problems.
pmc-13339013:
Vegar Stubberud and co-authors print water-repellent surfaces copied from a floating fern in a 2026 study. Salvinia molesta leaves trap air with hair-like structures that mix water-loving tips and water-shy sides. Copying that shape has been hard with standard methods.

Two-photon printing built the tiny hairs directly at high resolution in a single material. Varied print settings and tip shapes tested how geometry alone steers wetting. Printed surfaces reached contact angles above 135 degrees and held a water surface over 0.47 mm in the reported measures. Shape alone overcame the base material's natural wetting, aiding repellent and drag-cutting designs.
pmc-13340013:
Kanade Fujiwara, Tomoyuki Makino, and Toru Hamamoto measure sugar breakdown by single microbes in man-made soil in a 2026 study. Real soil mixes too many forces to credit one species. Two bacteria, Bacillus subtilis and Streptomyces cinnamoneus, grew alone and together for 14 days.

Bacillus breathed fast and high, while Streptomyces breathed slowly and lower as reported. Together, total breathing matched the Bacillus-alone level and tracked its share of DNA. Streptomyces instead cut soil acidity sharply despite low breathing. Man-made soil thus separates who burns carbon from who changes soil chemistry, clarifying microbe roles in the carbon cycle.
pmc-13340213:
Coastal bacteria living on particles carry richer plasmid loads than their free-floating neighbors, according to a 2026 metagenomic study by Zhendu Mao and colleagues. Working in the Pearl River Estuary and Daya Bay in South China, the team compared particle-attached and free-living fractions across a pollution gradient.

Plasmids in the attached fraction proved more varied, more often transferable, and packed with genes suited to life on particles. Modeling pointed to biofilm-forming genes as the main route by which lifestyle shaped plasmid variety. As pollution rose, so did plasmid diversity and the share of antibiotic and metal resistance genes, a pattern with clear weight for tracking resistance spread in coastal waters.
pmc-13340713:
Metal wear from hip replacements produced large inflammatory masses in two women, reported by Ahmad Hammad and colleagues in 2026. Patient A, 58, had her hip replaced 16 years earlier and came in with a deep vein thrombosis; scans revealed a huge pelvic pseudotumor pressing on vessels.

She improved after two-stage revision surgery and walked again. Patient B, 81, had severe metallosis with a broken socket wall, and damage plus infection made reimplantation impossible, so surgeons removed hardware, used vacuum wound care, and gave long antibiotics. The contrast shows how metal debris disease ranges from fixable to joint-destroying.
pmc-13340813:
Vector control modeled on the immune system outperformed the standard approach in a 2026 cluster-randomized trial in Arequipa, Peru, led by Michael Z. Levy. Sixty health-facility districts, averaging 2,271 households each, were split between an adaptive immune-style arm and a conventional military-style campaign against Chagas disease vectors.

By the planned March 2023 interim look, the immune arm had found and confirmed 23 infested households spread over 10 separate foci. The conventional arm found only 5, all in one focus. The adaptive arm spent more effort confirming each find, yet its detection rate per person-day was far higher, with a rate ratio of 3.66 reported.
pmc-13341413:
Shaohong Yu and colleagues mapped weight and joint disease in 2026 across many data banks, hunting weight cutoffs for sharp prevention. The study joined Global Burden of Disease 2021, NHANES 2007 to 2018, and gene wide data. Additive models drew the weight to joint disease curve with adjustment for confounders, while split models hunted cutoff effects.

From 1990 to 2021, age standardised joint disease rates and disability years were highest in high development regions, and rates rose in a curved way with weight. Gene based tests gauged causal effects on joint disease subtypes. Cutoffs from the work could sharpen weight based prevention for joint disease.
pmc-13341513:
Knocking out a master gene in nerve cells reshapes their electrical behavior, in a 2026 study by Silvia Cardani and colleagues. PHOX2B directs autonomic nervous system development, and its mutations cause neuroblastoma and a syndrome of failed breathing control, yet its target genes remain partly unknown.

Using CRISPR in IMR32 neuroblastoma cells, the team combined expression, binding, electrical, and imaging analyses. The knockout cells matured more in form yet fired oddly, with shifted resting voltage and weaker calcium responses. PHOX2B proved to repress ion channel genes including KCNQ5, SCN3A, and RYR2 directly. Checks in stem-cell-derived neurons from patients supported the developmental relevance.
pmc-13341613:
Plague bacteria reach the brain in a mouse model, in a 2026 study by Brian A. Smith and a large team. Plague meningitis complicates 6 to 11% of human cases yet had never been described in animal models of the pneumonic form, so mice were exposed to aerosolized Yersinia pestis CO92.

Bacteria appeared in brain homogenates by day 2 after challenge, and inflammatory signals such as IL-6 rose in brain tissue. Microscopy in mouse tissue, cross-checked against primate sections, supported central nervous system involvement. Characterizing how lung plague seeds the brain could inform treatment of one of its deadliest complications.
pmc-13342213:
Kerstin Uvnäs-Moberg and Maria Petersson review, in 2026, how the hormone oxytocin is released and what it does, with close attention to touch, social contact, and closeness. The authors draw on clinical evidence about gentle stroking and skin contact and the calm, social, and healing responses that follow.

The review sets out a two-step account in which light touch and later firmer contact activate different skin nerves that signal brain centers where oxytocin is made. Released oxytocin then supports social bonding, lowers stress, pain, and fear, and aids growth and repair. The authors also discuss birth, breastfeeding, parent-infant skin contact, and the harms that follow when close contact is lacking.
pmc-13342813:
Meng Li and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for a multicenter randomized trial on fixing femoral neck fractures with three cannulated screws. Freehand placement leans on repeated X-ray shots and can lack precision, so the trial tests an intelligent navigation system against the standard freehand method.

The plan enrolls 300 adults across centers, half in each group, with 12 months of follow-up after surgery. The main outcome is how many fluoroscopy images surgery needs, with healing, hip scores, blood loss, and caregiver burden also tracked. Enrollment began in June 2024 and runs to October 2026. A clear win could set a standard protocol for guided fracture repair.
pmc-13344013:
Chongfa Tang and co-authors show that a frontline antiviral signal can backfire during chlamydia infection in 2026. Type I interferon alone did nothing to genital epithelial cells, yet paired with Chlamydia trachomatis it fired inflammation far beyond what the bacterium triggered by itself, a synergy with tissue-damaging potential.

The team traced the effect to interferon raising levels of Toll-like receptor 3, a sensor that detects leftover viral-style RNA inside infected cells. Silencing or deleting that receptor killed the synergy, while blocking AKT, mTOR, or ERK signaling also dampened it. Downstream cascades through MAPK and AP-1 completed the chain. Calming these pathways could limit the overinflammation some patients suffer.
pmc-13346113:
Jamil E G Faccin and co-authors report six feeding trials, published in 2026. That test how much soybean meal can be added to corn-based diets for pigs at nursery, grower, and finishing stages. Groups ranged from small nursery pigs near 10 kg to finishers over 100 kg, with meal levels varied widely across trials.

Higher meal levels lowered feed intake and daily gain in the youngest nursery pigs, while pigs starting near 13.5 kg were less affected in the same kind of comparison. Grower pigs on corn diets gained faster with more meal, but that gain vanished when distillers grains were included. Late finishers showed no clear change in growth or carcass traits.
pmc-13347713:
Nokuthula Mbele, Zanine Moyce, and David Bishop explore how mothers felt after caesarean birth in Durban public hospitals, in a qualitative study from 2026. Interviews with 100 women at two government hospitals covered pain control, emotional support, and staff talk, with themes drawn from guided conversations plus short background questionnaires.

Seventy-seven women said they were satisfied overall, and only one voiced clear dissatisfaction, with good outcomes, solid pain relief, and a warm ward mood lifting scores most. Yet only a third would choose the operation again, and thin pre-surgery briefing, language gaps, low say in choices. Weak feeding or emotional support dragged feelings down, a split the authors call complex.
pmc-13348013:
Graham Little and co-authors present an automated method that segments deep grey matter structures using only diffusion tensor brain images, without the structural scans many clinical protocols lack. Their 2026 study deforms three-dimensional models to fit boundaries visible in diffusion maps, targeting five structures including the thalamus, striatum, and hippocampus.

Against standard structural segmentation in a test-retest sample, agreement was strong for half the ten side-specific structures. It was weak for the globus pallidus, amygdala, and right hippocampus. On inspection, though, the new method looked more accurate, and it gave smaller volumes throughout. Applied to a lifespan cohort of 357 people aged five to ninety, the diffusion measures followed distinct curves: diffusivity fell then rose after the early thirties, while directional measures varied by structure. The authors note these microstructural trajectories differ from volume trajectories, and offer the tool for large studies of deep grey matter microstructure.
pmc-13348413:
Solomon Maina and Leonard Tesoriero sequence a lettuce virus found in stored garlic, in an announcement from 2026. Isolate LY came from a garlic plant gathered in Yanco, New South Wales, in 1980 and kept in a herbarium since. Dried leaf RNA was read and rebuilt to give the full coding genome for lettuce necrotic yellows virus, a serious lettuce disease spread by aphids.

Gene order matched the family pattern, and the isolate shared 97.8 percent identity with a New Zealand isolate against 81.28 percent for another Australian isolate in the reported matches. Finding a lettuce virus hiding in garlic stock stresses quarantine checks on imported garlic breeding material.
pmc-13348713:
Gaetano La Rocca and co-authors charted in 2026 the course of lymphoid interstitial pneumonia in Sjögren disease. This rare lung pattern's clinical and lab traits remain poorly charted. Sjögren disease can affect lungs in several patterns. Telling them apart matters for outlook and treatment.

Fifty-five patients with CT-confirmed interstitial lung disease, seen in Pisa from 2019 to 2024, were sorted by team discussion and weighed across patterns. Symptoms, lung function, and disease activity scores were gathered. The weigh-up clarifies how lymphoid interstitial pneumonia acts next to other Sjögren lung patterns. It helps rheumatologists and lung doctors counsel patients and pick tracking and therapy.
pmc-13350013:
Qinwen Shi and co-authors studied in 2026 whether tumour spread on PET/CT forecasts outlook in advanced nasal-type extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, a rare and fierce disease. The max distance between the two farthest lesions, called Dmax, captures spread in a single number. Its value had been hinted at in other lymphomas.

Looking back at scans with LIFEx software, the team measured max uptake, metabolic tumour volume, total lesion glycolysis, and whole-body Dmax. Best cut-offs were set and forecast value was tested with Cox regression and log-rank tests. If Dmax on its own forecasts outcome, it could refine risk grouping and treatment strength for patients whose disease pattern, not only its volume, drives outlook.
pmc-13352113:
Sha Qiu and colleagues study the pharmacist role in clot prevention quality in a 2026 single-centre review. Prevention of venous thromboembolism often falls short of ideal standards in hospital care. Records covered chest and heart surgery inpatients from January 1 to June 30, 2025, guided by national quality indicators for clot care in China.

In total, 1,813 patients were enrolled with mean age of 62.1 years, and 64.6 percent sat at moderate risk. Patients were split into baseline, pilot, and full pharmacist groups by timing and depth of pharmacist input. Rates of drug, mechanical, combined, and standard prevention were compared, along with hospital clots, major bleeding, and related deaths.
pmc-13352413:
Haobin Pan leads a 2026 study of salt stress responses in watermelon using chemistry and gene profiling. Watermelon tolerates salt only moderately, which makes it a useful model for tolerance pathways. Two inbred lines were compared: HY17, which is salt-sensitive, and HY73, which is salt-tolerant. Seedlings at the three-leaf stage faced 150 mM salt for 2 days or 25 days.

Short-term defence in the tolerant line leaned on higher salicylic acid made through a phenylalanine route. Long-term tolerance leaned on arginine and myristic acid build-up, which helps water balance, clears reactive oxygen, and limits membrane damage. Gene checks named two aspartate transferase genes among the changed set. Findings guide breeding for salt-hardy watermelon.
pmc-13352513:
Sengsavang Aphayvong leads a 2026 study of charge flow and wear-out in manganese-doped bismuth ferrite films. Lasting reliability is the key hurdle for using such films in tiny piezoelectric devices. Films were grown on silicon by sputtering, and leakage currents were tested under both bias directions.

Leakage behaviour flipped sharply with polarity, traced to oxygen vacancies spread unevenly through the film depth. Near the vacancy-rich top surface, current followed trap-based routes at low fields and space-charge routes at high fields. Near the leaner bottom surface, flow stayed simple at low fields. Vacancies drifting under steady voltage piled up at one interface and drove the uneven wear-out, a risk designers must plan around.
pmc-13354113:
Andreina Dones and co-authors study whether trainee involvement lengthens surgery for pelvic organ prolapse in 2026. Fellowship settings show longer operating times with trainees but no extra harm, yet community practice pairs surgeons with residents or physician assistants instead. Records covered 108 repairs from June 2016 to July 2020 by one specialist at two community hospitals.

Resident-assisted cases numbered 77, or 71.3 percent, against 31 assistant-led cases. Operating time ran longer with residents, at 187.5 minutes versus 155.7 minutes, and stayed 49.0 minutes longer after adjustment. Overall complications looked similar, and urinary infections formed most events at 54 percent of 22. Training costs time, not safety, in these data.
pmc-13354313:
Boutaina Agdi and co-authors report spinal spread of pineoblastoma in a teen patient in 2026. The rare, grade 4 pineal tumour strikes mainly children and teens and spreads readily through spinal fluid. A 16-year-old girl with no prior illness had two weeks of sleep disturbance, right-sided squint, and forceful vomiting.

Brain scans showed a mixed pineal mass of about 28 by 26 mm with fluid build-up in the ventricles. Endoscopic drainage and biopsy confirmed pineoblastoma, and spine scans revealed multiple leptomeningeal nodules from fluid spread. With no standard protocol, an international expert advised a high-risk medulloblastoma-style plan: spine-wide radiation with weekly vincristine, then further chemotherapy.
pmc-13354413:
Ahmed Vadel Jidou and colleagues report surgery for acute bile duct inflammation tied to a spontaneous duct-to-gut fistula in 2026. A choledochoduodenal fistula joins the common bile duct to the duodenum and can drive cholangitis. A 65-year-old patient arrived with belly pain, fever, and jaundice.

CT scans showed air in the bile system and dense material in the duct, and bile MRI confirmed the fistula. Endoscopic drainage failed, so a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy was built and succeeded. Gallstones are the usual cause, though ulcers, tumours, and nearby inflammation also occur. The authors stress imaging as the diagnostic key and surgery as the fallback.
pmc-13354813:
Rabson R Nakey and others studied primary healthcare use among prostate cancer survivors in Tanzania, ran the snapshot study in 2026. Follow-up care in Tanzania remains concentrated in a few specialised centres, a model that strains a small oncology workforce. Primary care could support survivors closer to home, but how often survivors actually use it was unclear.

The study checked the share of post-care survivors who used primary healthcare services and tested which factors forecast use. Barriers such as distance, cost, and referral practice were considered with patient traits. Health planners gain evidence for shifting survivorship support toward primary care without leaving survivors without specialist backup.
pmc-13355213:
Xiaoping Jiang and co-authors describe in 2026 a light-based sensor for ultrasound and photoacoustic imaging, two methods that use sound to see inside the body. Standard sound sensors are bulky, narrow in range, and hard to blend with other imaging tools. Their sensor uses a tiny grating and a mirrored cavity to turn sound waves into light signals.

Three cavity sizes were built and tested, reaching a bandwidth above 130 megahertz with very low noise. The design is cheap to make, matches body tissue well, and can trade sensitivity against range by design choice. The authors see it as a practical step for sharper medical sound imaging.
pmc-13356613:
Rosita Zakeri and Adam A Nabeebaccus give a 2026 practical review for general doctors on heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. In this form, the heart pumps at a normal rate yet fills poorly, and it is now the most common heart failure type as populations age. Many patients are found only when admitted to hospital.

Diagnosis needs a structured mix of exam, blood markers, and heart ultrasound to show raised filling pressures and rule out other causes. Two drug classes now cut hospital stays and improve quality of life, and weight-focused care helps some patients. The authors stress early finding, fluid relief, and team care of other illnesses.
pmc-13357113:
Shuchang Lou and co-authors compared drugs for radiation-induced mouth sores in head and neck cancer patients in a 2026 network meta-analysis. The painful sores strike over 80 percent of these patients during radiation, and four routine drugs are used to prevent them, with little head-to-head evidence. The team pooled 29 trials with 2,276 patients, ranking the drugs across many outcomes at once.

Glutamine cut severe sore risk sharply versus rival drugs and reduced feeding tube use and treatment breaks. Amifostine best cut swallowing trouble. No drug clearly shortened sore duration or eased dry mouth. The authors name glutamine the best overall pick, pending stronger trials.
pmc-13359513:
Jianfang Wang and co-authors review single-cell methods in sheep and goats in a 2026 paper. Wool, meat, and milk quality all depend on how cells team up in skin, muscle, fat, and other tissues. New tools can now read gene activity cell by cell. The review gathers what these methods have revealed about how prized traits form in the two species.

Studies have mapped the cells behind wool growth, reproduction, and fat placement, among other traits. The authors also flag hurdles, from cost to sparse reference maps, and suggest ways forward. Better cell maps can steer breeding toward healthier, more productive animals.
pmc-13360213:
Shuang Dong and co-authors published a 2026 feeding study on growing pigs and added enzymes in feed. Plant feeds carry anti-nutrient factors that block pigs from using the feed well. The team's enzyme mix held protease, amylase, and pectinase, which break down protein, starch, and plant fiber parts. They tested the mix in a standard corn and soybean diet and in a mixed diet with varied ingredients.

The enzyme mix raised how well pigs took up nutrients on both diets. Growth results were also tracked under each feed plan. Work like this matters because feed is the biggest cost in pig farming, and better uptake means less waste. The authors say matching the enzyme mix to the diet type is the key point for farmers.
pmc-13360613:
Viktor Reiswich and co-authors carried out a 2026 scan of a DNA repair protein across a huge range of cancers. The protein, MRE11, helps fix broken DNA strands and sits at the core of a repair team. Cancers that lack it may react better to radiation and chemo. The team stained tissue samples from 134 tumor types, nearly 15,000 samples in all, to see how much MRE11 each held.

In healthy tissue, almost all cells showed strong MRE11 staining. In cancers, most tumors also stained strongly, and only 55 readable samples out of nearly 13,000 lacked the protein entirely. Just six tumor types had more than one such case. The work maps how rare this defect is, which helps doctors judge where testing for it is worth doing.
pmc-13360713:
Miraç Öz Kahya and co-authors review exercise testing in older heart and lung patients in a 2026 study. The test, called CPET, tracks heart, lung, and body responses while a patient exercises. Doctors use it before surgery and to find why exercise feels hard. Proof of its safety in older people with mixed heart and lung problems is still thin.

The team looked back at 235 patients tested at a major referral center. Of these, 112 were 65 or older, letting the team compare older and younger patients. They weighed test results, how many finished the test as planned, and any bad events during testing. Such data help clinics judge whether the test is safe and workable for frail older patients who need it most.
pmc-13360913:
Kseniia Kriukova and others studied high-rate waves after acute bleeding injury brain injury, in 2026. After-injury seizures may be foreseeable from markers of seizure growth, mainly sick high-rate waves. Whether these signals can be found early after injury in medical settings was unclear.

Scalp and in-skull EEG traces during the acute phase were studied for rate and location of sick waves. Early finding patterns were related to later seizures risk. Doctors gain evidence on whether bedside and in-skull traces can flag people most likely to develop seizures after bleeding brain injury.
pmc-13361113:
Ibtissem Sanah and co-authors improved gluten-free rice bread with farm leftovers in a 2026 food study. Rice bread without gluten often tastes plain and feels dense. The team added black cumin seed meal, left after oil pressing, and whey, a cheese-making by-product. A design method varied the amounts to find the best mix for brown rice and red rice loaves.

The best brown rice loaf, with the most seed meal, gained fiber and antioxidant power. It also came out softer and less chewy than the plain control loaf. The red rice version leaned on whey and showed a different balance of gains. The work shows how two waste streams can raise the food value of breads made for people who cannot eat gluten.
pmc-13361213:
Mariantonietta Peloso and co-authors surveyed toxic compounds in lupin foods sold in Italy in a 2026 study. Lupins are protein-rich beans gaining fans as plant diets grow, but they carry bitter alkaloids that can harm health. Europe has no shared limit for these toxins, so market checks matter. The team tested 28 shop products for 14 of these alkaloids with a precise lab method.

Dried lupins held by far the highest toxin load, on average near 13,700 milligrams per kilogram. Flours held far less, and the team also tested how well the standard debittering soak lowers toxins in dried seeds. Levels varied widely by food type. The results give regulators and makers hard numbers for setting safety limits and better processing.
pmc-13361613:
Festa Margherita and co-authors review how plant tissues respond to electric fields in a 2026 paper. The property at stake, dielectric permittivity, describes how a material polarizes under a changing electric field. Reading it can reveal the inner physical order of living tissue without cutting it open. The authors aim to explain where this response comes from in plants, keeping the math light.

They lay out the basic ways polarization happens and the time scales and frequencies involved. Water dominates the response in plant tissues, so its behavior gets close attention. The review then compares leaves, fruits, and roots, showing how permittivity shifts with structure and water content. Such readings could serve farming and food checks, sensing ripeness or damage from outside the plant.
pmc-13362313:
Kardelen Akin and co-authors followed children with a severe gut movement disorder in a 2026 study. Pediatric intestinal pseudo-obstruction makes the bowel act blocked without any physical blockage. It leads to intestinal failure, repeated hospital stays, and risk of death. The team reviewed all cases diagnosed at their referral center from 2011 to 2025, using European consensus criteria.

Thirty-two children were included, a bit over half of them girls, and nearly half had disease starting very early in life. Gene testing was done in 22 of the children. The review covers feeding support, surgeries, transplant, and long-term outcomes. Rare-disease series like this gather scattered experience into guidance for families and doctors facing a long, hard course.
pmc-13362513:
Yoshihito Kano wrote a 2026 review on drugs that target KRAS, one of the most common cancer-driving genes.
