KRAS faults drive many lung, bowel, and pancreas cancers, and for decades the protein was seen as impossible to drug. The review covers the first approved blockers, aimed at one fault type, and the push toward drugs for other types and for KRAS as a whole.

Newer plans include drugs for the G12D fault, broad RAS blockers, and protein degraders, often paired in combinations guided by blood tests for tumor DNA. Resistance still cuts responses short, so tracking how tumors adapt is a core theme. Kano maps where this fast field stands and what must come next.
pmc-13362713:
Marina Sánchez-Robles and colleagues present a 2026 survey of body aches among Spanish surgeons who perform knee replacement surgery. The work is physical: long hours standing, bent postures, and forceful steps during the operation. Seventy-two surgeons answered questions on where they hurt, how strong the pain feels, and how it affects their work, and the team built an early score that blends discomfort with interference.

About four in five surgeons reported work-related symptoms, most often in the lower back and neck. Average pain levels were low, yet a small share reported strong pain, sick leave, or even surgery of their own. Stance during the operation made no clear difference. The authors frame the score as a first draft for later, fuller studies.
pmc-13362813:
Masaaki Kasahara and colleagues present a 2026 dental lab study on how well PEEK posts grip the resin used to rebuild broken teeth. PEEK is a tough plastic used for posts inside treated roots, but its smooth surface bonds poorly. The team tested four surface options: none, sandblasting, a chemical primer, or both together, then pulled the posts out to measure grip, before and after heat cycling that mimics mouth aging.

Every treatment beat the bare post, and the combined treatment gripped best, with sandblasting alone next. Heat cycling did not weaken the treated groups, which hints at durable bonds. The findings give dentists a simple recipe, blast plus primer, for more secure rebuilds on PEEK posts.
pmc-13363113:
Michał Szyszka and others studied circulating plasma miRNAs in children with untreated primary hypertension, ran the ATHENA study in 2026. The role of miRNA in childhood hypertension was unclear, with whether training changes miRNA levels and how they relate to blood pressure and organ damage. A hypothesis-generating, pre-post design addressed those questions.

Fifty-six hypertensive children and fifty-nine healthy controls were studied, measuring miRNA-16, -21, -27a, -27b, -133a, and -145 before and after aerobic training, with medical, biochemical, vascular, and organ damage settings. Levels patterns and training replies were matched. Child cardiologists gain choice markers linking hypertension, training, and early organ injury in children.
pmc-13364213:
Nicoleta Mirela Marin and colleagues present a 2026 study on a water-cleaning material made by fixing the dye Congo red onto maize stalk waste. The dyed stalks then grab dissolved iron, chromium, and manganese from water. The team proved the dye stays anchored even in strong acid or base, and mapped how it binds. They tested uptake across acidity and dose levels, plus how to strip the metals back off for reuse.

At high pH the material removed over nine tenths of the manganese and most of the iron from test water. Spectra showed metals binding to carboxyl and phenol groups once those lost their protons. A mid-strength acid wash freed nearly all captured metal. The authors pitch the farm-waste adsorbent as a cheap, sturdy option for metal-laden effluents.
pmc-13364513:
Stack-Sanchez and colleagues used high-resolution brain imaging in 2026 to track how the hippocampus, a deep brain region central to memory, changes from childhood to old age. Their method, diffusion kurtosis imaging, follows water movement in tissue to reveal fine structure that standard scans miss. They scanned 363 healthy people aged 5 to 90 and mapped four subfields of the hippocampus.

Each measure followed its own path across life. Volume peaked in the mid-thirties to early forties, water mobility bottomed out near age 35. One structure marker rose steeply through youth before leveling near age 25, while another fell steadily across the whole span. Men showed larger volume and higher values of the structure marker than women, a sex gap standard scans did not show. One subfield stood out with higher values after age 20. The method, they say, adds new insight into development and aging.
pmc-13364713:
Qiji Li and co-workers pin in 2026 a gene chain that drives breast cancer spread to bone, where it eats bone away. A long non code RNA, named LCAL4, runs high in bone spread tumors and marks poor life odds. Cell and mouse tests show it drives the spread.

The RNA acts as a frame that brings a partner protein to a bone eat gene and turns it on. The gene's output wakes bone eat cells, and freed bone growth cues feed the tumor in a loop. Cuts to the chain stopped bone spread in mice. The chain is a clear drug aim.
pmc-13365113:
Agapios Sachinidis and co-workers flag a 2026 risk in science work: flash AI made top art for study sum ups that looks pro but says little. A good sum up art must pick the one core find and make it stick in the mind. AI tools tend to pile in more, not pick.

Tired teams may trust the slick look and skip the hard pick work, the editors warn. Shine can mask weak thought and fake depth. The note is not anti tool, but pro care: treat sum up art as thought work, check the point, and cut the gloss that adds no sense.
pmc-13365313:
Joana Ferreira and Tânia Gaspar studied health reading, well-being, and stress care among older adults, in 2026. Ageing increases stress, and effective stress care supports healthy ageing, yet low health reading undermines well-being for many older adults. Few studies had studied how reading, well-being, and stress coping relate jointly.

Levels of general and digital health reading were tested, gaps by age, gender, education, and senior school attendance were tested, and associations among reading, well-being, and stress care were studied. Higher reading tracked better well-being and coping. The study guides plans that build reading as a route to healthier ageing.
pmc-13366413:
Jana Schroeder and others tested aimed screening and clearing for methicillin-sensitive Staph aureus in planned hip and knee swap, in 2026. Nasal and throat settling with Staph aureus is a major risk factor for after-op wound illness after bone surgery, and pre-op clearing is urged by several rules. Real-world evidence on lasting value of set plans was limited.

A set pre-op screening and octenidine-based clearing plan was tested for long-term value in reducing op site sickness after planned arthroplasty. The study tests whether plan benefits persist in routine practice. Bone teams gain evidence for keeping clearing plans as a durable illness stopping measure.
pmc-13367513:
Madhulika Mahashabde and co-workers write in 2026 a letter on a study that casts a small RNA as a flaw free mark for lung press in long lung ill. The study claims full hit and full clear rates. Such a clean split in a mixed ill rings false, the trio argue.

No in set check, like split or re pull tests, backs the claim, they note. The ill call also rests on scan press cuts that new world rules have left for direct heart tube reads. A mark this strong needs a fresh, free pool and set rules prior to trust.
pmc-13370213:
Muhammad Waseem reviews a class of small RNAs that guard male fertility in grasses in a 2026 paper. In maize, rice, and related monocots, these phased small RNAs build up only in the anther, the pollen-making part of the flower. They resemble animal piRNAs in their abundance, germline focus, and timing.

The review traces how they are made: a microRNA trigger cuts a precursor, a copying enzyme builds a double strand, and cutting enzymes release 21- and 24-unit pieces. Those pieces then join Argonaute proteins to steer development, silence jumping genes, and respond to stress. The piece maps what is known, what varies across grass species, and which steps still need direct tests in breeding work.
pmc-13370313:
Janhavi Kulkarni and Suraj Kanase test in 2026 two aids for foot drop in stroke kin: shock pulse to a leg nerve, with or sans a brace. Weak lift of the foot cuts step clear and lifts fall risk. Thirty folks split by lot to pulse lone or pulse plus a light leaf brace for three weeks.

Both groups gain in step span, pace, and clear. The brace group gains more in clear and in a gait adapt score, with clear stats gaps. Joint use looks the safer pick for walk work after stroke, the team holds, at low cost and no drug load.
pmc-13370813:
Cristine D. Delnevo and colleagues describe a new centre for fast tobacco surveillance in the United States in a 2026 paper. New products, brands, and marketing moves have outpaced older monitoring, and the rapid rise of JUUL exposed gaps in speed and scope. The National Cancer Institute and the Food and Drug Administration funded the Center for Rapid Surveillance of Tobacco to close that gap.

The centre watches marketing, shop availability, sales, and youth and adult behaviour, combining those streams to spot early warning signs. Its framework moves from signal spotting to checking and judging each signal. The paper also points to case studies in the same issue, showing how rapid methods can feed regulators sooner, before a new product trend becomes entrenched.
pmc-13374313:
Xi Yang and colleagues report a staged bone repair method for chronic heel bone infection in a 2026 study. Calcaneal osteomyelitis after trauma is hard to clear and leaves a bone defect that threatens walking. Between 2021 and 2025, nine patients were treated with slow debridement plus a hemi-Masquelet technique using structural bone grafting.

All nine patients cleared infection after an average of 1.7 debridements, and sinus tracts, redness, and swelling largely resolved. Every patient achieved bony healing and could bear full weight without pain within a year. Average ankle and hindfoot function score was 93 out of 100. The small series suggests that slow, staged clearance plus structural grafting can restore both infection control and function.
pmc-13375113:
Kuldeep Rawat and co-authors taught computers to sort prostate cancer gene reads in a 2026 study. Men of African roots face this cancer more and die of it more, at a young age more often. Blood tests and tissue cuts for it still miss and overcall.

The team read 1,684 gene reads from a public bank and kept 1,662 after checks. Each read gave 67 traits, like code mix and three-part word rates. Seven sort tools were tried, with fake extra cases to bal­ance the rare class. Sharp gene sorts could one day back the blood test, most of all for high-risk men.
pmc-13378013:
Yang Yang and co-authors pooled heart scans in bowel ill in a 2026 review. Long bowel fire goes with more heart risk, but how the heart shifts was not summed. A total of 28 works held 1,613 sick folk and 1,303 sound peers.

Sick hearts showed thick walls on two sides and a weak squeeze, by small but clear steps. Strain reads were less keen too. Cuts by ill heat, age at start, and type gave mixed tales. The team calls for set, planned work to tell if heart checks should join bowel care as a fixed step.
pmc-13380213:
Yanling Zhong, Mu Xu, and Liangzhi Cai present a 2026 study predicting which patients will see a benign womb tumour return after surgery. The tumour type, called cellular uterine leiomyoma, can recur, but the risk factors were unclear. The team reviewed patients treated at a hospital in Fujian, China, between 2012 and 2021.

Of 176 patients, 76 saw the tumour return during follow-up. Three features raised the risk: having two or more tumours, a higher body mass index, and having endometriosis at the same time. The authors combined these into a chart that estimates each patient's personal risk. Such a tool could guide how closely patients are followed after surgery.
pmc-13380313:
Alberto Daniel Navarro Vergara and colleagues present a 2026 series of 56 children hurt when a foot was caught in the spokes of a motorcycle wheel. Such entrapment can crush and tear the foot and ankle badly. The study describes how the injuries looked and how they were first managed at a referral trauma centre.

Cases were treated between January 2023 and December 2025. About two in five children had high-severity injuries, and in over half the bone was exposed. The middle of the foot was the most often affected area. Many children needed several operations and a hospital stay. The series gives treating teams a clearer picture of this injury pattern in children.
pmc-13382813:
Philip Greulich argues that math and computer models can drive real discovery in biology, in a 2026 perspective piece. Models, he writes, turn loose ideas into clear, testable claims that data alone may not settle. He also shows how models can rule out neat stories that sound right but fail the numbers.

Clonal lineage tracing serves as the running example for a model-led workflow through the piece. A second theme is universality, where the same pattern appears across systems, and how to use it rather than be misled by it. The closing guide distills the approach into steps researchers can apply in daily work.
pmc-13383013:
Melodie M. Lynn and a large team ask whether amiodarone use before heart transplant affects children's recovery in a 2026 study. The heart rhythm drug has been linked to worse outcomes in adults, but child data were scarce. Records covered 156 patients aged 18 or younger who had transplants at one large center from 2015 to 2021.

Only 10 children had received the drug in the two weeks before surgery, and deaths did not differ between groups. Those children did show more severe early graft problems and needed more pacing and rhythm support drugs afterward. Dose and length of therapy did not change the pattern, the authors report.
pmc-13383213:
Kelvin H. M. Kwok and colleagues describe pregnancy outcomes in women with autoimmune disease across three Nordic countries in 2026 work. National health registers in Denmark, Finland, and Sweden supplied the data. The study covered 20,425 singleton pregnancies affected by one of five diseases, with rheumatoid arthritis the largest group.

Common problems included preeclampsia and early rupture of membranes, and emergency cesarean rates ranged from 10 to 21 percent. Between 6 and 18 percent of babies were born preterm, and newborn unit admission varied by disease and country. The multi-country picture gives clinicians a firmer base for counseling women who plan pregnancy with these conditions.
pmc-13383613:
Fatemeh Safari and a large team present a new nitrogen-rich energetic compound and its many molecular forms in 2026 work. The fused-ring compound, called TTT1, can gain or lose protons across a wide acidity range. Its charged form can arrange its hydrogens in several near-equal ways, called tautomers.

Computer work predicted four such forms close in energy, and two were caught in crystal salts. Oddly, the form predicted most stable never appeared in the crystals grown. One salt proved stable to heat, impact, and friction, and held its structure under pressure up to 2.8 gigapascals, which marks it as a notable new energetic material.
pmc-13385513:
Cara Jean Ronish describes two hands-on activities that teach medical physics with simple model objects called phantoms. Her 2026 case report presents a single lesson plan covering external beam radiation therapy and diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging, built from fabricated and shop-bought materials.

In the imaging activity, students use handheld survey meters and sealed radioactive check sources to hunt for a hidden tumour inside a phantom, meeting measurement variability and diagnostic uncertainty directly. In the therapy activity, a gelatin phantom holding an embedded target, with wooden skewers standing in for radiation beams shows why precision, geometry, and planning matter. First built for secondary students, the activities now serve audiences from middle school to community groups, and materials were shared at national meetings in 2025. Ronish explains how teachers can adjust depth and pacing for different learners.
pmc-13385813:
Stefan Mereiter's team shows tumor sugar coating shields breast cancer from immune attack, in a 2026 study. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, yet checkpoint inhibitors help only a minority. Tumor sialylation tracked inversely with T cell infiltration across breast cancer subtypes.

Blocking sialylation genetically or with drugs cut immunosuppressive neutrophil infiltration while raising CD8 effector and Tcf7 memory T cells in tumors. Sialylation lengthened the blood half-life of G-CSF, a driver of neutrophil suppression, and lowered MHC-I display. Disrupting sialylation sensitized resistant tumors to T cell killing and anti-PD-1 therapy, nominating a new immune target.
pmc-13386013:
Babu Francis and colleagues report a toddler with rickets from a new variant in the FGF23 gene in a 2026 case report. The girl, just under two years old, failed to improve after a single very large vitamin D dose. Blood work showed low phosphate, very high alkaline phosphatase, and poor kidney phosphate retention.

Whole-exome sequencing found a fresh deletion variant in FGF23, the hormone that lowers phosphate reabsorption, confirming dominant hypophosphatemic rickets. Phosphate and active vitamin D treatment improved her labs and clinical state. Iron treatment for mild anemia let doctors trim the phosphate dose, a practical point the authors highlight.
pmc-13386713:
Xingzhe Liu's team reports final survival and long-term safety of olaparib maintenance in relapsed ovarian cancer, in a 2026 phase IIIb analysis. PARP inhibitor maintenance in platinum-sensitive relapsed ovarian cancer lacked long-term Asian data. The L-MOCA study enrolled Asian patients with high-grade epithelial disease across China and Malaysia, giving oral olaparib 300 milligrams twice daily.

After a median follow-up of 73.4 months, median overall survival reached 51.0 months. Survival reached 64.4 months in BRCA-mutated patients versus 40.9 months in BRCA wild-type, and 54.4 months in HRD-positive versus 34.8 months in HRD-negative patients. No new safety signals emerged, and MDS/AML occurred in 1.3 percent of patients.
pmc-13389613:
Parsa Torkaman and colleagues systematically review, in 2026, how best to treat ramp lesions of the knee. These tears affect the rear edge of the inner cartilage pad and often occur alongside anterior cruciate ligament injuries, hurting knee stability.

Searching major databases to June 2025, the team kept 17 studies that met set criteria and pooled their results with random-effects methods. Different repair and non-repair approaches were compared for pain, function, and healing outcomes. Knee surgeons gain a combined summary where single studies disagreed, helping them weigh repair against other care when a ramp tear is found during ligament surgery. Readers also see the limits of the current proof, which rests on a modest number of studies.
pmc-13389813:
Habtamu Alemayehu and colleagues survey, in 2026, what horse and donkey owners in South Gondar Zone, northwest Ethiopia, know and do about internal parasites. These worms are a major drag on working equid health and output worldwide.

The community study covered 150 farmers and scored their knowledge, attitudes, and daily practices for parasite control. Scores were grouped into low, moderate, and high levels, then simplified to good or poor for models that hunted for linked factors. Animal health workers gain a baseline picture of where owner understanding is strong and where it fails. That picture can shape training on worming timing, drug choice, and pasture care. The region depends heavily on working equines.
pmc-13390013:
Ugyen Rinzin and colleagues report, in 2026, a prospective study of why people's hearts stopped before they reached hospital in Bhutan. Death rates after such arrests are high, and in low-resource settings the cause often stays unknown for lack of tests or post-mortem study.

From August 2023 to July 2024, the team followed every out-of-hospital cardiac arrest case brought to the emergency department of the national referral hospital until discharge, death, or the study end. Of 110 patients, most were men and most arrests occurred outside hospital care. Emergency doctors and policy makers in similar settings gain rare prospective cause data that can guide prevention, from heart disease care to faster community response.
pmc-13390913:
Keziah N Keizer leads a 2026 multi-laboratory check of screening methods meant to catch a hard-to-detect resistant Escherichia coli. The strain produces OXA-244, an enzyme that breaks down carbapenem antibiotics, and it is emerging across Europe while slipping past routine tests.

Twelve isolates carrying various resistance enzymes, plus non-target strains, were sent blind to five Dutch clinical microbiology laboratories. Each laboratory ran its own screening and confirmation protocol, and results were compared. Hospital laboratory managers gain a practical ranking of which algorithm combinations actually detect this stealthy strain, a prerequisite for stopping its silent spread between patients. Five labs faced one set of germs with no hints, so the ranks show which checks find the strain and which let it slip past. That kind of blind test is hard to fake and easy to trust.
pmc-13392813:
Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, acting through its publisher, retracts a study claiming that lucidumol A fights colorectal cancer and calms cell inflammation. The compound is purified from the reishi mushroom Ganoderma lucidum. The notice, published in 2026, follows an investigation sparked by a third party and comments on the PubPeer discussion site about suspect images. The original authors were asked to explain and did respond.

Editors found that two panels of a cell migration figure at different doses share overlapping areas, meaning both came from one larger image. One panel also appears in an earlier retracted article by the same group, under different conditions. Judging the reply insufficient, the editors state they have lost confidence in the results. The authors support and agree with the decision to retract.
pmc-13392913:
EFSA's Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed, chaired in this opinion by Roberto Edoardo Villa, reviewed whether bentonite clay should keep its licence as a feed additive. Bentonite serves two jobs: stopping feed from caking in storage for all farm species, and soaking up fungal toxins in feed for pigs, poultry, and cattle. The European Commission asked for the review, and maker BASF supplied proof the product still matches its licence terms.

Finding no new evidence to upset earlier judgements, the EFSA panel held that bentonite stays safe for animals, consumers, and the environment under current rules. For workers handling it, the clay is not a skin irritant but mildly irritates eyes and can sensitise skin and airways, so exposure by any route counts as a risk to minimise. Efficacy needed no fresh check for a renewal.
pmc-13393913:
Chao Yan leads a twenty-one-author study of how Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection weakens asthma control in children. Clinical records covered one hundred forty-five children with asthma. The team layered in microbe detection, drug sensitivity work, and metabolite profiling. They then mirrored the question in allergic mice with and without the infection. The clinical signal was clear: children carrying the bacterium alongside asthma were much likelier to have poorly controlled disease.

The infecting strains in positive samples shared one genotype and all carried a mutation known to blunt macrolide antibiotics. In mice the infection worsened allergic symptoms, airway twitchiness, allergy marker levels, and lung tissue damage scores. Gene reads showed shifted airway microbes and altered signals and metabolite patterns. The authors say the joined evidence supports screening and tailored care when the two coincide.
pmc-13394413:
Kieran G. Stakem and colleagues ask, in 2026, what sets how well radical plastics carry electric charge. These plastics hold stable radical units, named TEMPO, along their backbones. The team built chains by joining two ring-shaped building blocks, swapping one to change the spacer between radicals. They checked radical counts with magnetic tests and modelled the chain shapes.

Stiff spacers placed radicals closer than soft ones of like length. Still, charge flow in solid samples tracked the glass point, the heat at which the plastic softens. Blends and block chains that shifted that point shifted flow too. The authors say heat behaviour, not spacing alone, rules these materials.
pmc-13394813:
Giuseppe Fumai, Francesco Menolascina, and Claudio Morelli argue, in a 2026 editorial, that nurses in nuclear plants need radiation training built for them. Europe sets strict rules on dose tracking and worker safety. Those rules speak mostly of physics and plant design, not of nursing skills. Ward nurses often know little about radiation response, the authors note.

Willingness to help in a crisis turns on mood and job factors as much as facts. Long low-dose exposure also links to stress and burnout in staff. The editorial offers a four-part training frame covering protection, crisis readiness, resilience, and well-being. It is put forward as a testable plan, not a proven course.
pmc-13395913:
Bruno Ruiz Brandão da Costa and a large team of co-authors report field work from São Paulo, Brazil, published in 2026. Their subject is how four native Atlantic Forest tree species defend their leaves against ozone and seasonal stress. They compared an urban site with a peri-urban one across dry and rainy seasons.

The group measured ascorbate and glutathione pools, three antioxidant enzymes, total phenols, and a marker of lipid damage, then paired those tests with leaf anatomy and cell death assays. Species identity shaped the profiles far more than place did. Casearia sylvestris held the steadiest balance with little tissue harm, while two porous-leaved species showed more damage, and harm rose in the rainy season for all four.
pmc-13396413:
Komarov and co-authors trace, in 2026, the evolutionary origin of histone H3.4, a variant protein that packages DNA in sperm-producing cells and is essential for male fertility in mice and men. Their phylogenetic analysis shows the eutherian gene arose from an ancestral H3.2 gene before placental and marsupial mammals diverged, over 100 million years ago, and has since evolved under positive selection, accumulating changes faster than its marsupial counterpart.

To test which changes matter, the team reverted three altered amino acids in mouse H3.4 back to the canonical histone versions, on a background lacking the normal gene. The triple reversion cut testis weight by over 40 percent, stalled meiosis, killed developing sperm cells, and disturbed thousands of genes during sperm maturation. Testing each residue alone showed positions 24 and 42 promote spermatogenesis, while position 98 is neutral. The study ties specific evolutionary substitutions to reproductive fitness.
pmc-13397513:
Published in 2026 with no named author, the article sets out a staged plan for reshaping the female torso when a single long operation would be unsafe. The patients in view have high body weight, poor tissue quality, past surgical damage or clashing breast and torso shapes. Doing everything at once can starve skin flaps, break wounds open and force costly hospital care.

Stage one reshapes the waist and belly with a wrap-around cut, a wide repair of the belly wall, fat removal that spares blood vessels and pubic reshaping. A later stage can lift or rebuild the breasts and add fat grafts, plus arm or back work where wanted. Splitting the load across sittings aims for a safer path to a balanced shape.
pmc-13397613:
Ruben Dario Arias Pérez and co-authors ask what failure really means after surgical repair of a torn knee cruciate ligament. Their 2026 narrative review finds the word used in clashing ways across studies. One paper may count only a torn graft, another only repeat surgery, and others lean on looseness measures or patient complaints alone.

Because definitions swing so widely, reported failure rates cannot be compared fairly between studies. Causes also vary, spanning technique, biology, fresh injury and patient factors, and current consensus notes admit the muddle without fixing it. The authors argue for one shared definition tied to both clinical findings and what the knee can actually do.
pmc-13397713:
Norbert Alexander Lang and co-authors test a web app for teaching dental students how to plan brace treatment. Their 2026 randomised trial at RWTH Aachen University compares the Orthotrainer app against classic planning with plaster models and printed records. Orthodontic planning demands orderly reasoning from findings to a treatment choice, a skill students must practise case by case.

Twenty-eight students were split between digital and hands-on training, each group completing two matched sessions after a baseline check. Ease of use and user experience were scored on standard scales, and a final paper-based exam tested whether skills carried over. Twenty-seven teachers from four universities also reported how they mark analogue work, adding context on marking load.
pmc-13398713:
Minju Kim and colleagues evaluated a tongue-base operation as part of multilevel surgery for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. Their 2026 case series covers 92 patients whose airway blockage involved the tongue base, treated with endoscope-guided coblation, a precise technique that shrinks tissue with controlled energy. Sleep apnea from multilevel blockage often resists single-site surgery, so measuring this added step matters.

Mean breathing pause index fell from 47.3 events per hour before surgery to 27.8 at six months, and two thirds of patients showed significant sleep improvement, with a 56.1 percent overall success rate. Oxygen lows, sleep efficiency, and REM sleep also improved. Pain was the most common complaint and rarely lasted long. The paper supports the technique as a relatively safe adjunct, while its single-center, uncontrolled design limits comparison with other options.
pmc-13399013:
Qun Fang writes a 2026 letter faulting a diabetes study for skipping thyroid antibody tests. The study under discussion, by Zheng and colleagues in the Journal of Diabetes Investigation, concluded that hypothyroidism independently raises the risk of cognitive impairment in type 2 diabetes. Its grouping and dose-response work were sound, Fang grants, but one omission clouds the claim.

Patients were sorted by TSH and FT4 alone, without the peroxidase and thyroglobulin antibodies that mark autoimmune thyroid disease, the top cause of hypothyroidism worldwide. Autoimmune inflammation itself can injure neurons, so the letter argues the study cannot tell hormone lack from immune attack as the true driver. Adding antibody testing would refine risk sorting in future work.
pmc-13399113:
Li and co-authors build, in 2026, a fluorescence probe that detects microRNA-21, a lung cancer signal molecule, at almost unimaginably low concentrations. Their design couples a cyanine dye to a tetrazine quencher on an RNA scaffold; meeting the target triggers a bioorthogonal reaction that releases the dye to glow. Computational screening minimized the energy gap between the dye's bright state and the tetrazine's dark state, achieving a background fluorescence quantum yield below 0.01 before activation.

The reaction, powered by target recycling so each microRNA molecule triggers many probes, reached a detection limit of 3.58 times ten to the minus eighteen molar, with a linear range from 100 attomolar to 100 nanomolar in their measurements. Activation boosted fluorescence 214-fold when the target reacted. The probe imaged microRNA-21 with high contrast in living cells and tissues and distinguished lung cancer patients from healthy individuals in clinical samples, supporting its diagnostic promise.
pmc-13399313:
Ayinula Tuohetali and colleagues packaged a redesigned plant compound into nanoparticles to treat hydatid disease, a parasitic liver infection, in a 2026 study. The infection, cystic echinococcosis, comes from a tapeworm larva. Harmine, an alkaloid from Peganum harmala, kills the parasite yet is too toxic to nerves for clinical use. The team built a safer relative called H-2-168 and loaded it into biodegradable PLGA particles.

The particles came out as uniform spheres averaging 198 nanometers across, trapping 88.6 percent of the drug inside, as the researchers report. After thirty days of oral dosing, the nanoparticle version outperformed the free compound against the parasite. It also helped liver tissue regenerate, eased inflammation, and slowed liver scarring. Harm to the liver and to cells generally fell compared with the unpackaged drug. The authors call the formulation promising for this neglected disease. Long-term safety and the best dosing schedule still need study.
pmc-13399613:
Wolterink and co-authors evaluate, in 2026, whether a single perioperative dose of intravenous dexamethasone improves recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. Their retrospective comparison covered 309 patients operated between 2013 and 2023. Of them, 187 received the steroid around surgery and 122 served as controls, with adjustment for age, sex, body mass, diabetes, smoking, and prior opioid use.

The dexamethasone group reported better upper-extremity function and less pain interference at six weeks, three months, and six months, all significant. Pain scores stayed lower long-term: one-point-nine against three-point-one on the ten-point visual scale at twelve months, and one-point-zero against one-point-eight at twenty-four months, though only 37 percent of patients completed two-year follow-up. For small and medium tears, patients on the steroid hit meaningful pain improvement more often early on. Regression confirmed dexamethasone independently predicted that early benefit, with an odds ratio of 1.67.
pmc-13399713:
Matthew D Benson and team asked whether cartilage damage worsens outcomes after isolated meniscal root repair. Their 2026 work reviews repairs from 2012 to 2022, defining failure as retear confirmed by MRI, repeat surgery, or conversion to total knee replacement. Surgeons had worried that existing cartilage disease might doom root repairs.

Among 63 isolated medial root repairs, 51 patients had cartilage disease. Overall, 7.9 percent underwent reoperation, 9.5 percent showed retear, and 4.8 percent later received total knee replacement. Failure rates did not differ significantly between patients with and without cartilage disease on any of the three outcomes. The work reassures surgeons that cartilage damage alone need not block root repair, while its retrospective, single-center design limits certainty.
pmc-13400413:
Yuting Lin and colleagues describe, in 2026, the setup and testing of an ultra-fast proton beam line for FLASH radiotherapy. FLASH gives radiation at very high dose rates, over 40 gray per second, and may spare healthy tissue while still controlling tumors. Putting such a beam into planning software is a key step toward wider study.

Working on a single-room proton system, the team measured point doses and beam profiles for a high-energy scanning beam. They built a model in the RayStation planning system and checked it with chambers, film and light detectors. The beam passed the rate target with steady output, giving labs a validated framework for preclinical FLASH work.
pmc-13400613:
Asmaa Ibrahim, Mervat Abd El Aal, Hayam El-Zahed and Ahmed F Mabied model, in 2026, a blended plastic material designed to sense carbon dioxide and humidity. The mix combines polyvinyl alcohol with zinc oxide and graphene oxide. Such tunable composites are attractive for cheap gas sensors, but their behavior needs prediction before building.

Using quantum chemistry calculations, the team mapped the blend structure and found strong internal bonds stabilizing it. Adding the two nanomaterials shrank the electronic energy gap sharply and raised the electric dipole, signs of better charge movement. Both water and carbon dioxide stuck favorably to the surface, and carbon dioxide produced the strongest electronic response. The authors present the blend as a promising sensor candidate.
pmc-13400713:
Juan Esteban Muñoz Montoya and José Leonardo Guerrero Cardozo write, in 2026, a letter raising three points about new AO Spine recommendations on spinal alignment in adult deformity surgery. The recommendations described four strategies for assessing balance and planning operations. The letter writers praise the publication while flagging gaps in one classic model it uses.

Their main concern is the Roussouly classification, which sorts spinal shapes using the sacral slope angle. Because degeneration changes that angle over time, older patients can be misclassified. They note a published update of the system that accounts for degenerative change, which the recommendations omit. The letter asks that future guidance incorporate that refinement.
pmc-13401013:
Theofanis Mavrepis and colleagues pilot, in 2026, a handheld heat camera for triaging infections where a heart pump cable exits the skin. Patients with implanted left ventricular assist devices face driveline infections. Current checks detect them slowly or imprecisely. A quick, contact-free heat read could speed decisions.

Fifty patient episodes were imaged at one center, six with clinically diagnosed infection. Skin around the cable ran much warmer in infected cases. Heat values separated infection well. A derived threshold caught every infection while clearing about three fifths of non-infected cases. Each extra degree of warmth raised infection odds. The authors stress the threshold is exploratory and needs outside validation.
pmc-13401213:
Cleber J N Chaves and co-authors report a 2026 study of how heat and cold tolerance strategies vary among tropical plants at different elevations. They ask whether community diversity and evolutionary history explain that variation. The setting is Brazil's Atlantic Forest, from sea level to about 2,200 metres.

During 2023 and 2024 the team surveyed plant communities at seven sites, focusing on the bromeliad Pitcairnia flammea and the species growing with it, including other monocots, dicots, and ferns. For each site they measured diversity, species cover, and phylogenetic structure. They also measured photosynthetic heat and cold tolerance, expressed as T50 values, plus leaf traits, in the focal species and dominant neighbours, letting them compare community-wide patterns with variation inside one species.
pmc-13402013:
Wataru Omori and colleagues describe two older inpatients with severe major depression who were being readied for electroconvulsive therapy, then improved on medicines alone. One, a man in his late 70s, carried a pacemaker for complete heart block and was relapsing on duloxetine. The other, a woman in her late 80s, had a clipped brain aneurysm and was worsening despite mirtazapine, risperidone, and added duloxetine.

In both cases doctors crossed over from duloxetine to venlafaxine extended-release, kept mirtazapine going, and raised venlafaxine to 150 mg per day under close watch. Scores on the 21-item GRID-Hamilton scale fell into the remission range, appetite and eating improved, and the planned shock therapy was called off. The pair of cases argues for one careful drug review before shock therapy in frail older patients.
pmc-13402213:
Takahiro Asano and co-authors follow a 79-year-old man on the blood thinner edoxaban whose left adrenal mass kept growing until it looked like adrenal cancer. A first scan after a fall showed a 56 millimeter lump. Over fifteen months it grew to 83 millimeters, and a PET scan lit up mildly in both the adrenal lump and a right thigh lesion. Hormone tests and a targeted scan for adrenal tumors came back negative.

Surgeons removed the gland by keyhole surgery, and tissue study showed an organized blood clot with calcium and iron deposits, not cancer. A biopsy of the thigh lesion showed the same clot material. Asano and the team blame bleeding fed by blood thinners and repeated falls. Their warning: an old, organizing clot can grow and glow on scans exactly like a malignancy, so it belongs on the list for enlarging adrenal masses.
pmc-13402313:
Sheela S Sinharoy and a large trial team ask whether cleaner cooking changes blood hemoglobin in pregnant women, using the HAPIN randomized trial across Guatemala, Peru, India, and Rwanda. Homes in the trial got liquefied petroleum gas stoves and fuel, or kept cooking with wood and other biomass. The analysis covered 3178 women, with hemoglobin and 24-hour personal pollution measures taken three times across pregnancy.

Women in the gas group ended with hemoglobin higher by 0.074 grams per deciliter than controls, a small but statistically supported gain. Looking at exposure itself, each added part per million of carbon monoxide tracked with hemoglobin higher by 0.015 grams per deciliter in the reported models. Fine particles and black carbon showed no such link. The authors stop short of a mechanism and call for work on how smoke exposure moves blood values during pregnancy.
pmc-13402713:
Chao-Guang Ji and co-authors capture the atomic shape of Retron-Eco8, a bacterial immune system that kills infected cells to stop phage spread, and show how a phage protein trips it. The system joins a reverse transcriptase, a non-coding RNA, and a DNA-cutting effector. Frozen-state microscopy caught the complex idle and active, as four-part assemblies holding their effector locked in an off pose.

Infection changes the picture: the phage single-stranded DNA binding protein grabs the system DNA scaffold, springs the lock, and wakes the nuclease, which then shreds both phage and host DNA. The host own version of that protein cannot trip the switch, and the phage protein must bind DNA and cluster to work. That pickiness keeps the suicide system aimed at true infection. The authors say the mechanism should aid retron-based biotechnology tools.
pmc-13403213:
Joan Hansen and colleagues interview Danish women about the psychosexual fallout of testing positive for high-risk human papillomavirus in cervical screening. Denmark, like many countries, is switching to HPV-based screening for its higher sensitivity, but a sexually transmitted result carries stigma cytology never did. Twenty-one women aged 30 to 60, referred for colposcopy at Gødstrup Hospital, gave in-depth interviews analyzed thematically.

Results arriving by mail left women anxious about cancer, confused about next steps, and without immediate support; general practitioners reassured when reachable, but access varied. The virus sexual nature triggered guilt, shame, feelings of uncleanliness, and distance from their own bodies, and it strained partnerships and intimacy. Even the reassuring colposcopy visit felt heavy, with a pressure to simply comply muting open talk. The authors call for holistic, informative support around results.
pmc-13404113:
Jin-He Liu and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how makers of mRNA medicines clean their product and strip out a harmful twin-strand by-product. mRNA shots proved their worth in COVID vaccines, yet leftover bits from lab synthesis can stir unwanted immune alarms. The twin-strand form is the worst of those leftovers, since it can also block protein making.

Two broad fixes exist, the review explains. Labs can wash the twin strands out after synthesis, using columns or cellulose steps. Better still, they can stop the strands forming at all, with tuned enzymes, additives, or smarter templates. Pros and cons of each route guide the choice.
pmc-13404413:
Katrine Rasmussen led a 2026 pilot trial of fun virtual reality sessions for stress relief inside a closed psychiatric intensive care unit in Denmark. Locked wards leave patients few ways to feel in control. Twenty-six patients joined during the virtual reality year, against nine in a plain year, well under the planned draw.

Patients who used the headsets told of calmer mood and a welcome escape from distress. Sessions also gave staff and patients a shared activity that warmed their bond. Staff gaps in know-how and trust held use back, despite the warm patient response. Within-session distress eased in the numbers as well, matching the stories told.
pmc-13404613:
Federica Fogliazza and colleagues review gene therapy for beta-haemoglobin disorders in a 2026 narrative survey. The group covers sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia, among the most common single-gene disorders worldwide. Standard care with transfusions, iron removal and stem cell transplant helps many patients but carries toxicity and donor limits.

Searching PubMed through 2025, the authors sort treatments into gene addition and gene editing. pmc-13407613:

pmc-13407713:

pmc-13407813:

pmc-13408013:

pmc-13408113:

pmc-13408613:

pmc-13408713:

pmc-13408813:

pmc-13409113:

pmc-13409613:

pmc-13410413:

pmc-13410613:

pmc-13410713:

pmc-13410913:

pmc-13412013:

pmc-13412113:

pmc-13412313:

pmc-13414313:

pmc-13418513:

pmc-13419413:

pmc-13422813:

pmc-13423913:

pmc-13424613:

pmc-13426413:

pmc-13426713:

pmc-13427313:
