pmc-13427413:
Yehui Fu and coauthors tested whether carbon trading pushes firms toward energy-saving innovation in a 2026 study of Chinese listed manufacturers. Using 3.09 million patent texts from 2008 to 2023, the team applied a large language model to identify energy-saving technological innovation at firm level, a narrower target than general green patenting. Staggered difference-in-differences estimation then measured the trading scheme's effect as regions adopted it at different times.

Trading significantly promoted energy-saving innovation, robust across checks, through higher carbon-risk exposure, substitution between subsidies and market incentives, and correction of market inefficiencies. Effects ran stronger in firms with lower pollution baselines in the mechanism analysis. Firm by firm counts, built from a vast pile of filed claims to new goods, give the test a scale few polls of plant chiefs could hope to match.
pmc-13427813:
Laura Bandini and colleagues pool studies on vitamin D in pregnancy and later autism and attention-deficit diagnoses in children. Both conditions mix genes and surroundings, and the biology linking a mother's vitamin D to child brain development stays unclear.

Fifteen studies qualified, with 8 on autism, 5 on attention deficit, and 2 on both, searched to February 2026. High versus low maternal vitamin D lined up with lower risk, at a ratio of 0.91 for autism and 0.90 for attention deficit, with a dose-response pool across the full range. Parents and clinicians get a careful link, not proof that supplements prevent either condition.
pmc-13427913:
Tufan Agah Kartum and co-authors dissect, in a 2026 anatomy study, the layered tissues that complicate a wide skull-base approach. The cranio-orbito-zygomatic approach swings open bone around the eye and cheek to reach deep targets. Its wide exposure endangers branches of the facial nerve that cross the temple layers. The team performed the approach on 10 cadavers, studying both sides of each head.

They traced how scalp layers, the temporal fascia, and nerve branches relate at each step. Facial nerve branches run in a defined layer between the galea, the scalp's tough sheet, and the temporal fascia. Following one fascia layer downward opened a natural plane toward the cheek prominence without crossing the nerves. Skull-base surgeons gain a clearer map for protecting facial movement during a demanding exposure.
pmc-13428313:
Lilian Almeida Nascimento Rabêlo and colleagues test, in a 2026 dental materials study, how a year in water changes two filling resins. Semidirect restorations are built outside the mouth and given extra hardening, often in an autoclave, before fitting. One resin held special glass fillers that can release helpful minerals; the other was a standard nanohybrid resin. Forty-eight discs were made, half with the extra hardening step, and all were stored in distilled water for twelve months.

The mineral-filler resin changed color more over the year than the standard resin. Extra hardening made no difference to color change in either material. Surface roughness rose in every group after storage, again regardless of hardening. Microscope checks matched those results. Dentists choosing materials for visible restorations get a caution about long-term shade drift with the mineral type.
pmc-13428813:
Peter Rhodes writes an essay on medicine and crowd madness, using the COVID years as context for a wider warning. Individual judgment, he argues, is fragile, and people can be swept into a shared thought window by mass narrative or by the certainty of a totalised mind.

Loss of the self to the group can run from small group-think to literal crowds and on to global propaganda and technocratic control. Milgram's obedience tests and Hannah Arendt's phrase about the banality of evil frame the risk, with the bureaucrat as a new kind of wrongdoer. Readers get a polemic that asks science, too, to check its own crowds.
pmc-13429113:
Hamza Abedallaa, Zuheir Al-Shehabi, and Nader Abedallaa review, in a 2026 study, eighteen years of testicular cancer care at one Syrian hospital. Testicular cancer is the commonest cancer in males aged 15 to 39 and among the most curable. The Latakia center's records covered 318 patients from its opening in 2007 through late 2025. The team sorted tumors by type and stage and checked risk features used to plan treatment after surgery.

Median age at diagnosis was 32 years. Germ cell tumors dominated, split almost evenly between seminoma and non-seminoma forms, with mixed tumors the largest single subgroup. Most patients arrived at stage I, the earliest stage, though seminomas presented early more often. Risk features such as vessel invasion were tallied for each group. The pattern matches global reports, and the authors call for more regional research from Syria and the Middle East.
pmc-13430413:
Asta Nyvang Rank and colleagues surveyed orthodontic specialists in Denmark and Sweden for a 2026 study on judging when braces are needed and when care should start. Nearly 500 certified specialists received a 20-item survey built around nine patient cases. Each case came with photos, head drawings, and notes on how the teeth meet.

Replies from 219 specialists showed clear gaps between regions and between the two countries. Danish replies lined up more closely, which the authors link to shared national guidance. Swedish replies spread more widely. Digital referral tools were more common in Sweden, yet their use went with more choices to watch a case rather than judge need at once. The findings point to uneven practice even among trained experts.
pmc-13430913:
Fanfan Cao and colleagues set out a systematic-review protocol on acceptance and commitment therapy for weight stigma. Such stigma brings negative attitudes and stereotypes, linked to body-image distress, eating disorders, depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidal thoughts.

Acceptance and commitment therapy, a third-wave talking therapy, aims to build psychological flexibility and values-led action, and it shows promise against stigma. Yet evidence stays limited and fragmented, often missing stigma's many dimensions. This protocol plans a synthesis of how well the therapy cuts stigma and improves related mental health, giving therapists a clearer evidence verdict.
pmc-13431013:
Ketfi and Ben Saad compare two yardsticks for lung function tests in healthy Algerian adults. Spirometry grades breathing against reference equations. The Global Lung Function Initiative replaced its 2012 race specific equations with race neutral ones in 2023, to remove race as a medical input. Their 2026 study runs both equation sets over 488 healthy adults aged 18 to 85 who passed breathing tests. It compares the labels each set assigns.

The two yardsticks agreed on a normal label for about nine in ten people, so the headline barely moved. Under the surface, percent predicted values for the two main volumes ran several points higher under the neutral equations. Abnormal labels shifted too. More people were classed as obstructive, fewer as restrictive or non specific. Isolated low first second volume vanished as a class. Broad comparability, with real reclassification at the margins, is the fair summary for this population.
pmc-13431613:
Cinzia Auriti and co-authors reviewed the trials of spotting a common womb infection in 2026, centered on cytomegalovirus and its risks in pregnancy. The virus spreads widely, sleeps for life in the body, and can wake or strike again. A first infection during pregnancy carries the highest risk of passing to the unborn child.

Effects on children range from no signs at all to grave body-wide illness, slow growth of mind skills, and hearing loss. The review stresses fast checks for the mother, care in telling first bouts from fresh ones, and joined checks before and after birth, from scans to hearing tests. Drugs against the virus now exist for pregnancy and infancy, which sharpens the case for early flags. Wide screening of newborns earns a close look as a way to catch missed cases.
pmc-13431713:
Estella Castillon and colleagues describe three people whose patchy light skin follows Blaschko lines, tied to new post-conception ACTB gene variants. ACTB faults already link to several conditions, including a constitutional gain-of-function syndrome and somatic variants in birthmarks and muscle hamartomas.

Deep gene sequencing of skin biopsies from affected areas found the same missense variant, Arg335His, in two people, previously seen in a fetus in constitutional form. The third person carried a new insertion-deletion variant. Two of the three also showed neurodevelopmental features. The report widens the ACTB disease spectrum, showing that variants acquired after conception can paint skin in lines and affect the brain.
pmc-13432813:
Yongshu Wu and co-authors deleted a sensing gene in 2026 from a food-borne germ that sickens people, then watched how the loss cut both toughness and attack skill. The gene sits in a two-part alarm system that reads stress cues from the world around the cell. Germs without it grew poorly in acid, alkali, and salt strain.

The crippled strain also fared worse under strong acid, metal strain, and harsh oxygen strain, while a restored copy healed most gaps. Inside host cells, the strain broke in less well and moved more slowly. In mice, it filled liver and spleen more weakly and killed later. Gene voice reads under acid showed stress genes lit in odd patterns without the sensor. The authors cast the sensor as a twin pillar of survival and harm.
pmc-13433413:
Marko Balan and colleagues develop climate-conscious recommendations for critical care in Canada, under the Choosing Wisely banner. The climate crisis is framed as the largest health threat of the twenty-first century, and critical care's footprint can shrink if clinicians have safe guidance.

A national multidisciplinary working group refined a recommendation list between November 2023 and May 2024, drawing on content experts and literature review. A three-stage anonymous voting process selected and polished the final list. Clinicians and managers get evidence-based steps to cut intensive-care emissions without compromising patient safety.
pmc-13435913:
Charles W Tran and a large team pool blood tumor markers from more than 2,300 lung cancer patients in 2026. Six tumor proteins plus one swelling marker were read at start and at six weeks. Five trials of immune therapy mixes supply the data.

A learning model blends marker levels from both time points to rank survival risk. Its accuracy held in both squamous and non squamous test sets. One marker, CYFRA, carried the most weight in both lung types. Marker math matched costlier DNA blood tests in prior work. Cheap blood panels may guide care when DNA tests lag or fail.
pmc-13436013:
Fiona Lynch's team asked Australians living with rare or undiagnosed genetic conditions in 2026 what they think of automating genomic reanalysis. Re-reading old genome data against new knowledge can yield diagnoses, yet manual reanalysis is slow and rarely routine, so cases that could now be solved stay unsolved. Automated reanalysis could widen access, but worries about transparency, bias, data security, and trust had not been studied with affected people.

Twenty-three Australians in seven online focus groups voiced strong support for automation, while raising conditions around openness, accountability, and control of their data. Genomics services get a user-grounded mandate with guardrails: automate to find answers faster, but show the reasoning and protect trust. Policy makers should weigh these views before scaling automation.
pmc-13436213:
Kate Stoeckle and coauthors follow leukemia patients whose guts carry resistant germs into chemotherapy in 2026. The study enrolls 159 patients getting strong induction therapy with no preventive antibiotics. Stool checks at chemo start sorted patients by germ carriage.

Fifteen patients carried ESBL type germs, and seventeen carried AmpC type germs. Three of the ESBL carriers grew the same germ in blood during low white cell counts. Just one non carrier did so, a stark gap. AmpC carriage showed no such risk lift. Gut screening may flag who needs closer watch or tailored cover.
pmc-13436813:
Zuhal Mohmand's team surveyed young adults in 2026 on sedation during endoscopy after moving from pediatric to adult bowel care. Sedation habits differ between child and adult units, and that shift may color how patients with childhood-onset inflammatory bowel disease experience scopes. Ninety-seven patients aged eighteen to twenty-five, diagnosed around age fourteen, rated satisfaction, pain, discomfort, anxiety, and preparedness in both settings.

Deep sedation was far more common in pediatric care, and adult scopes brought lower sedation satisfaction plus more pain and discomfort, while anxiety and preparedness ratings did not differ. Patients cited thin communication and perceived low empathy as barriers, with education and compassion as helps. Transition teams get a clear prompt: explain adult sedation plainly and early.
pmc-13437813:
Jukka Sivonen and colleagues studied how feeling unable to afford adequate energy shapes Finnish views on climate action. Official energy poverty is reckoned from bills and income, yet a household can feel energy-poor without crossing those lines. Their 2026 study drew on a representative 2023 survey of 5,909 people and modeled support for fossil fuel taxes and two gentler climate nudges.

Higher felt energy poverty came with lower support for climate measures across the board. The authors split the harm of being left behind into two kinds. The sting of exclusion flows from the felt condition itself, whatever the meter says. Pure money harm from nudges, by contrast, lands more on people objectively poor in energy terms. Either way, climate policy ignoring energy hardship risks losing the very households it most needs onside. They advise pairing carbon measures with visible relief and honest messaging about who pays.
pmc-13438313:
Ahmed Hadj Hassen and colleagues reviewed research and gray sources on moving through airports with a disability. About sixteen percent of people live with disability, and air travel promises mobility that terminals often fail to deliver. Their 2026 scoping review reads the airport journey from curb to gate through five lenses: whether help exists, can be reached, is acceptable, is affordable, and truly works in practice.

Across the studies, access arrived in pieces. Ramps, lifts, and desks existed yet often failed to join into a usable whole, leaving travelers dependent on booked assistance. Needs beyond mobility drew the least attention, above all invisible disabilities such as cognitive or sensory ones staff cannot see. The authors insist compliance checklists are the wrong finish line: access is a living quality of the trip. Their map is meant to push airports from providing features toward guaranteeing a journey holding together.
pmc-13438813:
Bingjie Fu and colleagues coaxed one metal-containing aromatic ring system into reshaping itself into another. Aromatic compounds, prized for their stable ring currents, usually swap small pieces while keeping their skeleton; wholesale reshaping is known mainly from one classic pair of hydrocarbons. Their 2026 study starts from a fused metallacycle with a three-membered ring and ends at a charged six-membered metal ring.

Radical-trapping tests and modeling pointed to electrophilic attack followed by elimination, a familiar substitution pathway pushed somewhere new. Metal aromatics attract attention because the metal bends the rules of aromatic chemistry, opening structures carbon alone cannot reach. The authors frame the switch as proof aromatic frameworks can be re-cut, and a practical route into compounds otherwise hard to make. For chemists, a controlled reshaping reaction is a new kind of tool: edit the frame, not just the fittings.
pmc-13439013:
Diana Mager and colleagues asked parents of children with coeliac disease what makes safe food hard to secure, and what governments should do about it. Coeliac disease demands a strict gluten-free diet. Yet gluten-free staples cost one and a half to two times their ordinary versions, and many Canadian households with an affected child report food insecurity. Their 2026 study drew on fifty-nine parent-child pairs from a wider survey, with open-ended interviews.

Cost dominated: more than ninety percent named high prices, and nearly as many blamed absent food policy. Their policy asks were concrete: child tax credits led, backed by school nutrition education and official recognition of coeliac disease as a disability. The authors frame gluten-free food as medicine priced like a luxury. Their take-away: families have already drafted the agenda; what is missing is adoption and funding.
pmc-13439313:
Matteo Rocchetti and colleagues compare blood and kidney side effects across three pulsed field ablation systems used to treat atrial fibrillation. This ablation method uses electric pulses rather than heat, but the pulses can rupture red blood cells, a process called haemolysis. Their 2026 prospective study enrolled 239 patients.

Patients received the pentaspline, balloon-in-basket, or lattice-tip catheter, with blood tests before and 24 hours after the procedure. Only the pentaspline system caused significant depletion of haptoglobin, a protein that mops up free haemoglobin, and only that group saw acute kidney injury, in 4.9 percent of cases. Heart injury markers rose in all groups but were lowest with the lattice-tip catheter. No group showed clinically important falls in haemoglobin or lasting kidney damage. The authors conclude catheter design drives these differences.
pmc-13440713:
van de Wetering and Lee interviewed 11 Dutch teen climate activists aged 14 to 18. Through growth science, they sought to learn what young people get out of striking for the climate. Millions of teens have joined school strikes calling for action. The authors probed how activism connects to identity formation and age-salient motives.

Three themes fell out of the interviews. They were held online between September 2022 and 2023, with six female, two male, one non-binary, and two undisclosed teens. Activism was driven by wanting to build a just world. Accounts spanned solidarity with future generations and the Global South. It also worked as the teens' own choice, helping them explore and express who they are during the teen years. Finally, activism created a felt bond with some others, though not all. The authors suggest backing such involvement, since it channels teen growth needs well.
pmc-13442613:
Obaidul Hasan's team strengthened carbon fiber laminates in 2026 with aligned carbon nanofiber z-threads, tackling weak through-thickness shear between plies. Carbon fiber composites fail catastrophically under inter-ply shear, and unaligned nanoparticle interleaves had barely helped in-plane shear. Electrically aligned nanofibers were threaded through fiber gaps along the thickness direction, forming an interlocked multiscale network, then tested against controls and unaligned variants.

Half-percent z-threaded samples gained about twenty-six percent in shear strength, with toughness modulus gains near twenty-two percent for the higher loading, and failure localized to interlaminar zones rather than spreading across plies. Unaligned variants ran weaker and more brittle. Composite engineers get a threading method that reinforces the weak direction without sacrificing in-plane performance.
pmc-13446313:
Maruyama and colleagues showed in 2026 that a long first intron, a non-coding stretch inside the PROS1 gene, tunes how much protein S its owner makes across tissues. Protein S helps control blood clotting, and its shortage raises clot risk, yet standard gene tests that read only coding parts miss the cause in about half of affected families. The team probed the intron for regulatory elements in mice and humans.

Elements inside the intron adjusted protein S output in several tissues. Rare variants found there lowered activity in reporter tests, the lab assays that read out a regulatory element's strength. Such variants may explain part of the missing-cause group with protein S deficiency. The authors argue that diagnostic testing should extend into this intron, and that non-coding regulation deserves a routine place in the workup of inherited clotting disorders.
pmc-13446413:
Nelson, McGregor, and Lombrozo test whether stating a belief as a chance, rather than a yes or no, goes with intellectual humility, the habit of owning one's limits and fallibility. A belief framed as a probability admits doubt by design. Their 2026 paper reports two studies: one with 279 students and one with two nationally matched samples of about 270 adults each, covering political and moral beliefs.

Comparing people, the predicted link failed: those who framed more beliefs as chances were not more humble overall, in either sample. Comparing beliefs within the same person, the link appeared. Political and moral beliefs a person held as probabilities came with a humbler stance toward those very beliefs, even after allowing for how extreme the beliefs were. Framing may thus soften single beliefs without marking a humbler character, a hint that teaching chance based framing could cool hard disputes.
pmc-13447113:
Valentina Baderna and colleagues asked what decides how often a gene switch, called an enhancer, is active across a group of cells. Enhancers are DNA stretches that boost nearby genes when proteins called transcription factors bind them.

Using a method that reads single DNA molecules, the team measured how often chromatin, the packed form of DNA, opens at enhancers. Most single factors opened chromatin in only a small share of cells at a time. Added together, though, the binding of many factors set how often an enhancer switched on. Tests on hundreds of enhancers placed at a new genome spot showed the helper protein p300 was needed for full activation.
pmc-13447413:
A S Arya and Rahul Shukla analyse decentralised waste governance in Kerala, India, through a sociological lens in 2026 work. Most waste research focuses on trucks, rules and targets, leaving social effects underexamined. Kerala's Green Task Force model, staffed largely by women who collect sorted waste door to door, offers a rich case for asking how policy shapes everyday environmental roles.

Policy papers, institutional reports and operating guidelines were read with theories of governance, social structure and community trust. Official writing presents the model as building responsibility, participation and inclusion, with women workers gaining new public visibility. Whether daily life matches that picture remains unverified, since no fieldwork tested lived experience. The authors call for on-the-ground research into how households and workers actually experience the system.
pmc-13447813:
Jedidi, Kerkeni, and Ben Lahouel report a 25-year-old man with a painless cystic mass under the skin of his left shoulder blade region. It had grown slowly for five years before he sought care. Scans showed a well-defined cyst measuring about 9 by 5 by 9 centimeters. It sat in the soft tissue over the back ribs, with no cysts in lung or liver.

Blood serology for the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus came back positive. MRI supported a subcutaneous hydatid cyst. A hydatid cyst is a parasitic larval cyst. This soft-tissue form accounts for under 2 percent of hydatid cases. Surgeons excised the cyst completely. Tissue examination confirmed the diagnosis, with its layered germinal membrane visible under the microscope. His recovery was uneventful. He received two 28-day cycles of albendazole separated by a 14-day break, to reduce recurrence risk after surgery.
pmc-13448113:
Kim presents a 2026 editorial on restraint in endoscopic spine surgery, reviving a famous warning. In 1993 an editorial titled 'The Rape of the Spine' accused the field of overusing fusion for financial rather than clinical reasons; a 2015 revisit found little changed. Kim asks whether the fast-growing endoscopic era is destined to repeat that history of enthusiasm outrunning evidence.

Endoscopic techniques are a genuine advance in minimally invasive spine care, shrinking incisions and recovery. But fusion volumes once rose far faster than comparable operations, driven by incentives the editorial names plainly. Kim's imperative of restraint argues that new tools should narrow indications to patients who benefit, not widen them to whoever can be scheduled. The piece is a conscience check for a specialty at the start of its next expansion wave.
pmc-13448213:
Ksenia Anufrieva and colleagues map immune and stromal niches in skin from adults with dermatomyositis in 2026 spatial gene work. The autoimmune disease inflames skin and muscle and carries a strong cancer link, yet which tissue neighbourhoods mark cancer-associated cases was unknown. Comparison with a related skin condition, cutaneous lupus, sharpened what is unique to each disease subtype.

Cancer-linked lesions held scattered immune infiltrates rich in macrophages, or organised lymphoid clusters with dense B cell cores ringed by T cells, while blood vessel structure stayed preserved. Non-cancer skin instead showed dense myeloid infiltrates near injured vessel linings, with signals that drove stromal reshaping and loss of vessel-supporting fibroblasts. Both diseases shared strong interferon signals, while one interferon type appeared only in dermatomyositis skin.
pmc-13448813:
Mamadou Cherif Diallo and coauthors evaluate a 2026 time-domain electromagnetic survey method run inside deep mine galleries for mineral exploration at kilometer depths. Through 3D modeling, the team compared a small 250-by-5-meter gallery loop against a huge surface loop, then field-tested a gallery transmitter with borehole receiver at LaRonde mine near 3 kilometers depth.

Modeling showed the small gallery loop can out-perform the surface loop at depth, favoring more turns over longer loops. Secondary field polarity changes diagnose whether conductors sit above, below, or both sides. LaRonde measurements validated two known lenses and revealed an in-hole anomaly at 700 meters. Deep-gallery surveying looks feasible for exploring deep deposits.
pmc-13449313:
Meiling Chen and colleagues measure in 2026 a metabolic hormone, fibroblast growth factor 21, in the blood of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, asking whether it tracks disease activity and artery health. The study enrolled 187 patients treated at Xuzhou Central Hospital during 2023 and 2024, split by ultrasound into 118 with carotid plaque and 69 without, plus 139 healthy controls. Blood tests covered lipids, insulin resistance, inflammation, arthritis antibodies, and the hormone itself.

Patients carried far higher hormone levels than controls, about 805.7 against 203.8 picograms per milliliter, and those with plaque ran higher still. Levels rose alongside LDL cholesterol, insulin resistance, arthritis antibodies, disease activity scores, and artery wall thickness, and fell with use of disease-modifying drugs. In adjusted models the hormone stood as an independent factor linked to thicker artery walls. The authors propose it as a research marker for cardiovascular risk in this population.
pmc-13449913:
Patcharin Sihathip and co-authors dissect in 2026 a rare hemoglobin variant, Hb Chumphae, found in a Thai man whose anemia was far worse than the usual pattern predicts. The 44-year-old arrived with chronic anemia and an enlarged liver and spleen; his hemoglobin measured just 3.7 grams per deciliter and his red cell distribution width a striking 40.5 percent. Protein separation tests hinted at abnormal hemoglobin peaks, but their patterns mimicked another variant, Hb Bart's, making the true identity easy to miss.

DNA sequencing settled it. A missense change at codon ten swapped valine for aspartic acid in the alpha-globin chain. The same patient also carried the Southeast Asian deletion form of alpha-zero thalassemia. Together, in compound heterozygous state, the pair produced anemia more severe than classic hemoglobin H disease. The team built two DNA tests that can identify the variant directly and mapped its likely ancestral chromosome background.
pmc-13450413:
Zidian Xie and colleagues mapped e-cigarette talk on Twitter and X in 2026 using language-processing methods. E-cigarettes have grown popular, especially among youth and young adults, and online discussion shapes norms and policy debate. The team wanted a spatiotemporal picture of what people actually say.

Over three million related posts were collected from March 2021 to March 2023, leaving 2,140,439 non-commercial posts after cleaning. Human coders labeled 2,300 posts for relevance, sentiment, and likely user status, and those labels fine-tuned a RoBERTa model with good accuracy. Topic modeling then revealed the main themes in positive and negative posts. Public health teams gain a map of where and when vaping talk turns favorable or hostile.
pmc-13450513:
Zahedi and colleagues test whether a CT measurement can stand in for an invasive ultrasound in judging the heart's most dangerous narrowing. Their 2026 study compares two measures in 45 Iranian patients who had both tests within ninety days. One is the cross-sectional area of the left main coronary artery on CT angiography. The other is the minimal lumen area from intravascular ultrasound. A third had significant narrowing by the ultrasound standard.

The two measurements correlated strongly, at 0.93 across patients. A CT cut-off of about 6.2 square millimetres identified significant stenosis with about 96 percent diagnostic accuracy. Specificity was perfect in this cohort. Nobody above the threshold was misclassified as diseased. Sensitivity was about 88 percent. The authors present CT area as a reliable non-invasive metric for left main assessment and offer the threshold, derived in an Iranian population, for wider validation.
pmc-13450613:
Shengli Shi and co-authors hunt in 2026 for savory taste fragments in cod skin, a fish plant leftover that is often thrown away. Umami, the savory taste, comes from tiny protein pieces that switch on taste buds. The team broke cod skin down with enzymes and sifted the mix by size.

Taste panels and lab tools narrowed the field to five candidate fragments. Computer models then tested how each fragment docks with the umami taste switch on the tongue. One fragment stood out as strongly savory, while two others boosted the taste of a mix. The work gives food makers a path to natural taste boosters from fish waste.
pmc-13451213:
Vinoth Kumar Selvaraj and others turned e-waste and tire rubber into tough foam blends in 2026, to cut waste and make green building stuff. Waste from phones, boards, and tires piles up, and reuse in useful blends could cut costs and trash. The team glued three waste fillers with a resin binder.

Tests found a best mix of six parts waste foam, three parts tire bits, and just over seven parts waste board. That mix bore close to thirty-nine pressure units, far more than the plain foam base at just over fourteen units. Computer checks matched lab tests to within less than one percent, and scans showed an even spread of fillers. Builders gain a waste-based blend with proven strength.
pmc-13451813:
Esben Schroeder and co-authors present in 2026 a partly automated flow for counting and mapping cell cores along single muscle fibers. Hand counts of these cores are slow and prone to bias, which limits big studies of muscle change. Their flow pairs free image tools with custom code to read stained fiber images.

The code logs each core's place, shape, and tilt in three planes, plus its gaps to the fiber spine and to its nearest neighbors. Results roll up per fiber and per biopsy, joined with measures from a second imaging suite. The team offers the flow as a fast, repeatable base for large fiber data sets in muscle labs.
pmc-13451913:
Paula Timonen and co-authors survey in 2026 how Finnish drug stores took up digital and remote services in the first COVID-19 wave. Owners of all private community pharmacies in Finland were polled in late 2020, and 175 replied. Readiness to adopt new ways was scored with a known innovation scale, and stores were split into early and late adopters.

Remote services grew fast: medicine pickup lockers near doubled in share, and online sales rose by a third. Early adopters, about two fifths of stores, offered a wider digital range. Younger owners and high-volume stores showed more readiness. The authors link readiness to service growth, while noting the low reply rate may flatter the picture.
pmc-13452413:
A Ita Juwita and five co-authors test how place of origin and post harvest handling shape Liberica coffee beans from Indonesia. Their 2026 study compares beans from Jambi, Kayong, and Meranti, each handled by the natural dry method or the honey method. Liberica is a less common coffee species that draws growing trade interest across Southeast Asia.

Where a bean grew mattered most, shifting nearly every trait the team measured, while handling mainly changed moisture, fat parts, and antioxidant strength. Jambi honey beans held the most alkaloids, and Kayong natural beans held the most diterpenes, two groups of active plant chemicals. Meranti natural beans carried the most of a key acid group and showed the strongest antioxidant action. Growers can use the map of place and method to aim beans at buyers with set tastes.
pmc-13453013:
Yi Jiang and seven co-authors review ferroptosis, a cell death path driven by iron and fat damage, and its role in heart and vessel disease. Their 2026 review spans clogged arteries, aneurysms, valve disease, heart attack damage, and heart failure. The team lays out how the death path works, what controls it, and which drugs can block it.

Several drug types protected the heart and vessels in animal studies, among them iron binding drugs such as deferoxamine and deferiprone. Antioxidants such as vitamin E and lipoic acid also helped, as did a blocker named Ferrostatin-1. Natural products joined the list of agents that tame the iron driven damage. The authors frame the review as a map for turning these lab finds into new heart treatments.
pmc-13453713:
Reiko Kanno and others told of a three-button heart fix in 2026, for valve-sparing root swap in giant cell arteritis. This artery disease hits mid and large tubes, and root widening with a left main heart tube bulge is most rare. A plain one-button fix was ruled out once the bulge was cut away.

The team did a valve-sparing root swap with full cut-out of the left main bulge. The front descending and side tubes were sewed back on their own, to make a true three-button rebuild. The case, cleared by the Kobe board with patient consent, lays out the fix in full. Heart surgeons gain a fix for a rare shape where plain buttons fail.
pmc-13454113:
Kang Li and five co-authors map two decades of research joining childhood obesity with precocious puberty, the early onset of puberty. Their 2026 study pulls 2,506 papers from three databases across 2005 to 2025, written by 9,843 authors in 664 journals. Mapping tools chart output by country, center, and keyword, while a topic model sorts the themes on its own.

Output rose steadily, with the United States and China as the top contributors and Harvard the top center. The most prolific author logged 42 papers, and one pediatric endocrine journal led the venue list. The topic model found 15 themes in four clusters, from adrenal and puberty biology to the body wide damage of childhood obesity. The authors offer the map to help clinicians spot hot spots and new fronts in the field.
pmc-13454313:
Damico, Mathus, and Demchenko tackle a core problem in sugar chemistry in 2026: steering new bonds between sugars to face the right way. Their method uses a hydrogen bond, a weak pull between atoms, to deliver the partner sugar to one side of the growing chain. They built three donor sugars that differ only in where a helper group, called Pico, sits on the ring. They then tested each donor against a range of acceptor sugars.

All three donors gave good to high yields, but the bond direction hinged on Pico placement. Donors with Pico at the third or sixth position favored one link type. Pico at the fourth position favored the other, though less cleanly. The sixth position donor gave complete control in every test. The team then used it to build a four unit chain of amino sugars, with every step fully controlled.
pmc-13455313:

pmc-13457813:

pmc-13458713:

pmc-13459213:

pmc-13459913:

pmc-13460313:

pmc-13461413:

pmc-13461613:

pmc-13461713:

pmc-13462513:

pmc-13464013:

pmc-13464913:

pmc-13465013:

pmc-13466513:

pmc-13466813:

pmc-13467113:

pmc-13467513:

pmc-13467913:

pmc-13468113:

pmc-13471513:

pmc-13471613:

pmc-13472513:

pmc-13474713:

pmc-13474813:

pmc-13474913:

pmc-13476513:

pmc-13478213:

pmc-13478813:

pmc-13479413:

pmc-13479713:

pmc-13481413:

pmc-13482213:

A preventive suppository drug, not a rescue form, was given in over a third of cases and at times delayed the right drug. Timing and month patterns showed seizures strike without a schedule. The authors call for sharper training on spotting long seizures and reaching for the right medicine first.
pmc-13482513:
Afranie-Sakyi and colleagues check whether a sickle cell centre followed brain-health guidelines. Their 2026 letter examines the American Society of Hematology's 2020 recommendations on silent cerebral infarcts. These are small brain injuries without obvious stroke symptoms. The recommendations also cover monitoring thinking problems in sickle cell disease. The guidelines advise at least one brain MRI in adulthood for higher-risk patients.

Only 4.3 percent had an MRI done specifically to screen for silent infarcts, and rates did not improve after the guidelines appeared. Most scans were ordered because symptoms had already shown up, pointing to missed chances for early action.
pmc-13482613:
Dada and colleagues predict soil nutrient levels for a Johannesburg park in 2026 with a hybrid model that pairs an attention-based temporal neural network with gradient boosting. Farmers need field-level nutrient maps to dose fertilizer well, and the model digests elevation data, satellite imagery from two missions, and weather records together. The attention mechanism lets the network weigh which time points and signals matter for each nutrient.

Agreement with lab values reached 0.76 on the concordance scale, and the authors report clear gains over random forest, plain gradient boosting, and AdaBoost baselines across the nutrients tested. pmc-13483413:
Aydın Güneş and co-authors present a 2026 study of whether a quick neck ultrasound before surgery can flag a hard breathing-tube placement. Two classic checks, the lip bite test and mouth-opening grade, also carried signal. Hard mask breathing followed a different pattern, tied more to body traits and other illnesses than to any single scan number. With few hard cases overall, the authors call the scan figures exploratory and ask for bigger multicentre checks.
pmc-13485213:
Jane M Edgeloe sequences both organelle genomes of a reef-building brown alga to fill a gap in its family tree. Published in 2026, the work uses long-read sequencing on Cystophora brownii, a habitat-forming species of Australian and New Zealand temperate reefs that is retreating under warming in places. Gene content and order match fellow members of the order closely. Family trees place the species as sister to the rest of its family, hinting at an early split possibly dating to the Miocene. pmc-13488013:
Yousef Boobes leads a large team validating a fasting risk score for people with chronic kidney disease in a 2026 prospective study. Many patients wish to fast during Ramadan, yet fasting can be unsafe for some kidneys. The Ramadan and Kidney Disease score sorts patients into risk groups, and the team followed 220 patients through the fasting month using records and phone interviews before and after Ramadan.

About seven in ten patients completed all thirty days of fasting, while a smaller group stopped partway. Higher scores predicted less complete fasting and more serious adverse events, including hospital admission. A cutoff near the middle of the range separated likely fasters from others with fair accuracy. The authors offer the score as a shared decision aid.
pmc-13488113:
Mursyid Hasan Basri and colleagues build planning models for fairer health care access in West Java, Indonesia, in a 2026 study centered on Kota Bandung. Community health centers provide basic care, immunization, and maternal services, yet their locations lag behind fast, uneven city growth. The team forecast population to 2045, mapped daily demand on a fine spatial grid, and tested placement models that maximize coverage, cut travel time, or balance both goals.

Demand is projected to keep rising, with growth hotspots in areas now poorly served. Model runs show that well-placed new centers can widen coverage and shrink access gaps substantially. Planners can switch among the scenarios to match local budgets and priorities, the authors note.
pmc-13489713:
Marabini and colleagues studied involuntary retirement in 2026, asking how workplace climates shape whether older workers leave on their own terms. Between a tenth and two fifths of employees retire against their wishes, for reasons such as poor health, employer pressure, or hitting the standard pension age. Using Dutch panel data on 3,735 workers in 501 organizations, the team separated shared workplace climates from each worker's own reading of them.

Reaching the standard pension age was the most common reason for forced exit. Across workplaces, a climate that supported staff development cut involuntary retirement overall. Workers who saw their own workplace as more accommodating than their colleagues did, including on post-retirement work options, were also less likely to leave unwillingly. Distinct climates tied to distinct exit reasons. The authors argue that training and flexible policies widen older workers' real choices near retirement.
pmc-13490213:
Zhongqiao Lu, Deshan Zong, Zhongde Yang, and Bin Yue pool risk factors for rebleeding after acute lower gut bleeding in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Searches across four databases through May 2024 yielded twenty-nine studies with more than fourteen thousand patients, of whom about nineteen hundred bled again. Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently, and adjusted results were combined to judge which factors hold up together.

Age seventy or older, needing a transfusion, shock on arrival, high blood pressure, kidney disease, and high blood fats each raised rebleeding risk in pooled adjusted results. Painkiller use, active bleeding seen at colonoscopy, bleeding from colon pouches, and certain platelet-blocking drugs also raised risk. Steroids and blood thinners appeared in simpler analyses.
pmc-13490613:
Speleers and colleagues planned a radiotherapy technique that angles radiation planes out of the usual flat geometry to spare the heart, lungs, and gullet during left breast and lymph node treatment. Patients lie prone with a breath hold, already protective, but node coverage still doses nearby organs. Their 2026 planning study on eight patients compared standard coplanar arcs with tilted-plane arcs, checking hardware feasibility on a computer model of the treatment couch.

Tilting planes by fifteen to twenty degrees cut mean doses to heart, lungs, and esophagus simultaneously by more than twenty percent versus coplanar plans in this planning set. Angles within twenty degrees of the transverse plane proved physically deliverable on the ring-shaped treatment machines modeled. The prone crawl couch could slew to the needed positions without collisions in the feasibility model. Speleers argues non-coplanar planning deserves clinical rollout for high-dose node cases.
pmc-13491613:
Takayuki Takimoto and four co-authors report a 2026 imaging study of a rare scarring lung disease called idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis. The disease stiffens the upper lobes and restricts breathing for reasons that remain poorly understood. The team wondered whether stiff joints in the chest cage itself help limit how much the thorax can move.

Seventeen patients with the disease and fifteen with other lung diseases had CT scans taken while breathing in and out. Joint abnormalities, mostly abnormal calcium deposits near the breastbone joints, appeared in fourteen of the seventeen patients. Half showed clearly reduced chest motion, and every patient with reduced motion had joint changes. Chest motion tracked lung volume change closely, suggesting the cage, not only the lung, restricts breathing.
pmc-13491713:
Lauren C Houghton leads an eleven-author team comparing in 2026 estrogen breakdown products in women living in Mongolia, China, and the United Kingdom. Breast cancer rates are lowest in Mongolia, higher in China, and higher still in Britain, and hormone patterns have long been suspected as one explanation. Urine tests measured parent estrogens and thirteen metabolites in premenopausal women across the menstrual cycle.

British women generally carried higher total and parent estrogen levels than Asian women, while their ratio of metabolites to parent hormones was the lowest. Mongolian women showed the highest ratio of all three groups, with Chinese women in between. Parent estrogen levels differed little between the two Asian groups, though Mongolian women had higher metabolite totals. The pattern fits the countries' relative breast cancer risks and hints at a protective style of estrogen processing.
pmc-13491813:
Kostyantyn Dmytruk leads a thirteen-author team engineering in 2026 the yeast Komagataella phaffii to produce the receptor-binding domain of the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, a prime vaccine ingredient. Yeast factories are cheap and scalable, and the team built strains that either secrete the protein into the broth or display it on their outer surface like a billboard.

Small linker tweaks lifted secretion to fifty milligrams per liter with little protein trapped inside the cells. Microscopy confirmed surface display in the billboard strain. Mice injected with the purified protein made strong antibody responses, and their blood blocked the virus protein from latching onto its human receptor. Feeding mice the displaying yeast produced comparable results, supporting a whole-cell oral vaccine concept the authors want to develop further.
pmc-13492113:
Tamal Dey and Manoharan Shankar review in 2026 the sticky coating that makes some Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteria so dangerous. This trait, hypermucoviscosity, was long blamed on simply making more capsule sugar, but newer work shows the real change is longer, more uniform sugar chains. Extra slime helps the bacteria dodge immune cells and spread through the body.

Genes called rmp regulators were thought to control the trait, yet recent evidence shows ordinary strains can switch it on through single mutations in a capsule-building gene, wzc, gaining invasiveness fast. The same coating backfires on surfaces, weakening attachment to gut lining and medical devices, so the bacteria tune it up or down by setting. The review connects these mechanisms to infections of lung, blood, and urinary tract.
pmc-13492213:
Smits and colleagues test whether a three-dimensional heart tracing tracks recovery after resynchronization therapy in this 2026 multicenter study. Vectorcardiography rebuilds the heart's electrical activity in 3D from a standard ECG. Its QRS area measure has outperformed simple QRS duration. That was seen in earlier work on biventricular pacing. The team compared 116 patients receiving the newer left bundle branch area pacing or standard biventricular pacing, before treatment and six months later.

Both pacing styles shrank QRS area and T-wave area by roughly half and raised pumping efficiency similarly, with no significant differences between groups in the changes measured. Three-quarters of patients showed reverse remodelling, meaning the enlarged left ventricle shrank back toward normal. Only the reduction in QRS area, not pacing type or QRS duration, independently predicted that recovery in the adjusted analysis.
pmc-13493813:
Wang and co-authors designed a robot that installs hanging columns inside railway tunnels, a job that is currently labour-heavy, slow, and risky for workers on lifts. Their 2026 machine combines hoisting, gripping, lifting, and fitting gear on one vehicle. The team modelled its arm movements mathematically before building smooth motion paths. A hybrid solving method, mixing algebra with a genetic algorithm that evolves good answers, picks the arm posture that follows the shortest route.

Tests showed the robot's reach covered the full working range the tunnel job demands. Positioning proved extremely precise in the trials, with orientation errors below one part in a million on the reported scale and smooth, shock-free joint motion along the planned paths. The motion-shaping method kept operation efficient as well as gentle. The authors present the machine as a proven foundation for automating this installation work.
pmc-13494013:
Zanini and co-authors examine why weight gain is rising among people living with HIV whose virus is fully suppressed by long-term therapy. Modern treatment keeps people healthy for decades, so diet and activity now shape their risks. The 2026 study enrolled 176 patients at a northern Italian centre. It recorded what they ate, how closely they followed a Mediterranean diet, and how active they were, then split them by body mass index.

Just over half the group counted as overweight or obese. Those patients scored lower on diet adherence, a median of 10 against 11 for the normal-weight group, and drank beer and aperitifs more often, while activity levels looked the same. In adjusted analysis, each extra point of diet adherence came with lower odds of excess weight, whereas being heavy when therapy began multiplied the odds many times over. The authors call for diet-focused help designed for this population.
pmc-13494613:
Daniel E Roth and colleagues question, in a 2026 perspective, a common way of spotting catch-up growth in studies of child height in low- and middle-income countries. Stunting means a child is far shorter than expected for age. Some studies call it stunting reversal when a child crosses back above that line, and read the crossing as true catch-up growth.

The authors show with simulated data that such crossings arise from regression to the mean, the pull of extreme first measures toward average on retest. Their review of 69 studies from two decades found the trap named in only a fifth of papers, and few guarded against it. Over half drew catch-up claims from crossing counts or from splits by starting size, both prone to the artifact. They urge the field to drop threshold crossings and to fix past claims built on them.
pmc-13495313:
Xiangwen Shi and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a light-responsive gel for wounds infected with MRSA, a drug-resistant staph germ. Such wounds stall because germs persist, inflammation drags on, and tissue regrows slowly. Their gel sets with light and carries zinc-based particles plus a growth factor, set in a mixed gel base.

Under near-infrared light the gel warmed mildly to a set point and kept releasing zinc ions. In dishes it killed MRSA and another common germ, more so with light on, by tearing membranes and scrambling germ metabolism. It also calmed overactive immune cells, nudged them toward a healing state, and helped vessel cells move and form tubes. In infected rat wounds, gel plus light cut the germ load, sped closure, and grew new vessels. The authors present the gel as a full-course answer joining germ killing, immune calming, and repair.
pmc-13495513:
Xiaojian Cai and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 study, for metabolic genes that split healthy heart growth from harmful heart growth. The team mined gene data from mouse models of both kinds, then crossed the hits with known metabolism gene sets.

Twenty-two genes tied to the healthy pattern emerged, and a network pass named three hubs, HADHA, ACOX1, and GOT2, all linked to fat burning and cell energy. Tests in mice, rat heart cells, and human tissue agreed: the three ran high in healthy thickening and low in harmful thickening. Human diseased heart muscle confirmed the drop. The authors say the trio marks a metabolic fingerprint that may one day help doctors tell the two growth kinds apart.
pmc-13499013:
Kumar and colleagues profiled proteins inside vesicles shed into blood by certain brain cell types, aiming at earlier spotting of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 biomarker study. Standard blood tests cannot tell which brain cells a signal came from and miss scarce proteins. Kumar measured 122 proteins spanning Alzheimer's changes, degeneration, and inflammation with a sequencing-based assay. Each cell type's vesicles carried a distinct pattern. Mild impairment already showed early shifts in protective, inflammatory, and vascular markers in vesicles from neurons, microglia, and the myelin-making oligodendrocytes. The authors argue the blood platform can surface changes across many cell types long before dementia, supporting biomarker discovery.
pmc-13499113:
Ono and colleagues look for early signs that can show who may one day stop leukemia drugs safely. Their patients have chronic myeloid leukemia, a slow blood cancer driven by one faulty gene fusion. All got newer second-round kinase blockers, drugs that switch off that faulty signal.

The team drew on a trial with more than four hundred patients. A very deep fall in cancer gene levels by six months stood out as the key early sign. Patients who hit that mark had a strong chance of deep lasting control by three years. Such control is the gate for a safe trial stop of the drug. Six-month blood tests can thus sort patients early for stop plans.
pmc-13499713:
Sacco and colleagues test whether a body's electrical properties can help forensic doctors estimate time of death, a stubborn problem once the first day has passed. Bioelectrical impedance analysis, a bedside technique that passes a tiny current through tissue, is routine in living patients but barely explored after death. One derived value, the phase angle, rose moderately and consistently with time since death, while raw resistance and overall impedance tracked time poorly. The relationship curved: electrical change ran fast in the early hours and flattened later, matching the known biology of membrane breakdown and ion shifts. pmc-13500713:

Bare dots proved substantially toxic and blood-damaging, while the hogweed-coated dots achieved the highest cell survival and the least red cell rupture. pmc-13500813:
Sungho Park leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 imaging study that tests a faster form of 4D flow MRI for measuring turbulence in the aorta. In patients, the two methods agreed closely: peak total turbulent energy differed by about 5.0 percent in the ascending aorta and 7.4 percent across the whole aorta, neither difference reaching significance. In healthy participants, the fast method read much higher values, roughly double in the ascending aorta and triple across the whole region. The authors attribute that gap to the very low turbulence levels in healthy aortas.
pmc-13501713:

Monte Carlo simulations then stress-tested the method under varied conditions, and parameter recovery stayed accurate with stable estimates throughout. The authors position the framework as a flexible extension of randomized trial analysis for the era of phone-collected symptom data.
pmc-13502013:

Boosting fat-eating offers a new healing angle for plaque biology.
pmc-13503013:

The injury accounts for under three percent of such ruptures because the tendon normally withstands force. Such tears usually need a weakness, from kidney disease or diabetes to long steroid use. Surgical repair of both sides followed, the route back to walking.

The authors use the case to argue for monitoring, since a missed diagnosis means lasting joint damage.
pmc-13503913:

The authors frame the design as a way to cut labeling cost in eye care.
pmc-13504213:

The top dose raised stress-linked white cells, a warning sign. The authors back the middle dose for farm use, with care at higher levels.
pmc-13504813:

pmc-13506113:

pmc-13507013:

pmc-13507113:

pmc-13507213:

Ninety-three coffee-linked fungal types sat at higher modeled levels on forest relatives than on other hosts. Crop borders may quietly reshape forest understory health through relatedness.
pmc-13508213:

Patients who drank later reported less thirst, dry mouth, nausea, and weakness than those who waited six hours. View clarity and leftover fluid rates held up in both later-drinking groups, with no choking events. The one-hour group, though, showed a worrying drift toward more leftover fluid. The authors recommend drinking two hours before the exam as the best balance of comfort and safety.
pmc-13508413:
Kristine Sørensen and four co-authors track seven years of ambulance urgency and real patient severity in North Denmark, in 2026 work. Severity on scene was scored from vital signs with an early warning tool.

The share graded A slipped from 62 to 59 percent, while B rose in step. True critical illness stayed a steady share within each grade. Raw counts of critical patients still climbed each quarter, driven by rising total volume. Patients also grew older and carried more severe illness over the period. The authors read the pattern as more calls overall rather than looser grading, with real need growing alongside demand.
pmc-13509513:

Upgrading ranged widely, from fourteen to sixty-seven percent, and downgrading from five to twenty-six percent. The lowest biopsy grade carried the highest upgrading risk, at fifty-five to sixty-seven percent. pmc-13511913:

On 3,709 held-out simulations, it beat plain data-driven rivals, cutting average error by 5.3 percent overall. Gains were largest, 13.5 percent, in the slow-spreading regime where memory effects dominate, while other regimes stayed accurate. Once trained, it answers in a fraction of a millisecond instead of seconds of simulation, Zhu reports.
pmc-13512413:

Strains shared as little as about eighty percent of their NSP1 letters, showing wide diversity. Among all sequences, 290 amino-acid sites varied while ninety-three stayed completely conserved. Lineage 8 dominated the set, with over three hundred sequences, while lineage 3 had only four. Seven sites showed strong signs of positive selection, evolution favouring change, supported by three methods.
pmc-13514413:

The study covers one centre at one point in time, so it shows association rather than cause.
pmc-13515413:

The team combined sixteen mouse data sets. Human kidney cell data were included. Genetic analysis and patient blood samples were also used. The samples came from over two thousand patients. Uric acid and one related compound stood out. They were the only signals conserved across injury models. They peaked during the transition window. The failed-repair cells showed a matching pattern. It was a four-part pattern of purine pathway changes. It appeared in both acute and chronic disease.
pmc-13515713:

Tuning groove position, depth, and width together beat tuning them one by one, reaching 72.34 kilopascals of output pressure. Against a plain membrane, the tuned design more than doubled output pressure and lifted the pressure-bandwidth product by about 29 percent. Repeat runs varied by only 0.052 percent in output, Yu notes, showing the search lands on the same design reliably.
pmc-13515913:
Kairat Davletov leads a multicenter team reporting in 2026 how common poor sleep is among heart disease patients in Kazakhstan, and what travels with it. Sleep is now counted among the core measures of heart health, yet data from Central Asia have been scarce.

Nearly four hundred patients, assessed six to twenty-four months after a coronary event, completed a standard sleep questionnaire. About thirty-seven percent slept poorly. Anxiety was the only factor tied to poor sleep across the whole group once other traits were accounted for. Patterns split by sex: anxiety and lower schooling mattered most in women, while retirement and low activity mattered in men. The authors urge routine sleep and mood screening in cardiac follow-up care.
pmc-13516013:
Shakiba Rahimi and colleagues tested whether dietitian-led feeding plans shorten intensive care stays for critically ill patients in Tehran. The trial compared personal plans from dietitians against usual feeding directed by physicians alone.

The study covered 107 patients at two centres who were expected to stay at least five days. After adjustment, the dietitian group left intensive care about 2.5 days sooner than the control group. Nutrition risk scores also improved more in that group on two standard screening tools. New infections hit 7.7 percent of the dietitian group against 38.2 percent of controls, and pressure sores were rarer too. Death rates at 28 days did not differ, so Rahimi calls for randomised trials to confirm the gains.
pmc-13517713:
Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 a cheap clay extract as the calcium source for trapping arsenic with bacterial mineral-making. Microbially induced carbonate precipitation uses bacteria to form calcite that locks up pollutants, but pure calcium chemicals are costly. The team screened natural minerals and chose Baiyin attapulgite clay, richest in calcium with fewest toxic impurities.

In twenty-day water tests, the clay extract roughly doubled arsenic removal versus standard calcium chloride. Removal peaked at about two-thirds of the arsenic for both strains, far above blank controls near one-fifth. In thirty-day soil tests, clay plus bacteria cut the most available arsenic fraction from 0.115 to about 0.03 milligrams per kilogram. The authors present attapulgite extract as a low-cost, sustainable calcium source for large-scale cleanup.
pmc-13518713:
Caroline M Stüven and seven colleagues study photodynamic therapy for central serous chorioretinopathy in a large 2026 real-world cohort. In that condition, fluid collects under the retina and blurs vision. Light-activated drug therapy is a standard choice when fluid persists, yet doctors know little about which patients respond best or whether waiting hurts results.

Their review covered 115 patients treated at one center. Retinal thickness fell clearly after therapy, fluid cleared fully in 51.3 percent of eyes, and vision improved slightly. About 30 percent of eyes saw the fluid return, while repeat therapy helped again. Waiting longer before treatment linked to a weaker thickness response, supporting earlier action.
pmc-13518813:
Bingxiang Wu, Pengcheng Yang, Yiming He, and Huayang Liang propose a 2026 hybrid model for short-term electricity price forecasting. Good forecasts help markets run and grids stay reliable, yet prices depend on long time patterns plus network connections that most models handle separately. Training mixed data streams together can also create conflicting updates.

Their framework joins a Transformer encoder for time patterns, a graph neural network for network structure, and a gradient surgery method that calms training conflicts. Market records from PJM were fused with simulated sensor data from an IEEE 39-bus grid. Across five runs the fused model posted the lowest average error, with tighter uncertainty than the strongest rival baseline.
pmc-13519013:
Sunghwa Kang and five colleagues compute the best possible single-shot detection limits in 2026 for quantum illumination, a sensing trick that uses entangled light to spot a faint target in noise. Textbook intuition says maximally entangled many-part states should win. Their analysis of three- and four-part systems, spanning qubits up to four-level qudits, says otherwise.

The optimal recipe combines one maximally entangled pair with the rest, because entanglement among the signal parts themselves hurts performance. Multi-part states still beat the classic two-qubit benchmark in several cases. Quantum correlations explained the advantage except for the four-ququart case, which broke the pattern. Kang and co-authors supply exact limits against which real devices can be judged.
pmc-13519413:
Ghazala Khurshid and colleagues tested whether adding stem cells to bone grafts helps dental implants bond more firmly. Published in 2026, the trial split sixty patients at random into two groups, with one group receiving stem cells plus graft and the other graft alone, then followed both for six months. Firm bonding between living bone and implant, called osseointegration, decides whether an implant lasts, especially where bone quality is poor.

The stem-cell group showed higher implant stability scores, greater bone volume gain, and denser new bone than the graft-only group. Every implant survived in the stem-cell group, against a survival rate just under 97 percent in the control group. The authors present stem cells as a promising aid to implant healing, while the small size and short follow-up argue for larger trials. Readers get a compact, hopeful result with its limits in plain view.
pmc-13520313:
Tingjuan Huang and colleagues report in 2026 a targeted delivery system for acute liver injury using tiny vesicles shed by stem cells. Plain vesicles spread widely in the liver, so the team adds vitamin A to steer them toward stellate cells that drive scarring, carrying a gene called REDD1.

Lab tests showed stronger uptake by activated stellate cells, while animal tests showed better liver build-up. Treatment quieted stellate cell activity, lowered inflammation and cell death, and improved liver function and scarring measures. The design pairs a natural targeting trick with gene delivery, offering a template for more precise liver medicines.
pmc-13520713:
Gwyndolin M. Vail and colleagues argue in 2026 for course plans that honour student culture from the design stage. The aim is to keep more underrepresented students in science degrees. Past work coached teachers on delivery. Course blueprints got far less focus.

Good design values what students already know. Good design also links content with lived life. Real issues such as racial health gaps in the pandemic can build science identity. A new 2024 course at a mostly Black college tackles myths about race, genes and AI. Built-in support also cuts the load on each teacher in class.
pmc-13522513:
Mingguang Cui and seven colleagues published this 2026 synthetic biology study introducing VIPbodies, nanobodies, tiny antibodies, fitted with viral protease switches. Controlling a protein's binding activity, rather than its amount or location, has been a standing challenge. Each VIPbody carries a self-cleaving viral protease that keeps snipping the nanobody apart until an antiviral drug blocks the protease, letting the intact nanobody fold and grab its target.

Starting from prototypes against a red glowing protein, the team built versions answering to different protease-drug pairs, each working alone inside the same cell. Wired into gene circuits, the nanobodies gave drug-tunable gene expression and performed all six canonical Boolean logic operations, the building blocks of cell logic. They also steered cell death both ways, triggering two distinct death programmes through caspase coupling. The authors present VIPbodies as a compact, programmable framework for chemogenetic control of protein function and cell fate.
pmc-13522613:
Anqi Li and colleagues report a materials study, published in 2026. It covers 3D printing of chiral luminous materials. These glow with circularly polarised light. The twist of the light can be controlled. Keeping the twisted order intact during fast printing was a barrier. Curing usually disrupts how layers line up.

The team used a new curing method at the layer boundary. Each layer set within twenty seconds. The printed forms gave off twisted light in all directions. The twist effect was strong. Fine detail reached ten microns. The glow could even flip its handedness. This depended on the light setup or on the growth direction.
pmc-13523213:
Ying Tan and colleagues map the care journey of older patients with chronic lung disease in a 2026 qualitative study. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease care is often fragmented and focused on crises rather than long-term needs. In-depth interviews with older patients were analyzed thematically and assembled into a journey map spanning screening, diagnosis, hospital care, and home rehabilitation.

Themes covered management tasks, emotional experience, and pain points at each stage. Patients struggled to recognize early symptoms, carried ongoing burdens of symptom control, and faced barriers to lung rehabilitation, weak support, nutrition knowledge gaps, and worry about physical activity. The authors argue for a shift from episodic care to continuous support that combines digital tools, self-management education, and community resources across the whole pathway.
pmc-13523513:
Chunyan Zhao and colleagues map, in a 2026 data-driven review, the worldwide landscape of clinical trials for pulmonary fibrosis treatment. Pulmonary fibrosis covers chronic lung diseases where scarring impairs breathing and can end in respiratory failure. Knowing where trials cluster, and what they test, guides future strategy.

Searching a pharma intelligence database produced 1,203 interventional trials. Activity grew in three stages, with a surge in 2020, and concentrated in the United States with 316 trials and China with 285, while only 128 were multinational. Two established drugs still dominated, nintedanib in 94 trials and pirfenidone in 88. Endpoints focused on safety and on forced vital capacity, a breathing measure. The disease range widened beyond idiopathic disease, and the authors call for more collaboration and precision grouping.
pmc-13524613:
Munshi and colleagues studied in 2026 the protein Gα13, a signal relay inside cells, in pancreatitis, the painful inflammation of the pancreas. Samples from people with acute and chronic pancreatitis showed lower levels of this protein. The team then triggered pancreatitis in mice with a standard drug, comparing normal mice with mice whose pancreas lacked the protein, and added rapamycin, a drug that blocks the growth pathway mTOR.

Munshi found that mice without the pancreatic protein suffered worse injury to the enzyme-making acinar cells in both acute and chronic disease. Inflammation rose only mildly, and only in the chronic form. Loss of the protein also raised mTOR signalling. Rapamycin softened the acute injury in these mice but made chronic disease worse, a split result. The authors conclude Gα13 normally protects the pancreas, and mTOR blockade helps only in the acute setting.
pmc-13525913:
Lew and co-authors describe technology for measuring blood chemistry continuously during dialysis. Their 2026 paper addresses a practical gap: dialysis prescriptions could be tailored moment by moment if clinicians knew a patient's electrolytes and acid-base status in real time. Point-of-care devices using small whole-blood samples already return sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, urea, gases, and more within minutes.

The authors outline a setup that draws samples from the dialysis arterial line. It runs them on a point-of-care device installed in the machine itself. Results reach the clinician promptly for prescription adjustments. Derived measures such as the anion gap could flag problems like diabetic ketoacidosis or alcohol poisoning mid-session. They also flag pitfalls honestly: whole blood values differ from serum values, and arterial samples differ from venous ones, so readings must be interpreted with the sampling route in mind.
pmc-13526313:
Awang and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of massive biliary ascariasis, infestation of the bile ducts by the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, in a 73-year-old woman. The disease is common in tropical Southeast Asia, where warm climate, poor sanitation, and farm work sustain transmission. Worms wandering from the gut can block the bile ducts and mimic gallstone colic. Her ultrasound showed the worms in the ducts, a recurrence after earlier endoscopic clearance despite prior gallbladder removal.

Treatment used endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, a scope procedure that both confirms and clears duct blockage, and the team extracted fourteen worms. Anti-worm medicine after clearance is standard to kill gut worms and prevent recurrence. The authors note that such a heavy burden, especially in an elderly patient after gallbladder surgery, is rarely documented. They review imaging choices from ultrasound first to MR and CT when the picture is unclear.
pmc-13527613:
Urszula Radzikowska and others comment, in a 2026 editorial, on new evidence that glutamine breakdown acts as a metabolic checkpoint for protective immunity against tuberculosis. The discussed study found the enzyme GLS1, which starts glutaminolysis, raised in blood cells from patients with active tuberculosis and rising further after bacterial stimulation.

Blocking the enzyme in that study weakened the Th1 and Th17 helper T-cell responses that defend against the bacterium. It also cut energy production and let bacteria survive better inside macrophages. The effect was traced to histone marks maintained by a GLS1-derived metabolite and reversible with supplements. The editorialists stress context. The same checkpoint drives harmful responses in autoimmune disease, where blocking helps, yet sustains protective responses in tuberculosis, where blocking harms, shaping how future GLS1 drugs should be judged.
pmc-13527913:
Mohd Rashid Khan and seven colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of basket and umbrella trials in children's precision medicine. In a basket trial, one targeted drug is tested across several diseases sharing a genetic marker; an umbrella trial tests several drugs within one disease, split by marker. Such designs suit rare childhood conditions where patient numbers are small.

Searching three databases produced 1,867 records, of which 28 studies met the criteria for the final review, and topic modeling of 76 articles mapped the field's main themes. Basket designs appeared more often than umbrella designs, especially in early cancer and rare-disease work. The authors find these trials can speed drug development, provided statistical planning is careful and regulators are involved early.
pmc-13528813:
Rhoubi Asmae and colleagues report a 2026 hospital laboratory study from Oujda, Morocco, on iron stores and blood sugar control in diabetes. The team reviewed records for 1,412 patients who had both serum ferritin, a marker of body iron, and HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar, tested during 2023.

Ferritin showed no link with HbA1c in the 214 patients with type 1 diabetes. In the 1,198 patients with type 2 diabetes, the link was strongly positive, and ferritin rose steadily as sugar control worsened. Because the study looked at one point in time, the authors note it cannot prove ferritin changes cause poor control, and they call for follow-up studies over time.
pmc-13529113:
Wang and colleagues reported a 2026 case in which fever after stroke turned out to be caused by the antibiotic rather than by a new infection. A 45-year-old woman with a brain infarction complicated by pneumonia linked to her stroke received piperacillin-tazobactam. During treatment she developed high fevers while her neutrophils, infection-fighting white blood cells, kept falling.

Wang describes a search for infectious and other causes pointed to drug fever combined with agranulocytosis. A drug-reaction scoring scale rated the link as probable. Agranulocytosis is a near-absence of neutrophils, and her lowest count fell to critically low levels. Stopping the antibiotic and giving a growth factor that boosts white cell production, plus adjusting other antimicrobials, resolved the fever and restored her counts. There was no recurrence over a year of follow-up. The authors urge blood monitoring during long courses of this antibiotic.
pmc-13529613:
Leonard Knoedler and eight colleagues mine United States hospital data on chin surgery outcomes in a 2026 study. The database covered inpatient genioplasty from 2000 to 2022. It held 485 admissions, with a mean age near thirty-two. Just over half the patients were women. Most had private insurance and lived in richer areas.

Complications appeared in about ten percent of stays. Older patients suffered them at about fifteen percent, versus six percent in younger ones. Bone-cutting chin surgery made up about sixty-four percent of cases. It cost more, lasted longer in hospital, and drew more complications than soft methods. Long stays tracked with complications in both subgroups. Lower-income patients stayed longer despite similar complication rates. The authors flag fairness gaps and call for larger prospective work.
pmc-13529713:
Poonyaporn Poolborwornrak and three colleagues build a two-step cleanup for microplastics in lab wastewater in a 2026 study. Polyethylene bits from 0.15 to 1 millimeter were the target. Step one used clumping chemicals to gather the bits. Three clumpers were tried, with chitosan as a helper. Step two passed the water through a simple sand column.

Clumping worked best at neutral pH. One agent, PAC, cleared about seventy-seven percent of the finest bits alone. Alum and iron chloride trailed. Coupling clumping with sand at a slow flow changed the game. Total removal hit 99.93 percent in the best run. The authors pitch the pairing as cheap and scalable. Real wastewater, with mixed plastics and dirt, is the next test.
pmc-13530113:
Meng Cao and colleagues reviewed double emulsions that carry both water-loving and fat-loving nutrients for athletes. Published in 2026, the review covers water-in-oil-in-water droplets, which nest one water phase inside oil inside water, allowing two cargo types in one vehicle. Demand for tailored sports nutrition keeps growing as athletes seek performance, muscle, and recovery gains.

The review explains how cargo releases, why these droplets break down, and how to stabilize them, then surveys preparation methods and fabrication techniques. Sports uses center on supplements that deliver bioactive compounds in stable, functional forms. Future work points toward athlete-specific designs with better stability and targeted release. Readers get a design guide for a promising but finicky delivery format.
pmc-13530213:
Fengmin Xu, Zhenting He, and Qianqian Li search in 2026 for a gene signal that tracks inflammatory bowel disease activity without invasive testing. The illness mixes disturbed gut metabolism with a disordered immune setting. Machine learning sifted genes tied to a form of regulated cell death shaped by metabolism.

Three genes survived strict checks across separate patient groups and rose together during active disease phases. Single-cell data placed each gene in distinct gut cell types, from immune to lining to support cells. The trio links metabolism, immune entry, and cell death, offering a candidate signature for sorting patients.
pmc-13531213:
Florin-Leontin Lazar and co-authors describe in 2026 a stent-sparing strategy for a frail woman with disease in all three coronary arteries.
