The 76-year-old arrived with a heart attack pattern short of full blockage, plus a hard calcified branch junction and one fully closed artery. Shock struck when a side branch closed mid-procedure.

Drug-coated balloons reopened both branches without new stents after careful preparation that included shock-wave calcium cracking. A later session opened the closed artery with a mixed balloon and single-stent plan. One-year imaging showed healthy vessel widening, favoring minimal metal in frail patients.
pmc-13531813:
Shizuka Kudo, Tomoko Kodama, and Yuri Sasaki map social drivers of older adult suicide across Japanese medical regions in a 2026 ecological study. About 40 percent of Japanese suicide deaths in 2020 involved people aged 60 and over. Public data on income, living arrangements, work, habits, and illness were set against regional suicide rates.

Among men, rates rose with high blood pressure, smoking, daily drinking, living alone, and older-worker employment. Among women, rates fell where more mental health professionals practiced and where taxpayer income ran higher. The split pattern argues for prevention plans fitted to local conditions and to each sex.
pmc-13531913:
Donald A Redelmeier, C Mark Cheung, and Akash M Patel test in 2026 whether gut protein leakage explains low blood protein after heart surgery. Low albumin after major surgery is common and ominous, yet its cause stays murky. Thirty-eight consecutive cardiac surgery patients gave paired blood and stool samples for a clearance test of a marker protein.

Low albumin appeared in about 82 percent after surgery. The leakage test flagged protein-losing gut in about 39 percent. Every positive leakage result came with low albumin, giving perfect positive prediction in this small group, while sensitivity stayed near half. Leakage may explain some cases only.
pmc-13534213:
Sofia Solari-Hernandez and colleagues review in 2026 immune problems in Down syndrome, a condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. Extra gene copies over-activate interferon signals, a core immune alarm, and keep inflammation switched on. Both first-line and targeted immune defences show faults in cell numbers and function.

Clinically, people face higher risk of severe lung infections and weaker, shorter vaccine responses. Studies report more hospital care and deaths plus faster fading of antibody levels after vaccines. Readers gain a frame for tailoring prevention and vaccine plans for this group.
pmc-13534413:
Jeong-Hyun Ryu and colleagues test in 2026 how dose changes the effects of zinc oxide nanoparticles on bone-forming cells. The particles attract interest for medical use, yet benefits depend strongly on amount, and the best range was unclear. Extracts at four strengths were applied to pre-osteoblast cells in the lab.

The lowest strength boosted cell growth, survival, and bone gene activity, with more enzyme action and mineral build-up. The highest strength harmed cells clearly and showed strong toxicity. Readers learn that low doses may support bone repair while high doses must be avoided in material design.
pmc-13534613:
Jinning Liu and colleagues study in 2026 how to find and protect critical nodes in layered networks that link hospitals, water supply, and power supply. Failure in one layer can cascade into others, yet key nodes differ by structure and by stability. Their model weighs flow links between layers plus management coordination.

Two ranking methods together flagged both central nodes and unstable nodes as high risk for spreading failure. Protecting just a small set of flagged nodes curbed early cascade spread in tests. Managers gain a focused protection plan for linked infrastructure under stress.
pmc-13534713:
Jennifer M Mongiovi and colleagues study in 2026 whether contraceptive history shapes immune cell patterns inside ovarian tumours. Non-hormonal devices create local inflammation in the uterus, while pills suppress ovulation, and both link to ovarian cancer risk in unlike ways. Tumour samples came from 24 tissue arrays across six studies.

High-grade serous tumours held the highest shares of T cells overall. Ever using a device linked modestly to more killer T cells in tumours, while pill use for a year or more linked to fewer. Device use also linked to more exhausted T cells in some subgroups.
pmc-13536613:
Mengtong Sun and colleagues track in 2026 whether insulin resistance scores predict combined heart and metabolic disease in people with fatty liver disease. Over 109,000 UK Biobank adults with fatty liver but no such disease at entry were followed for near sixteen years. Nine scores built from blood sugar, fats, and body measures were compared.

Higher scores on all nine meant higher risk of combined disease later. Scores mixing waist and height or body mass led the list for risk and added small gains to standard prediction. Blood markers for inflammation and organ strain explained part of the links seen.
pmc-13538413:
Zhuming Bi and co-authors present a digital twin case for judging remaining life of used storage racks in a 2026 study aimed at small and medium firms. Virtual copies can guide reuse decisions, yet real benefit cases for smaller firms stay scarce. Four selected racks were modeled digitally and tested under worst-case loads for safety margins. Changing loads in design studies then showed how safety margins respond, supporting reuse and recycling choices.

Models supplied managers with evidence-based safety factors for each rack under harsh loading. Load sweeps clarified which racks tolerate heavier reuse and which need limits or retirement. The authors frame the assistive project as proof that twin methods can deliver practical sustainability gains beyond large firms, linking longer resource life to leaner manufacturing.
pmc-13539713:
Hyein Shin and Woohyeon Kim split health literacy into components and link each to health behaviors among South Korean adults in a 2026 survey study. National panel data supplied a sixteen-item literacy scale, reduced by component analysis into two dimensions. Adjusted models then tied each dimension to exercise, weight control, drinking, and smoking, with education splits checked.

One dimension captured active engagement, meaning finding, judging, and applying health information. The other captured compliance, meaning following given information. Higher active engagement raised odds of regular activity and weight control attempts. Compliance orientation lowered activity odds yet raised current drinking odds. Patterns were sharpest among adults without college education. The authors urge policies that build proactive, searching literacy.
pmc-13541913:
Ling Wang leads a 2026 five-year prospective study linking CT-measured changes in muscle and fat to declining strength and mobility in older adults. Muscle performance change sits at the heart of sarcopenia, the age-related wasting that leads to frailty.

One hundred twenty neighbourhood volunteers had CT scans, grip strength, and a timed stand-and-walk test at entry and again five years later. Muscle size and density shrank across back, pelvis, and thigh compartments, while fat grew more in women. In women each unit of front-thigh muscle loss tracked with weaker grip and slower walking. In men, one deep trunk muscle's density behaved in the opposite, protective direction.
pmc-13545213:
Jamil Hallak and AH Abdul Hafez presented a 2026 planning model for rebuilding waste services in Idlib Governorate in northwest Syria, a region recovering from conflict. Their mathematical model chooses where to place transfer stations, treatment plants, waste-to-energy facilities, and landfills while weighing cost, carbon emissions, and two kinds of risk. Formal local data were scarce, so the case drew on field information, geographic analysis, and judgments from eleven experts.

The preferred design opened three transfer stations, two treatment facilities, one energy plant, and two landfills, producing a large yearly electricity output. Carbon taxes, subsidies, and permit trading mainly shifted costs rather than the network itself. Readers get a template for infrastructure planning where records and institutions are thin.
pmc-13546713:
Hypatia Thobejane, Tlou Grace Manyelo, and Busisiwe Gunya fed Creole goats leaf meal from the Muni tree in 2026 to see whether a local plant feed can help control gut worms. Sixteen yearling male goats were assigned diets containing none of the leaf meal or three rising shares, up to 30 percent, for 42 days. Worm egg counts in dung were measured at the end.

Results were mixed across parasite types. One worm genus was absent at the middle dose yet appeared more at higher doses, while whipworm eggs and coccidian cysts fell as leaf meal rose. The authors read the pattern as enough promise to justify further work on the tree as a natural supplement, given that commercial dewormers are costly and resistance is growing.
pmc-13547213:
Doudou Cao, Enrico R. Crema, and Emma Pomeroy analyzed in 2026 body measurements from more than 90,000 adults in 213 groups across China to untangle what shapes human body form in one country. Their statistical models weighed climate, altitude, town versus countryside living, language group, and time period against height, weight, sitting height, and body breadth.

Bodies grew larger over recent decades, especially heavier, in step with economic development and city living. Northern groups stayed taller and heavier than southern ones, and men and women responded in similar ways. Rainfall, rather than temperature, was the strongest climate link, possibly acting through food production and disease. Highland and northeastern groups broke the general patterns, hinting at altitude adaptation and population history.
pmc-13547413:
Megan E Parker and a multinational team evaluated in 2026 crackers fortified with crickets and black soldier fly larvae as school snacks in Madagascar, where children often lack protein and iron. Laboratory checks cleared the snacks on germs and heavy metals and found solid nutrition, with protein near twelve to fourteen grams per hundred grams plus useful iron and zinc. The real test was whether children would eat them.

Among 187 schoolchildren, about four in five ate at least eighty percent of their portion, and nearly nine in ten chose the insect crackers over a plain control when offered both. Savory versions beat sweet ones. Caregivers in focus groups spoke positively and reported fuller, more energetic children. The authors present insect snacks as acceptable and safe.
pmc-13548713:
Jian Zhou and colleagues hunt in the blood for a T cell type that foreshadows success of combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy in advanced lung cancer, in a 2026 study. The patients came from a phase two trial of first-line treatment for non-small cell lung cancer. The team profiled their blood immune cells with multicolor flow methods. On samples from eight patients they layered single-cell gene and receptor sequencing.

A late-differentiated killer T cell marked by missing CD28 and carrying KLRG1 stood out: patients starting with more of these cells, and keeping them during treatment, fared better. Far from being exhausted leftovers, the cells had expanded in clones and could feed the tumor with fresh fighters. A zinc-linked pathway governed the subset, and adding zinc in mice strengthened treatment. The authors propose a convenient blood test and a possible zinc pairing.
pmc-13551513:
Eren Demir published a 2026 paper presenting a decision support tool meant to make hospital planning usable by managers and clinicians, not only modeling experts. Hospitals must balance rising demand against limited beds and staff, and existing tools often cover only parts of a system. The tool runs a discrete event simulation, a computer model of patient flow, spanning specialties and their connections with 360 input parameters.

Scenarios for 2023 to 2027 produced activity levels, bed and clinic needs, theatre use, and financial effects. One scenario, a virtual ward where patients are monitored at home, cut backlogs and eased resource strain from 113 percent to 80 percent in the reported run. Demir presents the adaptable tool as a way to test changes before committing resources.
pmc-13551713:
Jinhuo Wang, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 laboratory study of whether salvaged blood can be safely returned during liver cancer surgery. Machines that collect, wash, and return a patient's own blood save donor blood, yet might also return cancer cells. Blood from twenty patients was sampled at three stages: from the surgical field, after salvage processing, and after an added leukocyte depletion filter.

Cancer cells appeared in most samples at every stage, though counts fell significantly after processing in the reported comparisons. After three weeks of culture, cancer cell clusters grew only from untreated field samples, and none were detected after filtration. The authors read the combined process as stripping salvaged blood of viable tumor cells.
pmc-13552113:
In a 2026 study, Flor Torres-Juarez and ten colleagues examined a tuberculosis bacterium enzyme that appears to restrain the microbe's own virulence. Protein kinase F had poorly defined roles, though cell work tied it to limiting inflammasome activation. The team infected mice with a mutant strain lacking the kinase gene, comparing lung bacterial growth, inflammation, and survival against normal and restored strains.

The mutant made far more of a pro-virulence surface lipid and grew dramatically more in mouse lungs by late infection in the reported counts, with heavier lung inflammation alongside. The effect persisted in mice lacking the inflammasome sensor, ruling out that pathway as the explanation. Highly susceptible mice also died sooner with the mutant, leading the authors to cast the kinase as a brake on virulence through lipid suppression.
pmc-13554913:
Trevor T Lovell, Jennifer Ogrin, and Ahmad Elashery report a grapefruit clash that weakened a heart drug's safety in a 2026 case report. Their fifty-seven-year-old patient took mavacamten for a thickened, obstructed heart muscle. Over months the drug eased the obstruction while pumping strength held steady. Then he began drinking grapefruit energy drinks daily.

About two months later his pumping strength had slipped to a reduced range. Grapefruit blocks a liver enzyme that clears the drug, so levels likely climbed too high. Stopping both the drug and the drinks restored his heart strength. Restarting the drug alone, without grapefruit, caused no repeat fall. The authors warn that hidden diet clashes can push this narrow-window drug into harm.
pmc-13555513:
Md Nazmul Huda leads a seven-author team interviewing clinicians who run a crisis service for young people in mental distress in a 2026 Australian study. Emergency visits by children and teens in crisis have risen worldwide. The Safeguards Teams Program answers with fast outreach, short recovery-focused help, and trauma-aware care. Clinicians described what helped, what hindered, and what should change.

Flexible referrals, outreach-friendly structures, and chances to build skills eased the work. Clinicians valued that the service catches young people who fall outside other programmes' intake rules. Heavy demand strained workloads, and the care model felt unsettled in its early phase. Suggestions included co-design with local communities, a more flexible model, and staff with cultural awareness and specific skills.
pmc-13557013:
Nguyen-Ha and co-authors computed a 2026 theoretical study of aluminium clusters doped with a boron triangle, spanning cluster sizes from three to twenty-one atoms in three charge states. Density functional theory, a standard quantum chemistry method, mapped the lowest energy shapes. The clusters grow around a stable three boron unit while aluminium atoms accumulate around it.

At thirteen aluminium atoms the boron unit moves from outside to inside the cluster, Nguyen-Ha found. At eighteen aluminiums the boron triangle straightens into a line for neutral and positive clusters, but negative clusters keep the triangle because that charged unit is exceptionally stable. Adding boron improved the stability of the aluminium frameworks in every charge state studied. Certain magic sizes grabbed extra electrons almost as eagerly as halogen atoms do, earning quasi-halogen behaviour.
pmc-13558313:
Alexandra Villalpando-Solórzano and five colleagues pooled in 2026 studies testing whether one gene variant raises blood levels of the HIV drug efavirenz. The drug often causes liver and nervous system side effects, and the liver enzyme that clears it, CYP2B6, varies by inheritance. Their meta-analysis searched four databases for studies, up to March 2025, comparing efavirenz concentrations across the three forms of a single letter change in that enzyme's gene.

Five studies with 373 patients who had both HIV and tuberculosis qualified. People with two copies of the variant form carried clearly higher drug levels than either of the other groups, while those two groups barely differed from each other. Higher levels were not directly tied to side effects in the pooled data, yet the authors support genetic testing to fine-tune dose and lower toxicity risk.
pmc-13558613:
Jack Lee Smith, Christina Antoniou, and Ruaridh Alexander released in 2026 a Python tool, stratapy, that draws geological layer logs from simple text or spreadsheet input. Stratigraphic logs are the basic picture geologists make of rock layers in a cliff or drill core, and drawing them by hand is slow and hard to reproduce. Existing software is patchy and often bound to one specialty, so the authors built for accessibility first.

Non-programmers can produce publication-quality logs through plain parameter choices, while specialists can still customise deeply. The package ships standard rock pattern fills, a curated symbol library, automatic alignment with the geological time column, and slots for samples and notes. Panels can be joined into correlated multi-log figures for complex systems. The authors aim to standardise log illustration across research and industry, and to modernise a daily Earth science workflow.
pmc-13558713:
Sreekanth Rallapalli and Weiwei Jiang assembled in 2026 a cyberthreat detector that lets three nature-inspired search algorithms tune a sequence-learning network in turn. Signature-based intrusion systems miss novel and shape-shifting attacks. Their design hands feature selection to a firefly algorithm. A whale algorithm tunes the network settings. A grey wolf algorithm sets the ensemble weights. Each search method is named for the animal behaviour it imitates. A long short-term memory network does the classifying.

Thirty independent runs on two standard benchmark collections returned accuracies near ninety-nine percent with a false positive rate a little above one percent. Formal paired tests confirmed the gains were statistically solid rather than lucky runs. The authors judge the hybrid fit for near-real-time defence, with one clear caveat. The benchmarks are archived traffic. Live networks must validate the system before anyone trusts it at the perimeter.
pmc-13559513:
Søren S Olesen and colleagues chart the natural course of recurrent acute pancreatitis using Danish national registries. Their 2026 cohort study included 45,338 adults hospitalized with a first pancreatitis episode between 2000 and 2022. Recurrence meant a new hospital episode at least ninety days after the previous one. The team modeled how risk changes as episodes pile up.

Nearly seven thousand patients, 15.2 percent of the cohort, went on to recurrent disease during a median follow-up of 4.5 years. The twelve-month risk of yet another attack climbed from 17 percent after one recurrence to 46 percent after five. Gaps between episodes shortened as their number grew, a wear-out pattern the statistical models confirmed. Most returns happened within a year. The authors suggest that prevention trials will recruit most efficiently by targeting patients who already carry several episodes, since their near-term risk is highest.
pmc-13560113:
Xuanming Hu, Meilin Wen, and Shunfang Liu compare exercise formats for blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes through a network meta-analysis. Their 2026 study pooled sixteen randomized trials with 744 participants, searched across four databases to October 2025. Moderate continuous training faced two interval styles: short bursts of sixty seconds or less, and long intervals of two minutes or more.

All three exercise types lowered glycated hemoglobin and fasting glucose compared with no exercise. Long intervals produced the largest drops and ranked first for both outcomes in the ranking analysis. Long intervals also beat moderate continuous training on glycated hemoglobin in the main analysis, though that edge faded in a sensitivity check removing one trial. Fasting glucose showed no clear differences among the active formats. Insulin resistance improved markedly only under long intervals. The authors present long-interval training as the leading option, on modest evidence.
pmc-13560213:
Chen Liu, Jiali Zhang, and Liu Yang use unsupervised machine learning to sort high-risk newborns into hearing-risk phenotypes. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 447 babies in a neonatal unit, clustering demographic, perinatal, and diagnostic data by a medoid method suited to mixed data types. A decision tree then translated the clusters into bedside rules.

Four phenotypes appeared. Term babies with jaundice failed hearing screening least often, at 20.5 percent of their group in the reported rates. Preterm boys with respiratory illness failed most, at nearly half. Preterm girls sat between, and term babies with respiratory or infectious problems scored moderately. Simple rules emerged, such as boys under a stated birth weight failing at very high rates. Network analysis showed respiratory illness, infection, and prematurity forming a tangled core, while jaundice stood apart. The authors argue pattern-based sorting complements single-factor thinking.
pmc-13562513:
Anita Csizmarik and thirteen colleagues hunt for a blood signal that warns when a prostate cancer drug is about to fail. Enzalutamide, a hormone-blocking drug, extends life in advanced prostate cancer, yet many tumours resist it from the start. No test currently guides that choice. The 2026 team first grew prostate cancer cell pairs, one sensitive and one resistant to the drug, and compared their genes and DNA. Three candidates emerged, among them a stretch called UCA1 and the androgen receptor gene.

The researchers then counted copies of each candidate in cell-free DNA from patients' blood serum. Groups covered 20 men on enzalutamide, 20 on a related drug, and 40 on chemotherapy. Extra UCA1 copies went with shorter survival on enzalutamide, while extra receptor copies mattered for the related drug only. The authors suggest a simple blood count could help doctors pick the right drug sooner.
pmc-13562613:
Yasmeen A. S. H. Hameed and seven colleagues spin a triple-duty nanofibre membrane that pulls toxic mercury from water and shows biological activity. The 2026 membrane blends a tough plastic, PVDF, with chitosan from natural sources and a layered aluminium-copper mineral. A battery of imaging and surface tools confirmed the blend and revealed a porous mat rich in chemical groups that grip metal ions. Batch tests varied dose, acidity, and contact time to find the best uptake conditions.

At the sweet spot, mildly acidic water and 100 minutes of contact, each gram of membrane held about 423 milligrams of mercury. Uptake followed a chemical-binding pattern and absorbed heat as it ran. Beyond cleanup, the mat killed breast and liver cancer cells in a dose-dependent way and mopped up free radicals. The authors pitch the material for water purification first, with medical uses as a longer-term prospect.
pmc-13562713:
Xianhuan Luo and six colleagues model how much strain a glued-on fibre sensor feels when the structure beneath it stretches. Fibre Bragg grating sensors watch wind turbine blades for damage, prized for small size and immunity to electrical noise. The catch sits in the glue: the adhesive layer between blade and fibre absorbs part of the strain, so readings understate it. Their 2026 paper builds a model for the end-bonded layout, where the sensor is fixed at its ends.

The model spells out how the glue's stiffness, its Poisson behaviour, and its thickness drain transfer efficiency, along with the sensor's gauge length. Finite element simulations, a stress test, then checked the formulas. Both routes agreed on the governing patterns. The authors offer the model as a design guide: choose glue and geometry on paper, and the sensor on the blade reports strain more faithfully.
pmc-13563913:
Leyao Qian and colleagues describe laboratory and feeding trials, published in 2026, of a blended plant extract tested in the fish Acrossocheilus fasciatus. The mixture combined four plant sources and was first checked for its ability to stop Streptococcus agalactiae, a bacterium that harms farmed fish.

A dose mixed into feed at a low rate gave the best survival after bacterial challenge and caused no harm to growth. Treated fish showed healthier liver and gut tissue and a gut microbe mix with more helpful bacteria and fewer harmful types. Fish farmers and researchers get a candidate alternative to antibiotics, with dose and safety details spelled out.
pmc-13569313:
Shuai Yuan and colleagues write, in a 2026 letter reporting a nationwide Swedish cohort study, about fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. Their question is whether it raises the risk of peripheral artery disease in step with liver severity. Biopsy records from twenty-eight pathology departments were linked to national registers covering care, medicines, and deaths.

Adults with biopsy-proven fatty liver were followed from their biopsy or first matching diagnosis code, with other liver diseases and alcohol misuse excluded. The design lets risk be graded across tissue severity stages rather than treating fatty liver as one uniform condition. Clinicians watching heart and vessel risk in liver patients get population-scale evidence organized by how advanced the liver changes are.
pmc-13570913:
Musa İşnas's team tested wormwood leaf extracts, plain and nano, against diabetes damage in rats, in a 2026 study. Diabetes drives oxidant stress that injures liver, kidney, and pancreas, and plant extracts are candidates for easing that harm. The team induced diabetes in 48 female rats and gave ethanolic lyophilised or nano Artemisia haussknechtii extracts at two doses for 21 days.

Diabetic rats showed persistent high glucose, weight loss, abnormal fats, and suppressed oxidant defences, all of which improved dose-dependently with treatment. The high-dose nanoparticle form performed best, normalising insulin, HbA1c, and C-peptide markers and markedly sparing tissue damage. The authors present the plant, especially in nano form, as a promising complement against diabetes-related oxidant injury.
pmc-13571713:
Laura Maté Miguel and Pablo Pazos Lama report, in a 2026 case written in Spanish, a 62-year-old man in intensive care after an ischemic stroke. His central venous catheter tore the innominate vein, a large vein behind the upper chest. The line had been placed under ultrasound through the left subclavian vein, and the first chest film looked reassuring.

Two days later he became unstable, with kidney failure, fluid around both lungs, and fluid squeezing the heart. CT imaging with contrast sent through the catheter itself showed the tear leaking into the chest cavity, and a vein study confirmed it. The catheter was removed in an operating room with a blocking balloon ready, no new leak appeared, and recovery went well. The authors stress imaging when decline has no clear cause.
pmc-13572313:
Wan and colleagues fed two probiotic strains to heavy finishing pigs in 2026 to compare how each shapes fat, inflammation, and meat quality. Two hundred eighty-eight pigs were split into three diet groups for forty-two days: plain feed, or feed with one of two Lactobacillus strains, given daily. Probiotics are marketed to trim fat, but strains are often lumped together despite different habits.

Both strains lowered stress hormone and inflammation signals in blood, raised a calming immune factor, and cut saturated fat in the loin muscle. The second strain went further on fat: thinner backfat, more lean meat, and smaller fat cells, through a metabolic switch pathway the team measured. The first strain instead improved the meat itself, making it more tender with less internal fat. The authors say producers should pick strains by goal.
pmc-13572413:
Szymon Plewa, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 lab method for measuring amino acids tied to proline use in skin cells. Proline helps build collagen and plays a part in wound healing and swelling. Sound measures of proline and its partner compounds are needed to study those paths.

The method pairs liquid chromatography, which sorts compounds in a fluid stream, with a precise mass detector. The team checked the method for straight-line response, range, repeat results, accuracy, and stability, and all checks passed. It then measured the target amino acids in lysates of HaCaT cells, a lab skin cell line, with success. The authors note that the setup can add more compounds later. It can also extend to other complex samples from living tissue.
pmc-13573413:
Aurélien Cornil, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 umbrella review of what drives protective behaviour in pandemics. Masks, hand hygiene, and distancing saved lives in COVID-19, and future crises will need the same habits. The team gathered past reviews to sort the factors that help or hinder those habits.

From 86 records, 11 reviews met the bar, covering COVID-19 plus flu, SARS, MERS, and Ebola. Factors fell in three bands: who people are, what they think and trust, and the world around them. Trust in credible sources, belief that steps work, and clear multi-channel messages helped. False claims, conspiracy beliefs, and lack of supplies blocked action. Age, gender, and schooling cut both ways across habits. The authors urge tailored, honest messaging and fair access to supplies.
pmc-13574513:
Lunavath and colleagues report in 2026 a cross-sectional study of gum health and oral health-related quality of life in postmenopausal women. In this group, estrogen loss is suspected of accelerating periodontal breakdown and so denting daily comfort and function.

The team examined 266 women attending a tertiary government hospital. They charted bleeding, pocket depth, and attachment loss tooth by tooth, and scored quality of life with the fourteen-item oral health impact questionnaire. The average numbers of teeth with bleeding, and of teeth with pockets and attachment loss, were significantly associated with the quality-of-life score. The correlations themselves were weak. More teeth showing bleeding tracked with slightly lower impact scores in some domains, while more teeth with pockets and attachment loss tracked with slightly worse scores overall in this sample.
pmc-13574813:
Benjamin Lefranc, with twelve colleagues, reports a 2026 find of a new chemical twist in frog skin peptides. Frog secretions brim with small protective peptides, often reshaped after the cell builds them. Two peptides from the giant gladiator treefrog carried a reshaping never before confirmed in any backboned animal.

Mass and magnetic tools read the pair's makeup, and lab-made copies confirmed the read. Their head unit was a ring-shaped form of the amino acid tryptophan, built by a classic ring-closing reaction. Computer models pegged that unit as the spot where electrons move most freely, a hint at redox work. In radical-mopping tests, the reshaped peptides scored lower than their plain kin. The find widens the known menu of natural peptide edits and shows how inventive frog skin chemistry runs.
pmc-13575113:
Ileana Quiñones and colleagues shared a large brain-imaging resource for studying how minds that speak many languages handle language. Language use relies on a known left-brain network, but how it varies from person to person, above all across lives lived in two or more tongues, remains little studied. Their 2026 data paper presents NEUROLINGUA, MRI scans from 725 healthy adults aged 18 to 82 in a Basque-Spanish setting, plus language history and test scores.

In the scanner, people did hear-and-read tasks plus number tasks, allowing side-by-side checks across senses. Early checks tied brain structure to social background and thinking, and showed the functional scans pinpoint the language network as expected. The authors offer the set as a top resource for studying how language networks bend to fit varied language lives.
pmc-13575313:
Jaegeun Cho and colleagues studied 231,386 Korean adults in the 2024 Community Health Survey to test whether an inflammation-related lifestyle score tracks with quality of life. The score combined smoking, drinking, physical activity, and body mass index into one measure. Quality of life was rated with a five-dimension health questionnaire, and depressive symptoms were checked with a nine-item mood scale.

Higher lifestyle scores lined up with poorer quality of life after other health and demographic factors were taken into account. That link was clearly stronger among people with depressive symptoms than among people without them. The results suggest that daily habits and mood should be weighed together when health workers try to understand why quality of life differs across a population.
pmc-13576813:
Sarah A Sacco leads a 2026 study feeding cell cultures with acids from the cell's own energy cycle to control acidity in drug-making reactors. Chinese hamster ovary cells dominate production of therapeutic proteins. Three cycle acids, malic, succinic, and alpha-ketoglutaric, replaced the usual carbon dioxide bubbling in two industrial antibody-making cell lines.

Carbon tracing showed deep rewiring of central metabolism under every acid feed, with clear differences between the two lines. Fed cultures ran the energy cycle harder, leaned less on glucose, and spilled less lactate. The alpha-ketoglutaric feed split the lines on nitrogen handling: one made more glutamine and cleared ammonia, the other stockpiled glutamate instead. Antibody output per cell rose later in the runs. The authors back acid feeding as a combined acidity and metabolism lever.
pmc-13577013:
Il-Rae Cho and colleagues mapped which part of the H-1 parvovirus outer shell lets the virus enter human cancer cells. H-1 parvovirus already kills HeLa cells in the laboratory, while the closely related Kilham rat virus does not. By building hybrid viruses that swapped segments of the VP2 shell protein, the team narrowed the key region step by step.

A minimum stretch from amino acid 208 to 435 set infectivity, yet it could not sustain infection on its own. Two further segments, plus variable regions named VR4b and VR8, were also required. Hybrids carrying all of these pieces infected human lung and pancreatic cancer cells, pointing to precise shell regions that could guide future cancer-targeting virus designs.
pmc-13578213:
Jakub Kufel and colleagues describe a 2026 machine learning tool that finds breathing tubes on chest X-rays of adults. A tube placed for a ventilator must sit at the right depth, and doctors judge that by the gap between the tube tip and the carina, the point where the windpipe splits. Reading that gap by hand takes time in busy intensive care units.

Six doctors marked tubes and windpipes on close to four thousand X-rays to train the model, which paints both structures on each scan. On outside test scans its outlines matched the doctors well, and its gap readings missed the true value by a few millimeters on average. The authors see the tool as support for staff, not a stand-in for them.
pmc-13579713:
Yuhang Wu and colleagues weigh which early pregnancy risks drive low birth weight in central China, and how many cases could be prevented, in a 2026 study. More than thirty four thousand pregnant women were followed from 2013 to 2019, split into those with and without pregnancy diabetes. Six changeable risks were scored from the first months, from older mother age to missed folic acid.

Five risks mattered in each group, with one swap: secondhand smoke in the diabetes group and alcohol in the other. Low education carried the largest preventable share in both groups, ahead of low body weight and older age. In total about a fifth of low weight births in the diabetes group and a third in the other group traced to the five risks. Tailored early care is the authors' prescription.
pmc-13579913:
Li Guo and colleagues test whether a stiffness reading from ultrasound can flag moderate to severe chronic kidney disease, in a 2026 study. One hundred fifty two patients across all five disease stages had standard scans plus shear wave readings, which time tiny ripples through tissue to gauge firmness. A combined scoring sheet that folds in size, layer thickness, and brightness was also computed for each kidney.

The stiffness of the outer kidney layer sorted stage three and beyond with strong accuracy. It rarely cried wolf, which makes it handy for ruling disease in, yet it missed about a third of cases, so a soft reading cannot rule disease out. The combined score sorted nearly as well. The authors back the pair for staging help in clinic, with the miss rate as the caveat.
pmc-13590913:
Hailing Yu leads a team testing flat titanium based sheets as a cancer treatment for triple negative breast cancer, a form that lacks the usual drug targets. The sheets act like enzymes, turning peroxide found in tumors into highly reactive oxygen. Under near infrared light they also heat up. Heat and reactive oxygen together wreck cell power stations and disarm a key guard protein, pushing cells toward an iron linked death called ferroptosis, here reached without iron itself.

In mouse tumors the approach slowed growth and stirred immune attack, drawing in killer T cells and flipping macrophages to a fighting mode. Yu and the team present the sheets as a way to beat tumor resistance by joining catalytic, heat, and immune effects in one platform.
pmc-13591913:
Lynn Huisman, Harriët Jager-Wittenaar, and Martine J Sealy survey, in 2026, how aware older Dutch adults are of malnutrition and what social factors track with that awareness. Spotting undernutrition early matters, since it erodes strength, independence, and survival. Their sample held 216 people aged 65 and up living at home in the northern Netherlands. Each filled in a scale that scores knowledge of malnutrition signs and risks.

Most respondents scored in the upper half of the scale, the team found. Women scored higher than men. A larger social network also paired with higher awareness, even after other traits were weighed. Huisman and the team advise public health work that builds social ties and spreads clear cues about eating too little in old age.
pmc-13592313:
Fabienne Weber and four colleagues review, in 2026, how lab made sugars help scholars read and use anti-glycan antibodies. A sugary coat wraps human and microbe cells, and antibodies patrol it for odd patterns that betray germs or cancer. Natural glycans vary wildly, which long blocked clean study. Fresh synthesis routes, including automated assembly lines, now deliver pure, defined structures on demand.

With pure sugars in hand, teams can profile which antibodies a person carries, hunt markers of disease, and raise therapeutic antibodies on purpose. Vaccine design also gains, since exact sugar targets can be built into shots. Weber and the team map these uses and flag the promise for care tailored to each patient's own antibody mix.
pmc-13592413:
Christophe Lavenn leads a 2026 team unlocking hidden flex in a soft porous crystal with one small ligand swap. Flexible frameworks can gulp gas in sudden steps, prized for storage, yet design rules for that flex stay murky. Swapping a benzene based linker for a pyridine cousin added a nitrogen that welcomes hydrogen bonds from acetylene gas. The change woke dormant flex in the lattice.

Pore volume swelled by nearly threefold under gas, and acetylene uptake rose five times over the parent material. Uptake also climbed in distinct steps and favored acetylene over close cousins ethylene and ethane. Lavenn and the team credit hydrogen bonding for steadying the open form, and offer the swap as a general design hint.
pmc-13592813:
Michel Godel and six colleagues follow how infants at high and low likelihood of autism process speech sounds. Late babbling and first words often precede an autism diagnosis, hinting that early speech machinery differs. Their team recorded 83 brain wave sessions from 44 infants between two and twenty two months old. Babies heard streams of three syllable words from many voices, and brain tracking of syllables and words was measured alongside a word recognition test.

High likelihood infants tracked syllables more weakly, and that weakness tracked with weaker verbal scores at twenty months. Their pattern finding itself stayed intact, though their brain response to new words ran smaller. Voice variety briefly disrupted word splitting near twelve months only in low likelihood babies. Godel and the team favor long, passive brain measures for catching such early forks.
pmc-13593713:
Marco Antonio Delaye-Martínez and colleagues weighed adding breathed colistin to vein colistin for burn patients with drug-proof lung germs in Mexico City. Fifty patients from 2011 to 2017 were read back, with 41 on breathing-machine lung infections and 9 on hospital lung infections. Thirty-one had both drugs and the rest had vein drug alone, with Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas germs most common.

Both-drug care brought more lung distress, more blood-pressure drug use, more days on a breathing machine, worse organ scores, and more days in intensive care. Airway spasm hit 13 percent, and one patient bled into the lungs. Death in thirty days did not shift. Breathed colistin added no gain here, and trials that look ahead are due.
pmc-13598313:
Niels G Mede and Sophia C Volk talked with fifteen uni science spokespeople in varied lands on public backlash. Backlash can come from crowds, pols, news folk, or peers, from fair gripes to threats and hits. Spokespeople stand in the firing line both as marks and as shields for beset scientists.

The authors map views of backlash, its toll on people and schools, fight-back plans, and setting facts such as topic, route, and land politics. They set tests to split fair gripe from foul abuse and note both bad and good fallout. Plans that act early and plans that react, they urge, can guard staff and the public trust in science.
pmc-13600313:
Jiayi Wang and colleagues trace a gene-silencing pathway that drives scarring in diseased kidneys. Kidney fibrosis, the buildup of scar tissue, drives chronic kidney disease, yet the switches that turn scar-forming cells on are only partly known. The team studied UHRF1 and G9a, two proteins that place chemical marks on DNA packaging and turn genes off.

Both proteins were raised in fibrotic human and mouse kidneys, and in activated fibroblasts, the cells that lay down scar tissue. Removing UHRF1 only from fibroblasts eased fibrosis in mice and lowered G9a activity. The pair settles on the promoter of KLF15, a gene that normally holds fibrosis back, and silences it with repressive marks. Blocking the pathway restored KLF15 and softened the scarring. The authors present this UHRF1 and G9a axis as a fresh drug target for slowing kidney failure.
pmc-13612613:
Jiumeng Zhang and colleagues read past work on ways to line up long-term health data from varied cohorts so joint reads can run. Joint reads give big data pools and fresh asks, but cohorts rarely gauge the same traits the same way. By strict scope-review rules, the team sifted 1,234 hits down to 35 papers with person-level line-up methods.

Three ways stood out for table-type poll data: spread-based ways, the share-score model, and latent-trait models. Fit hangs most on the old gauge scales and on whether the aim trait can be read straight or just through signs, and the choice shapes how half-seen traits are dealt with. No paper used machine-led auto ways, which leaves room for new tools and a choice map.
pmc-13612913:
Densenbal Dansran leads a large team reporting a 2026 study of lung health among 143 small-scale gold miners in a northern province of Mongolia. In July 2024 the miners answered structured interviews, had physical exams and chest X-rays, and blew into a spirometer, a device that measures how well the lungs move air. The team recorded where each miner worked, how much dust they faced, and whether they wore N95 masks.

About 23.8 percent of the miners had lung function below 80 percent of the level expected for them. Surprisingly, no single work factor, including dust level or mask use, showed a clear statistical link with poor lung function once age, sex, and smoking were taken into account. The findings still give local health services a baseline picture of breathing problems in this hard-to-reach workforce.
pmc-13615013:
Shaniece Criss leads a team reporting in 2026 on how power shapes public health in Greenville County, South Carolina, through the Equity in Public Health Initiative. Health gaps grow from unequal power over money, rules, and whose voice counts. The team held seven focus groups with 68 Black and Hispanic residents and interviewed sixteen officials, staff, and advocates between March and December 2024.

Residents described visible power in unfair funding, closed processes, and barriers to taking part in civic life. Hidden power ran through churches, schools, nonprofits, and social media that link residents to decision makers. A third, invisible layer lay in how income, race, immigration status, and language shaped what people believed was possible. The study gives counties a map of where community power can be built.
pmc-13615913:
Tsugihisa Sasaki, Tsutomu Sounou, and Tomomi Higashide review in 2026 surgery results for tear drainage damage caused by S-1, a widely used oral cancer drug in Japan. The drug can scar or block the narrow channels that drain tears from the eye, leaving patients with constantly watering eyes. The multi-centre review covered 51 patients, 89 affected sides in all, with an average age near 69 years.

Cases were sorted into six groups by where the blockage sat, from the tear opening to shared channels deeper in. A simple snip procedure for blocked openings succeeded in 32 of 34 sides, while tube placement worked in every case in its small group. Tighter, double-sided blockages were the hard core of the series. Matching the operation to the blockage site, the authors show, is the key to dry eyes.
pmc-13616313:
Péter Salamon and colleagues measure, for the first time directly, how a flowing liquid crystal generates electricity when sheared, a property called the direct piezoelectric effect. Piezoelectricity was long thought to belong to solid crystals, yet a new class of liquid crystals with built-in electric order breaks that rule. Earlier work measured only the reverse effect, voltage causing motion. This team sheared two standard compounds of the class while recording the electric current produced.

By varying heat, rhythm, and strain, and pairing the readings with flow measurements, they extracted firm coupling numbers for the shear mode. Both liquids gave similar values, matching the earlier reverse-effect figures. A flow-alignment mechanism is proposed to explain the signal. Soft materials that turn touch into current could serve in flexible sensors and energy harvesters that bend instead of break.
pmc-13617113:
Daria Malich and Andrii Vasylyshyn review how testosterone shapes the default mode network, the brain system active during self-focused thought, social thinking, and mood regulation. Their systematic search of PubMed in March and April 2026 gathered human brain-imaging studies from the past fifteen years. Ten studies met the criteria, each checked with quality tools matched to its design.

Testosterone-related changes clustered in self-referential hubs such as the medial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, and angular gyrus. Effects differed sharply by sex and developmental stage and depended on the form and size of hormone exposure. Links ran mainly to emotional reactivity and self-related processing, including aggression control and body self-identification, rather than to outward thinking tasks. Because studies varied so much, the authors say firm causal claims are not yet possible and call for long-term randomized studies.
pmc-13617613:
Muhammad Adnan Bashir and six colleagues review greener ways to form carbon-nitrogen bonds, the linkages at the heart of most medicines, dyes, agrochemicals, and advanced materials. Water, cheap, safe, and abundant, is their chosen reaction medium. The review stresses that water does far more than replace a toxic solvent: its hydrogen bonding, surface effects, and proton shuttling actively reshape how reactions proceed.

Coverage spans reactions run on water and in water, sorted into metal-free processes, transition-metal catalysis, and emerging electrochemical and light-driven methods. For each family the authors weigh reaction scope against what is known about water's mechanistic roles, including gathering oily reactants together and stabilizing catalysts. They close with opportunities for designing aqueous bond-forming reactions on purpose rather than by accident, aiming at cleaner production of nitrogen-containing compounds.
pmc-13617713:
Steffi Kar Kei Yuen and fourteen colleagues test how bendy new suction ureteral access sheaths are, in a laboratory study for the European Association of Urology endourology section. These flexible sheaths snake across the kidney's drainage junction so surgeons can suck out stone fragments directly from a target chamber. The team measured maximum bending angles for four commercial brands across three sizes, with the working channel empty or holding laser fibers of two thicknesses.

Smaller sheaths, the two narrower sizes, bent significantly better than the largest size across every brand when paired with a thin disposable scope. Advancing the sheath itself bent the tip more effectively than deflecting the scope inside it. Which laser fiber occupied the channel, by contrast, made no significant difference to bending. The authors say these performance details help surgeons pick equipment combinations that can actually reach difficult kidney chambers.
pmc-13619013:
Aurore A. Perrault and four colleagues test whether sleeping on a gently rocking bed helps people who sleep badly, extending the team's earlier success with good sleepers. Sixteen young adults who struggled to fall or stay asleep, and whose recorded sleep confirmed the problem. They spent an adjustment night in the laboratory, then one night on a bed rocking slowly sideways. A second night used the same bed held still, with memory tested each night.

The rocking night fragmented sleep less: participants spent less time awake and in light sleep, objective sleep efficiency rose, and they rated their sleep better. Brain recordings showed the rocking motion entraining sleep rhythms, boosting fast spindles and slow oscillations during deep sleep, replicating the effect seen in good sleepers. Memory consolidation did not improve. The authors offer this as early evidence that rocking could serve as an add-on for some chronic insomnia.
pmc-13620113:
Panagiotis Poulis and four colleagues investigated a side effect of the chemical tweak that made COVID-19 mRNA vaccines practical. The modified building block, called m1Psi in the study, calms immune alarms and stabilizes the message. Earlier work hinted it can also make ribosomes slip and read the message in the wrong frame. The team measured that slipping with glowing reporter genes in cells, a rebuilt translation system, and single-molecule microscopy.

Slipping rose on one short sequence pattern where the reading machinery paused. At that pause the modified block weakened the grip between message and transfer RNA and nudged the transfer RNA into a slip-prone shape. Swapping the pattern for two nearby alternatives erased the effect entirely. The authors say vaccine designers can keep the useful modification while simply avoiding the risky sequence when they optimize the code.
pmc-13620213:
Moby Solangi and four colleagues report what four decades of tracking say about dolphin lifespans in Mississippi Sound. In 1982, fifty bottlenose dolphins there were freeze-branded during a health study and followed by their marks. Later photo-identification surveys, which recognize dolphins by fin shapes, kept watch over the same population.

Ten of the branded dolphins were still being seen between 2011 and 2026. Seven of the survivors are now over thirty years old, and one is confirmed at forty-seven, a striking age for the species. Two of the living dolphins show long-term loyalty to the same home waters. Because mark tracking has limits, the authors caution that ages and fidelity need continued checking. They urge keeping the surveys going, since these dolphins also serve as sentinels for the health of the whole sound.
pmc-13620813:
Si-Yu Ma and five colleagues describe two new species of wood-inhabiting fungi found in a tropical rainforest national park on China's Hainan Island. Fungal diversity in the tropics remains poorly mapped, and these fungi belong to Biscogniauxia, a genus of carbon-crust fungi that live on bark and wood. The team combined close study of spore and fruiting body shapes with family trees built from three gene regions.

One new species, named for Diaoluo Mountain, shows flat fruiting crusts and spores with a bold straight germ slit running nearly the spore's length. The second, named for the Jianfeng range, carries tube-shaped spore chambers and spores with a faint slit plus a small opaque appendage on one side. Gene trees confirmed both stand apart from known relatives. The paper adds full descriptions, illustrations, and an identification key for the whole genus.
pmc-13621813:
Mary Leick and three co-authors review records of liver transplant patients who switched to everolimus, a drug used to lower reliance on older immune-suppressing medicines that can harm the kidneys. The question was whether the timing of the switch changes kidney outcomes. Patients at one academic medical centre were grouped by how soon after transplant the switch happened.

Eighty patients were included. Those switched within six months showed kidney gains that held at one month and at twelve months after the change. A later group gained at one month but not at twelve, and the latest group gained at neither point. The trade-off was rejection, proven by tissue sampling, which was most common in the earliest group. The authors conclude that early switching protects kidneys best but needs care because rejection risk runs high.
pmc-13622913:
Vasileios Sotirios Akrivos and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review that hunts for spin in studies comparing two versions of the Latarjet operation for shoulders that keep dislocating. Spin means presenting results in a slanted way that makes one method look better than the data support. The operation moves a piece of bone to stabilise the joint, open or through small scopes.

The reviewers screened comparative studies from the last twenty years and checked each one against a spin classification system. Four in five of the twenty-five studies showed at least one form of spin. Selective reporting was the most common problem, followed by missing discussion of limits and claims of differences that were never tested statistically. Studies judged weaker in design carried more spin per paper. Funding and declared conflicts made no difference. The authors warn readers to check the numbers behind claims in this surgical debate.
pmc-13623013:
Alessio Maione and a large surgical team compare kneecap ligament repair results in patients whose knee anatomy sits at the borderline of normal. The medial patellofemoral ligament holds the kneecap in its groove, and rebuilding it can stop repeated dislocations. Surgeons debate whether patients with slightly abnormal bone shapes need extra bone surgery on top of the ligament repair.

The team reviewed fifty-one patients, covering fifty-five knees treated between 2013 and 2023, and split them into standard and borderline anatomy groups. After an average follow-up of nearly eight years, both groups improved strongly on pain and function scores. Final scores and redislocation rates were much the same in the two groups, and stacking several borderline features did not worsen results. The authors conclude that ligament repair alone serves well-chosen borderline patients, and bone procedures should wait for clearly abnormal anatomy.
pmc-13624013:
Yusuke Matsui and a large engineering-medical team published a 2026 test of a robot that drills needles into bone under CT guidance. Placing biopsy and treatment needles into bone by hand is slow and exposes staff to radiation. Their remote-controlled robot adds a rotating drill plus force feedback that adjusts pushing speed as resistance changes.

The team attempted insertions into the spine, pelvis, and thigh bones of three pigs, six tries per site. Every insertion succeeded. Angle errors between plan and final needle stayed tiny, well under a degree in most planes, with the thigh bone the least exact. Insertion times ran from about twenty seconds in spine and pelvis to about a minute in the dense thigh bone. No adverse events occurred. The authors call the system feasible and accurate in animals, a step toward human trials.
pmc-13624313:
Kayoung Han and colleagues show that star-shaped brain support cells, astrocytes, step in to manage blood flow only when sensory demand lasts. Brief stimulation draws a standard response, but the brain needs a gear for sustained activity, and the study compares five-second against twenty-second stimulation in animals using optical imaging and microscopy.

Long stimulation, not short, switched on a relay inside astrocytes: a water channel let the cell swell, and the swelling opened a calcium gate. The calcium then triggered release of a signalling molecule, D-serine, through a second channel. That signal boosted neuron activity and blood volume, and it set the resting tightness of brain arteries. Removing any relay part in mice broke the long-stimulus response while sparing the short response, and supplying the missing signal molecule restored it. The work assigns astrocytes a duration-sensing role in matching blood supply to demand.
pmc-13626313:
Ayaka Tajiri and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, refine a cheaper way to forecast how antibody drugs behave in human blood. Developers usually scale up doses from cynomolgus monkeys, whose cost keeps rising, so this team used common marmosets, far smaller primates. Two arthritis and bowel drugs, golimumab and ustekinumab, were given four times each, and size-based scaling math, averaged with three earlier antibodies, predicted the human curves.

Ustekinumab's human profile was matched excellently, while golimumab's fade rate came out slightly off. Immune reactions against the human drugs were tiny or brief, clearing a key worry about repeat dosing. The authors settle on provisional scaling values and present marmosets as a workable stand-in for early pharmacokinetic work.
pmc-13627113:
Kim and colleagues use a Korean cohort to ask whether alcohol's link to liver cancer grows with age. Hepatocellular carcinoma, the liver cancer, is an established cost of heavy drinking, but age specific risk was murky. Their 2026 study follows 3.9 million adults who had a health exam in 2009. It records drinking level and cancer cases over a median of more than eleven years. The analysis splits into twenty year age bands.

Twenty thousand people developed liver cancer in follow up. A dose trend, rising risk with rising intake, reached clear levels only at sixty and over. Heavy drinking raised risk in both the forty to fifty nine band and the sixty plus band. The raise was far larger in the older group, near half again the risk of non drinkers there. Prevention talks, the authors suggest, should press hardest on middle aged and older heavy drinkers.
pmc-13628913:
Zhilin Hu and twelve colleagues asked why a usually mild childhood leukaemia sometimes turns risky. The danger comes when a second mutation is present. Their 2026 study concerns leukaemia carrying the AML1-ETO fusion. It asks what a matching KIT mutation in exon 17 does to outlook and drug response.

The team mined a database of 957 child patients. The exon 17 mutation largely wiped out the fusion type's survival edge. Tests on marrow samples from sixteen patients in Shenzhen hinted at broad drug resistance. Standard chemotherapy drugs seemed to fail against it. Gene activity pointed to one gene, SOCS1, switched up in the resistant pattern. The authors argue for finer risk grouping by KIT profile. They also urge study of the linked signalling axis as a treatment target.
pmc-13629413:
Marcus Brady and Rachel Crespo-Otero benchmark the computer methods used to simulate what a propeller-shaped molecule does after absorbing light. The molecule, a three-bladed rotor, mostly wastes the energy as motion rather than glowing, and simulation results depend heavily on which electronic-structure theory drives the calculation.

Running surface-hopping dynamics under several methods, the pair mapped the crossing points where the molecule drops between energy states. One method relaxed the molecule far faster than the others, and the preferred crossing point was consistent across approaches, though a second crossing changed character between theory levels. A spin-flip method produced the richest outcomes, including a bicyclic product. The study questions how far push-button excited-state tools can be trusted for photochemistry.
pmc-13629813:
Lijun Sun and five colleagues compared the two home dialysis methods for people whose kidneys have failed, asking which better preserves the kidney function patients still have. Their single-centre retrospective study followed fifty-three Chinese patients starting treatment, nineteen on the automated overnight method and thirty-four on the manual daytime method.

Both groups began with similar remaining function and urine output. By six months the automated group's residual function had fallen significantly further, and its yearly rate of decline was clearly faster. Statistical modelling tied the automated method itself, plus higher starting function, to quicker loss. The authors advise weighing this trade-off when choosing a starting modality, since lingering kidney function strongly shapes dialysis patients' health.
pmc-13630113:
Anna Dankers and nine colleagues catalogued the yardsticks hospitals used to run and judge their services during COVID-19. Their review screened five databases. It sought European inpatient studies from 2020 to late 2024. It then pulled out every distinct yardstick in use.

Ninety-four studies yielded 459 separate yardsticks. They grouped into six families, from health outcomes to access times. The same measure often carried unlike definitions across hospitals. Like ideas also hid under unlike names. That made comparison treacherous. Most studies used the yardsticks to compare pandemic care with the time before. Few blended health and logistics views. The authors offer the catalogue as groundwork. Standard, crisis-ready hospital dashboards could grow from it.
pmc-13631313:
Outammassine Abdelkrim and ten colleagues publish a global atlas of the Asian bush mosquito. Their study appeared in 2026. Aedes japonicus invades readily and thrives in varied containers of water. It can carry dengue, Zika, West Nile, and several other viruses. Yet it draws a fraction of the attention given to its famous cousins.

The team gathered three quarters of a century of sightings, from 1950 to 2025. They mined journals, national surveys, and biodiversity stores. Each record was cleaned and geolocated through strict quality control. The result is 4,618 verified points. It is the first dedicated global store for the species. The authors offer it as working infrastructure. Distribution mapping, invasion tracking, and disease risk assessment can all build on it.
pmc-13631713:
Francesca M Cohn and seven colleagues present a lab method for telling apart six look-alike coral species in French Polynesia. These Pocillopora corals build reefs across the Indo-Pacific, yet their shapes vary so much that eyes alone cannot name them reliably. Genetic naming usually needs sequencing, which costs money and needs facilities that field teams may lack. Their method uses DNA cutting patterns instead.

The protocol works on two known marker regions, one from mitochondria and one from a histone gene. Cutting the DNA with chosen enzymes gives each species its own pattern of fragment sizes. In blind checks done both on computer predictions and in the lab, the method named every species correctly. Because the test is cheap and fast, similar protocols could help reef surveys, conservation work, and restoration projects in other regions.
pmc-13635213:
Yige Cao and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study testing whether yeast-derived particles can strengthen the tuberculosis vaccine. The BCG vaccine protects children well but guards adults unevenly against lung tuberculosis. The team added whole beta-glucan particles, fiber pieces from fungal cell walls that wake up immune cells. In dishes, the particles sharpened macrophages, the cells that first meet the vaccine bacteria, improving how they swallowed, digested, and displayed bacterial parts to T cells.

The effect ran through a known sensing pathway in those cells. Breaking that pathway erased the gains and weakened T cell responses. In mice, giving the particles at a separate site from the vaccine worked best and calmed early lung inflammation. The pairing strengthened memory T cell responses and improved control of a tuberculosis challenge while reducing lung damage. The authors propose the particles as a vaccine helper worth developing further.
pmc-13636613:
Peter J. Halfmann and six colleagues published this 2026 study building nanoparticle vaccines against the coronaviruses behind many common colds. Two endemic viruses, OC43 and HKU1, spread widely through airways and can hit older and immune-weakened people hard. Their spike proteins keep evolving, and a large animal reservoir adds spillover risk. The team mounted spike proteins from three virus versions onto nanoparticles and also made a two-in-one version pairing two of them.

Vaccinated mice produced strong spike-targeting antibodies. The antibodies reached across to matched virus relatives, a hopeful sign for breadth. The paired vaccine matched the single versions against each of its targets, losing nothing by combining. The authors frame the work as groundwork for vaccines against this whole virus family. A future universal cold vaccine is the distant prize, and knowing the antibody landscape of these spikes is a needed early step.
pmc-13638713:
Niangmei Cheng and seven colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study on why liver cancer can stop responding to the drug lenvatinib. That drug is a first-line treatment for liver cancer that cannot be removed by surgery, but resistance often develops over time.

Sequencing of resistant cancer cells pointed to a change in the p53 gene called R280S. Cells carrying that change survived lenvatinib better in dishes and in mouse tumors, partly because the altered protein raised Bcl-2, a protein that blocks cell death, and lowered BAX. The work names one route to resistance that future drugs might try to close.
pmc-13639013:
Teerachai Amnuaylojaroen and one colleague present MSEA-Daily, a 2026 climate dataset for mainland Southeast Asia. The dataset gives daily rain and temperature values on a four-kilometer grid for Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam across the years 1981 to 2014.

The builders blended monthly TerraClimate values with daily patterns from satellite rain data and a weather reanalysis, then checked results against seventy-seven weather stations. Temperature matched station records closely, while heavy rainfall extremes were understated somewhat. The dataset reproduces monsoon timing and El Niño patterns, supporting farm planning, water modeling, and studies of climate extremes in the region.
pmc-13644513:
Zengqian Hou and twenty-three colleagues present a 2026 prospectus on searching for signs of life beyond Earth and judging which planets could host it. The piece appears as China's deep space program shifts from engineering-led missions toward science-led design.

The authors review world research and name three urgent themes: what makes a planet habitable, how to hunt biosignatures, and how life and environments evolve together. For each theme they sharpen the core questions and propose target worlds and detection settings for future missions. The analysis is offered as theoretical backing for the top-level design of China's planetary exploration.
pmc-13647113:
Yunfeng Xiang, Daoxue Xiong, and Xiangjun Liu review a rising lung pathogen in cystic fibrosis care, bacteria of the Achromobacter group. Once rare in airway samples, these germs now appear in up to a tenth of patients in European and North American registries. They also strike people with weak immunity outside cystic fibrosis. Naming the exact species is error-prone, treatment thresholds are missing for most species, and resistance mechanisms stack together.

The review pulls together outbreak reports, spread data, and new European cutoff values for judging drug sensitivity in the lead species. A framework links loss of swimming ability, biofilm growth, and resistance into one story of how the germ adapts inside the cystic fibrosis airway. Sticky biofilms and dormant persister cells help infections endure. The authors set priorities: standard ways to identify the germ and proper clinical development of virus-based phage therapy.
pmc-13648013:
Karim and colleagues built in 2026 the first zebrafish knockouts of the three ataxin-1 family genes, to learn what these genes do in health. A warped form of one gene causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 1, a brain disease that steals balance and movement. The team cut each gene in turn with CRISPR, a gene editing tool, and tracked growth, movement, and gene activity in the fish.

All three knockouts cut early survival and slowed larval growth a bit. Fish that lacked the first gene moved poorly in light but swam near normal in the dark. Fish that lacked the other two genes were just sluggish overall. As adults, the first group again fared worst on swim tests. Gene readouts in young larvae showed broad shifts tied to nerve growth, immune cell travel, and a light sensing module in the first knockout.
pmc-13649513:
Ning Lin and seven colleagues studied why blood vessel muscle cells react in split ways to stretch: some die off, while others multiply. Both paths harm artery health under high blood pressure. The team stretched the cells in the lab and traced how a scaffold protein inside each cell set its fate.

Cells with distinct scaffold levels made distinct amounts of a harmful oxygen signal in their power units. That signal switched on both a growth path and a death path through one shared chain. A plant compound, berberine, calmed both paths by damping the chain's first link. Treated cells showed less growth and less death under stretch. The authors pitch the compound as a lead for stretch-linked artery disease.
pmc-13649713:
Georgios P. Skandalakis and six colleagues introduce a set of 23 papers on how new tools sharpen brain surgery. Brain surgery has always paired deep knowledge of anatomy with the latest technology. The pieces come from 181 authors at centres worldwide.

Anatomy work maps fine structures such as the blood supply of an eye-movement nerve and a lab model of tumour surgery. Tech pieces cover virtual reality planning for aneurysm care, live ultrasound, and mixed reality guides for tumour removal. Others test robot-guided biopsies and printed guides shaped to one patient. Spine tumour viewing and tissue checks round out the set. The editors stress that gains must still pass tests of accuracy and real-world value.
pmc-13649913:
Deniz Tasdemir and Hatice Ceylan spoke with 21 adults in Türkiye who went back on dialysis after a donated kidney failed, for a study published in 2026. A failed transplant breaks a life story, not just a body: the hope of freedom from the machine ends, and grief and doubt follow.

Four themes came from the talks. First came raw distress, doubt, and loss. Faith then served two roles: a comfort in pain and a tool for remaking meaning, which let people reframe their suffering and hold on to hope. Kin and friends backed that work. The authors urge clinics to weave spiritual care into the support offered at this hard turn.
pmc-13650013:
Kumaragurubaran Karthik and three colleagues open a collected set of studies on how bacteria that live inside host cells develop resistance to antibiotics. Germs such as the tuberculosis bacterium and Brucella species shelter within cells, where many drugs reach poorly, so resistance in these species is especially hard to treat.

The editorial previews six articles that use genome comparison, mutation analysis, and family-tree reconstruction to trace how resistance arises and spreads during infection in people and animals. One highlighted study examines a tuberculosis enzyme and finds that an existing drug, clofazimine, blocks it strongly, which may help explain how that drug works. Other pieces cover Bartonella species, which cause illnesses from cat-scratch disease to trench fever. Together the collection argues that reading resistance history in genomes can guide better treatment choices.
pmc-13650313:
Caroline Morizot and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, update five years of evidence on a stool test for hidden gut inflammation in people with rheumatic diseases. The test measures calprotectin, a protein released by activated white cells, and it is already standard in bowel disease care, yet joint and muscle conditions can inflame the gut quietly.

Studies from 2020 to 2025 centered on spondyloarthritis, a spinal inflammatory disease, where a large share of patients showed raised values that often matched inflammation seen under the microscope. Values also tracked gut symptoms and sometimes disease activity. Common painkillers pushed readings up, while biologic drugs generally pushed them down, which complicates interpretation. Evidence in rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia stayed thin. The authors call the test promising for the spinal disease group but note that differing cutoffs and study designs still block firm clinical rules.
pmc-13650613:
Muxin Tang and three colleagues trace four generations of colorectal cancer organoids, the miniature tumors grown from patient tissue that now anchor precision cancer research. Organoids matter because this cancer varies enormously between patients and resists treatment inside a complex local environment that flat cell cultures cannot copy.

The first generation simply embedded cells in a gel, proving three-dimensional growth was possible. Media refinements and co-culture then let tumor and supporting cells interact. Engineering brought microfluidic chips and bioprinting for scale and control. The newest generation applies artificial intelligence to read organoid shapes, forecast drug response, and sketch patient digital twins. The authors compare the generations on fidelity, throughput, cost, and clinical promise, and they recommend shared organoid banks, AI woven into workflows, and clear rules to move the technology into care.
pmc-13650713:
Yang and colleagues reported in 2026 on whether carbon-ion radiotherapy, a treatment using heavy charged particles, can be planned well for melanoma tumors inside the eye. Their software relies on a local effect model, which estimates how strongly the beam affects living tissue. Past clinical success came from a Japanese center using a different dose model, so the two dose scales needed a fair way to be compared.

Yang's team set the conversion factor between the two dose scales at 0.65 for a stated total dose, then checked plans against simulations and real measurements. The checks matched closely, with dose gaps mostly within about 1.6 percent and passing rates of at least 94 percent in their main test. Tumors at least 10 millimetres across could be treated with scan-based planning, supporting wider use of this eye-saving treatment.
pmc-13651513:
Angelina Tyumina and five colleagues engineer a negative feedback loop out of pure chemistry. It is the kind of self-damping circuit that living cells use everywhere and that synthetic chemists struggle to build in a modular way. Their loop rests on an exchange reaction between sulfur-bearing molecules called thiols and ring compounds called tetrazines.

The exchange converts sluggish tetrazines into redox-active ones, meaning they can now accept electrons and collapse into a reduced form through two competing routes. Those reduction routes eat the very thiols the exchange needs, so the system's output throttles its own input: textbook negative feedback in miniature. A microfluidic flow setup showed that neighboring chemical groups on the thiol carriers, extra thiols or acid groups, could amplify the effect. The authors propose their recipe as a transferable module for building reaction networks that behave further from equilibrium, closer to living chemistry.
pmc-13651613:
Matilda Dirawy and seven co-authors make salts of naringin, a citrus flavonoid, as cheaper growth promoters for lab-grown meat. Growing meat from cells stalls in the market on the price of growth factors. Naringin's known biological activity makes it attractive, except that the natural compound barely dissolves in water.

Turning it into phenolate salts with four varied partner ions fixed the solubility problem to varying degrees. The sodium and potassium salts dissolved readily, while the calcium and bulky ammonium versions dissolved less. Full chemical checks confirmed the structures. Soaking the salts in acid brought back the original flavonoid, proving the chemistry reversible. Early cell studies suggest chosen salts can support the cell growth that lab-grown meat output needs. The authors claim the first full report on this salt family and pitch it as a cost-cutting ingredient for the trade.
pmc-13651813:
Joice Zuckermann and nine colleagues cost out stem cell transplantation before and after a hospital introduced therapeutic drug monitoring. The monitoring measures drug levels to steer doses of three powerful agents used around transplant. The question was whether the extra testing pays for itself in a procedure famous for its price.

Forty-four patients in each era were compared with a detailed time-driven costing method, and prices were adjusted to a common date. Average cost per patient ran near thirty thousand dollars overall.
